Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 1:

The discussion of the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Alif, Lam, Mim (1) Allah, there is no god but He﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the meaning of His saying "Alif Lam Mim" earlier, in what suffices so that it need not be repeated at this point. [See what has passed, 1: 205-224.] Likewise the explanation of His saying "Allah" [See what has passed, 1: 122-126.]

* *

As for the meaning of His saying "there is no god but He": it is a report from Allah, mighty and majestic, informing His servants that divinity belongs to Him alone, to the exclusion of anything else among the gods and rivals, and that worship is not fitting or permissible except to Him, because He alone is Lord and singular in divinity; that everything other than Him is His possession, and everything besides Him is His creation, with no partner in His authority and dominion. [The construction of the phrase: "informing His servants that divinity is His alone ... "] As a proof from Him, may His remembrance be exalted, against them, that since this is so, it is not lawful for them to worship other than Him, nor to associate anyone with Him in His authority, since every deity other than Him is His possession, and every object of veneration other than Him is His creation, and it is incumbent upon the possession to devote obedience to its owner and to direct service to its master and provider; and making known to whoever was among His creation, on the day that this was revealed to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ by sending it down to him and sending it to them through his tongue, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, [The context: "and making known to whoever was among His creation ... remaining upon the worship of an idol"] remaining upon the worship of an idol, or a statue, or the sun, or the moon, or a human, or an angel, or other things which the children of Adam remained upon in worshipping and deifying [Al-ilahah: the worship of a god, as already explained in its commentary, 1: 124.] and taking it, other than its owner and creator, as a god and lord, that he is remaining in error, and deviating from the clear path, and riding a path other than the straight way, by directing worship to other than Him, while no one has the right to divinity except Him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: It has been mentioned that Allah began the revelation of this surah with the opening that He began with: the negation of "divinity" being for other than Him, and describing Himself with what He described Himself with at its beginning, as a proof from Him against a group of Christians who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ from Najran and disputed with him concerning Jesus, peace be upon him, and deviated concerning Allah. So Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down concerning their matter and the matter of Jesus, from this surah, some eighty-odd verses from its beginning, as a proof against them and against those who held their view, to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. They refused except to remain upon their error and disbelief, so he invited them to mubahala, and they refused that, and they asked to pay the jizya, and he ﷺ accepted it from them, and they returned to their lands.

However, although the matter is as such, and it was them that the argument was directed at, whoever among the rest of mankind shares their meaning in disbelieving in Allah, and taking what is other than Allah as lord, god and object of worship, is also bound by the proof with which Allah, blessed and exalted, argued against the one about whom these verses were revealed, and is refuted in the Furqan with which He distinguished between him and them for His Messenger ﷺ.

* *

The narration from those whose statements we mentioned concerning the revelation of the opening of this surah, that it was revealed concerning the people whose description we have given, of the Christians:

6543 - Muhammad ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far, who said: The delegation of Najran came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: sixty riders, among them fourteen men of their nobles. Among the fourteen, three men to whom their affairs returned: "al-Aqib," the commander of the people, their man of judgment and holder of their counsel, the one whose decision they never depart from, and his name was "Abd al-Masih"; and "al-Sayyid," their pillar, the owner of their caravan and their gathering place, and his name was "al-Ayham"; and Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah, brother of Bakr ibn Wa'il, their bishop, their rabbi, their imam, and the master of their madrasa. [The madrasa (with the mim kasra and the dal sakin): is the house in which they study their books; by his saying "master of their madrasa" is meant their scholar who studied the books, giving them fatwas and speaking the proof in their religion.] Abu Harithah had been honoured among them and had studied their books until his knowledge of their religion was good; the kings of Rome who were Christians had honoured him, supported him, served him, built churches for him, and bestowed honours upon him, because of what reached them of his knowledge and his diligence in their religion. [In the printed edition: "in his religion"; I have kept what is in the manuscript and Ibn Hisham.]

Ibn Ishaq said, Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr said: [In Ibn Hisham: "When they came ... "] They came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Madinah, and they entered upon him in his mosque after he had prayed the afternoon prayer, wearing striped Yemeni cloaks, jubbas and mantles, in [the bearing of men] of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b. [What is between the brackets is an addition that is necessary, from Ibn Hisham's text. The hibarat (with the ha kasra and the ba fatha) are the plural of hibarah, a striped cloth of Yemeni fabric, which is among the fine garments.] He said: Some of the companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who saw them that day said: We have not seen after them a delegation like them! And their prayer time came, so they stood to pray in the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Leave them!" So they prayed facing east.

He said: The names of the fourteen among them to whom their affairs returned were: "al-Aqib," who is "Abd al-Masih," and al-Sayyid, who is "al-Ayham," and "Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah," brother of Bakr ibn Wa'il, and Aws, and al-Harith, and Zayd, and Qays, and Yazid, and Nubayh, and Khuwaylid, and Amr, [In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and Khuwaylid ibn Amr," which is an error; the correct reading is from Ibn Hisham.] and Khalid, and Abd Allah. And Yuhannas: among sixty riders. From among them, "Abu Harithah ibn 'Alqamah" and "al-Aqib," Abd al-Masih, and "al-Ayham" al-Sayyid spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they were of Christianity according to the religion of the king, [In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and he is of Christianity," and the correct reading is from Ibn Hisham.] with differences among them regarding their matter. They say: "He is God," and they say: "He is the son of God," and they say: "He is the third of three," and so is the saying of Christianity.

They argue for their saying "He is God" that he used to give life to the dead, heal the sick, inform of the unseen, and create from clay the likeness of a bird, then breathe into it so that it becomes a bird, and all of that by the permission of Allah, to make it a sign for the people. [In Ibn Hisham: "and that We may make it a sign for the people," as in the verse.]

They argue for their saying "He is the son of God" that they say: "He had no father who is known, and he spoke in the cradle, a thing that none of the children of Adam before him had done." [In the printed edition: "with a thing that he did not do," which is corrupt speech; the correct reading is from the manuscript. In Ibn Hisham: "and this, none of them did".]

They argue for their saying "He is the third of three" by the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic: "We have done, and We have commanded, and We have created, and We have decreed." They say: "If He were one, He would not have said 'We' but 'I have done, I have commanded, I have decreed, and I have created,' but He is He, and Jesus, and Mary."

In all of that of their saying the Qur'an was revealed, and Allah mentioned to His Prophet ﷺ their saying in it.

When the two rabbis spoke to him, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to them: "Submit!" They said: "We have submitted." He said: "You have not submitted, so submit!" They said: "Yes, we have submitted before you!" He said: "You have lied. What prevents you from Islam is your claim that God has a son, your worship of the cross, and your eating of the pig." They said: "Then who is his father, O Muhammad?" The Messenger of Allah ﷺ fell silent concerning them and did not answer them, so Allah revealed concerning that, of their saying and the difference of their matter entirely, the beginning of "Surat Al 'Imran" up to some eighty-odd verses of it. So He said: "Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting," [In the printed edition and the manuscript "Alif Lam Mim" is not mentioned; I have added it from Ibn Hisham.] so He opened the surah by declaring Himself free of what they said, and affirming His singularity in creation and command, with no partner in it, as a refutation of what they had invented of disbelief and what they had made as rivals with Him, and as a proof against them by their saying about their companion, to make their error known to them. So He said: "Allah, there is no god but He," meaning: there is no partner with Him in His command.

6544 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting," he said: The Christians came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and disputed with him concerning Jesus son of Mary, and they said to him: "Who is his father?" and they spoke falsehood and slander against Allah, "there is no god but He, He has not taken a consort nor a son." So the Prophet ﷺ said to them: "Do you not know that there is no son except that he resembles his father?" They said: "Yes!" He said: "Do you not know that our Lord is living and does not die, and that Jesus will come upon him extinction?" They said: "Yes!" He said: "Do you not know that our Lord is the Sustainer over everything, who protects it, guards it, and provides for it?" They said: "Yes!" He said: "Does Jesus possess any of that?" They said: "No!" He said: "Do you not know that Allah, mighty and majestic, nothing is hidden from Him on earth or in heaven?" They said: "Yes!" He said: "Does Jesus know any of that except what he was taught?" They said: "No!" He said: "Our Lord shaped Jesus in the womb as He willed; do you know that?" They said: "Yes!" [In the manuscript and al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 3 there is the text: "Our Lord shaped Jesus in the womb as He willed. He said: Do you not know that our Lord does not eat food nor drink drink," although al-Durr al-Manthur has dropped "he said" from this phrase. As for al-Baghawi (margin of Ibn Kathir's tafsir) 2: 93: "Our Lord shaped Jesus in the womb as He willed, and our Lord does not eat or drink." I have left what is in the printed edition as it is, lest it come from another copy in which this existed.] He said: "Do you not know that our Lord does not eat food, nor drink drink, nor void waste?" They said: "Yes!" He said: "Do you not know that Jesus was carried by his mother as a woman carries, then she delivered him as a woman delivers her child, then he was nourished as a child is nourished, then he used to eat food, drink drink, and void waste?" They said: "Yes!" He said: "How then can this be as you claim?" He said: They recognised it, then they refused except denial, so Allah, mighty and majestic, revealed: "Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 2:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Al-Hayyu al-Qayyum (2)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The reciters differed regarding this.

The reciting of the common reciters (qurra' al-amsar) is ﴿al-Hayyu al-Qayyum﴾.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Ibn Mas'ud, as it is related from them, recited it: ﴿al-Hayyu al-Qayyumu﴾.

* *

It is also reported from 'Alqamah ibn Qays that he used to recite: ﴿al-Hayyu al-Qayyimu﴾.

6545 - Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Uthham ibn 'Ali related to us, saying: al-A'mash related to us, from Ibrahim, from Abu Ma'mar, who said: I heard 'Alqamah reciting: "al-Hayyu al-Qayyim."

I said: "Did you hear it from him?" He said: "I do not know."

6546 - Abu Hisham al-Rifa'i related to us, saying: Waki' related to us, saying: al-A'mash related to us, from Ibrahim, from Abu Ma'mar, from 'Alqamah, the same.

* *

It is also related from 'Alqamah something contrary to that, namely:

6547 - Abu Hisham related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah related to us, saying: Shaybān related to us, from al-A'mash, from Ibrahim, from Abu Ma'mar, from 'Alqamah, that he recited: "al-Hayyu al-Qayyam."

Abu Ja'far said: The reading which, in our view, it is not permissible to depart from in this matter is that which the reciters of the Muslims have transmitted through widespread transmission (naql mustafid), not by collusion or prior agreement, by inheritance [[In the printed edition: "tashaghur" with a ghayn, which is an error; see above p. 127 note 2. And see what I said about the phrase "wirathah" above p. 127 note 3.]], and that which was established in their codices (masahif). That is the reading of the one who recites "al-Hayyu al-Qayyumu."

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿al-Hayyu﴾

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of His words "al-Hayy" (the Ever-Living). [[See the explanation of "al-Hayy" above, 5: 386, 387.]]

Some of them said: The meaning of this, from God, dhikruhu, is that He described Himself as enduring, and negated death from Himself, which is permissible for whoever else among His creatures.

Those who said this:

6548 - Muhammad ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "al-Hayy" is the One who does not die, though 'Isa was killed and crucified according to their claim, meaning according to the claim of the rabbis who disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from among the Christians of Najran. [[The report: 6548 - Sirat Ibn Hisham 2: 225, and it is part of the preceding report: 6543.]]

6549 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words "al-Hayy," he said: He says: the Living who does not die.

* *

Others said: The meaning of "al-Hayy," which Allah, mighty and majestic, meant in this verse and described Himself with, is that He is the one for whom the management of everything He wills and desires is easy; nothing He wills can be withheld from Him, and that He is not like the one who has no management, from among the gods and rivals.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is that He has enduring life, which has never ceased to be an attribute of His and will not cease to be so. They said: He described Himself with life because He has life, just as He described Himself with knowledge because He has knowledge, and with power because He has power.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of that, in my view: [[See the explanation of "al-Hayy" above, 5: 386, 387.]] He described Himself with enduring life that has no perishing and no cessation, and negated from it what befalls every living creature among His creatures of perishing and the cessation of life at the coming of its term. So He informed His servants that He is the one deserving worship and divinity from His creatures, the Living who does not die and does not perish, unlike every one who is taken as a lord besides Him, who dies, and every one claimed as a god besides Him, who perishes. He argued against His creatures that whoever perishes, passing away, and dies, ceasing to exist, cannot be a god deserving to be worshipped instead of the God who does not perish and does not die. And that God is the One who endures, who does not die, does not perish, and does not cease, and He is Allah, there is no god but Him.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿al-Qayyum﴾

Abu Ja'far said: We have mentioned the differences of the reciters in this, and which of them we choose, and the reason for which we chose what we chose.

* *

As for the interpretation of all the readings that we mentioned the reciters recited, they are close in meaning. The meaning of all of them is: the one who sustains (al-qayyim) everything, provides for it, manages it, and disposes of it as He wills and desires, with change, alteration, increase and decrease, as:

6550 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa ibn Maymun related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Najih related to us, from Mujahid, regarding the words of Allah, majestic is His praise: "al-Hayy al-Qayyum," he said: The one who stands over everything.

6551 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Huthayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

6552 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "al-Qayyum," the one who watches over everything, guards it, provides for it.

* *

Others said: "The meaning of that is: the one who stands in His place." They directed it to the enduring standing with which there is no cessation or movement, and that Allah, mighty and majestic, negated from Himself, by describing Himself with it, change and movement from place to place, and the occurrence of transformation that happens to human beings and to other creatures.

Those who said that:

6553 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "al-Qayyum," the one who stands in His place of authority over His creatures, who does not cease; and 'Isa ceased, according to their claim, meaning according to the claim of the rabbis who disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ) from the people of Najran concerning 'Isa, from his place where he was, and went from it to another. [[The report: 6553 - In the manuscript and the printed edition: "Umar ibn Ishaq," which is a clear error; this is Abu Ja'far's chain to "Muhammad ibn Ishaq," on whom his tafsir turns. This report completes the two preceding reports: 6543, 6548, in Sirat Ibn Hisham 2: 225. And the printed and manuscript editions have another error: "al-qiyam 'ala makanih," for "al-qa'im 'ala makanih," and the correct wording is from Sirat Ibn Hisham.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two interpretations is what Mujahid and al-Rabi' said, that this is a description by Allah, mighty and majestic, of Himself as the one who stands over the affair of everything, in its provision and the warding off of harm from it, its protection, its management, and its disposal by His power. It is from the Arabs' saying: "So-and-so stands over the affair of this town," meaning: the one who takes charge of managing its affairs.

So "al-Qayyum," since that is its meaning, is "al-Fay'ul" from the speaker's saying: "Allah stands over the affairs of His creatures." Its original form is "al-Qayyuwum," but the first "waw" of "al-Qayyuwum," since a still "ya'" preceded it while it was moving, was changed into a "ya'," and it and the "ya'" before it were made into a doubled "ya'." This is because the Arabs do so with a moving "waw" when a still "ya'" precedes it. [[See what was said above in the explanation of "al-Qayyum": 5: 388, 389; here there is an addition regarding "al-qiyam" and "al-qayyim" which was not mentioned there.]]

* *

As for "al-Qayyam," its original form is "al-Qiwwam," which is "al-Fay'al" from "qama yaqumu," and the moving "waw" of "qiwwam" was preceded by a still "ya'," so both became a doubled "ya'."

Had "al-Qayyum" been "Fa'ul," it would have been "al-Quwwum," but it is "al-Fay'ul." Likewise "al-Qayyam," had it been "al-Fa''al," it would have been "al-Qawwam," as it is said "al-sawwam wa al-qawwam" (those who fast much and those who stand much in prayer), and as He, mighty is His praise, said: ﴿Be steadfast upholders of justice, witnesses for Allah﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 8]. But it is "al-Fay'al," so it is said "al-Qayyam."

* *

As for "al-Qayyim," it is "al-Fay'il" from "qama yaqumu," the moving "waw" was preceded by a still "ya'," so both became a doubled "ya'," as it is said "fulan sayyidu qawmihi" (so-and-so is the lord of his people) from "sada yasudu," and "hadha ta'am jayyid" (this is good food) from "jada yajudu," and what is similar to that.

* *

These words came in this form because it was intended for the purpose of emphasis in praise, so "al-Qayyum," "al-Qayyam," and "al-Qayyim" are more emphatic in praise than "al-Qa'im." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, Allah willing, used to prefer the reading "al-Qayyam," because that is the prevalent pattern of the speech of the people of the Hijaz in triliteral forms with "ya'" and "waw," so they say of a man who often makes goldsmithing "al-Sayyagh" (instead of "al-Siyagh"), and they say of a man who turns around much "al-Dayyar." [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 110.]] It has been said that the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿Leave not upon the earth any of the disbelievers a dayyar﴾ [Surah Nuh: 26] are really "dawwar," "fa''al" from "dara yadur," but it was revealed in the dialect of the people of the Hijaz, and was confirmed thus in the codex.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 3:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, says: O Muhammad, indeed your Lord, the Lord of Jesus and the Lord of everything, is the Lord who sent down to you the Book — by "the Book" he means the Qur'an — "in truth," meaning: in truthfulness regarding what the People of the Torah and the Gospel differed about, and what your interlocutors disputed with you about, namely the Christians of Najran and all other people of polytheism. "Confirming what was before it" means: by this he means the Qur'an, that it confirms what came before it of the books of God which He sent down to His prophets and messengers, and verifies what the messengers of God brought from Him. [[In the manuscript it reads "wa-makhfu ma ja'at bihi rusul Allah" [and obscuring what the messengers of God brought], which is an error; the correct reading is what is in the printed edition.]] Because the sender of all of that is one, there would be no disagreement in it; had it come from other than Him, there would have been much disagreement.

* *

Those who engage in interpretation have said the same as what we have said.

Among those who said that:

6554 – Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, saying: Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "confirming what was before it" — he said: for what preceded it, of a book or a messenger.

6555 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "confirming what was before it," for what preceded it, of a book or a messenger.

6556 – Muhammad ibn Humayd related to me, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq related to me, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "He has sent down to you the Book in truth," i.e., in truthfulness regarding what they differed about. [[The report 6556 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6553 above.]]

6557 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it" — he says: the Qur'an; "confirming what was before it" of the books that had passed before it.

6558 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to me, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His saying: "He has sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it" — he says: confirming what came before it of a book and a messenger.

* *

The interpretation of His, may His praise be exalted, saying: ﴿And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel﴾ (3) ﴿before, as guidance for mankind﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this He, may His praise be exalted, means: "And He sent down the Torah" upon Moses, "and the Gospel" upon Jesus, "before" — i.e., before the Book which He sent down to you. By His saying "guidance for mankind" He means: a clarification for people from God regarding what they differed about concerning the oneness of God and the confirmation of His messengers, and the description of you, O Muhammad, that you are His prophet and messenger, [[In the printed edition: "wa-mufidan ya Muhammad annaka nabiyyi rasuli" ... In the manuscript it reads thus: "wa-hafiyka ya Muhammad bi-annaka nabiyyi wa-rasuli", the first letter being ḥā', the second fā', the third yā', and the fourth resembling dāl, though more like kāf. I have judged the word to be "na'tiyak" [your description], because when God described Muhammad as His prophet and messenger, people differed about this attribute. Likewise this delegation of the Christians of Najran did, as is clear from their account in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham. His saying "wa-na'tika" is joined to "concerning the oneness of God and the confirmation of His messenger," meaning "and concerning your description." As for what appears in the printed edition, it is corrupt both in context and in meaning.]] and other matters of the laws of God's religion, as follows:

6559 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel before, as guidance for mankind" — they are two books which God sent down, in which there is a clarification from God and a safeguard for whoever adheres to them, believes in them, and acts by what is in them.

6560 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "And He sent down the Torah and the Gospel" — the Torah upon Moses and the Gospel upon Jesus, just as He sent down the books upon those who came before him. [[The report 6560 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6556. In the printed edition it reads "upon those who came before them"; the correct reading is from the manuscript and the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 4:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿And He revealed the Furqan﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: and He revealed the decisive distinction between truth and falsehood concerning that over which the factions and the people of the religions differed regarding the matter of Jesus and other things.

* *

We have already explained earlier that "al-Furqan" is an intensive form (al-fu'lan) derived from the saying "God distinguished (faraqa) between truth and falsehood," meaning He separated them by His granting victory to the truth over falsehood, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "yafsilu baynahuma ... bil-haqq" in the present tense; the correct reading is the past tense, as I have established it.]] either through the conclusive proof or through subjugation and dominance by strength and might. [[See what has passed: 1:98, 99 / then 3:448. In the printed edition it reads "bil-aydi" with a yā' at the end, which is an error. Al-Ayd: severity and strength.]]

* *

The people of interpretation said the same as what we have said on this, except that some of them directed its interpretation toward the meaning that He made a separation between truth and falsehood concerning the matter of Jesus, and others toward the meaning that He made a separation between truth and falsehood in the rulings of the sacred laws.

Mention of those who said: its meaning is "the distinction between truth and falsehood concerning the matter of Jesus and the factions":

6561 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "And He revealed the Furqan," i.e., the separation between truth and falsehood concerning what the factions differed over regarding the matter of Jesus and other things. [[Report 6561 is the remainder of the reports whose last is 6560.]]

* *

Mention of those who said: the meaning of that is "the distinction between truth and falsehood in the rulings and the laws of Islam":

6562 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "And He revealed the Furqan," it is the Qur'an, which He sent down upon Muhammad, and by which He distinguished between truth and falsehood, so He made lawful its lawful things and made unlawful its unlawful things, and legislated its laws, and set its limits, and prescribed its obligations, and explained its clarifications, and commanded obedience to Him, and forbade disobedience to Him.

6563 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And He revealed the Furqan," he said: the Furqan is the Qur'an, which distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation we mentioned from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr on this is more correct than the interpretation we mentioned from Qatadah and al-Rabi'. And the meaning of "al-Furqan" in this place is: God made a separation between His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and those who disputed with him concerning the matter of Jesus and concerning other of his affairs, by the conclusive decisive proof that silenced them and their counterparts among the people of disbelief in God.

We said this view is closer to the correct, because God's report of His sending down the Qur'an, before His report of His sending down the Torah and the Gospel in this verse, has already passed in His saying: "He has sent down to you the Book with truth, confirming what was before it." There is no doubt that this "Book" is the Qur'an and nothing else, so there is no point in repeating it a second time, since there is no benefit in repeating it when it has already been mentioned and reported about from the beginning.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Indeed, those who denied God's signs and His proofs of His oneness and divinity, and that Jesus is a servant of His, and who took the Messiah as a god and lord, or claimed for God a son, will have from God a severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection.

* *

"Those who disbelieved" are those who denied the signs of God, and "the signs of God" are God's indicators, proofs and arguments. [[See the language indexes earlier under "kafara" and "aba".]]

* *

This statement from God, mighty and majestic, indicates the meaning of His saying "And He revealed the Furqan," that it refers to the distinction which is a proof for the people of truth against the people of falsehood. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "annahu ma'nan bihi al-fasl 'an alladhi huwa hujjah..." The word "'an" is clearly an extra inserted by the scribe's haste, so I have dropped it. The context that follows confirms this.]] Because He followed it with His saying: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God," meaning: indeed those who denied that distinction and the Furqan which He sent down as a separator between the one who is right and the one who is wrong, "will have a severe punishment," a warning from God to whoever opposes the truth after its clarity to him and departs from the path of guidance after the proof has been established against him. Then He informed them that He is "Exalted in Might" in His authority, that no one who wants to punish them can be prevented by any preventer, no barrier can stand between Him and it, and no one can dare to oppose Him in it. And that He is "Owner of Retribution" against whoever denies His proofs and arguments after they have been established against him and after their clarity to him and his knowledge of them.

* *

Those of the people of interpretation said the same as what we have said on this.

Mention of those who said that:

6564 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution," i.e., indeed God takes retribution against whoever disbelieves in His signs after knowing them and recognizing what came from Him concerning them. [[Report 6564 is from the remainder of the reports whose last is number 6561.]]

6565 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God will have a severe punishment, and God is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution,"

.........................................................................

............................................................................ [[The dots mark what was lost from the continuation of report 6565, and the reports after it, if there were any reports after it. The same is found in the printed edition and all the other manuscripts available to us.]]

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven﴾ (5)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means by this: Indeed, nothing that is on the earth or nothing that is in the heaven is hidden from Allah. He says: How then could it be hidden from me, O Muhammad, while I am the Knower of all things, what these people who dispute with you concerning the signs of Allah from the Christians of Najran about Jesus son of Mary, in their saying that they say about him? As:

6566 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "Indeed, nothing is hidden from Allah, on the earth or in the heaven," meaning: He knows what they intend, what they plot, and what they liken [to Allah] by their saying about Jesus, when they made him a lord and a god, while they have from His knowledge something other than that, out of deception regarding Allah and disbelief in Him. [[The report 6566 is from the remaining reports whose last is number 6564, from the Sirah of Ibn Ishaq.]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means by this: Allah is the One who forms you, making you shapes and figures in the wombs of your mothers however He wills and chooses, so He makes this one a male and this one a female, this one black and this one red. Through this He informs His servants that all who are contained in the wombs of women, whom He formed and created however He willed, [[In the printed edition: "mimman sawwarahu" without the fa' at its beginning. The correct reading is from the manuscript.]] and that Jesus son of Mary is among those whom He formed in the womb of his mother and created in it however He willed and chose, and that if he were a god he would not have been one contained in his mother's womb, for the Creator of what is in the wombs is not contained by the wombs; rather, wombs contain only created beings. As:

6567 - Ibn Humayd related to me, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills," meaning: [["ay" is missing from the manuscript and the printed edition; I have added it from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham, and the method of Ibn Ishaq in the preceding reports follows this.]] Jesus was indeed among those formed in the wombs; they do not deny or reject this, just as others of the children of Adam were formed, so how could he be a god when he was in that station?  [[The report 6567 is from the remaining reports whose last is number 6566 from Ibn Ishaq.]]

6568 - al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills," meaning: He formed Jesus in the womb however He willed.

* *

Others have said concerning this:

6569 - Musa ibn Harun related to us, saying: Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, from Abu Malik, and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ, [his] saying: "He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills," he said: When the drop enters the wombs, it flies in the body for forty days, then it becomes a clot for forty days, then it becomes a lump of flesh for forty days. When it reaches the time to be shaped, Allah sends an angel to form it. The angel comes with dust between his two fingers, and mixes it into the lump of flesh, then kneads it with it, then forms it as he is commanded, and says: Male or female? Wretched or happy? What is its provision? What is its lifespan? What are its deeds? What are its calamities? Allah decrees, and the angel records. When that body dies, it is buried where that dust was taken. [[The chain of this report was discussed previously in number 168. The hadith on the creation of the human in its mother's belly with other wording and other chain is in Muslim 16:189-195, and in al-Bukhari in the Book of "Beginning of Creation," in the chapter on mention of the angels, and in the Book of "Menstruation," chapter: "Formed and not formed."]]

6570 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, [his] saying: "He it is who forms you in the wombs however He wills," [He is] capable, our Lord, to form His servants in the wombs however He wills, male or female, black or red, complete in its creation or incomplete.

The discussion concerning His saying: ﴿There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ [3:6]

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This statement is a declaration by God, may His remembrance be exalted, that He is free of having any rival or equal in His lordship, or that divinity could belong to anyone other than Him. It is also a refutation of those who said what they said about Jesus, namely the delegation of Najran who came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and all who held the same view as them concerning Jesus, and of everyone who claimed a deity alongside God or acknowledged the lordship of another. [[His words "and of everyone who claimed ..." are coordinated with his words "and a refutation of those who said ..."]] Then, may His praise be exalted, He informed His creatures of His attribute, as a warning to whoever worshipped other than Him or associated anyone else with Him in worship, saying: ﴿He is the Almighty﴾, who cannot be helped by anyone against one who seeks to take vengeance upon him, and from whom no refuge or shelter can save him. [["Wa'l" (with a fatha on the waw and a sukun on the hamza, on the pattern of sami'a) means the refuge (mawil), the shelter to which one who fears flees. "LajA'" (with a fatha on the lam and the jim) means the shelter, the stronghold in which one seeks protection.]] This is because of His might, before which every creature is humbled and to which every existing thing submits. [[See the lexical indexes (ʿ-z-z) mentioned earlier.]] Then He informed them that He is ﴿the All-Wise﴾ in His management and in His clearing of Himself before His creatures, and in His sending His proofs to them, so that whoever perishes among them perishes after clear evidence, and whoever lives among them lives after clear evidence. [[See the lexical indexes (ḥ-k-m) mentioned earlier.]] As related:

6571 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Then He said, meaning the Lord, mighty and majestic: exalting Himself and affirming His oneness, free of what they ascribed alongside Him: ﴿There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾. He said: "The Almighty" in His victory over those who disbelieve in Him, whenever He wills, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "in His victory (nusrah)", which is an error in meaning, since "nusrah" is a noun from "nasr" (help) and has no place here. The correct reading is "intiṣār", which means vengeance; "intaṣara minhu" means he took vengeance upon him.]] and "the All-Wise" in His excuse and proof addressed to His servants. [[In Ibn Hisham: "in His proof and His excuse to His servants", which is preferable because of the placement of "to" (ila) in the sentence. "A'dhara ilayhi i'dhaaran and 'udhran" means he reached the utmost in guiding him, so that no room for excuse remained.]]

6572 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': ﴿There is no god but Him, the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾, he says: Mighty in His retribution, wise in His command.

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 3, verses 7–8 (part 1 of 7):

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), they are the mother of the Book, and others that are allegorical (mutashabihat)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His praise, "It is He who has sent down to you the Book," meaning that God, from whom nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden, is the One who has sent down to you the Book. By "the Book" He means the Qur'an.

* *

We have already explained earlier the reason why the Qur'an is called "a Book," so there is no need to repeat it here. [[See what has preceded, 1:99, then 3:86, and the language indexes.]]

* *

As for His saying, "in it are verses that are decisive," it means: from the Book there are verses. By "verses" He means the verses of the Qur'an.

As for "decisive" (muhkamat), these are the verses that have been made firm through clear explanation and detail, and whose proofs and arguments have been established for what they were made into evidence for: lawful and unlawful, promise and warning, reward and punishment, command and prohibition, report and parable, admonition and lessons, and what is similar to these.

* *

Then, exalted is His praise, He described these "decisive verses" as being: "they are the mother of the Book." He means by this that they are the foundation of the Book, in which are the pillars of the religion, the obligations and the prescribed limits, and all else that people need in matters of their religion, and the obligations imposed upon them in this world and the next.

* *

He called them "the mother of the Book" only because they are the principal part of the Book and the place to which its people turn when they need it. The Arabs do likewise: they call whatever gathers and unifies a thing its "mother." Thus the banner of a people that gathers them in the armies is called "their mother," and the one who manages the principal affairs of a village or town is called "its mother."

We have already explained this earlier in a way that suffices without repetition. [[See what has preceded, 1:107–108.]]

* *

He made "the mother of the Book" singular and did not pluralize it, saying "mothers of the Book," although He said "they" (hunna). This is because He meant that all the decisive verses together are "the mother of the Book," not that each verse of them is "the mother of the Book." Had the meaning been that each verse of them is "the mother of the Book," it would undoubtedly have been said: "they are the mothers of the Book." A parallel to God's saying, "they are the mother of the Book," in the interpretation we have given regarding the singular "mother," where it is the predicate of "they," is His saying, may He be remembered: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [Surah al-Mu'minun: 50], and He did not say "two signs," because the meaning is: We made both of them together one sign, since their meaning was one in that they were made a lesson for people. Had the meaning been to report about each of them separately, that He made each a lesson for people, it would have been said: "We made the son of Mary and his mother two signs," for each of them had a lesson for them. That is because Mary bore a child without a man, and her son spoke, speaking as a child in the cradle, so that in each of them there was a sign for the people. [[In the printed edition: "if the meaning was one and their two [states]..." which is meaningless; the copyist of the manuscript misread it, as the final alif in "wāḥidan" fell at the position of the fa' of "fīmā" unpointed, so he took it as "wa-ihdāhumā" and changed "ja'alā" into "ja'alnā." And "if its meaning was the report..." is the correct reading from the manuscript.]]

* *

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "they are the mother of the Book" was said, and not "they are the mothers of the Book," in the manner of quotation (ḥikāyah), as a man says, "I have no helpers (anṣār)," and you reply, "I am your helper (anṣāruka)," or "I have no equal (naẓīr)," and you reply, "we are your equal (naẓīruka)." [[Perhaps the correct reading is: "I have no helper (naṣīr)," and you reply, "we are your helper (naṣīruka)." What is in the printed edition and the manuscript is undoubtedly correct.]] He said: It is similar to "leave me alone regarding two dates (damratān)," and he recited for a man of the Fuq'as tribe: [[He is Manzur ibn Murthid ibn Farwa al-Fuq'asi al-Asadi. It is also said: "Manzur ibn Farwa ibn Murthid," and he is the same as "Manzur ibn Hubbah al-Fuq'asi al-Asadi," "Hubbah" being his mother, by whom he was known.]]

She presented herself to me at a place of halting (ḥall),
like a mare presenting herself at the grazing-tether (ṭawal),
a presenting that did not fall short in slaying me.

[[Majalis of Tha'lab: 602 (many verses of this rajaz), and Sharh Shawahid al-Shafiyah: 248–251, and Sirr Sina'at al-I'rab (the science of grammatical inflection) 1:177–179, then 235, and Lisan al-Arab under (ṭawal), (qatal), and elsewhere. In the Majalis of Tha'lab, the version of the first verse is "bi-majāz ḥall," and the last is "'an qatlalī," and there is no evidence in this version. Lisan al-Arab mentions the variation in its transmission. "Ṭawal" (with a kasra on the ṭa', and a fatḥa on the waw and an unshaddated lam, as in the rajaz) is the mountain that is tethered for the animal so it can graze in it; the poet only doubled the letter. Lam ta'al: did not fall short. The pronoun in this poem refers to his beloved, about whom he says before these verses: "Who will I have from the separation of Layla? Who will I have? ... and the cord of her union that has come undone?"]] "ḥall," meaning: he alights at it. [[In the printed edition: "kull, meaning: it is recounted by way of quotation," which is corrupt speech. But how strange it is for the one who wanted to correct it to say: "Perhaps its original is, as is understood from the context: he did not say 'from slaying,' and he brought it in quotation." He wanted to correct it but repeated the words, which is the most absurd. However, the reader who copied from the manuscript did not read its text well, and he corrupted it badly; but it is clear as I have written it from the manuscript's script.
As for his saying "bi-makān ḥall," it is vocalized in pen in Lisan al-Arab and in Majalis of Tha'lab with tanwin on "makān" and "majāz," and kasra on the ḥā' of "ḥall." I do not think this is correct, for I have not found them saying "makān ḥall" with a kasra on the ḥā'; rather it is with a fatḥa on it, as an annexed construction and not as an adjective: "ḥalla bi-l-makān ḥulūlan wa-ḥallan," meaning: he alighted at it.
As for his saying "on quotation" in the context of his saying "and he recited for a man of the Fuq'as...."]] — "on quotation," because it was in the accusative before that, as one says: "The prayer was called, 'the prayer, the prayer!'" quoting the speaker who said: "The prayer, the prayer!"

He said: Some of them said: it is in fact "an qatlā lī," but he took it as "'an," because "an" in his dialect takes "'an" in its place, and the accusative is by way of command, as if you had said: "a striking for Zayd."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This is a view that has no meaning. For all these examples which he cited are undoubtedly quotations by those who quote them, of what was reported from the words of another and the utterances he spoke; and it is known that God, exalted is His praise, did not quote from anyone his saying "mother of the Book," so that it could be said that He brought it out in the manner of quoting one who said it thus. [[In the manuscript: "brought it out in the place of quotation," and the pure correct reading seems to be what is in the printed edition. This is a distortion from the haste of the copyist, who wanted to write "makhraj," then the pen added a lam, then he reviewed a rā', then dropped the jīm.]]

* *

As for His saying "wa-ukhar" (and others): it is the plural of "ukhrā" [feminine of "other"]. [[See what has preceded, 3:459. In the printed edition: "plural of ākhar," and in the manuscript, without a madda on the alif; I preferred that it be "ukhrā," due to what has passed in his words on that and what will come shortly after, and because it is the analogy.]]

* *

Then the grammarians differed about the reason why "ukhar" was not declined (ṣarf).

Some of them said: "ukhar" was not declined because it is an adjective (na't), its singular being "ukhrā," just as "jumaʿ" and "kutaʿ" were not declined, because they are adjectives.

* *

Others said: "ukhar" was not declined because of the extra yā' that is in its singular, and because its plural is built on its singular in not taking declension. They said: "ukhrā" was not declined just as "ḥamrā'" and "bayḍā'" were not declined, in indefinite and definite forms, because of the added long vowel in them and the hamza in place of a waw. [[I have left his phrase "with the waw" as it is, for I was not able to determine its addition, nor did I know what he meant by it, except that he meant the shortened feminine alif, like the one in "ḥublā." And "ukhrā" has the extended feminine alif.]] Then the plural of "ḥamrā'" and "ukhrā" diverged: the plural of "ukhrā" was built on its singular, so it became "fuʿal" and "ukhar," [[What seems more likely to me is that his saying "fuʿal" is an addition by the copyist.]] so its non-declension was kept as the non-declension of "ukhrā"; and the plural of "ḥamrā'" and "bayḍā'" was built against its singular, so it was declined, becoming "ḥumr" and "bayḍ." So because their states differ in the plural, their inflection differed for them in declension. And because their states agree in the singular, their states agreed in it.

* *

As for His saying "mutashābihāt" (allegorical), its meaning: alike in recitation, different in meaning, as He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿And they were given it in semblance﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 25], meaning alike in appearance, different in taste. [[See what has preceded, 1:385–394.]] And as He said, reporting about those among the Children of Israel who said: ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confusing to us﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 70], meaning by that: they have become confusing to us in description, though their kinds differ. [[See what has preceded, 2:209–211.]]

* *

The meaning of the statement, then, is: He who nothing on earth or in heaven escapes, is the One who has sent down to you, O Muhammad, the Qur'an; in it are verses that are decisive by clear explanation, which are the foundation of the Book upon which your pillar and the pillar of your community in religion rest, and to which your recourse and theirs is directed in what He has made obligatory upon you and them of the laws of Islam; and other verses, which are alike in recitation and different in meanings.

* *

The interpreters have differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book, and others that are allegorical," and what is the decisive (muhkam) of the verses of the Book, and what is the allegorical (mutashābih) of it?

Some of them said: the "decisive" verses of the Qur'an are those acted upon, and they are the abrogating (nāsikhāt) or those that establish rulings; and the "allegorical" verses are those whose practice has been abandoned, the abrogated (mansūkhāt).

Those who said this:

6573 – Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: al-Awwam informed us, from one who related to him, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive." He said: They are the three verses from here: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 151–152], to three verses more, [[In the printed edition: "that are here," which is an error, for the verses, as you see, are from Surah al-An'am. I have confirmed what is in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:4. See the takhrij at the end of the report.]] and the one in "Banu Isra'il": ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 23–39], to the end of the verses. [[The report 6573: this is its chain as it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition. I fear that something may have dropped from its chain, "from Abu Ishaq," after "qāla akhbaranā al-Awwām." "Al-Awwām" is al-Awwām ibn Hawshab, who narrates from Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i. As for his saying in the chain "from one who related to him," that is so, because the one from whom Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i narrated is "Abd Allah ibn Qays," who is mentioned as narrating this report, and the one who narrates from him is Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i, and no one is known to have narrated from him except Abu Ishaq. (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib 5:365.) This same report was narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:288 through the route: "Ali ibn Salih ibn Hayy, from Abu Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Qays, from Ibn Abbas." Its text: "Decisive verses: they are those in al-An'am: Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden—to the end of the three verses." Al-Hakim said: "Sahih," and al-Dhahabi agreed. For this reason I feared that "from Abu Ishaq" had dropped from al-Tabari's chain, but I did not record it in his text.]]

6574 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih related to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." The decisive: its abrogating, its lawful and unlawful, its limits and its obligations, and what is believed in and acted upon. He said: "And others that are allegorical": the abrogated, its earlier and later parts, its parables and its divisions, and what is believed in but not acted upon.

6575 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: "It is He who has sent down to you the Book," to "and others that are allegorical": the decisive ones, which are the mother of the Book, are the abrogating, by which one is religiously bound and acts. The allegorical are the abrogated, by which one is not religiously bound.

6576 – Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah al-Hamadani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book," to His saying: "all is from our Lord." As for the decisive verses, they are the abrogating ones by which one acts; and as for the allegorical ones, they are the abrogated.

6577 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." The "decisive" is the abrogating by which one acts, in which God made lawful what is lawful and forbade what is unlawful. As for the "allegorical," it is the abrogated, which is not acted upon but is believed in.

6578 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "decisive verses." He said: the decisive is what is acted upon.

6579 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book, and others that are allegorical." He said: "The decisive": the abrogating by which one acts. And "the allegorical": the abrogated, which is not acted upon but is believed in.

6580 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: "verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." He said: the abrogating. "And others that are allegorical": he said: what has been abrogated and left, which is recited.

6581 – Ibn Wakī' related to me, saying: my father related to us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said: The decisive is what has not been abrogated, and what is allegorical in it is what has been abrogated.

6582 – Yahya ibn Abi Talib related to me, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: "verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." He said: the abrogating. "And others that are allegorical": he said: the abrogated.

6583 – It was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh relate, saying: Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive": meaning the abrogating by which one acts. "And others that are allegorical": meaning the abrogated, which is believed in but not acted upon.

6584 – Ahmad ibn Hazim related to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from al-Dahhak: "In it are verses that are decisive": he said: what has not been abrogated. "And others that are allegorical": he said: what has been abrogated.

* *

Others said: the "decisive" verses of the Book are those in which God has made clear the explanation of its lawful and unlawful; and the "allegorical" among them are those whose parts resemble one another in meaning, though their wordings differ.

Those who said this:

6585 – Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive": what is in it of the lawful and unlawful; and whatever else is apart from that is "allegorical," confirming one another. It is like His saying: ﴿And He leads none astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 26], and like His saying: ﴿Thus does God place defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 125], and like His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Surah Muhammad: 17].

6586 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

Others said: the "decisive" verses of the Book are those that admit of only one interpretation; and the "allegorical" among them are those that admit of several interpretations.

Those who said this:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 7–8 (part 2 of 7):

6587 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr related to me concerning "He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat)": they contain the proof of the Lord, the protection of the servants, and the repelling of adversaries and falsehood; there is no altering or distorting them from what they were established upon = [In the text of Ibn Hisham: "there is no altering of them ... from what they were placed upon."] "and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)", in truthfulness [In the printed edition: "and others that are ambiguous," and the correct reading is from the manuscript and Ibn Hisham. The phrase "in truthfulness" is not in the text of Ibn Hisham, but it is present in the manuscript.], they admit of alteration, distortion and interpretation; God tested His servants by them, as He tested them with the lawful and the unlawful; they are not turned to falsehood nor distorted away from truth. [The report 6587 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is 6571, transmitted by him from Ibn Ishaq.]
* *
Others said: The meaning of "the decisive (muhkam)" is what God has made firm in it of the verses of the Qur'an, and the narratives of the nations and their messengers who were sent to them, which He detailed by clarifying that for Muhammad and his community. "And the ambiguous (mutashabih)" is what the wording has made ambiguous of their narratives when repeated in the surahs, by relating them with the agreement of wording and the difference of meanings, and by relating them with the difference of wording and the agreement of meanings. [In the printed edition: "so the narrative of the agreement of wording ... and the narrative with difference of wording ..." which is corrupt; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]
Mention of those who said this:
6588 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, and he recited: "Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm and then detailed from One Wise and Acquainted" [Surah Hud: 1], and he said: He mentioned the account of the Messenger of God ﷺ in twenty-four verses of it: [That is, of Surah Hud; this enumeration that follows is in the order of the codex.] and the account of Noah in twenty-four verses of it. Then he said: "That is from the news of the unseen" [Surah Hud: 49], then he mentioned "And to 'Ad" and recited until he reached "and seek forgiveness of your Lord" [[It seems he means that he recited until he reached this verse of Surah Hud: 89. But this verse is in the account of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, so I do not know what he said after: "then he proceeded, then he mentioned Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb". My guess is that the text of his statement is: "then he proceeded. He mentioned Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb ..." with the second "then" dropped. See the following note.]] Then he proceeded. Then he mentioned Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb and finished with that. This is the clarification of that, the clarification of "whose verses have been made firm and then detailed" = [In the printed edition and manuscript: "this is certainty of that, certainty of ..." and it seems the correct reading is what I have set down.
Moreover, I did not find this report elsewhere, but I found al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 3: 320, in the tafsir of "Surat Hud", saying: "Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Ibn Zayd, may God be pleased with him, that he recited: 'Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm' and said: they are all Meccan and firm, meaning Surat Hud, 'and then detailed.' He said: Then he mentioned Muhammad ﷺ, and judged between him and those who opposed him, and recited: 'The likeness of the two parties', the whole verse. Then he mentioned the people of Noah, then the people of Hud, and this was the detailing of that, and its beginning was firm. He said: My father, may God be pleased with him, used to say that - meaning: Zayd ibn Aslam."
Therefore, I preferred the correction mentioned earlier in the previous note, and I preferred that "yaqin" in both places be "tabyin".] He said: The ambiguous is the mention of Moses in many places, and it is ambiguous, and it is all one meaning. And ambiguous: "then take her (fa-uslukh) therein" [and] "carry therein" (uhmil fiha), "insert your hand" (usluk yadaka), "enter your hand" (adkhil yadaka), "a serpent moving swiftly" (hayyatan tas'a), "a manifest serpent" (thu'ban mubin) = [From his words "He said: The ambiguous ..." it is an interjection within his discussion of the detailing of the narratives in "Surat Hud" and the enumeration of the verses of each narrative. As for the verses mentioned here, this is the explanation of their places in order: "Surat al-Mu'minun: 27" / "Surat Hud: 40" / "Surat al-Qasas: 32" / "Surat al-Naml: 12" / "Surat Ta Ha: 20" / "Surat al-A'raf: 107" and "Surat al-Shu'ara: 22."] He said: Then he mentioned Hud in ten verses of it, [Salih in eight verses of it, Abraham in eight other verses, Lot in eight verses of it, Shu'ayb in thirteen verses, and Moses in four verses; all of this judges between the prophets and their peoples in this surah. That amounted to one hundred verses of Surat Hud.] Then he said: "That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; some of them are standing and some are harvested" [Surah Hud: 100]. And he said concerning the ambiguous in the Qur'an: whoever God intends with trial and misguidance says: "What is the matter with this that it is not so? What is the matter with this that it is not so?"
* *
Others said: Rather, the "decisive (muhkam)" of the verses of the Qur'an is what the scholars know the interpretation of, and understand its meaning and explanation; and the "ambiguous (mutashabih)" is what no one has any way to know, of what God has kept the knowledge of to Himself apart from His creatures, such as the report on the time of the coming forth of Jesus son of Mary, the time of the sun rising from the west, the establishment of the Hour, the end of the world, and what is similar to that, for no one knows that. They said: God has named "the ambiguous" among the verses of the Book the disjointed letters found at the beginnings of some surahs of the Qur'an, such as "Alif Lam Mim", "Alif Lam Mim Sad", "Alif Lam Mim Ra", "Alif Lam Ra", and what is similar to these, because they are ambiguous in wording and agree with the letters of abjad reckoning. Some Jews in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ hoped to learn from them the knowledge of the duration of Islam and its people, and to know the end of the lifespan of Muhammad and his community [In the printed edition: "the term of his community," which is a misreading by the printer; I have kept what is in the manuscript: al-akl (with a vowel on the first letter and a sukun): the span of life; see the note on p. 196, note 1.], so God refuted their hope in that and informed them that what they sought to know of that through these ambiguous letters they would not reach, nor through anything else, and that this is known only to God.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This is a saying reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab [In the printed edition: "ibn Rabab," which is an error; the correct reading is what I have set down, and "Ri'ab" with a kasra on the ra. See what preceded at 1: 216 and what will come in note 4, where the reference is.] that this verse was revealed concerning him [the word "him" refers to this saying, not to "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah"]; and we have mentioned the report of that from him and from others who said similarly, in the interpretation of that in the tafsir of God's words: "Alif Lam Mim. That is the Book; there is no doubt in it" [Surah al-Baqarah: 2].
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This saying we have mentioned from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah is closer to the interpretation of the verse. That is because all that God the Mighty and Majestic has sent down of the verses of the Qur'an upon His Messenger ﷺ, He sent down only as a clarification for him and his community and as guidance for the worlds; and it is not permissible that there be in it what they have no need of, nor that there be in it what they need and then there is no way for them to know its interpretation. Since that is so, then everything in it that the creatures need [In the printed edition: "for His creatures," and in the manuscript: "muhlaqihi," the first letter appearing as an obliterated mim; the correct reading is what I have set down.], even if in some of it there is what they are independent of regarding some of its meanings = [and if the need compels them to it in many meanings] [This sentence between the parentheses appears thus in the printed edition, and similarly in the manuscript, though the word "idtarrathu" is written without dots. It is a sentence whose meaning is not clear, and I fear that the copyist may have omitted lines from this place, so the speech became confused for us and for him! Dropping this sentence from the context does no harm. But I have left it as it is, placed it between brackets, and enclosed it between lines, so that its place and the place of the omission, which I judged to be an oversight by the copyist, may be known.] = such as the saying of God the Mighty and Majestic: "On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or earn good through its faith" [Surah al-An'am: 158]. So the Prophet ﷺ informed his community that the sign which God, may His praise be exalted, informed His servants that when it comes faith will not benefit a soul that had not believed before it, is the rising of the sun from the west. [See the detail of that and its reason in the interpretation of the verse in the Tafsir of al-Tabari 8: 71-77 (Bulaq).] So what the servants needed of knowledge of that is their knowledge of the time when repentance benefits, by its description, without limiting it by a number of years, months or days. [In the printed edition: "after by the years ...", and in the manuscript: "after the years ...", and it is clear that the copyist dropped the second dal from "bi-'adad".] God has clarified that to them through the evidence of the Book, and made it clear to them through His Messenger ﷺ, explained. As for what they have no need to know of it, [In the printed edition: "there is no need for them" with a lam, and I have kept the correct reading from the manuscript.] it is the knowledge of the length of the period between the time of the revelation of this verse and the time of the occurrence of that sign, for that is something they have no need to know in religion or in worldly life. That is the knowledge which God, may His praise be exalted, has kept to Himself apart from His creatures, and withheld from them. That, and what is similar to it, is the meaning which the Jews sought to know regarding the duration of Muhammad ﷺ and his community, by means of His saying "Alif Lam Mim", "Alif Lam Mim Sad", "Alif Lam Ra", "Alif Lam Mim Ra" and similar disjointed letters, the ambiguous ones, of which God, may His praise be exalted, informed that they would not grasp the interpretation before it, and that its interpretation is known only to God.
Since the ambiguous is what we have described, then everything else is decisive. For it cannot be free of either being decisive in that it has one meaning with no interpretation other than one interpretation, and it has become sufficient by hearing it without need of an explanation that clarifies it [In the printed edition and manuscript "mubayyanah," but the mim in the manuscript does not look like a mim, and the correct reading of the text is what I have set down]; or it is decisive, even though it has many aspects and interpretations and variation in many meanings. The indication of the meaning intended by it is either from God's clarification, may He be remembered, concerning it, or from the clarification of His Messenger ﷺ to his community. And the knowledge of that will not be lost to the scholars of the community, for what we have already explained.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: "They are the mother of the Book" [Surah Ali 'Imran: 7]
Abu Ja'far said: We have already given the explanation of the interpretation of that with the evidence attesting to the soundness of what we have said about it. [See what preceded shortly: 170.] We will now mention the differences of the people of interpretation concerning it, for they differed in its interpretation.
Some of them said: The meaning of His saying "they are the mother of the Book" is: they are those in which are the obligations, the limits and the rulings, like what we have said about it.
Mention of those who said that:
6589 - Imran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd related to us, from Yahya ibn Ya'mur, that he said concerning this verse: "They are the decisive, the mother of the Book." Yahya said: They are those in which are the obligations and the limits and the pillar of religion; and he struck an example for that, saying: "The mother of the cities" is Mecca, "the mother of Khurasan" is Merv, and "the mother of travellers" is the one to whom they entrust their affairs and who looks after them on their journey; he said: That one is their mother. [The report 6589: "Imran ibn Musa al-Farra" and "Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id" whose biographies have passed under number 2154. See the note on the report number 6591, next.]
6590 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying "they are the mother of the Book": they are the sum of the Book.
* *
Others said: Rather, what is meant by that is: the opening surahs from which the Qur'an is derived.
Mention of those who said that:
6591 - Imran ibn Musa related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd related to us, from Abu Fakhitah, that he said concerning this verse: "Of it are decisive verses; they are the mother of the Book": "the mother of the Book" are the openings of the surahs, from which the Qur'an is derived - "Alif Lam Mim. That is the Book", from it "al-Baqarah" was derived, and "Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but He" from it "Al 'Imran" was derived. [The report 6591: "Abu Fakhitah" is Sa'id ibn 'Alaqah al-Hashimi, mawla of Umm Hani, a trustworthy narrator whose biography is in al-Tahdhib. See the preceding report number 6589. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 4 narrated them as one abridged report and said: "From Ishaq ibn Suwayd that Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Abu Fakhitah debated this verse: 'they are the mother of the Book'; Abu Fakhitah said ... and Yahya ibn Ya'mur said ..." and he gave what is in these two reports in abridged form.]
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation"
Abu Ja'far said: God, may His praise be exalted, means by that: As for those in whose hearts is inclination away from the truth and deviation from it.
* *
It is said from it: "Such-and-such deviated from the truth, so he deviates from it, deviation, deviating, and deviation (zaygh), and he caused deviation (az-agahu Allah)" when He inclines him, "so He inclines him (yuzighuhu)." And from it is His saying, may His praise be exalted: "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us" [Surah Ali 'Imran: 8]: do not incline them away from the truth.
* *
Those of the people of interpretation said in accordance with what we have said regarding that:
Mention of those who said that:
6592 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to me, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation": i.e., inclination away from guidance. [The report 6592: it is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6587, from Ibn Ishaq.]
6593 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning God's saying "in whose hearts is deviation": he said: doubt.
6594 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.
6595 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," he said: from the people of doubt.
6596 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas = and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," as for deviation, it is doubt.
6597 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid: he said: "zaygh" is doubt = Ibn Juraij said: "Those in whose hearts is deviation" are the hypocrites.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: "So they follow that of it which is ambiguous"
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous," is meant: what its wordings are ambiguous and its meanings are varied through aspects of interpretation, so that they may confirm, through their claim of falsehoods of interpretations regarding it, the deviation and inclination from the path of truth which they are upon, a deception on their part through it upon whoever's knowledge of the aspects of its interpretation and the variation of its meanings is weak, as:
6598 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous": they impose the decisive upon the ambiguous, and the ambiguous upon the decisive, and they deceive, and God deceives them.
6599 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous," i.e., what is distorted from it and turned, [In Ibn Hisham: "i.e., what is turned from it," with no "distorted."] so that they may confirm by it what they invented and innovated, so that it would be a proof for them for what they said and a doubt. [The report 6599 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6592, by his isnad from Ibn Ishaq. The text in Ibn Hisham's Sirah 2: 226 is: "so that it would be a proof for them, and for them a doubt about what they said."
I have left what is in the tafsir here as it is, because his transmission from Ibn Ishaq differs from the transmission of Ibn Hisham.]
6600 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous," he said: the door through which they went astray and perished, seeking its interpretation.
* *
Others said regarding that, with what:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 7–8 (part 3 of 7):
