6601 - Muhammad ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His words: "So they follow that which is ambiguous of it" (﴿فَيَتَّبِعُونَ مَا تَشَابَهَ مِنْهُ﴾), that they follow the abrogated (al-mansukh) and the abrogating (al-nasikh), saying: "What is the matter with this verse, which is acted upon in such-and-such a way, alongside this verse? [[In the printed edition: "majaz hadhihi al-ayah" (the meaning of this verse); the manuscript is unclear, and I have preferred reading it as "makan".]] The first was left and this other one was acted upon? Would it not have been the case that acting upon this verse came before the first one, which was abrogated arrived? And what is the matter with it that it promises punishment to whoever does a deed that punishes him [in] the Fire, and in another place: whoever does it, it has not made the Fire obligatory?"
* *
The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning who is meant by this verse.
Some of them said: It refers to the delegation of the Christians of Najran who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and disputed with him with what they disputed with him, and argued with him by saying: "Do you not claim that Jesus is the Spirit of Allah and His Word?" And they interpreted in that regard what they say about it of disbelief.
Mention of those who said that:
6602 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: They intended — meaning the delegation who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Christians of Najran — and argued with the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "Do you not claim that he is the Word of Allah and a Spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes!" They said: "Then it is enough for us!" So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord," then Allah, His praise be exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 59], the verse.
* *
Others said: Rather, this verse was revealed concerning Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, and his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and the group who debated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the measure of the duration of his nation's lifespan and the lifespan of his community, [[In the printed edition: "ajalahu wa ajal ummatihi"; see the explanation of "al-akl" above, p. 180, note 1.]] and they wanted to know that from his saying: "Alif Lam Mim," "Alif Lam Mim Sad," "Alif Lam Ra," and "Alif Lam Ra." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said concerning them: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation" — meaning these Jews whose hearts are inclined away from guidance and truth — "they follow that which is ambiguous of it," meaning: the meanings of these disjointed letters which admit of varied inflection and different interpretations, "seeking discord."
We have already mentioned the report concerning this earlier, at the beginning of the surah in which "al-Baqarah" is mentioned. [[See the earlier report, no. 246.]]
* *
Others said: Rather, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meant by this every innovator in his religion who introduces an innovation opposing what His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent with, by an interpretation he interprets from some verses of the Qur'an that admit of interpretations, even though Allah has made clear the explanation of that, either in His Book or on the tongue of His Messenger.
Mention of those who said that:
6603 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord." Qatadah, whenever he recited this verse, "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," would say: "If they are not the Haruriyyah and the Sabaiyyah, [["al-HarurIyyah" are the Kharijites, who gathered at Harura on the outskirts of Kufa; their first gathering there and their arbitration occurred when they opposed Ali. As for "al-Sabaiyyah," they are attributed to Ibn al-Sawda', the Jew "Abdullah ibn Saba'," who said to Ali: "You are you," meaning that the Imam has a divine portion, exalted is Allah far above that, so Ali exiled him to al-Mada'in. The manuscript has "al-Sabaiyyah," and the printed edition has "al-Sabi'iyyah"; I have preferred the manuscript's reading because it is so in most books.]] then I do not know who they are! By my life, among the people of Badr and al-Hudaybiyah who witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the Pledge of Ridwan, from the Emigrants and the Helpers, there is a lesson for whoever seeks information, and a warning for whoever takes heed, for whoever has understanding or sight. [[This refers to the lesson of Badr, when his companions advised the Messenger of Allah to leave the first position he had taken for the position they advised him toward, and the lesson of al-Hudaybiyah, when some of the companions of the Pledge of Ridwan said what they said in disliking the treaty the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concluded between himself and Quraysh. In this is proof of the corruption of the doctrine of the Kharijites and the doctrine of the Sabaiyyah.]] The Kharijites went out, and the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at that time were numerous in Medina, Syria and Iraq, and his wives were alive at that time. By Allah, not a single male or female among them ever became a Harurite, nor did they approve of what they were upon, nor did they support them in it; rather, they would narrate the defect of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in regard to them and the description with which he described them, and they hated them in their hearts and opposed them with their tongues, and by Allah their hands were harsh upon them when they met them. By my life, if the matter of the Kharijites were guidance, it would have gathered together, but it was misguidance, so it scattered. Likewise, when a matter is from other than Allah, you will find much disagreement in it. They have been trying to manage this matter for a long time. [[Alaṣa al-amr: he managed it and attempted it. Alaṣa fulanan 'ala hadha al-amr: he steered him toward the thing he wanted.]] Have they ever succeeded in it, or prospered? Glory be to Allah! How does the last of these people not take heed from the first of them? If they were upon guidance, Allah would have made it manifest, granted it victory and supported it, [[In the printed edition: "aflahahu" with a non-dotted ha; in the manuscript it is undotted, and the correct reading is with jim: aflaja Allah hujjatahu, meaning He made his proof manifest and gave him victory, i.e., success and triumph.]] but they were upon falsehood, which Allah refuted and crushed. So they are as you have seen them: whenever a generation of them emerges, Allah refutes their argument, exposes their claims, and sheds their blood. If they conceal it, it is a wound in their hearts and a grief upon them; and if they make it manifest, Allah sheds their blood. That, by Allah, is an evil religion, so avoid it. By Allah, Judaism is an innovation, Christianity is an innovation, the Harurites are an innovation, and the Sabaiyyah are an innovation; no Book has been sent down with them and no Prophet has laid them down as a tradition.
6604 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation." The people sought the interpretation, erred in the interpretation, and attained the discord, so they followed what was ambiguous of it, and thereby they perished. By my life, among the companions of Badr and al-Hudaybiyah who witnessed the Pledge of Ridwan... and he mentioned something similar to the report of Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from him.
6605 - Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, both saying: Isma'il ibn Ulayyah related to us, from Ayyub, from Abdullah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book" up to His words: "And none will take heed except those of understanding," and then said: "When you see those who dispute about it, they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." [[The hadith: 6605 — al-Tabari narrated this hadith here through eleven chains, all from the narration of Ibn Abi Mulaykah, except one, which is hadith 6611. The narrators differed on Ibn Abi Mulaykah: some narrate it from him directly from Aisha, and some narrate it from him from al-Qasim from Aisha. Both are authentic, as will come.
Ibn Abi Mulaykah is Abdullah ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Mulaykah al-Qurashi al-Makki, a major, trustworthy Successor (tabi'i) who heard Aisha and others of the Companions. Al-Bukhari recorded his biography in al-Saghir, p. 131; Ibn Sa'd 5:347-348; Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/99-100; and al-Mus'ab in Nasab Quraysh, p. 293.
Al-Tirmidhi said (4:80), after narrating the hadith through both routes, as will come: "Thus many narrated this hadith from Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Aisha, and they did not mention in it: from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad. Rather, Yazid ibn Ibrahim mentioned it from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad in this hadith. And Ibn Abi Mulaykah is Abdullah ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, and he also heard from Aisha."
Yazid ibn Ibrahim did not alone mention "al-Qasim" in the chain, as al-Tirmidhi claimed. The clarification of that will come, Allah willing.
Al-Hafiz said in Fath al-Bari (8:157): "Ibn Abi Mulaykah heard much from Aisha, and an intermediary often enters between them. And it has been differed upon concerning him in this hadith..."
The hadith, from this route, through Ibn Ulayyah from Ayyub, was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (6:48, Halabi) from Ibn Ulayyah with this chain. Likewise Ibn Majah (47) narrated it from Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash — the shaykh of al-Tabari here — from Ibn Ulayyah, with it.
This Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash is biographed in al-Tahdhib, which says: "Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy, and said: he sometimes related strange reports from his father."
Ibn Abi Hatim did not record his biography, nor did al-Khatib mention him in Tarikh Baghdad, although he resided there, as in al-Tahdhib.
Ibn Kathir (2:97) mentioned the hadith according to the Musnad narration, then said: "Thus this hadith occurs in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from the narration of Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, without anyone between them." Then he pointed to Ibn Majah's narration and other narrations which will be mentioned later.
But "Ya'qub" occurs in Ibn Kathir instead of "Ayyub"! This is a copyist's or printer's error. In the Musnad it is correctly "Ayyub".]]
6606 - Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: I heard Ayyub, from Abdullah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, that she said: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book" up to "And none will take heed except those of understanding." She said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who dispute about it — or he said: who dispute about it — they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." Mutar said, from Ayyub, that he said: "So do not sit with them; they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." [[The hadith: 6606 — Ibn Abd al-A'la: he is Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani; his biography has passed at 1236.
Mutar: he is Ibn Tahman, with a fatha on the ta and sukun on the ha, al-Warraq. He is trustworthy, and some have spoken of him concerning his memory. He died in 125.
This hadith, through this route, was narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, no. 75 in our edition, from the route of Asim ibn al-Nadr al-Ahwal, from al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman, with this chain.
Ibn Hibban said after narrating it: "Ayyub heard this report from Mutar al-Warraq and Ibn Abi Mulaykah together."
This is an error, which we failed to point out there, since we understood it in its correct meaning and did not notice the wording! Ibn Hibban intends to say: "Ayyub and Mutar al-Warraq heard this report together from Ibn Abi Mulaykah."
Either what is established there is a slip of the pen by Ibn Hibban, or it was an oversight by the copyists. Ibn Hibban could not have been unaware that Mutar al-Warraq did not meet Aisha, and he has mentioned him among the trustworthy (al-Thiqat, pp. 344-345), and mentioned that he narrates from Anas ibn Malik, and that he died in 125, it was said 129. Nevertheless, this was not granted to him, for Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Marasil, p. 78, narrated from Abu Zur'ah, who said: "Mutar did not hear anything from Anas. It is mursal."
But what troubles Ibn Hibban's statement — if it is read in the correct form we mentioned — is that al-Tabari's narration here is explicit that Mutar heard it from Ayyub with the addition he added to the wording of the hadith. Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman would have heard it from Ayyub in abridged form, with the wording "fa-ahdharuhum," and heard it from Mutar al-Warraq from Ayyub in full, with the other wording. This, Allah willing, is the correct view. Mutar and Ayyub are of the same generation.]]
6607 - Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Wahhab related to us, saying: Ayyub related to us, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with a similar meaning. [[The hadith: 6607 — Abd al-Wahhab is Ibn Abd al-Majid al-Thaqafi; his biography has passed at 2039. This hadith, through this route, was narrated by Ibn Majah (47) from Ahmad ibn Thabit al-Jahdari and Yahya ibn Hakim, both from Abd al-Wahhab, with it.
Ibn Kathir (2:97) pointed to it from Ibn Majah's narration, then said: "Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Abdi narrated it in his Musnad from Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, with it."]]
6608 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similarly. [[The hadith: 6608 — This is the preceding hadith, through Ma'mar from Ayyub. Ibn Kathir (2:97) pointed to it, saying: "Likewise Abd al-Razzaq narrated it from Ma'mar from Ayyub, and likewise others narrated it from Ayyub."
Ibn Kathir did not mention another takhrij for this narration of Ma'mar. The manuscript of Abd al-Razzaq's Tafsir in the Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah has a lacuna from the end of Surat al-Baqarah to the beginning of Surat al-Nisa'.]]
6609 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: al-Harith informed us, from Ayyub, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)," the whole verse. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, and those who dispute about it, they are the ones Allah meant; they are those whom Allah mentioned, so do not sit with them." [[The hadith: 6609 — al-Harith is Ibn Bunhan al-Jurmi al-Basri. He is very weak. Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir 1/2/282: "munkar al-hadith" (denounced in narration). He said the same in al-Saghir, p. 185. In al-Tahdhib, from al-Tirmidhi in al-Ilal al-Kabir, from al-Bukhari: "munkar al-hadith, he does not mind what he narrates, and he is very weak." Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/91-92) narrated from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said: "A righteous man, but he was not known for hadith, and he did not memorize it; munkar al-hadith."
Despite the weakness of this al-Harith, the basic hadith is authentic, through the other chains, preceding and following.]]
6610 - Ibn Waki' related to us, saying: Abu Usamah related to us, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: I heard al-Qasim ibn Muhammad narrate, from Aisha, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear, they are the foundation of the Book," then he recited to the end of the verses, and said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, then they are those whom Allah named, so beware of them." [[The hadith: 6610 — Ibn Waki' is Sufyan ibn Waki', who is weak, as we explained at 1692. Abu Usamah is Hammad ibn Usamah al-Kufi, the hafiz; his biography has passed at 2995. Yazid ibn Ibrahim al-Tustari al-Basri, the hafiz: trustworthy and firm. Ahmad, Waki', Abu Hatim and others declared him trustworthy, and Ibn Ma'in considered him more firm than Jarir ibn Hazim.
This chain is one of the narrations of this hadith in which "al-Qasim ibn Muhammad" is added between Ibn Abi Mulaykah and Aisha. Both are authentic. It is among the additions in a connected chain: Ibn Abi Mulaykah heard it from Aisha and heard it from al-Qasim from Aisha, so he narrated it in both ways, sometimes thus and sometimes thus.
This hadith, through this route, was narrated by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi (1433) from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with this chain, similar, somewhat abridged.
It was narrated by al-Bukhari (8:157-159, Fath), Muslim (2:303-304), and Abu Dawud (4598), all three from al-Qa'nabi, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with this chain.
Al-Tirmidhi (4:80) narrated it from Abd ibn Humayd, from Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with it, similarly, and said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."
Ibn Hibban narrated it in his Sahih, no. 72 in our edition, from the route of Abdullah — Ibn al-Mubarak, the Imam, Shaykh al-Islam — from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with it.
Yazid ibn Ibrahim did not alone mention the addition of "al-Qasim" between Ibn Abi Mulaykah and Aisha; a different chain will come at 6615 with the addition of al-Qasim, and it will also come after this at 6611 from the narration of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 3, verses 7–8 (part 4 of 7):**

6611 - Ali ibn Sahl told us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim told us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: "They follow that which is ambiguous of it" [the verse], and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has warned you about them. So when you see them, then beware of them." [[Hadith 6611. Ali ibn Sahl al-Ramli, Tabari's shaykh: his biography has already passed at 1384. al-Walid ibn Muslim al-Dimashqi, scholar of Syria: his biography has already passed at 2184.
Abd al-Rahman: he is Ibn al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. His biography has already passed at 2836.
This is a sound chain. It is a strong, sound supporting narration (mutaba'ah) for the version of Ibn Abi Mulaykah from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad.
Ibn Kathir cited it (2: 98), then said: "Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another route, from al-Qasim, from Aisha, with the same wording."
See the following hadith: 6615.
His saying "nazaʿa Rasul Allah" (the Messenger recited): one says "intaza'a" with a verse or a poem, meaning he quoted it as evidence. It is also said of a man who derives the meaning of a verse from the Books of God: "He has derived a good meaning" (qad intaza'a maʿnan jayyidan), and "nazaʿahu", meaning he extracted it. Perhaps by her saying "nazaʿa" here she meant: he cited as evidence, or he recited citing it. See the next hadith after this one.]]

6612 - Ali told us, saying: al-Walid told us, from Nafi ibn Umar, from [Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who told me] Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you see them, then beware of them." Then he recited: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it," and they do not act upon its clear (muhkam) verses. [[Hadith 6612. Nafi ibn Umar ibn Abd Allah ibn Jumayl, al-Jumahi al-Qurashi al-Makki: trustworthy. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "Firm, firm, sound in hadith." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/86, Ibn Sad 5: 363, Nasab Quraysh by al-Mus'ab: 400, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/456, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1: 213.
In the manuscript and the printed edition here it reads "Nafi an Umar" instead of "Nafi ibn Umar". This is an error. The correction comes from al-Fath 8: 157, where he is mentioned among those who narrated this hadith "from Ibn Abi Mulaykah without mention of al-Qasim", "...and Nafi ibn Umar, and Ibn Jurayj, and others." We have also corrected it from Ibn Kathir, as we will mention.
Then in both the original copies there is another error, worse than that and more shameful! In them it reads: "an Nafi, an Umar, an Aisha"!! So "Ibn Abi Mulaykah" was dropped from the chain, and then his explicit statement of hearing from Aisha was dropped.
We have corrected the chain and restored what the copyists had mistakenly omitted, namely what we added after the word "an" between the markers of addition: [Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who told me].
We took this addition from Ibn Kathir 2: 98, where he said: "Ibn Jarir narrated it, from the hadith of Rawh ibn al-Qasim and Nafi ibn Umar al-Jumahi, both from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha. Nafi said in his narration: 'from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who told me Aisha', and so he mentioned it."
This is the correct reading, and it was the copyists' omission that caused the lost part of the chain here. Praise be to God.
Furthermore, the hadith will come again: 6614, through this route, in the correct form, from the narration of Khalid ibn Nizar, from Nafi, who is Ibn Umar al-Jumahi, "from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha".]]

6613 - Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb told me, saying: my paternal uncle told us, saying: Shabib ibn Said informed me, from Rawh ibn al-Qasim, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about this verse: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation, and none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge..." He said: "When you see those who dispute concerning it, they are the ones whom Allah meant, so beware of them." [[Hadith 6613. Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb: his biography has already passed at 2747. His paternal uncle is Abd Allah ibn Wahb.
Shabib ibn Said al-Tamimi al-Habati al-Basri: Ibn al-Madini said: "Trustworthy. He used to travel to Egypt for trade, and his book is a sound book." In Egypt Ibn Wahb heard from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/234, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/359.
"al-Habati": with an unpointed initial letter ha' and a dotted ba' with one dot. It is a nisba to "al-Habatat", a clan of Tamim.
Rawh ibn al-Qasim al-Tamimi al-Anbari al-Basri: trustworthy. Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, and others declared him trustworthy. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah said: "I have not seen anyone who sought hadith while elderly with better memory than Rawh ibn al-Qasim."
Ibn Kathir indicated this chain at 2: 98, as we quoted his words at the previous chain.]]

6614 - Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam told me, saying: Khalid ibn Nizar told us, from Nafi, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, regarding this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book," [the verse], "they follow it," meaning they recite it. Then he [the Prophet] said: "When you see those who dispute concerning it, beware of them, for they are the ones whom Allah meant." [[Hadith 6614. Khalid ibn Nizar ibn al-Mughirah al-Ayli: trustworthy. He is biographed only in al-Tahdhib. His shaykh Nafi is Ibn Umar al-Jumahi.
This hadith repeats hadith 6612, from the narration of Nafi al-Jumahi, and it confirms what we mentioned, that the link dropped from that chain.
So these: Ayyub, Nafi ibn Umar, and Khalid ibn Nizar all narrated it from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, directly, without an intermediary "al-Qasim" between them. Indeed Nafi ibn Umar explicitly stated that Ibn Abi Mulaykah heard it from Aisha, as passed at 6612.
Abu Amir al-Khazzaz followed them in this:
Al-Tirmidhi narrated it at 4: 80, from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from Abu Amir al-Khazzaz, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, without mention of al-Qasim.
Abu Amir al-Khazzaz (with dotted letters) is Salih ibn Rustum. His biography has already passed at 5458.
Ibn Kathir mentioned this follow-up at 2: 98, and the Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) in al-Fath 8: 157. Its chain is sound.
Also Said ibn Mansur narrated it, from Hammad ibn Yahya, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, as Ibn Kathir reported at 2: 98. It is a sound chain.
Ibn Jurayj also followed them. The Hafiz mentioned it in al-Fath 8: 157, but did not name who narrated it. I have not found it in any other source among those available to me.]]

6615 - Ibn Wakiʿ told us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun told us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim, from Aisha, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book, in it are verses that are clear (muhkamat), they are the mother of the Book," to the end of the verse. He said: "They are those whom Allah named. So when you see them, then beware of them." [[Hadith 6615. This is also a sound chain. But it has the addition of "al-Qasim" between Ibn Abi Mulaykah and Aisha, like the narration of Yazid ibn Ibrahim from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, passed at 6610.
It refutes the claim of al-Tirmidhi that Yazid ibn Ibrahim alone transmitted this addition, as we mentioned at 6605. For Hammad ibn Salamah followed him in this, in this chain.
Similarly Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it in his Musnad: 1432, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aisha.
Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi gathered the two narrations, that of Yazid and that of Hammad, in his narration from both of them. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from his father, from Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim al-Tustari and Hammad ibn Salamah together, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aisha. Ibn Kathir cited it at 2: 98 from Ibn Abi Hatim, and the Hafiz indicated it in al-Fath 8: 157.
Earlier, at 6611, was the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father, from Aisha. This and that show that Hammad ibn Salamah narrated it from two shaykhs who both took it from al-Qasim: he narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim and from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, both from al-Qasim.
There is another follow-up from al-Qasim whose chain details we do not know. For Ibn Kathir said at 2: 98: "Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another route, from al-Qasim, from Aisha, with the same wording." He did not mention what that route is or its chain, and the Hafiz did not indicate it in al-Fath.
There is also a hadith whose origin al-Suyuti mentioned at 2: 5, and he attributed it further to al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: What the apparent meaning of this verse indicates is that it was revealed concerning those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over the ambiguous part of what was sent down to him from the Book of Allah, either concerning the matter of Jesus, or concerning the term of his own lifespan and the lifespan of his community. [[In the printed edition: "either the term of his life and the term of his community", the correction from the manuscript. A similar distortion occurred already at p. 180, note 1, p. 187, note 1, and in the first volume of the commentary, p. 217, note 4. The word "akl" (with a dammah on the alif and a sukun on the kaf) means provision, because it is eaten. From it is said of the span of life a person lives in this world "akl". One says of the dead: "his akl has ended", meaning his term has finished and his life has passed away.]]

And it is more fitting for it to concern those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over its ambiguity regarding his term and the term of his community, because his saying: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah," indicates that this is information about the term which they wanted to know through the ambiguous matter that none but Allah knows. As for the matter of Jesus and its causes, Allah has informed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his community of it, and clarified it for them. It is known that the verse only meant what was hidden about the terms (al-ajal). [[In the printed edition: "...that he did not mean except what was hidden from the individuals (al-ahad)", which has no meaning. In the manuscript: "that he did not mean by it except what was hidden in it from the individuals," so I judged the correct reading to be as I have written it, "al-ajal", plural of ajal, which is what they wanted to know of the term of this community. The copyist here often erred through haste.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿seeking discord﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the meaning of that.

Some of them said: the meaning of that is: seeking shirk (polytheism).

Mention of those who said that:

6616 - Musa ibn Harun told me, saying: Amr ibn Hammad told us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "seeking discord", he said: the desire for shirk.

6617 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: Ishaq told us, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, regarding His saying: ﴿seeking discord﴾, meaning shirk.

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: seeking doubts (al-shubuhat).

Mention of those who said that:

6618 - Muhammad ibn Amr told me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "seeking discord", he said: doubts, by which they were destroyed.

6619 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "seeking discord", the doubts; he said: they were destroyed by it.

6620 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "seeking discord", he said: the doubts. He said: and the doubts are what they were destroyed by.

6621 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr: "seeking discord", that is confusion (al-labs). [[The report: 6621. This is the remainder of the earlier reports, the last of which is number 6599, with its chain from Ibn Ishaq.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The more correct of the two opinions regarding this, in terms of correctness, is the view of the one who said: its meaning is "the desire for doubts and confusion."

* *

So the meaning of the speech is then: As for those in whose hearts is inclination away from the truth and a turning away from it, they follow from the verses of the Book those whose wording is similar, and which admits of diverting its interpreter's meaning into various directions of interpretation [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "and it admits its diversion into various directions of interpretation", and I am certain this is a copyist's error, because the preceding pronouns are all plural and the following ones are all singular, which does not work. I judged that the copyist read "sarf sarfuhu" (without alif in "sarfuhu", as was written in older times), thought it an error, so he removed the first "sarf" and kept the second "sarfuhu", and the pronouns became confused.]] – by its admitting of different meanings – desiring confusion for themselves and for others, using it as proof for their falsehood toward which their hearts were inclined, rather than the truth which Allah made clear and explained by the clear verses of His Book.

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: And this verse, although it was revealed concerning those from among the polytheists whom we mentioned it was revealed concerning, it also refers to every innovator in the religion of Allah who has an innovation toward which his heart has inclined, interpreting some of the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an, then argues and disputes with it against the people of truth, and turns away from the clear proofs of its clear verses, desiring by that to create confusion for the people of truth among the believers, and seeking knowledge of the interpretation of what is ambiguous to him of it, whoever he may be, and whatever kind of innovators he is, whether from among the Christians, the Jews, the Magians, or he is a Sabaʾi, [[It is written here as "sabaʾiyyan", and we have said that in the earlier passages it was written "sabaʾiyyan". I have left this spelling as it is, and it is correct.]] or a Harurite, or a Qadarite, or a Jahmite, as he, peace be upon him, said: "When you see those who dispute with it, they are the ones whom Allah meant, so beware of them," and as:

6622 - Yunus told me, saying: Sufyan informed us, from Mamar, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, from Ibn Abbas – and the Kharijites were mentioned in his presence and what they experience (yulqawna) when hearing the Qur'an – [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "and what they encounter at the flight (al-firar)", which is words with no meaning. He only meant that Ibn Abbas was mentioned to have described the Kharijites' humility, worship and submissiveness when hearing the Qur'an, which is well known of the Kharijites, and they are the ones described in the famous hadith: "you will belittle your prayer compared to theirs." Therefore I am certain that the reading in the manuscript is what I have adopted. This is confirmed by Ibn Abbas's reply: "They believe in its clear verses, and they perish at its ambiguous verses," expressing his astonishment at their actions in their humility, and at their misguidance in their innovated interpretation, by which they made the blood and property of the Muslims lawful.]] he said: They believe in its clear verses, and they perish at its ambiguous verses! And Ibn Abbas recited: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah," [the verse].

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: We only said the view we mentioned as the more correct of the two interpretations concerning His saying: "seeking discord," because those concerning whom this verse was revealed were people of polytheism, and by seeking the interpretation of what they sought its interpretation, they only intended to create confusion for the Muslims and to use it as an argument against them, in order to turn them away from the truth they were upon. So there is no sense in saying: "They did that out of desire for shirk," when they were already polytheists.

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿and seeking its interpretation﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of "al-ta'wil" which Allah, great is His praise, meant by His saying: "and seeking its interpretation."

Some of them said: the meaning of that is: the term (al-ajal) which the Jews wanted to know, concerning the expiry of the period of the matter of Muhammad ﷺ and the matter of his community, through the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah) according to the reckoning of the abjad (jummal), "Alif Lam Mim", "Alif Lam Mim Sad", "Alif Lam Ra", "Alif Lam Mim Ra", and what is similar to these of terms.

Mention of those who said that:

6623 - al-Muthanna told me, saying: Abd Allah ibn Salih told us, saying: Muawiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His saying: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah", meaning its interpretation is the Day of Resurrection, "except Allah".

* *

Others said: rather, the meaning of that is: "the consequences of the Qur'an." They said: "They only wanted to know when the abrogating (nasikh) of the rulings which Allah, great is His praise, had legislated for the people of Islam before its coming would arrive, abrogating what He had legislated before that."

Mention of those who said that:

6624 - Musa told me, saying: Amr told us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and seeking its interpretation", they wanted to know the interpretation of the Qur'an – which is its consequences. Allah said: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah", and its interpretation, its consequences, is: when will the abrogating part of it come and abrogate the abrogated?

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: "and seeking the interpretation of what is ambiguous of the verses of the Qur'an, interpreting it – since it has many aspects and variations of interpretations – according to what is in their hearts of deviation, and the misguidance they have acquired."

Mention of those who said that:

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verses 7–8 (part 5 of 7):**

٦٦٢٥ - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, concerning "and seeking its interpretation" (*wa-ibtigha'a ta'wilihi*): this refers to what they had fallen into of error in their saying [[In the printed edition: "in his saying," but the correct reading is from the manuscript and Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 226. His words after this, "We created, and We decreed," are a detached statement, pointing to what preceded from the beginning of this long, continuous report, which al-Tabari relates in scattered form from Ibn Ishaq. This is mentioned in report no. 6543 above, p. 153, lines 3–4, where he said: "They argue from their saying, 'He is the third of three,' with God's words: 'We did, We commanded, We created, We decreed.' They say: If He were one, He would only have said, 'I did, I decreed, I commanded, I created'; but He is He, with Jesus and Mary."]] "We created" and "We decreed."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The view stated by Ibn 'Abbas, that "seeking the interpretation" which the people sought in the ambiguous verses is knowledge of the end of the term and the time of the Hour, and what we have mentioned from al-Suddi, that they sought and desired knowledge of a time that has already come before its arrival [["jaa'" is an active participle from the verb "jaa'a, yajee'u, fahuwa jaa'," and the sentence's context is: "The view stated by Ibn 'Abbas ... and what we have mentioned from al-Suddi ... is closer to the truth."]] — is closer to the truth, although al-Suddi overlooked the meaning of this in one respect, by restricting it to the view that its meaning is: the people sought knowledge of the time of the coming of the abrogating (*nasikh*, that which abrogates an earlier ruling) of what had already been made firm before that.

We only said that the people's seeking knowledge of the time that has already come before its arrival, whose knowledge is concealed from them and from others, by means of the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an [[His words "by means of the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an" are a continuation of their saying, "the people's seeking knowledge of the time..." It is a prepositional phrase, related to "seeking."]] is closer to the meaning of His words "and seeking its interpretation," because of what we have already shown from God's report, exalted is His praise, that this interpretation is known only to God. There is no doubt that the meaning of His words "We decreed" and "We did" has been known in its interpretation by many of the ignorant among the polytheists, let alone the people of faith and those firmly rooted in knowledge among them.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿None knows its interpretation except God. And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, exalted is His praise, He means: None knows the time of the Hour, and the end of the term of Muhammad's community [[In the printed edition: "the term of Muhammad's lifetime"; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript; see the note above, p. 196, no. 1.]] and what will happen, except God, apart from anyone else among mankind who hoped to attain knowledge of it through reckoning, astrology, and soothsaying. As for those firmly rooted in knowledge, they say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord." They do not know it; rather, their superiority in knowledge over others regarding this is knowing that God is the One who knows it, apart from anyone else of His creatures.

* *

The people of interpretation (*ahl al-ta'wil*) differed concerning the interpretation of this, and whether "those firmly rooted" is conjoined to the word "God," meaning that knowledge of the interpretation of the ambiguous verses is attributed to them, or whether their mention is a new statement [[In the printed edition: "or are they a new statement"; I have restored what is in the manuscript.]] meaning a report about them that they say, "We believe in the ambiguous verses, and we affirm that knowledge of them is known only to God"?

Some said: The meaning of this is: None knows the interpretation of that except God alone, by Himself. As for those firmly rooted in knowledge, the report about them begins with their saying, "We believe in the ambiguous and the decisive verses, and all of it is from God."

Those who said this:

٦٦٢٦ - Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Hakam related to me, saying: Khalid ibn Nizar related to us, from Nafi', from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from 'A'ishah, concerning His words "and those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it'": She said: Their firmness in knowledge was that they believed in its decisive and its ambiguous verses, and did not know its interpretation. [[Report 6626: see the earlier report no. 6614 and the note on it.]]

٦٦٢٧ - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ibn Tawus, from his father, who said: Ibn 'Abbas used to say: ﴿None knows its interpretation except God, and those [in knowledge] firmly rooted say, "We believe in it."﴾ [[In the printed edition: "and those firmly rooted say," without the waw. The correct form includes it, since it will come on p. 204, line 13, that Ibn 'Abbas used to recite it that way. I lean toward the view that the correct text originally read "Ibn 'Abbas used to recite" and "None knows its interpretation...", but the copyist, in his haste, wrote "say" instead of "recite," then dropped the waw from "and those firmly rooted say..." So I have restored the waw, which is the pure correct reading, God willing. For this reason I added [in knowledge] between the brackets, because this is a reading of the verse, not an explanation from Ibn 'Abbas, and no one among the reciters is reported to have omitted [in knowledge].]]

٦٦٢٨ - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Abi al-Zinad informed me, saying: Hisham ibn 'Urwah said: My father used to say concerning this verse, "None knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge," that those firmly rooted in knowledge do not know its interpretation, but they say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."

٦٦٢٩ - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih related to us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah related to us, from Abu Nuhayk al-Asadi, concerning His words "None knows its interpretation except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge": He would say: You recite this verse, and it is cut off: "None knows its interpretation except God," and then "those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.'" So their knowledge ends at their saying what they said.

٦٦٣٠ - al-Mathna related to us, saying: Ibn Dukayn related to us, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mawhab related to us, saying: I heard 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz say: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge": the knowledge of those firmly rooted in knowledge of the interpretation of the Qur'an ends at their saying, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."

٦٦٣١ - Yunus related to me, saying: Ashhab informed us, from Malik, concerning His words "None knows its interpretation except God": he said: Then he began and said, "And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.'" And they do not know its interpretation.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: None knows its interpretation except God and those firmly rooted in knowledge, and they, with their knowledge of it and their firmness in knowledge, say, "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."

Those who said this:

٦٦٣٢ - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: I am among those who know its interpretation.

٦٦٣٣ - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge" know its interpretation, and say, "We believe in it."

٦٦٣٤ - al-Mathna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge know its interpretation, and say, 'We believe in it.'"

٦٦٣٥ - It was related to me from 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "And those firmly rooted in knowledge" know its interpretation, and say, "We believe in it."

٦٦٣٦ - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "And none knows its interpretation" that which He intended, what He intended, [[This is as it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition, and in Ibn Kathir's *Tafsir* 2: 100. As for Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 226, it has "i.e., that by which they intended what they intended," and the correct reading seems to be what is in the *Tafsir*; his words "what He intended" are an interrogative. As for his words "that which He intended," it means that which God, glorified is He, intended. What is in Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* is also correct, and the pronoun in "they intended" refers to those who follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation; this is what they intended.]] "except God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord.'" How could it differ, when it is one word from one Lord? [[From his words "all of it is from our Lord" to his words "from one Lord" is an addition from the text of Ibn Hisham's narration in the *Sirah* 2: 226; there is no doubt that the copyist dropped it through haste and inattention.]] Then they referred the interpretation of the ambiguous verses to what they knew of the interpretation of the decisive verses, which have no interpretation for anyone except one interpretation. Thus the Book became consistent by their saying, and its parts confirmed one another; the proof was established by it, the excuse was made manifest by it, falsehood was dispelled by it [[The verb "zaha" yazīḥu zayḥan and "inzaha" are both intransitive: they mean to go away, to recede, and to vanish.]] and unbelief was crushed by it. [[Report 6636 is the remainder of the earlier reports, the last of which is no. 6625, with its chain of transmission from Ibn Ishaq. It is in Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 226.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the one who holds the first view, and says that those firmly rooted do not know the interpretation of that, and that God only reports about them their belief and their affirmation that it is from God, he makes "those firmly rooted in knowledge" the subject, according to the view of the Basrans, and makes its predicate "say, 'We believe in it.'" As for the view of some Kufans, it is the pronoun referring back to them in "say." And according to some of them, it is the whole predicate clause about them, which is "say."

* *

As for the one who holds the second view, and claims that those firmly rooted know its interpretation, he conjoins "those firmly rooted" to the word "God," and puts them in the nominative by conjunction with it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in our opinion is that they are in the nominative by their predicate clause that follows them, which is "say," because of what we have already explained: that they do not know the interpretation of the ambiguous verses which God, mighty and majestic is He, mentioned in this verse. It is also, as has reached me, in the reading of Ubayy: ﴿and those firmly rooted in knowledge say﴾ [[see the earlier note on report 6627, p. 202, line 7, note 2.]], as we mentioned from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite it. And in the reading of 'Abd Allah: ﴿Its interpretation is only with God, and those firmly rooted in knowledge say﴾.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for the meaning of "ta'wil" (interpretation) in the speech of the Arabs, it is explanation, return, and destination. Some transmitters recited the verse of al-A'sha:

"Because she was, of her love, interpreting [ta'awwul] / the interpreting [ta'awwul] of a spring-born foal that has been weaned and has come to submit"

[[His Diwan: 88; *Majaz al-Qur'an* by Abu 'Ubaydah 1: 86; *al-Sahibi*: 164; *Lisan al-'Arab* (sahiba), (rab'), (awwala), (wala). Then what will come shortly after of mention of another version, which I have not found in any other source so far.

As for the other version which came in *Lisan al-'Arab* (rab'), (wala), it is:
"Because she was a distant nawa [homeland] / the following [tawali] of a spring-born foal that has been weaned and has come to submit"

Al-Rab'i: the one born at the start of the litter. "Al-saqab" is the plural of "saqb" (with fatha then sukun): the young of a she-camel at the moment she gives birth, which is called "salil," before it is known whether it is male or female; once it is known that it is male, it is "saqb." "Asshaba" means: became humbled, submitted, and obeyed. This verse, in this version I mentioned here, has been explained by al-Azhari, who said: "Thus have I heard the Arabs recite it, and they explained 'the following of the spring-born foal' as coming from *muwala*, which is distinguishing one thing from another. It is said: 'We separated the foals from their mothers, so they followed,' meaning we weaned them from them at the completion of the year, and the *muwala* becomes intense for them, and their yearning for their mothers increases. A pen is made for them in which they are held, and the mothers are let loose in a direction of their pastures. When they are separated from their young, the young are let loose in a direction other than that of the mothers, and they graze alone, and continue in that, and after days become accustomed [to it]. Al-A'sha informed us that his beloved's homeland was intense upon him, so he yearned for her as the yearning of the spring-born foal when it is weaned from its mother. He informed us that this weaned foal continues in the following, and that it becomes accustomed as the young camel does. Al-Azhari said: I only explained this verse because the transmitters, when its meaning became unclear to them, stumbled in extracting it and confused it, and did not know from it what the people know from their witnesses in their desert."]]

As for the first version, Abu Ja'far explained it in what follows. As for his second version, which is his words "the followers of her love," I did not know its meaning, and I fear that its correct form is "the yearnings of her love." The "nazā'i'" is the plural of "nazī'ah," as it is said: a she-camel *nāzi'* from the she-camels *nawāzi'*. A *nazī'ah* she-camel is one that yearns for her homeland. A camel "nazaʿa" to its homeland: it yearned and longed.]

Its origin is from "āla al-shay' ilā kadhā," meaning it reached it and returned to it: "yaʾūlu awlan," and "awwaltuhu ana" means I made it reach it. It has been said that His words "and better in interpretation" [Sura al-Nisa': 59; Sura al-Isra': 35] mean "in recompense," because "recompense" is that to which the matter of the people has come and returned.

By his words "ta'awwul ḥubbihā" he means: the explanation of her love and its return. [[In the manuscript: "and the explanation of her love..." with an added waw, which is an error. This is the text of Abu 'Ubaydah in *Majaz al-Qur'an* 1: 87, which contains an error, as the editor thought that his words "its explanation" meant the explanation and clarification of this word, so he placed two dots after it thus: "its explanation: and its return," and then the waw in "and its return" has no meaning. The correct form is what we have written.]] He only means by this that her love was small in his heart, then it grew from smallness to greatness, and it kept growing until it became fully grown, and became old, like the small young camel which kept growing until it became fully grown and became large like its mother. [[See *Majaz al-Qur'an* by Abu 'Ubaydah 1: 87.]]

This verse is also recited as:
"Because she was the followers of her love / the following of a spring-born foal that has been weaned and has come to submit" [[See p. 204, note 4.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, "We believe in it"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By "those firmly rooted in knowledge" He means the scholars who have perfected their knowledge, understood it, and memorized it by memorization, into whose knowledge and understanding of what they have known no doubt or confusion enters.

* *

The root of that is from "the firmness of a thing in a thing," which is its establishment and its penetration into it. It is said from it: "Faith became firm (*rasikha*) in the heart of so-and-so, so he is firm, with firmness (*rasakh*) and firmness (*rusukh*)." [[His words "rasakhan" (firmness): this is a verbal noun that the dictionaries of the language have not mentioned.]]

* *

A report has been related about their description from the Prophet ﷺ, which is what follows:

٦٦٣٧ - Musa ibn Sahl al-Ramli related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah related to us, saying: Fayyad ibn Muhammad al-Raqqi related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Adam related to us, from Abu al-Darda' and Abu Umamah, who both said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked: Who is the one firm in knowledge? He said: "He whose right hand is true, whose tongue is truthful, whose heart is upright, and whose belly is chaste; that is the one firm in knowledge." [[Hadith 6637: Fayyad ibn Muhammad al-Raqqi: al-Bukhari mentioned him in *al-Tarikh* 4/1/135, and Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/87, and neither mentioned any criticism of him.
'Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Adam: Ibn Abi Hatim mentioned him, 2/2/197, and said: "He related from Abu al-Darda', Abu Umamah, and Wathilah ibn al-Asqa': that the Prophet ﷺ was asked: How will the prophets be raised? Fayyad ibn Muhammad al-Raqqi related from him ... I asked my father about him, and he said: I do not know him. And this is a false hadith."
Al-Dhahabi mentioned him in *al-Mizan*, and al-Hafiz in *al-Lisan*, and they related from Ahmad, who said: "His hadiths are fabricated." There is no good word in his biography about him, and it is enough that Ahmad accuses him of fabrication.]]

* *

٦٦٣٨ - al-Mathna and Ahmad ibn al-Hasan al-Tirmidhi related to me, saying: Nu'aym ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Fayyad al-Raqqi related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Awdi related to us = he said: He had met some companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ = he said, Anas ibn Malik, Abu Umamah, and Abu al-Darda' related to us: that the Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about those firmly rooted in knowledge, and he said: "He whose right hand is true, whose tongue is truthful, whose heart is upright, and whose belly and private parts are chaste; that is the one firm in knowledge." [[Hadith 6638: It is the previous hadith with a slight addition, and the addition of "Anas ibn Malik."
But in this chain is "'Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Awdi." The more probable view is that this is an error by one of the transmitters or by the copyists, and that its correct form is like the earlier chain, "'Abd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Adam." As for "'Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Awdi," it is certainly other than this one. He was mentioned earlier at no. 5461. His biography in Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/200 states that he "related from Salim ibn 'Abd Allah, from Hafsah, concerning the middle prayer; Abu Bishr Ja'far ibn Abi Wahshiyah related from him." The difference in generation between them is clear. Moreover, al-Awdi is reliable, while the narrator here is a liar.
The hadith was also related by Ibn Abi Hatim, from Muhammad ibn 'Awf al-Himsi, from Nu'aym ibn Hammad, from Fayyad al-Raqqi: "'Abd Allah ibn Yazid related to us," with this chain. He did not mention that he is "al-Awdi." In Ibn Kathir it occurs as "'Ubayd Allah" instead of "'Abd Allah," and this is an error.]]

Al-Haythami mentioned it in *Majma' al-Zawa'id* 6: 324, "from ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid ibn Adam, who said: Abu al-Darda', Abu Umamah, Wathilah ibn al-Asqa' and Anas ibn Malik narrated to me ..." And he said: "Al-Tabarani narrated it, and ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid is weak." Thus in al-Tabarani's narration he added a fourth Companion, namely Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'.

Al-Suyuti mentioned it in 2: 7, from these four Companions, and attributed it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani. This is a laxity on his part, for "Wathilah ibn al-Asqa'" does not appear in the narration of al-Tabari or of Ibn Abi Hatim, but only in the narration of al-Tabarani.

Then al-Suyuti mentioned roughly its meaning from the narration of Ibn ʿAsakir: "From the route of ʿAbd Allah ibn Yazid al-Awdi, I heard Anas ibn Malik say ..."

This indicates that the addition of "al-Awdi" is an error by one of the narrators, not by the copyists.

* *

A group of the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) have said: God, mighty and majestic, named these people "those firmly rooted in knowledge" because of their saying: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."

Those who said this:

6639 – Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Jabir, from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it'" [in the manuscript and the printed edition: "those firmly rooted in knowledge ..." without the waw; I have confirmed the text of the verse]. He said: "Those firmly rooted" are those who say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."

6640 – Musa narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge," they are the believers, for they say: "We believe in it" – in its abrogating and its abrogated [verses] – "all of it is from our Lord."

6641 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, Ibn ʿAbbas said, ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam said: "Those firmly rooted in knowledge" – and their knowledge is their saying – Ibn Jurayj said: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it'," and they are those who say: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us﴾, and they say: ﴿Our Lord, indeed You will gather the people for a Day about which there is no doubt﴾, and so on.

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying "they say, 'We believe in it'," it means that those firmly rooted in knowledge say: "We affirm what is ambiguous (mutashabih) among the verses of the Book, and that it is true, even if we do not know its interpretation (ta'wil)." And:

6642 – Ahmad ibn Hazim narrated to me, saying: Abu Nuʿaym narrated to us, saying: Salamah ibn Nubayt narrated to us, from al-Dahhak: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it'," he said: "the clear (muhkam) and the ambiguous (mutashabih)."

* *

Discourse on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿All of it is from our Lord﴾.

Abu Jaʿfar said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "all of it is from our Lord," He means: all of the clear (muhkam) part of the Book and the ambiguous part of it are "from our Lord," that is, His revelation and inspiration to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), as:

6643 – Ibn Wakiʿ narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Jabir, from Mujahid, from Ibn ʿAbbas, concerning His saying: "All of it is from our Lord," he said: it means what has been abrogated (mansukh) of it and what has not been abrogated.

6644 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: "And none knows its interpretation except God and those firmly rooted in knowledge," they said: "All of it is from our Lord": they believed in its ambiguous part and acted upon its clear part.

6645 – It was related to me from ʿAmmar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ, concerning His saying: "All of it is from our Lord": they say, "The clear and the ambiguous are from our Lord."

6646 – Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge say, 'We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord'," – we believe in the clear and we practise by it, and we believe in the ambiguous and we do not practise by it, and all of it is from God. [In the printed edition: "yu'minu ... wa-yadinu," both with the yaʾ; the context requires that they be with the nun.]

6647 – Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, concerning His saying: "And those firmly rooted in knowledge," – they act upon it: they say, "We act upon the clear and believe in it, and we believe in the ambiguous and do not act upon it, and all of it is from our Lord."

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: The grammarians (ahl al-ʿArabiyyah) differed regarding the status of "kull" (all) when a pronoun is implied in it. Some of the Basran grammarians said: The omission of the referent that "kull" is annexed to is permissible in this position, [in the printed edition: "idha jaza hadhf al-murad," and the earlier editors noted that it is superfluous from the copyist's pen!! The cause of that is the copyist's poor handwriting, which they did not read well,] because it is a noun, as He said: ﴿Indeed, we are all therein﴾ [Surah Ghafir: 48], meaning: "Indeed, we are all therein." He said: "Kull" does not have an implied pronoun in it when it is an adjective. One does not say, "I passed by the people, all (kull)." An implied pronoun is in it only when you make it a noun. If it were "innā kullan fīhā" as an adjective, it would not be permissible, because the implied pronoun in it is weak and does not operate in every position.

* *

Some of the Kufan grammarians held that the implied pronoun in it is the same whether it is an adjective or a noun. For it is impermissible, in their view, for what follows it to be omitted unless it is sufficient in itself from what it would be annexed to of the pronoun, and it is impermissible for it to be sufficient in one state and not sufficient in another. He said: The way of "kull" and "baʿḍ" (some) in indicating what follows them, and their sufficiency from it, is one meaning in every state, whether it is an adjective or a noun. [See what has preceded regarding "kull" in 3: 195 / then 5: 509.]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: This second view is more fitting by analogy, for when it is sufficient in itself from what has been omitted from it in one state, because it indicates it, the ruling concerning it is that whenever it is found indicating what follows it, it is sufficient from it.

* *

Discourse on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And none takes heed except people of understanding (ulu al-albab)﴾ (7).

Abu Jaʿfar said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: none is mindful, admonished, and restrained from saying about the ambiguous verses of the Book of God what he has no knowledge of, except the people of intellect (ʿuqul) and restraint (nuha) [see what has preceded in the interpretation of "yadhkuru" 5: 580 / 6: 5, and in the interpretation of "al-albab": 3: 68 / then 4: 162 / then 5: 80]. And:

6648 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr: "And none takes heed except people of understanding," he says: "And none takes heed in such a matter," – meaning: in returning the interpretation of the ambiguous to what is known of the interpretation of the clear, until the two agree upon one meaning – "except people of understanding." [The report: 6648 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6636 with its chain from Ibn Ishaq.]

* *

Discourse on the interpretation of His saying: ﴿Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us, and grant us from Yourself mercy. Indeed, You are the Bestower﴾ (8).

Abu Jaʿfar said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: those firmly rooted in knowledge say: "We believe in what is ambiguous among the verses of the Book of God, and that it and the clear part of its verses are from the revelation of our Lord and His inspiration." They also say: "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us," meaning that they say – out of longing toward their Lord that He turn away from them what He tested those with deviant hearts with, namely the following of the ambiguous verses of the Qur'an, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation, which none knows but God – : O our Lord, do not make us like those whose hearts have deviated from the truth and so have turned away from Your way. "Do not let our hearts deviate" means: do not incline them so that they turn away from Your guidance after You have guided us to it, and have granted us success in believing in the clear and the ambiguous of Your Book. "And grant us," O our Lord, "from Yourself mercy," meaning: grant us from Yourself success and steadfastness in what we are upon, of acknowledging the clear and the ambiguous of Your Book. "Indeed, You are the Bestower," meaning: indeed You are the Giver to Your servants of success and rectitude for steadfastness in Your religion and the affirmation of Your Book and Your messengers, as:

6649 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr: "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us," that is: do not incline our hearts, even if we incline with our bodies [in the printed edition: "bi-ajsadina," which has no meaning and is a distortion of the transmission from Ibn Ishaq; the correct reading is from the manuscript and Ibn Hisham 2: 226. "Ahdath" is the plural of "hadath," meaning action. They ask God to make their hearts firm in faith, even if their actions incline toward some disobedience] – "and grant us from Yourself mercy." [The report: 6649 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6648.]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: In God's praise of these people by what He praised them with – their longing toward Him that He not let their hearts deviate, and that He grant them mercy from Him as help for them to remain steadfast in what they are upon of sound insight into the truth they hold fast to – is what makes clear the error of the statement of the ignorant Qadariyyah [the Qadariyyah are the deniers of divine decree and attributes, meaning the Mu'tazilah] that God's deviating the heart of whomever of His servants He deviates from His obedience, and turning it away from it, is injustice. For if that were as they claimed, those who said, "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us," would be more deserving of blame than of praise. For if the matter were as they claimed, these people would only be asking their Lord – by their asking Him that He not deviate their hearts [in the printed edition: "masalatihim" without the bāʾ; the correct reading is from the manuscript] – that He not wrong them or be unjust to them. That would be ignorance on the part of the asker, for God, may His praise be exalted, does not wrong His servants nor is He unjust to them. He has informed His servants of that and negated it of Himself by His saying: ﴿And your Lord is not ever unjust to the servants﴾ [Surah Fussilat: 46]. There is no sense in asking Him to be in a quality which He has informed them He possesses. In the corruption of what they said in this respect is clear evidence that the deviation by God, mighty and majestic, of the heart of whomever of His servants He deviates from His obedience is justice. Therefore whoever longs toward Him that He not deviate him deserves praise, because he has directed his longing to its proper object and placed his request in its proper place, together with the abundance of reports from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) of his longing toward his Lord in that, together with his station with Him and his honour with Him.

6650 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Umm Salamah: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion!" Then he recited: "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us," to the end of the verse. [The report: 6650 – this is a sound chain. ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram is trustworthy; his biography has passed at 1605. Shahr ibn Hawshab is also trustworthy, as we said at 1489. This report is abridged. It will come in full at 6652, where we will takhrij it, God willing. It will come with a longer version than this and abridged compared to that, at 6658.]

6651 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Waki' narrated to us, from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Asma', from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), similarly. [The report: 6651 – this chain is also sound. But here it is from Shahr's transmission from Asma', who is the daughter of Yazid ibn al-Sakan al-Ansariyyah. The previous one is from Shahr's transmission from Umm Salamah, the Mother of the Believers. I have not found it from the report of Asma' except in this narration in al-Tabari, and a narration mentioned by Ibn Kathir, from Ibn Mardawayh. Ibn Kathir said in 2: 102 after mentioning the previous report of Umm Salamah: "Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through Muhammad ibn Bakkar, from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Umm Salamah, from Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan, who said she heard her narrate: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to frequently make his supplication ..." – and he mentioned something similar to the following narration of this report. Then Ibn Kathir said: "Thus did Ibn Jarir narrate it, from the report of Asad ibn Musa, from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, similar to it." Then he said: "He also narrated it from al-Muthanna, from al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal, from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, similar to it." It is clear and evident that his saying in Ibn Mardawayh's narration, "from Umm Salamah, from Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan," is an error beyond doubt. It appears to be an error by the copyists, in adding the particle "ʿan" (from). The correct version is: "from Umm Salamah, Asma' ..." As for "Asma' bint Yazid ibn al-Sakan al-Ansariyyah": she is a well-known Companion, the paternal cousin of Muʿadh ibn Jabal, and her kunyah is "Umm Salamah." Shahr ibn Hawshab is known for narrating from her; indeed Ibn al-Sakan said: "He is the one most narrated from her." He was one of her mawali. We have never heard that "Umm Salamah, Mother of the Believers" narrated from this Asma', nor from any other Companion. As for Ibn Kathir's reference to the two reports of al-Tabari from "Asad ibn Musa" and "al-Hajjaj ibn Minhal" – from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram – which are the two reports coming at 6652 and 6658 – it is problematic, for it suggests that it is like Ibn Mardawayh's narration: "from Umm Salamah, Asma' bint Yazid." Perhaps Ibn Kathir went this way, supposing that these reports in al-Tabari – 6650, 6652, 6658 – in which "from Umm Salamah" appears, are meant to be "Umm Salamah Asma' bint Yazid." If this is what he supposed, then he has erred in his supposition. For "Umm Salamah" in these three reports is, with certainty, the Mother of the Believers, as will come in the takhrij of the next report, which follows this: 6652.]

6652 – al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: al-Hajjaj ibn al-Minhal narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram al-Fazari narrated to us, saying: Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated to us, saying: I heard Umm Salamah narrate: that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to repeat in his supplication, saying: "O God, Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion!" She said: I said: "O Messenger of God, does the heart really turn?" He said: "Yes. There is no human being among the children of Adam whom God created but his heart is between two of the fingers of His fingers. If He wills, He sets it upright, and if He wills, He turns it aside. So we ask God, our Lord, that He not turn our hearts aside after He has guided us, and we ask Him to grant us from Himself mercy; indeed He is the Bestower." She said: I said: "O Messenger of God, will you not teach me a supplication to supplicate with for myself?" He said: "Yes. Say: 'O God, Lord of the Prophet Muhammad, forgive me my sin, remove the rage of my heart, and protect me from misleading trials.'" [The report: 6652 – this is the extended version, to which we referred at 6650, and it will come abridged somewhat at 6658, as we said before. The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in abridged form – in the Musnad of Umm Salamah, the Mother of the Believers – 6: 294 (Halabi), from Waki', from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Umm Salamah: "That the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: 'O Turner of the hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion.'" This is similar to the previous report, 6650, except that Abu Kurayb added the recitation of the verse in it. Ahmad also narrated it – in her Musnad – 6: 301–302, from Hashim – that is Ibn al-Qasim Abu al-Nadr – from ʿAbd al-Hamid ibn Bahram, with this chain, similarly, except that he said at its end: "And protect me from misleading trials, what You have given me life for." Then he narrated it abridged, without mention of the verse, and without "so we ask God, our Lord" etc., 6: 315 (Halabi), from Muʿadh ibn Muʿadh, who said: "Abu Kaʿb, the owner of the silk, narrated to us, saying: Shahr ibn Hawshab narrated to me, saying: I said to Umm Salamah: 'O Mother of the Believers, what was the Messenger of God's (ﷺ) most frequent supplication when he was with you?'..." Then ʿAbd Allah ibn Ahmad said after it: "I asked my father about Abu Kaʿb? He said: 'Trustworthy, and his name is ʿAbd Rabbih ibn ʿUbayd.'" Similarly al-Tirmidhi narrated it, 4: 266, from Abu Musa al-Ansari, from Muʿadh ibn Muʿadh, with it, and said: "This is a good hadith." Abu Kaʿb, the owner of the silk, ʿAbd Rabbih ibn ʿUbayd al-Azdi al-Jarmuzi: Yahya ibn Saʿid, Ibn Maʿin and others also declared him trustworthy. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/41–42. Al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id three times, 6: 325, 7: 210, 10: 176, from the narration of the Musnad, and he pointed out that al-Tirmidhi narrated part of it, and he defected it in two places through Shahr ibn Hawshab, "and he is weak, though he has been declared trustworthy." And in the last he said: "its chain is good." Al-Suyuti mentioned it in 2: 8, and added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah, without distinguishing between the narrations. Imam al-A'immah Ibn Khuzaymah narrated it in the Kitab al-Tawhid, p. 55, from the narration of Ibn Wahb, from Ibrahim ibn Nushayt al-Wa'lani, from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Husayn al-Makki, from Shahr ibn Hawshab, from Umm Salamah, similarly. This chain is also sound. Abu Bakr al-Ajurri narrated it in the Kitab al-Shari'ah, p. 316, from two other routes, from Umm Salamah. In the printed edition: "ma khalaqa Allah min bashar, min bani Adam" with the words transposed. I have adopted what is in the manuscript, which agrees with all the other narrations containing this phrase.]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verses 7–8 (part 7 of 7):**

6653. Muhammad ibn Mansur al-Tusi told me, saying: Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Zubayri told us, saying: Sufyan told us, from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from Jabir, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." Some of his family said to him: "Are we feared for, when we have believed in you and in what you have brought?" He said: "Indeed the heart is between two of the fingers of the Merciful, may He be blessed and exalted, He turns it with them thus." [Abu Ahmad moved his two fingers.] Abu Ja'far said: "And al-Tusi joined his two fingers together."

[[Hadith 6653: Muhammad ibn Mansur ibn Dawud al-Tusi al-Abid, the teacher of al-Tabari: trustworthy (thiqah). Ahmad praised him, and al-Nasa'i and others declared him trustworthy.
This hadith was also narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:288-289, through al-A'mash, with this same chain. He authenticated it according to the conditions of Muslim. However, the beginning of its chain, from al-Hakim to al-A'mash, is not mentioned, because there is a lacuna (kharm) at this point in the manuscripts of al-Mustadrak. I have inserted it from al-Dhahabi's Talkhis.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 2:9, and added its attribution to al-Tabarani in al-Sunnah.
Al-Tirmidhi alluded to it, 3:199, as we will mention in the hadith after it.
His saying "yuqallibu bihima" (he turns with them) is the correct reading, as established in the manuscript. In the printed edition it reads "yuqallibu bihi."
His saying "wasaqa bayna isbaihayh": "wasaqa al-shay'" means he gathered it. He means: he joined his two fingers.]]

6654. Sa'id ibn Yahya al-Umawi told me, saying: Abu Mu'awiyah told us, saying: al-A'mash told us, from Abu Sufyan, from Anas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) would often say: "O Turner of hearts, make my heart firm upon Your religion." We said: "O Messenger of God, we have believed in you and affirmed what you have brought, so are we feared for?" He said: "Yes, indeed the hearts are between two of the fingers of God, He turns them, may He be blessed and exalted."

[[Hadith 6654: Ahmad narrated it in al-Musnad: 12133 (vol. 3, p. 112, Halabi edition), from Abu Mu'awiyah, from al-A'mash, with this chain.
Then he narrated it again: 13731 (vol. 3, p. 257, Halabi edition), from Affan, from Abd al-Wahid, from Sulayman ibn Mihran, who is al-A'mash, with it.
Al-Tirmidhi narrated it, 3:199, from Hannad, from Abu Mu'awiyah, with it. Then he said: "This is a good, sound hadith. Likewise, more than one narrator related it from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from Anas. Some of them related it from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from Jabir, from the Prophet (ﷺ). The hadith of Abu Sufyan from Anas is more authentic."
Al-Tirmidhi intends to give a defect (ta'lil) to the hadith before this one. This defect is not valid. Abu Sufyan Talhah ibn Nafi' is a trustworthy Successor (tabi'i), who heard from Jabir and from Anas, and the authors of the six books related from him. A Successor often hears one hadith from two Companions.
Al-Hakim narrated it, 1:526, in abridged form, from the route of Abu Mu'awiyah, from al-A'mash, and he and al-Dhahabi authenticated it.
Ibn Majah narrated it in a longer form by another route, 3834, through Ibn Numayr, from al-A'mash, from Yazid al-Raqqashi, from Anas. Al-Busayri said in his Zawa'id: "The hadith revolves around Yazid al-Raqqashi, and he is weak."
The hafiz al-Damyati erred, as you see, in his claim that it revolves around Yazid al-Raqqashi; here it is through the narration of al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan, from Anas, like the narration of al-Raqqashi. So it is not unique to him.
Al-Bukhari combined the two routes in al-Adab al-Mufrad, p. 100. He narrated it abridged, through Abu al-Ahwas: "from al-A'mash, from Abu Sufyan and Yazid, from Anas."
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 2:8, and added its attribution to Ibn Abi Shaybah.]]
