6655. Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam told me, saying: Bishr ibn Bakr told us; and Ali ibn Sahl told me, saying: Ayyub ibn Bishr told us, both from Ibn Jabir, who said: I heard Busr ibn Ubayd Allah say: I heard Abu Idris al-Khawlani say: I heard al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an al-Kilabi say: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "There is no heart except that it is between two of the fingers of the Merciful: if He wills, He sets it upright, and if He wills, He makes it deviate." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "O Turner of hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your religion." The Scale is in the hand of the Merciful; He raises some peoples and lowers others until the Day of Resurrection.

[[Hadith 6655: Bishr ibn Bakr al-Tinnisi: trustworthy and reliable. Al-Shafi'i and al-Humaydi and others narrated from him. Al-Bukhari related from him.
Ayyub ibn Bishr: I have not found a narrator by this name, nor anything close to it in spelling, except narrators named "Ayyub ibn Bushayr," who are not of this generation and would not be in this chain. Among the narrators from Ibn Jabir is "Ayyub ibn Suwayd al-Ramli." It is very likely that his fellow townsman "Ali ibn Sahl al-Ramli" narrated from him. But the corruption (tashif) of "Suwayd" into "Bishr" is unlikely.
Ibn Jabir: he is Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir, al-Azdi al-Shami al-Darani. He is trustworthy, and the compilers related from him. Ibn al-Madini said: "He is counted in the second generation of the jurists of the people of Sham after the Companions."
Busr ibn Ubayd Allah al-Hadrami al-Shami: a trustworthy Successor. The compilers related from him. Abu Musahir said: "He is the most retentive of the students of Abu Idris," meaning al-Khawlani.
"Busr" is with a damma on the bah and sukun on the sin. His father "Ubayd Allah" is a diminutive form. In the printed edition here it reads "Bishr," and this is a corruption. This also occurred in some of the hadith sources we will mention, and in some of them his father's name is given as "Abd Allah," which is also an error. Both are to be corrected wherever they occur.
Abu Idris al-Khawlani: A'idh Allah ibn Abd Allah. His biography has already passed at 4840.
Al-Nawwas: with a fatha on the nun and a shaddah on the waw. He is a well-known Companion. The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 17707 (vol. 4, p. 182, Halabi edition), from al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Ibn Jabir, with this chain.
Ibn Majah narrated it: 199, through Sadaqah ibn Khalid, from Ibn Jabir, with it. Al-Busayri said in his Zawa'id: "Its chain is sound."
Imam al-A'immah Ibn Khuzaymah narrated it in Kitab al-Tawhid, p. 54, and Abu Bakr al-Ajurri in Kitab al-Shari'ah, pp. 317-318, both through al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Ibn Jabir.
Al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak 2:289, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, p. 248, from al-Hakim, through Muhammad ibn Shu'ayb ibn Shabur, from Ibn Jabir. Al-Hakim and al-Dhahabi authenticated it according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim).
This place in al-Mustadrak is defective in the printed original from which it was published, so the editor inserted it from al-Dhahabi's abridgment. However, the chain of this route can be derived from al-Bayhaqi's narration from al-Hakim.
Al-Hakim also narrated it, 4:321, from Abu al-Abbas al-Asamm, from Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam, the teacher of al-Tabari at the first chain here, with this chain.
He also narrated it, 1:525, from al-Asamm, from Bahr ibn Nasr, from Bishr ibn Bakr, from Ibn Jabir, with it.
Al-Hakim said in both places: "This is a sound hadith according to the conditions of Muslim!" It is strange that al-Dhahabi agreed with his authentication according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs in the route of Ibn Shabur. Ibn Shabur, although trustworthy, had nothing narrated from him in the two Sahihs. Then he agreed with his authentication according to the conditions of Muslim in the route of Bishr ibn Bakr. Al-Bukhari related from Bishr ibn Bakr, but Muslim did not narrate anything from him!!
Al-Suyuti mentioned the hadith, 2:9, and added its attribution to al-Nasa'i. He means the Sunan al-Kubra, because he did not narrate it in the Sunan al-Sughra.]]

6656. Umar ibn Abd al-Malik al-Ta'i told me, saying: Muhammad ibn Ubaydah told us, saying: al-Jarrah ibn Malih al-Bahrani told us, from al-Zubaydi, from Juwaybir, from Samurah ibn Fatik al-Asadi, who was one of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "The scales are in the hand of God; He raises some peoples and lowers others. The heart of the son of Adam is between two of the fingers of the Merciful; when He wills, He makes it deviate, and when He wills, He sets it upright."

[[Hadith 6656: Umar ibn Abd al-Malik ibn Hakim al-Ta'i al-Himsi, the teacher of al-Tabari: I have found only a brief biography of him in al-Tahdhib, which says: "al-Nasa'i narrated from him and said: Saleh (sound)."
Muhammad ibn Ubaydah: I do not know who he is, nor have I found a biography of him, except that al-Tahdhib mentions him as a teacher of Umar ibn Abd al-Malik al-Ta'i, and names him "Muhammad ibn Ubaydah, al-Maddi, al-Yamani." I find no meaning for this nisbah "al-Maddi" with two dal's. It is possible that it is a corruption of "al-Madari" with a ra', a nisbah to "Madar," with a fatha on the mim and dal and a ra' at the end, a village in Yemen, twenty miles from Sana'a, as in Mu'jam al-Buldan 7:416.
Al-Jarrah ibn Malih al-Bahrani, with a fatha on the ba' and sukun on the ha', al-Himsi: trustworthy, and well known among the people of Sham. He is different from "al-Jarrah ibn Malih ibn Adi," the father of "Waki' ibn al-Jarrah."
Al-Zubaydi, with a damma on the zay: he is Muhammad ibn al-Walid ibn Amir al-Zubaydi, Abu al-Hudhayl al-Himsi, its judge. He is trustworthy and firm. Ibn Sa'd said (7/2/169): "He was the most knowledgeable of the people of Sham in legal opinions and hadith." Al-Awza'i used to prefer Muhammad ibn al-Walid over all who heard from al-Zuhri.
Juwaybir: this is how it appears in al-Tabari. The apparent and probable view is that it is a distortion by the copyists, and Juwaybir, who is Ibn Sa'id al-Azdi, has no part in this hadith. Juwaybir is very weak, as we explained at 284. The hadith is known rather from "Jubayr ibn Nufayr," as will come.
Samurah ibn Fatik al-Asadi: thus it is established in al-Tabari as "Samurah" with a mim, which would then be vowelled with a damma on the first letter and a fatha on the sin. This is one view of his name.
The correct and preferred view is that his name is "Sabrah," with a fatha on the sin and a sukun on the ba'.
There is another Companion whose name is "Samurah ibn Fatik al-Asadi," other than this one. Likewise al-Bukhari distinguished between them in al-Tarikh al-Kabir: 2/2/188 for "Sabrah," and 178 for "Samurah." He mentioned this hadith under "Sabrah." Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim distinguished between them, 1/2/295 for "Sabrah," and 155 for "Samurah."
It has also been said of the other Companion, whose name is "Samurah," that it is "Sabrah." This is either confusion among the narrators or a corruption. The preferred view, which the hafiz confirmed in al-Isabah 3:63-64, 131-132, is that they are two, as we said, and that the narrator of this hadith is "Sabrah."
I did not dare to change what is in al-Tabari's text to the correct preferred reading "Sabrah," because the other view exists. Perhaps it occurred to him in his narration this way.
"Sabrah," as we said, has a sukun on the ba'. In the vocalization of his biography in al-Isabah there is a severe error, for the hafiz said: "with a fatha on its first letter and a kasra on its second"; no one has said this about the name "Sabrah" at all. Indeed, he himself vocalized the name "Sabrah" with a sukun on the ba' in other biographies. The name of this Companion is also vocalized with a sukun in al-Dhahabi's al-Mushtabih, p. 255. No other name with this spelling and a kasra on the ba' is mentioned. Likewise al-Hafiz did in Tabsir al-Muntabih. So what occurred in al-Isabah is only an oversight on his part, may God have mercy on him, a slip of the pen.
"Al-Asadi," in this biography, is with a fatha on the hamzah and a sukun on the sin. It is "al-Azdi." It is pronounced this way with the sin and with the zay. Abu al-Qasim stated this in the Tabaqat of Homs, as the hafiz said in al-Isabah.
This hadith was narrated by al-Bukhari in al-Kabir, in the biography of "Sabrah ibn Fatik." He said: "Haywah ibn Shurayh told us, Muhammad ibn Harb told us, from al-Zubaydi, from one who narrated to him, from Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Sabrah ibn Fatik, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: The scales are in the hand of God; He raises a people and lowers a people, and the heart of the son of Adam is between two of the fingers of the Lord, Mighty and Majestic; when He wills, He sets it upright, and when He wills, He makes it deviate."
Thus it is established through an unnamed narrator between al-Zubaydi and Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from him, as al-Bukhari narrated.
The hafiz said in al-Isabah: "It came to me in the Gharaib of Shu'bah, by Ibn Mandah, through Jubayr ibn Nufayr, from Sabrah ibn Fatik, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: The Scale is in the hand of the Merciful; He raises peoples and lowers others, the hadith. He also narrated it through another route, and said: Samurah."
We do not know whether in the narration of Ibn Mandah the unnamed man from Jubayr ibn Nufayr is present, or whether he is identified by name in it. I think that if his name were unnamed in it, the hafiz would have clarified this. It is possible that this unnamed man is "Abd al-Rahman ibn Jubayr ibn Nufayr," for he narrates from his father, and al-Zubaydi narrates from him.
What, in my view, supports that this unnamed man is mentioned by name in some narrations is that al-Haythami mentioned this hadith in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7:211, "from Samurah ibn Fatik al-Asadi," then said: "al-Tabarani narrated it, and its narrators are trustworthy."
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 2:8, and attributed it to al-Bukhari in his History, and to Ibn Jarir and al-Tabarani. He added nothing.
In the printed edition: "if He wills ... and if He wills." I have established what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the narration in al-Bukhari's al-Kabir.]]

6657. Al-Muthanna told me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr told us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us, from Haywah ibn Shurayh, who said: Abu Hani' al-Khawlani informed me that he heard Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli say: I heard Abd Allah ibn Amr ibn al-As say: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Indeed the hearts of all the sons of Adam are between two of the fingers of the Merciful, like one heart; He turns it however He wills." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O God, Turner of hearts, turn our hearts to Your obedience."

[[Hadith 6657: Abu Hani' al-Khawlani, with a fatha on the khay and a sukun on the waw: he is Humayd ibn Hani' al-Misri. He is trustworthy and well known.
Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Hubuli, with a damma on the ha' and the ba': he is Abd Allah ibn Yazid al-Ma'afiri, with a fatha on the mim and the ayn, al-Misri. He is a trustworthy Successor. He is one of the ten Successors whom Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz dispatched to teach the people of Ifriqiyah their religion. See the book Riyad al-Nufus by Abu Bakr al-Maliki, vol. 1, pp. 64-65, and Tabaqat Ulama Ifriqiyah by Abu al-Arab, p. 21.
The hadith was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad: 6569, from Abu Abd al-Rahman, who is al-Muqri', from Haywah ibn Shurayh, with this chain.
Muslim narrated it, 2:301, from Zuhayr ibn Harb and Ibn Numayr, both from Abu Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri'.
Abu Bakr al-Ajurri narrated it in Kitab al-Shari'ah, p. 316, by two chains, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, p. 248, both through al-Muqri'.
Al-Suyuti mentioned it, 2:9, and added its attribution to al-Nasa'i.]]

6658. Al-Rabi' ibn Sulayman told us, saying: Asad ibn Musa told us, saying: Abd al-Hamid ibn Bahram told us, saying: Shahr ibn Hawshab told us, who said: I heard Umm Salamah narrate that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to often say in his supplication: "O God, make my heart firm upon Your religion." She said: I said: "O Messenger of God, do hearts indeed turn?" He said: "Yes. There is no creature of God among the sons of Adam, no human being, except that his heart is between two of the fingers of God. If He wills, He sets it upright, and if He wills, He makes it deviate. So we ask God, our Lord, that He not make our hearts deviate after He has guided us, and we ask Him to grant us mercy from Him; indeed He is the Bestower."

[[Hadith 6658: It is an abridgment of the hadith 6652. I have given its takhrij there, and pointed to this there.
In the manuscript and the printed edition here it reads: "min bani Adam bashar" (among the sons of Adam, a human being). It is likely that the better reading is "min bashar" (of a human being), as in the other narrations.]]

The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 3, verses 7–8 (part 1 of 7):

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), they are the mother of the Book, and others that are allegorical (mutashabihat)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His praise, "It is He who has sent down to you the Book," meaning that God, from whom nothing on earth or in heaven is hidden, is the One who has sent down to you the Book. By "the Book" He means the Qur'an.

* *

We have already explained earlier the reason why the Qur'an is called "a Book," so there is no need to repeat it here. [[See what has preceded, 1:99, then 3:86, and the language indexes.]]

* *

As for His saying, "in it are verses that are decisive," it means: from the Book there are verses. By "verses" He means the verses of the Qur'an.

As for "decisive" (muhkamat), these are the verses that have been made firm through clear explanation and detail, and whose proofs and arguments have been established for what they were made into evidence for: lawful and unlawful, promise and warning, reward and punishment, command and prohibition, report and parable, admonition and lessons, and what is similar to these.

* *

Then, exalted is His praise, He described these "decisive verses" as being: "they are the mother of the Book." He means by this that they are the foundation of the Book, in which are the pillars of the religion, the obligations and the prescribed limits, and all else that people need in matters of their religion, and the obligations imposed upon them in this world and the next.

* *

He called them "the mother of the Book" only because they are the principal part of the Book and the place to which its people turn when they need it. The Arabs do likewise: they call whatever gathers and unifies a thing its "mother." Thus the banner of a people that gathers them in the armies is called "their mother," and the one who manages the principal affairs of a village or town is called "its mother."

We have already explained this earlier in a way that suffices without repetition. [[See what has preceded, 1:107–108.]]

* *

He made "the mother of the Book" singular and did not pluralize it, saying "mothers of the Book," although He said "they" (hunna). This is because He meant that all the decisive verses together are "the mother of the Book," not that each verse of them is "the mother of the Book." Had the meaning been that each verse of them is "the mother of the Book," it would undoubtedly have been said: "they are the mothers of the Book." A parallel to God's saying, "they are the mother of the Book," in the interpretation we have given regarding the singular "mother," where it is the predicate of "they," is His saying, may He be remembered: ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾ [Surah al-Mu'minun: 50], and He did not say "two signs," because the meaning is: We made both of them together one sign, since their meaning was one in that they were made a lesson for people. Had the meaning been to report about each of them separately, that He made each a lesson for people, it would have been said: "We made the son of Mary and his mother two signs," for each of them had a lesson for them. That is because Mary bore a child without a man, and her son spoke, speaking as a child in the cradle, so that in each of them there was a sign for the people. [[In the printed edition: "if the meaning was one and their two [states]..." which is meaningless; the copyist of the manuscript misread it, as the final alif in "wāḥidan" fell at the position of the fa' of "fīmā" unpointed, so he took it as "wa-ihdāhumā" and changed "ja'alā" into "ja'alnā." And "if its meaning was the report..." is the correct reading from the manuscript.]]

* *

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: "they are the mother of the Book" was said, and not "they are the mothers of the Book," in the manner of quotation (ḥikāyah), as a man says, "I have no helpers (anṣār)," and you reply, "I am your helper (anṣāruka)," or "I have no equal (naẓīr)," and you reply, "we are your equal (naẓīruka)." [[Perhaps the correct reading is: "I have no helper (naṣīr)," and you reply, "we are your helper (naṣīruka)." What is in the printed edition and the manuscript is undoubtedly correct.]] He said: It is similar to "leave me alone regarding two dates (damratān)," and he recited for a man of the Fuq'as tribe: [[He is Manzur ibn Murthid ibn Farwa al-Fuq'asi al-Asadi. It is also said: "Manzur ibn Farwa ibn Murthid," and he is the same as "Manzur ibn Hubbah al-Fuq'asi al-Asadi," "Hubbah" being his mother, by whom he was known.]]

She presented herself to me at a place of halting (ḥall),
like a mare presenting herself at the grazing-tether (ṭawal),
a presenting that did not fall short in slaying me.

[[Majalis of Tha'lab: 602 (many verses of this rajaz), and Sharh Shawahid al-Shafiyah: 248–251, and Sirr Sina'at al-I'rab (the science of grammatical inflection) 1:177–179, then 235, and Lisan al-Arab under (ṭawal), (qatal), and elsewhere. In the Majalis of Tha'lab, the version of the first verse is "bi-majāz ḥall," and the last is "'an qatlalī," and there is no evidence in this version. Lisan al-Arab mentions the variation in its transmission. "Ṭawal" (with a kasra on the ṭa', and a fatḥa on the waw and an unshaddated lam, as in the rajaz) is the mountain that is tethered for the animal so it can graze in it; the poet only doubled the letter. Lam ta'al: did not fall short. The pronoun in this poem refers to his beloved, about whom he says before these verses: "Who will I have from the separation of Layla? Who will I have? ... and the cord of her union that has come undone?"]] "ḥall," meaning: he alights at it. [[In the printed edition: "kull, meaning: it is recounted by way of quotation," which is corrupt speech. But how strange it is for the one who wanted to correct it to say: "Perhaps its original is, as is understood from the context: he did not say 'from slaying,' and he brought it in quotation." He wanted to correct it but repeated the words, which is the most absurd. However, the reader who copied from the manuscript did not read its text well, and he corrupted it badly; but it is clear as I have written it from the manuscript's script.
As for his saying "bi-makān ḥall," it is vocalized in pen in Lisan al-Arab and in Majalis of Tha'lab with tanwin on "makān" and "majāz," and kasra on the ḥā' of "ḥall." I do not think this is correct, for I have not found them saying "makān ḥall" with a kasra on the ḥā'; rather it is with a fatḥa on it, as an annexed construction and not as an adjective: "ḥalla bi-l-makān ḥulūlan wa-ḥallan," meaning: he alighted at it.
As for his saying "on quotation" in the context of his saying "and he recited for a man of the Fuq'as...."]] — "on quotation," because it was in the accusative before that, as one says: "The prayer was called, 'the prayer, the prayer!'" quoting the speaker who said: "The prayer, the prayer!"

He said: Some of them said: it is in fact "an qatlā lī," but he took it as "'an," because "an" in his dialect takes "'an" in its place, and the accusative is by way of command, as if you had said: "a striking for Zayd."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This is a view that has no meaning. For all these examples which he cited are undoubtedly quotations by those who quote them, of what was reported from the words of another and the utterances he spoke; and it is known that God, exalted is His praise, did not quote from anyone his saying "mother of the Book," so that it could be said that He brought it out in the manner of quoting one who said it thus. [[In the manuscript: "brought it out in the place of quotation," and the pure correct reading seems to be what is in the printed edition. This is a distortion from the haste of the copyist, who wanted to write "makhraj," then the pen added a lam, then he reviewed a rā', then dropped the jīm.]]

* *

As for His saying "wa-ukhar" (and others): it is the plural of "ukhrā" [feminine of "other"]. [[See what has preceded, 3:459. In the printed edition: "plural of ākhar," and in the manuscript, without a madda on the alif; I preferred that it be "ukhrā," due to what has passed in his words on that and what will come shortly after, and because it is the analogy.]]

* *

Then the grammarians differed about the reason why "ukhar" was not declined (ṣarf).

Some of them said: "ukhar" was not declined because it is an adjective (na't), its singular being "ukhrā," just as "jumaʿ" and "kutaʿ" were not declined, because they are adjectives.

* *

Others said: "ukhar" was not declined because of the extra yā' that is in its singular, and because its plural is built on its singular in not taking declension. They said: "ukhrā" was not declined just as "ḥamrā'" and "bayḍā'" were not declined, in indefinite and definite forms, because of the added long vowel in them and the hamza in place of a waw. [[I have left his phrase "with the waw" as it is, for I was not able to determine its addition, nor did I know what he meant by it, except that he meant the shortened feminine alif, like the one in "ḥublā." And "ukhrā" has the extended feminine alif.]] Then the plural of "ḥamrā'" and "ukhrā" diverged: the plural of "ukhrā" was built on its singular, so it became "fuʿal" and "ukhar," [[What seems more likely to me is that his saying "fuʿal" is an addition by the copyist.]] so its non-declension was kept as the non-declension of "ukhrā"; and the plural of "ḥamrā'" and "bayḍā'" was built against its singular, so it was declined, becoming "ḥumr" and "bayḍ." So because their states differ in the plural, their inflection differed for them in declension. And because their states agree in the singular, their states agreed in it.

* *

As for His saying "mutashābihāt" (allegorical), its meaning: alike in recitation, different in meaning, as He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿And they were given it in semblance﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 25], meaning alike in appearance, different in taste. [[See what has preceded, 1:385–394.]] And as He said, reporting about those among the Children of Israel who said: ﴿Indeed, the cows have become confusing to us﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 70], meaning by that: they have become confusing to us in description, though their kinds differ. [[See what has preceded, 2:209–211.]]

* *

The meaning of the statement, then, is: He who nothing on earth or in heaven escapes, is the One who has sent down to you, O Muhammad, the Qur'an; in it are verses that are decisive by clear explanation, which are the foundation of the Book upon which your pillar and the pillar of your community in religion rest, and to which your recourse and theirs is directed in what He has made obligatory upon you and them of the laws of Islam; and other verses, which are alike in recitation and different in meanings.

* *

The interpreters have differed regarding the interpretation of His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book, and others that are allegorical," and what is the decisive (muhkam) of the verses of the Book, and what is the allegorical (mutashābih) of it?

Some of them said: the "decisive" verses of the Qur'an are those acted upon, and they are the abrogating (nāsikhāt) or those that establish rulings; and the "allegorical" verses are those whose practice has been abandoned, the abrogated (mansūkhāt).

Those who said this:

6573 – Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: al-Awwam informed us, from one who related to him, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive." He said: They are the three verses from here: ﴿Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 151–152], to three verses more, [[In the printed edition: "that are here," which is an error, for the verses, as you see, are from Surah al-An'am. I have confirmed what is in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:4. See the takhrij at the end of the report.]] and the one in "Banu Isra'il": ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 23–39], to the end of the verses. [[The report 6573: this is its chain as it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition. I fear that something may have dropped from its chain, "from Abu Ishaq," after "qāla akhbaranā al-Awwām." "Al-Awwām" is al-Awwām ibn Hawshab, who narrates from Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i. As for his saying in the chain "from one who related to him," that is so, because the one from whom Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i narrated is "Abd Allah ibn Qays," who is mentioned as narrating this report, and the one who narrates from him is Abu Ishaq al-Subay'i, and no one is known to have narrated from him except Abu Ishaq. (Tahdhib al-Tahdhib 5:365.) This same report was narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:288 through the route: "Ali ibn Salih ibn Hayy, from Abu Ishaq, from Abd Allah ibn Qays, from Ibn Abbas." Its text: "Decisive verses: they are those in al-An'am: Say: Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden—to the end of the three verses." Al-Hakim said: "Sahih," and al-Dhahabi agreed. For this reason I feared that "from Abu Ishaq" had dropped from al-Tabari's chain, but I did not record it in his text.]]

6574 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih related to us, from Ali ibn Abi Talha, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." The decisive: its abrogating, its lawful and unlawful, its limits and its obligations, and what is believed in and acted upon. He said: "And others that are allegorical": the abrogated, its earlier and later parts, its parables and its divisions, and what is believed in but not acted upon.

6575 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: my father related to me, saying: my paternal uncle related to me, saying: my father related to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His saying: "It is He who has sent down to you the Book," to "and others that are allegorical": the decisive ones, which are the mother of the Book, are the abrogating, by which one is religiously bound and acts. The allegorical are the abrogated, by which one is not religiously bound.

6576 – Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas; and from Murrah al-Hamadani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet (ﷺ): "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book," to His saying: "all is from our Lord." As for the decisive verses, they are the abrogating ones by which one acts; and as for the allegorical ones, they are the abrogated.

6577 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." The "decisive" is the abrogating by which one acts, in which God made lawful what is lawful and forbade what is unlawful. As for the "allegorical," it is the abrogated, which is not acted upon but is believed in.

6578 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "decisive verses." He said: the decisive is what is acted upon.

6579 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "It is He who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book, and others that are allegorical." He said: "The decisive": the abrogating by which one acts. And "the allegorical": the abrogated, which is not acted upon but is believed in.

6580 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: "verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." He said: the abrogating. "And others that are allegorical": he said: what has been abrogated and left, which is recited.

6581 – Ibn Wakī' related to me, saying: my father related to us, from Salamah ibn Nubayt, from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, who said: The decisive is what has not been abrogated, and what is allegorical in it is what has been abrogated.

6582 – Yahya ibn Abi Talib related to me, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak regarding His saying: "verses that are decisive, they are the mother of the Book." He said: the abrogating. "And others that are allegorical": he said: the abrogated.

6583 – It was related to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh relate, saying: Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive": meaning the abrogating by which one acts. "And others that are allegorical": meaning the abrogated, which is believed in but not acted upon.

6584 – Ahmad ibn Hazim related to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from al-Dahhak: "In it are verses that are decisive": he said: what has not been abrogated. "And others that are allegorical": he said: what has been abrogated.

* *

Others said: the "decisive" verses of the Book are those in which God has made clear the explanation of its lawful and unlawful; and the "allegorical" among them are those whose parts resemble one another in meaning, though their wordings differ.

Those who said this:

6585 – Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu Asim related to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "In it are verses that are decisive": what is in it of the lawful and unlawful; and whatever else is apart from that is "allegorical," confirming one another. It is like His saying: ﴿And He leads none astray thereby except the defiantly disobedient﴾ [Surah al-Baqarah: 26], and like His saying: ﴿Thus does God place defilement upon those who do not believe﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 125], and like His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance and gives them their piety﴾ [Surah Muhammad: 17].

6586 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

Others said: the "decisive" verses of the Book are those that admit of only one interpretation; and the "allegorical" among them are those that admit of several interpretations.

Those who said this:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 7–8 (part 2 of 7):

6587 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr related to me concerning "He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat)": they contain the proof of the Lord, the protection of the servants, and the repelling of adversaries and falsehood; there is no altering or distorting them from what they were established upon = [In the text of Ibn Hisham: "there is no altering of them ... from what they were placed upon."] "and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)", in truthfulness [In the printed edition: "and others that are ambiguous," and the correct reading is from the manuscript and Ibn Hisham. The phrase "in truthfulness" is not in the text of Ibn Hisham, but it is present in the manuscript.], they admit of alteration, distortion and interpretation; God tested His servants by them, as He tested them with the lawful and the unlawful; they are not turned to falsehood nor distorted away from truth. [The report 6587 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is 6571, transmitted by him from Ibn Ishaq.]
* *
Others said: The meaning of "the decisive (muhkam)" is what God has made firm in it of the verses of the Qur'an, and the narratives of the nations and their messengers who were sent to them, which He detailed by clarifying that for Muhammad and his community. "And the ambiguous (mutashabih)" is what the wording has made ambiguous of their narratives when repeated in the surahs, by relating them with the agreement of wording and the difference of meanings, and by relating them with the difference of wording and the agreement of meanings. [In the printed edition: "so the narrative of the agreement of wording ... and the narrative with difference of wording ..." which is corrupt; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]
Mention of those who said this:
6588 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, and he recited: "Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm and then detailed from One Wise and Acquainted" [Surah Hud: 1], and he said: He mentioned the account of the Messenger of God ﷺ in twenty-four verses of it: [That is, of Surah Hud; this enumeration that follows is in the order of the codex.] and the account of Noah in twenty-four verses of it. Then he said: "That is from the news of the unseen" [Surah Hud: 49], then he mentioned "And to 'Ad" and recited until he reached "and seek forgiveness of your Lord" [[It seems he means that he recited until he reached this verse of Surah Hud: 89. But this verse is in the account of Shu'ayb, peace be upon him, so I do not know what he said after: "then he proceeded, then he mentioned Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb". My guess is that the text of his statement is: "then he proceeded. He mentioned Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb ..." with the second "then" dropped. See the following note.]] Then he proceeded. Then he mentioned Salih, Abraham, Lot and Shu'ayb and finished with that. This is the clarification of that, the clarification of "whose verses have been made firm and then detailed" = [In the printed edition and manuscript: "this is certainty of that, certainty of ..." and it seems the correct reading is what I have set down.
Moreover, I did not find this report elsewhere, but I found al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 3: 320, in the tafsir of "Surat Hud", saying: "Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Ibn Zayd, may God be pleased with him, that he recited: 'Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been made firm' and said: they are all Meccan and firm, meaning Surat Hud, 'and then detailed.' He said: Then he mentioned Muhammad ﷺ, and judged between him and those who opposed him, and recited: 'The likeness of the two parties', the whole verse. Then he mentioned the people of Noah, then the people of Hud, and this was the detailing of that, and its beginning was firm. He said: My father, may God be pleased with him, used to say that - meaning: Zayd ibn Aslam."
Therefore, I preferred the correction mentioned earlier in the previous note, and I preferred that "yaqin" in both places be "tabyin".] He said: The ambiguous is the mention of Moses in many places, and it is ambiguous, and it is all one meaning. And ambiguous: "then take her (fa-uslukh) therein" [and] "carry therein" (uhmil fiha), "insert your hand" (usluk yadaka), "enter your hand" (adkhil yadaka), "a serpent moving swiftly" (hayyatan tas'a), "a manifest serpent" (thu'ban mubin) = [From his words "He said: The ambiguous ..." it is an interjection within his discussion of the detailing of the narratives in "Surat Hud" and the enumeration of the verses of each narrative. As for the verses mentioned here, this is the explanation of their places in order: "Surat al-Mu'minun: 27" / "Surat Hud: 40" / "Surat al-Qasas: 32" / "Surat al-Naml: 12" / "Surat Ta Ha: 20" / "Surat al-A'raf: 107" and "Surat al-Shu'ara: 22."] He said: Then he mentioned Hud in ten verses of it, [Salih in eight verses of it, Abraham in eight other verses, Lot in eight verses of it, Shu'ayb in thirteen verses, and Moses in four verses; all of this judges between the prophets and their peoples in this surah. That amounted to one hundred verses of Surat Hud.] Then he said: "That is from the news of the towns which We relate to you; some of them are standing and some are harvested" [Surah Hud: 100]. And he said concerning the ambiguous in the Qur'an: whoever God intends with trial and misguidance says: "What is the matter with this that it is not so? What is the matter with this that it is not so?"
* *
Others said: Rather, the "decisive (muhkam)" of the verses of the Qur'an is what the scholars know the interpretation of, and understand its meaning and explanation; and the "ambiguous (mutashabih)" is what no one has any way to know, of what God has kept the knowledge of to Himself apart from His creatures, such as the report on the time of the coming forth of Jesus son of Mary, the time of the sun rising from the west, the establishment of the Hour, the end of the world, and what is similar to that, for no one knows that. They said: God has named "the ambiguous" among the verses of the Book the disjointed letters found at the beginnings of some surahs of the Qur'an, such as "Alif Lam Mim", "Alif Lam Mim Sad", "Alif Lam Mim Ra", "Alif Lam Ra", and what is similar to these, because they are ambiguous in wording and agree with the letters of abjad reckoning. Some Jews in the time of the Messenger of God ﷺ hoped to learn from them the knowledge of the duration of Islam and its people, and to know the end of the lifespan of Muhammad and his community [In the printed edition: "the term of his community," which is a misreading by the printer; I have kept what is in the manuscript: al-akl (with a vowel on the first letter and a sukun): the span of life; see the note on p. 196, note 1.], so God refuted their hope in that and informed them that what they sought to know of that through these ambiguous letters they would not reach, nor through anything else, and that this is known only to God.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This is a saying reported from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Ri'ab [In the printed edition: "ibn Rabab," which is an error; the correct reading is what I have set down, and "Ri'ab" with a kasra on the ra. See what preceded at 1: 216 and what will come in note 4, where the reference is.] that this verse was revealed concerning him [the word "him" refers to this saying, not to "Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah"]; and we have mentioned the report of that from him and from others who said similarly, in the interpretation of that in the tafsir of God's words: "Alif Lam Mim. That is the Book; there is no doubt in it" [Surah al-Baqarah: 2].
* *
Abu Ja'far said: This saying we have mentioned from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah is closer to the interpretation of the verse. That is because all that God the Mighty and Majestic has sent down of the verses of the Qur'an upon His Messenger ﷺ, He sent down only as a clarification for him and his community and as guidance for the worlds; and it is not permissible that there be in it what they have no need of, nor that there be in it what they need and then there is no way for them to know its interpretation. Since that is so, then everything in it that the creatures need [In the printed edition: "for His creatures," and in the manuscript: "muhlaqihi," the first letter appearing as an obliterated mim; the correct reading is what I have set down.], even if in some of it there is what they are independent of regarding some of its meanings = [and if the need compels them to it in many meanings] [This sentence between the parentheses appears thus in the printed edition, and similarly in the manuscript, though the word "idtarrathu" is written without dots. It is a sentence whose meaning is not clear, and I fear that the copyist may have omitted lines from this place, so the speech became confused for us and for him! Dropping this sentence from the context does no harm. But I have left it as it is, placed it between brackets, and enclosed it between lines, so that its place and the place of the omission, which I judged to be an oversight by the copyist, may be known.] = such as the saying of God the Mighty and Majestic: "On the day when some of the signs of your Lord come, faith will not benefit a soul that did not believe before, or earn good through its faith" [Surah al-An'am: 158]. So the Prophet ﷺ informed his community that the sign which God, may His praise be exalted, informed His servants that when it comes faith will not benefit a soul that had not believed before it, is the rising of the sun from the west. [See the detail of that and its reason in the interpretation of the verse in the Tafsir of al-Tabari 8: 71-77 (Bulaq).] So what the servants needed of knowledge of that is their knowledge of the time when repentance benefits, by its description, without limiting it by a number of years, months or days. [In the printed edition: "after by the years ...", and in the manuscript: "after the years ...", and it is clear that the copyist dropped the second dal from "bi-'adad".] God has clarified that to them through the evidence of the Book, and made it clear to them through His Messenger ﷺ, explained. As for what they have no need to know of it, [In the printed edition: "there is no need for them" with a lam, and I have kept the correct reading from the manuscript.] it is the knowledge of the length of the period between the time of the revelation of this verse and the time of the occurrence of that sign, for that is something they have no need to know in religion or in worldly life. That is the knowledge which God, may His praise be exalted, has kept to Himself apart from His creatures, and withheld from them. That, and what is similar to it, is the meaning which the Jews sought to know regarding the duration of Muhammad ﷺ and his community, by means of His saying "Alif Lam Mim", "Alif Lam Mim Sad", "Alif Lam Ra", "Alif Lam Mim Ra" and similar disjointed letters, the ambiguous ones, of which God, may His praise be exalted, informed that they would not grasp the interpretation before it, and that its interpretation is known only to God.
Since the ambiguous is what we have described, then everything else is decisive. For it cannot be free of either being decisive in that it has one meaning with no interpretation other than one interpretation, and it has become sufficient by hearing it without need of an explanation that clarifies it [In the printed edition and manuscript "mubayyanah," but the mim in the manuscript does not look like a mim, and the correct reading of the text is what I have set down]; or it is decisive, even though it has many aspects and interpretations and variation in many meanings. The indication of the meaning intended by it is either from God's clarification, may He be remembered, concerning it, or from the clarification of His Messenger ﷺ to his community. And the knowledge of that will not be lost to the scholars of the community, for what we have already explained.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: "They are the mother of the Book" [Surah Ali 'Imran: 7]
Abu Ja'far said: We have already given the explanation of the interpretation of that with the evidence attesting to the soundness of what we have said about it. [See what preceded shortly: 170.] We will now mention the differences of the people of interpretation concerning it, for they differed in its interpretation.
Some of them said: The meaning of His saying "they are the mother of the Book" is: they are those in which are the obligations, the limits and the rulings, like what we have said about it.
Mention of those who said that:
6589 - Imran ibn Musa al-Qazzaz related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd related to us, from Yahya ibn Ya'mur, that he said concerning this verse: "They are the decisive, the mother of the Book." Yahya said: They are those in which are the obligations and the limits and the pillar of religion; and he struck an example for that, saying: "The mother of the cities" is Mecca, "the mother of Khurasan" is Merv, and "the mother of travellers" is the one to whom they entrust their affairs and who looks after them on their journey; he said: That one is their mother. [The report 6589: "Imran ibn Musa al-Farra" and "Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id" whose biographies have passed under number 2154. See the note on the report number 6591, next.]
6590 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying "they are the mother of the Book": they are the sum of the Book.
* *
Others said: Rather, what is meant by that is: the opening surahs from which the Qur'an is derived.
Mention of those who said that:
6591 - Imran ibn Musa related to us, saying: Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Suwayd related to us, from Abu Fakhitah, that he said concerning this verse: "Of it are decisive verses; they are the mother of the Book": "the mother of the Book" are the openings of the surahs, from which the Qur'an is derived - "Alif Lam Mim. That is the Book", from it "al-Baqarah" was derived, and "Alif Lam Mim. Allah, there is no god but He" from it "Al 'Imran" was derived. [The report 6591: "Abu Fakhitah" is Sa'id ibn 'Alaqah al-Hashimi, mawla of Umm Hani, a trustworthy narrator whose biography is in al-Tahdhib. See the preceding report number 6589. Al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 4 narrated them as one abridged report and said: "From Ishaq ibn Suwayd that Yahya ibn Ya'mur and Abu Fakhitah debated this verse: 'they are the mother of the Book'; Abu Fakhitah said ... and Yahya ibn Ya'mur said ..." and he gave what is in these two reports in abridged form.]
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation"
Abu Ja'far said: God, may His praise be exalted, means by that: As for those in whose hearts is inclination away from the truth and deviation from it.
* *
It is said from it: "Such-and-such deviated from the truth, so he deviates from it, deviation, deviating, and deviation (zaygh), and he caused deviation (az-agahu Allah)" when He inclines him, "so He inclines him (yuzighuhu)." And from it is His saying, may His praise be exalted: "Our Lord, do not let our hearts deviate after You have guided us" [Surah Ali 'Imran: 8]: do not incline them away from the truth.
* *
Those of the people of interpretation said in accordance with what we have said regarding that:
Mention of those who said that:
6592 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to me, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation": i.e., inclination away from guidance. [The report 6592: it is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6587, from Ibn Ishaq.]
6593 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning God's saying "in whose hearts is deviation": he said: doubt.
6594 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.
6595 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih related to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn 'Abbas: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," he said: from the people of doubt.
6596 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, in a report he mentioned from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas = and from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some companions of the Prophet ﷺ: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," as for deviation, it is doubt.
6597 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid: he said: "zaygh" is doubt = Ibn Juraij said: "Those in whose hearts is deviation" are the hypocrites.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: "So they follow that of it which is ambiguous"
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous," is meant: what its wordings are ambiguous and its meanings are varied through aspects of interpretation, so that they may confirm, through their claim of falsehoods of interpretations regarding it, the deviation and inclination from the path of truth which they are upon, a deception on their part through it upon whoever's knowledge of the aspects of its interpretation and the variation of its meanings is weak, as:
6598 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas: "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous": they impose the decisive upon the ambiguous, and the ambiguous upon the decisive, and they deceive, and God deceives them.
6599 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous," i.e., what is distorted from it and turned, [In Ibn Hisham: "i.e., what is turned from it," with no "distorted."] so that they may confirm by it what they invented and innovated, so that it would be a proof for them for what they said and a doubt. [The report 6599 is the remainder of the preceding reports, the last of which is number 6592, by his isnad from Ibn Ishaq. The text in Ibn Hisham's Sirah 2: 226 is: "so that it would be a proof for them, and for them a doubt about what they said."
I have left what is in the tafsir here as it is, because his transmission from Ibn Ishaq differs from the transmission of Ibn Hisham.]
6600 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Juraij, from Mujahid concerning His saying: "so they follow that of it which is ambiguous," he said: the door through which they went astray and perished, seeking its interpretation.
* *
Others said regarding that, with what:

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 7–8 (part 3 of 7):

6601 - Muhammad ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning His words: "So they follow that which is ambiguous of it" (﴿فَيَتَّبِعُونَ مَا تَشَابَهَ مِنْهُ﴾), that they follow the abrogated (al-mansukh) and the abrogating (al-nasikh), saying: "What is the matter with this verse, which is acted upon in such-and-such a way, alongside this verse? [[In the printed edition: "majaz hadhihi al-ayah" (the meaning of this verse); the manuscript is unclear, and I have preferred reading it as "makan".]] The first was left and this other one was acted upon? Would it not have been the case that acting upon this verse came before the first one, which was abrogated arrived? And what is the matter with it that it promises punishment to whoever does a deed that punishes him [in] the Fire, and in another place: whoever does it, it has not made the Fire obligatory?"
* *
The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning who is meant by this verse.
Some of them said: It refers to the delegation of the Christians of Najran who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and disputed with him with what they disputed with him, and argued with him by saying: "Do you not claim that Jesus is the Spirit of Allah and His Word?" And they interpreted in that regard what they say about it of disbelief.
Mention of those who said that:
6602 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: They intended — meaning the delegation who came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Christians of Najran — and argued with the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "Do you not claim that he is the Word of Allah and a Spirit from Him?" He said: "Yes!" They said: "Then it is enough for us!" So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord," then Allah, His praise be exalted, revealed: ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with Allah is like the likeness of Adam﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 59], the verse.
* *
Others said: Rather, this verse was revealed concerning Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab, and his brother Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and the group who debated with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning the measure of the duration of his nation's lifespan and the lifespan of his community, [[In the printed edition: "ajalahu wa ajal ummatihi"; see the explanation of "al-akl" above, p. 180, note 1.]] and they wanted to know that from his saying: "Alif Lam Mim," "Alif Lam Mim Sad," "Alif Lam Ra," and "Alif Lam Ra." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said concerning them: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation" — meaning these Jews whose hearts are inclined away from guidance and truth — "they follow that which is ambiguous of it," meaning: the meanings of these disjointed letters which admit of varied inflection and different interpretations, "seeking discord."
We have already mentioned the report concerning this earlier, at the beginning of the surah in which "al-Baqarah" is mentioned. [[See the earlier report, no. 246.]]
* *
Others said: Rather, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, meant by this every innovator in his religion who introduces an innovation opposing what His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) was sent with, by an interpretation he interprets from some verses of the Qur'an that admit of interpretations, even though Allah has made clear the explanation of that, either in His Book or on the tongue of His Messenger.
Mention of those who said that:
6603 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord." Qatadah, whenever he recited this verse, "As for those in whose hearts is deviation," would say: "If they are not the Haruriyyah and the Sabaiyyah, [["al-HarurIyyah" are the Kharijites, who gathered at Harura on the outskirts of Kufa; their first gathering there and their arbitration occurred when they opposed Ali. As for "al-Sabaiyyah," they are attributed to Ibn al-Sawda', the Jew "Abdullah ibn Saba'," who said to Ali: "You are you," meaning that the Imam has a divine portion, exalted is Allah far above that, so Ali exiled him to al-Mada'in. The manuscript has "al-Sabaiyyah," and the printed edition has "al-Sabi'iyyah"; I have preferred the manuscript's reading because it is so in most books.]] then I do not know who they are! By my life, among the people of Badr and al-Hudaybiyah who witnessed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) the Pledge of Ridwan, from the Emigrants and the Helpers, there is a lesson for whoever seeks information, and a warning for whoever takes heed, for whoever has understanding or sight. [[This refers to the lesson of Badr, when his companions advised the Messenger of Allah to leave the first position he had taken for the position they advised him toward, and the lesson of al-Hudaybiyah, when some of the companions of the Pledge of Ridwan said what they said in disliking the treaty the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concluded between himself and Quraysh. In this is proof of the corruption of the doctrine of the Kharijites and the doctrine of the Sabaiyyah.]] The Kharijites went out, and the companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at that time were numerous in Medina, Syria and Iraq, and his wives were alive at that time. By Allah, not a single male or female among them ever became a Harurite, nor did they approve of what they were upon, nor did they support them in it; rather, they would narrate the defect of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in regard to them and the description with which he described them, and they hated them in their hearts and opposed them with their tongues, and by Allah their hands were harsh upon them when they met them. By my life, if the matter of the Kharijites were guidance, it would have gathered together, but it was misguidance, so it scattered. Likewise, when a matter is from other than Allah, you will find much disagreement in it. They have been trying to manage this matter for a long time. [[Alaṣa al-amr: he managed it and attempted it. Alaṣa fulanan 'ala hadha al-amr: he steered him toward the thing he wanted.]] Have they ever succeeded in it, or prospered? Glory be to Allah! How does the last of these people not take heed from the first of them? If they were upon guidance, Allah would have made it manifest, granted it victory and supported it, [[In the printed edition: "aflahahu" with a non-dotted ha; in the manuscript it is undotted, and the correct reading is with jim: aflaja Allah hujjatahu, meaning He made his proof manifest and gave him victory, i.e., success and triumph.]] but they were upon falsehood, which Allah refuted and crushed. So they are as you have seen them: whenever a generation of them emerges, Allah refutes their argument, exposes their claims, and sheds their blood. If they conceal it, it is a wound in their hearts and a grief upon them; and if they make it manifest, Allah sheds their blood. That, by Allah, is an evil religion, so avoid it. By Allah, Judaism is an innovation, Christianity is an innovation, the Harurites are an innovation, and the Sabaiyyah are an innovation; no Book has been sent down with them and no Prophet has laid them down as a tradition.
6604 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation." The people sought the interpretation, erred in the interpretation, and attained the discord, so they followed what was ambiguous of it, and thereby they perished. By my life, among the companions of Badr and al-Hudaybiyah who witnessed the Pledge of Ridwan... and he mentioned something similar to the report of Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from him.
6605 - Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash and Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, both saying: Isma'il ibn Ulayyah related to us, from Ayyub, from Abdullah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book" up to His words: "And none will take heed except those of understanding," and then said: "When you see those who dispute about it, they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." [[The hadith: 6605 — al-Tabari narrated this hadith here through eleven chains, all from the narration of Ibn Abi Mulaykah, except one, which is hadith 6611. The narrators differed on Ibn Abi Mulaykah: some narrate it from him directly from Aisha, and some narrate it from him from al-Qasim from Aisha. Both are authentic, as will come.
Ibn Abi Mulaykah is Abdullah ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abdullah ibn Abi Mulaykah al-Qurashi al-Makki, a major, trustworthy Successor (tabi'i) who heard Aisha and others of the Companions. Al-Bukhari recorded his biography in al-Saghir, p. 131; Ibn Sa'd 5:347-348; Ibn Abi Hatim 2/2/99-100; and al-Mus'ab in Nasab Quraysh, p. 293.
Al-Tirmidhi said (4:80), after narrating the hadith through both routes, as will come: "Thus many narrated this hadith from Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Aisha, and they did not mention in it: from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad. Rather, Yazid ibn Ibrahim mentioned it from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad in this hadith. And Ibn Abi Mulaykah is Abdullah ibn Ubayd Allah ibn Abi Mulaykah, and he also heard from Aisha."
Yazid ibn Ibrahim did not alone mention "al-Qasim" in the chain, as al-Tirmidhi claimed. The clarification of that will come, Allah willing.
Al-Hafiz said in Fath al-Bari (8:157): "Ibn Abi Mulaykah heard much from Aisha, and an intermediary often enters between them. And it has been differed upon concerning him in this hadith..."
The hadith, from this route, through Ibn Ulayyah from Ayyub, was narrated by Ahmad in al-Musnad (6:48, Halabi) from Ibn Ulayyah with this chain. Likewise Ibn Majah (47) narrated it from Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash — the shaykh of al-Tabari here — from Ibn Ulayyah, with it.
This Muhammad ibn Khalid ibn Khidash is biographed in al-Tahdhib, which says: "Ibn Hibban mentioned him among the trustworthy, and said: he sometimes related strange reports from his father."
Ibn Abi Hatim did not record his biography, nor did al-Khatib mention him in Tarikh Baghdad, although he resided there, as in al-Tahdhib.
Ibn Kathir (2:97) mentioned the hadith according to the Musnad narration, then said: "Thus this hadith occurs in the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from the narration of Ibn Abi Mulaykah from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, without anyone between them." Then he pointed to Ibn Majah's narration and other narrations which will be mentioned later.
But "Ya'qub" occurs in Ibn Kathir instead of "Ayyub"! This is a copyist's or printer's error. In the Musnad it is correctly "Ayyub".]]
6606 - Ibn Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman related to us, saying: I heard Ayyub, from Abdullah ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, that she said: The Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book" up to "And none will take heed except those of understanding." She said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who dispute about it — or he said: who dispute about it — they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." Mutar said, from Ayyub, that he said: "So do not sit with them; they are the ones Allah meant, so beware of them." [[The hadith: 6606 — Ibn Abd al-A'la: he is Muhammad ibn Abd al-A'la al-San'ani; his biography has passed at 1236.
Mutar: he is Ibn Tahman, with a fatha on the ta and sukun on the ha, al-Warraq. He is trustworthy, and some have spoken of him concerning his memory. He died in 125.
This hadith, through this route, was narrated by Ibn Hibban in his Sahih, no. 75 in our edition, from the route of Asim ibn al-Nadr al-Ahwal, from al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman, with this chain.
Ibn Hibban said after narrating it: "Ayyub heard this report from Mutar al-Warraq and Ibn Abi Mulaykah together."
This is an error, which we failed to point out there, since we understood it in its correct meaning and did not notice the wording! Ibn Hibban intends to say: "Ayyub and Mutar al-Warraq heard this report together from Ibn Abi Mulaykah."
Either what is established there is a slip of the pen by Ibn Hibban, or it was an oversight by the copyists. Ibn Hibban could not have been unaware that Mutar al-Warraq did not meet Aisha, and he has mentioned him among the trustworthy (al-Thiqat, pp. 344-345), and mentioned that he narrates from Anas ibn Malik, and that he died in 125, it was said 129. Nevertheless, this was not granted to him, for Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Marasil, p. 78, narrated from Abu Zur'ah, who said: "Mutar did not hear anything from Anas. It is mursal."
But what troubles Ibn Hibban's statement — if it is read in the correct form we mentioned — is that al-Tabari's narration here is explicit that Mutar heard it from Ayyub with the addition he added to the wording of the hadith. Al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman would have heard it from Ayyub in abridged form, with the wording "fa-ahdharuhum," and heard it from Mutar al-Warraq from Ayyub in full, with the other wording. This, Allah willing, is the correct view. Mutar and Ayyub are of the same generation.]]
6607 - Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Abd al-Wahhab related to us, saying: Ayyub related to us, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), with a similar meaning. [[The hadith: 6607 — Abd al-Wahhab is Ibn Abd al-Majid al-Thaqafi; his biography has passed at 2039. This hadith, through this route, was narrated by Ibn Majah (47) from Ahmad ibn Thabit al-Jahdari and Yahya ibn Hakim, both from Abd al-Wahhab, with it.
Ibn Kathir (2:97) pointed to it from Ibn Majah's narration, then said: "Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Abdi narrated it in his Musnad from Abd al-Wahhab al-Thaqafi, with it."]]
6608 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similarly. [[The hadith: 6608 — This is the preceding hadith, through Ma'mar from Ayyub. Ibn Kathir (2:97) pointed to it, saying: "Likewise Abd al-Razzaq narrated it from Ma'mar from Ayyub, and likewise others narrated it from Ayyub."
Ibn Kathir did not mention another takhrij for this narration of Ma'mar. The manuscript of Abd al-Razzaq's Tafsir in the Dar al-Kutub al-Misriyyah has a lacuna from the end of Surat al-Baqarah to the beginning of Surat al-Nisa'.]]
6609 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: al-Harith informed us, from Ayyub, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, wife of the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)," the whole verse. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, and those who dispute about it, they are the ones Allah meant; they are those whom Allah mentioned, so do not sit with them." [[The hadith: 6609 — al-Harith is Ibn Bunhan al-Jurmi al-Basri. He is very weak. Al-Bukhari said in al-Kabir 1/2/282: "munkar al-hadith" (denounced in narration). He said the same in al-Saghir, p. 185. In al-Tahdhib, from al-Tirmidhi in al-Ilal al-Kabir, from al-Bukhari: "munkar al-hadith, he does not mind what he narrates, and he is very weak." Ibn Abi Hatim (1/2/91-92) narrated from Ahmad ibn Hanbal, who said: "A righteous man, but he was not known for hadith, and he did not memorize it; munkar al-hadith."
Despite the weakness of this al-Harith, the basic hadith is authentic, through the other chains, preceding and following.]]
6610 - Ibn Waki' related to us, saying: Abu Usamah related to us, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: I heard al-Qasim ibn Muhammad narrate, from Aisha, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: "He it is who has sent down to you the Book; in it are verses that are clear, they are the foundation of the Book," then he recited to the end of the verses, and said: "When you see those who follow what is ambiguous of it, then they are those whom Allah named, so beware of them." [[The hadith: 6610 — Ibn Waki' is Sufyan ibn Waki', who is weak, as we explained at 1692. Abu Usamah is Hammad ibn Usamah al-Kufi, the hafiz; his biography has passed at 2995. Yazid ibn Ibrahim al-Tustari al-Basri, the hafiz: trustworthy and firm. Ahmad, Waki', Abu Hatim and others declared him trustworthy, and Ibn Ma'in considered him more firm than Jarir ibn Hazim.
This chain is one of the narrations of this hadith in which "al-Qasim ibn Muhammad" is added between Ibn Abi Mulaykah and Aisha. Both are authentic. It is among the additions in a connected chain: Ibn Abi Mulaykah heard it from Aisha and heard it from al-Qasim from Aisha, so he narrated it in both ways, sometimes thus and sometimes thus.
This hadith, through this route, was narrated by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi (1433) from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with this chain, similar, somewhat abridged.
It was narrated by al-Bukhari (8:157-159, Fath), Muslim (2:303-304), and Abu Dawud (4598), all three from al-Qa'nabi, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with this chain.
Al-Tirmidhi (4:80) narrated it from Abd ibn Humayd, from Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with it, similarly, and said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."
Ibn Hibban narrated it in his Sahih, no. 72 in our edition, from the route of Abdullah — Ibn al-Mubarak, the Imam, Shaykh al-Islam — from Yazid ibn Ibrahim, with it.
Yazid ibn Ibrahim did not alone mention the addition of "al-Qasim" between Ibn Abi Mulaykah and Aisha; a different chain will come at 6615 with the addition of al-Qasim, and it will also come after this at 6611 from the narration of Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father.]]

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 3, verses 7–8 (part 4 of 7):**

6611 - Ali ibn Sahl told us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim told us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father, from Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited: "They follow that which is ambiguous of it" [the verse], and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has warned you about them. So when you see them, then beware of them." [[Hadith 6611. Ali ibn Sahl al-Ramli, Tabari's shaykh: his biography has already passed at 1384. al-Walid ibn Muslim al-Dimashqi, scholar of Syria: his biography has already passed at 2184.
Abd al-Rahman: he is Ibn al-Qasim ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr. His biography has already passed at 2836.
This is a sound chain. It is a strong, sound supporting narration (mutaba'ah) for the version of Ibn Abi Mulaykah from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad.
Ibn Kathir cited it (2: 98), then said: "Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another route, from al-Qasim, from Aisha, with the same wording."
See the following hadith: 6615.
His saying "nazaʿa Rasul Allah" (the Messenger recited): one says "intaza'a" with a verse or a poem, meaning he quoted it as evidence. It is also said of a man who derives the meaning of a verse from the Books of God: "He has derived a good meaning" (qad intaza'a maʿnan jayyidan), and "nazaʿahu", meaning he extracted it. Perhaps by her saying "nazaʿa" here she meant: he cited as evidence, or he recited citing it. See the next hadith after this one.]]

6612 - Ali told us, saying: al-Walid told us, from Nafi ibn Umar, from [Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who told me] Aisha, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "When you see them, then beware of them." Then he recited: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it," and they do not act upon its clear (muhkam) verses. [[Hadith 6612. Nafi ibn Umar ibn Abd Allah ibn Jumayl, al-Jumahi al-Qurashi al-Makki: trustworthy. Ahmad ibn Hanbal said: "Firm, firm, sound in hadith." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 4/2/86, Ibn Sad 5: 363, Nasab Quraysh by al-Mus'ab: 400, Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/456, and Tadhkirat al-Huffaz 1: 213.
In the manuscript and the printed edition here it reads "Nafi an Umar" instead of "Nafi ibn Umar". This is an error. The correction comes from al-Fath 8: 157, where he is mentioned among those who narrated this hadith "from Ibn Abi Mulaykah without mention of al-Qasim", "...and Nafi ibn Umar, and Ibn Jurayj, and others." We have also corrected it from Ibn Kathir, as we will mention.
Then in both the original copies there is another error, worse than that and more shameful! In them it reads: "an Nafi, an Umar, an Aisha"!! So "Ibn Abi Mulaykah" was dropped from the chain, and then his explicit statement of hearing from Aisha was dropped.
We have corrected the chain and restored what the copyists had mistakenly omitted, namely what we added after the word "an" between the markers of addition: [Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who told me].
We took this addition from Ibn Kathir 2: 98, where he said: "Ibn Jarir narrated it, from the hadith of Rawh ibn al-Qasim and Nafi ibn Umar al-Jumahi, both from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha. Nafi said in his narration: 'from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who told me Aisha', and so he mentioned it."
This is the correct reading, and it was the copyists' omission that caused the lost part of the chain here. Praise be to God.
Furthermore, the hadith will come again: 6614, through this route, in the correct form, from the narration of Khalid ibn Nizar, from Nafi, who is Ibn Umar al-Jumahi, "from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha".]]

6613 - Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb told me, saying: my paternal uncle told us, saying: Shabib ibn Said informed me, from Rawh ibn al-Qasim, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha: that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about this verse: "As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow that which is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation, and none knows its interpretation except Allah. And those firmly grounded in knowledge..." He said: "When you see those who dispute concerning it, they are the ones whom Allah meant, so beware of them." [[Hadith 6613. Ahmad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Wahb: his biography has already passed at 2747. His paternal uncle is Abd Allah ibn Wahb.
Shabib ibn Said al-Tamimi al-Habati al-Basri: Ibn al-Madini said: "Trustworthy. He used to travel to Egypt for trade, and his book is a sound book." In Egypt Ibn Wahb heard from him. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, al-Kabir 2/2/234, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1/359.
"al-Habati": with an unpointed initial letter ha' and a dotted ba' with one dot. It is a nisba to "al-Habatat", a clan of Tamim.
Rawh ibn al-Qasim al-Tamimi al-Anbari al-Basri: trustworthy. Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, and others declared him trustworthy. Sufyan ibn Uyaynah said: "I have not seen anyone who sought hadith while elderly with better memory than Rawh ibn al-Qasim."
Ibn Kathir indicated this chain at 2: 98, as we quoted his words at the previous chain.]]

6614 - Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Hakam told me, saying: Khalid ibn Nizar told us, from Nafi, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, regarding this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book," [the verse], "they follow it," meaning they recite it. Then he [the Prophet] said: "When you see those who dispute concerning it, beware of them, for they are the ones whom Allah meant." [[Hadith 6614. Khalid ibn Nizar ibn al-Mughirah al-Ayli: trustworthy. He is biographed only in al-Tahdhib. His shaykh Nafi is Ibn Umar al-Jumahi.
This hadith repeats hadith 6612, from the narration of Nafi al-Jumahi, and it confirms what we mentioned, that the link dropped from that chain.
So these: Ayyub, Nafi ibn Umar, and Khalid ibn Nizar all narrated it from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, directly, without an intermediary "al-Qasim" between them. Indeed Nafi ibn Umar explicitly stated that Ibn Abi Mulaykah heard it from Aisha, as passed at 6612.
Abu Amir al-Khazzaz followed them in this:
Al-Tirmidhi narrated it at 4: 80, from Muhammad ibn Bashshar, from Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi, from Abu Amir al-Khazzaz, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, without mention of al-Qasim.
Abu Amir al-Khazzaz (with dotted letters) is Salih ibn Rustum. His biography has already passed at 5458.
Ibn Kathir mentioned this follow-up at 2: 98, and the Hafiz (Ibn Hajar) in al-Fath 8: 157. Its chain is sound.
Also Said ibn Mansur narrated it, from Hammad ibn Yahya, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from Aisha, as Ibn Kathir reported at 2: 98. It is a sound chain.
Ibn Jurayj also followed them. The Hafiz mentioned it in al-Fath 8: 157, but did not name who narrated it. I have not found it in any other source among those available to me.]]

6615 - Ibn Wakiʿ told us, saying: Yazid ibn Harun told us, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim, from Aisha, from the Prophet ﷺ, regarding this verse: "He it is who sent down to you the Book, in it are verses that are clear (muhkamat), they are the mother of the Book," to the end of the verse. He said: "They are those whom Allah named. So when you see them, then beware of them." [[Hadith 6615. This is also a sound chain. But it has the addition of "al-Qasim" between Ibn Abi Mulaykah and Aisha, like the narration of Yazid ibn Ibrahim from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, passed at 6610.
It refutes the claim of al-Tirmidhi that Yazid ibn Ibrahim alone transmitted this addition, as we mentioned at 6605. For Hammad ibn Salamah followed him in this, in this chain.
Similarly Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it in his Musnad: 1432, from Hammad ibn Salamah, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aisha.
Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi gathered the two narrations, that of Yazid and that of Hammad, in his narration from both of them. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it from his father, from Abu al-Walid al-Tayalisi, from Yazid ibn Ibrahim al-Tustari and Hammad ibn Salamah together, from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Aisha. Ibn Kathir cited it at 2: 98 from Ibn Abi Hatim, and the Hafiz indicated it in al-Fath 8: 157.
Earlier, at 6611, was the narration of Hammad ibn Salamah from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim, from his father, from Aisha. This and that show that Hammad ibn Salamah narrated it from two shaykhs who both took it from al-Qasim: he narrated it from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Qasim and from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, both from al-Qasim.
There is another follow-up from al-Qasim whose chain details we do not know. For Ibn Kathir said at 2: 98: "Ibn Mardawayh narrated it through another route, from al-Qasim, from Aisha, with the same wording." He did not mention what that route is or its chain, and the Hafiz did not indicate it in al-Fath.
There is also a hadith whose origin al-Suyuti mentioned at 2: 5, and he attributed it further to al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il.]]

* *

Abu Jaʿfar said: What the apparent meaning of this verse indicates is that it was revealed concerning those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over the ambiguous part of what was sent down to him from the Book of Allah, either concerning the matter of Jesus, or concerning the term of his own lifespan and the lifespan of his community. [[In the printed edition: "either the term of his life and the term of his community", the correction from the manuscript. A similar distortion occurred already at p. 180, note 1, p. 187, note 1, and in the first volume of the commentary, p. 217, note 4. The word "akl" (with a dammah on the alif and a sukun on the kaf) means provision, because it is eaten. From it is said of the span of life a person lives in this world "akl". One says of the dead: "his akl has ended", meaning his term has finished and his life has passed away.]]

And it is more fitting for it to concern those who disputed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ over its ambiguity regarding his term and the term of his community, because his saying: "and none knows its interpretation except Allah," indicates that this is information about the term which they wanted to know through the ambiguous matter that none but Allah knows. As for the matter of Jesus and its causes, Allah has informed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and his community of it, and clarified it for them. It is known that the verse only meant what was hidden about the terms (al-ajal). [[In the printed edition: "...that he did not mean except what was hidden from the individuals (al-ahad)", which has no meaning. In the manuscript: "that he did not mean by it except what was hidden in it from the individuals," so I judged the correct reading to be as I have written it, "al-ajal", plural of ajal, which is what they wanted to know of the term of this community. The copyist here often erred through haste.]]

* *

On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿seeking discord﴾

Abu Jaʿfar said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed regarding the meaning of that.
