As for His words "and wretched is the resting-place": "and wretched is the bed, Hell, to which you will be gathered." [[See what was passed at 4:246.]] Mujahid used to say something like this:

6671 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His words: "and wretched is the resting-place," he said: "Wretched is what they have prepared for their souls."

6672 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 13 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah, and another disbelieving﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Say, O Muhammad, to those who disbelieved among the Jews who are among the people of your city: "There has already been a sign for you," meaning: a sign and an indication of the truth of what I say, that you will be overcome, and a lesson (ʿibrah), as:

6673 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah: "There has already been a sign for you," a lesson and reflection.

6674 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' the like of it, except that he said: and a reflection (mutafakkar).

* *

"In two armies" means: in two groups and two parties. "Al-fi'ah" (a company, a group) is a body of people. "Which met" for battle; one of the two armies was the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and those with him from among those who witnessed the Battle of Badr, and the other was the polytheists of Quraysh.

"One fighting in the way of Allah" means: a group fighting in obedience to Allah and for His religion, and they are the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions. "And another disbelieving" means: they are the polytheists of Quraysh, as:

6675 - Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, narrated to me, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr or ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah": the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) at Badr. "And another disbelieving": the disbelieving party of Quraysh.

6676 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr or ʿIkrimah, from Ibn ʿAbbas, the like of it.

6677 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿIkrimah: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah": Muhammad (ﷺ) and his Companions. "And another disbelieving": Quraysh on the day of Badr.

6678 - Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿIsa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies": He said: concerning Muhammad and his Companions, and the polytheists of Quraysh on the day of Badr.

6679 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

6680 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah": He said: that was the day of Badr, when the Muslims and the disbelievers met.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: "One fighting in the way of Allah" is in the nominative (raf'), and it was previously said "in two armies," with the sense: one of them is fighting in the way of Allah, by way of a new beginning (ibtida'), as the poet said: [It is Kuthayyir ʿAzzah.]

So I was like one with two legs: one leg sound, and a leg on which time has cast (its harm), so it became paralysed (shallat)

[Diwan 1: 46; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 192; Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu ʿUbaydah 1: 87; Sibawayh 1: 215; al-Khizanah 2: 376; and many others. It will come in the tafsir 30: 58 (Bulaq). It is from his famous rhymed qasidah in -t, and this line is linked to a wish he expressed in the preceding verses...]

And as Ibn Mufarrigh said: [I have not found the attribution of this poetry to Ibn Mufarrigh; it is without doubt by al-Najashi al-Harithi, from his poem on Mu'awiyah and ʿAli, and it is mostly in al-Wahshiyyat of Abu Tammam; the battle of Siffin: 601-605.]

So I was like one with two legs: one leg sound, and a leg with misfortune of the vicissitudes

[al-Wahshiyyat no. 183; Hamasah of Ibn al-Shajari: 33; Khizanat al-Adab 2: 378. Azd Shanu'ah and Azd ʿUman were two tribes that fought at Siffin...]

"As for the one which was sound, then Azd Shanu'ah; and as for the one which was paralysed, then Azd ʿUman."

Thus the Arabs do in every repeated item that corresponds to an earlier one, when the repetition is followed by a predicate: you return it to the case of the first occurrence once, and you resume it a second time in the nominative, and you put it in the accusative in complete and incomplete verbs; and all of that has been put in the genitive, so that it is governed by return to the beginning of the speech, as if he meant, when he uses the genitive: "So I was like one with two legs, like the one with a sound leg and a sick leg." Likewise the genitive in His saying "fi'ah" is permissible, by return to His saying "in two armies which met," in "a group fighting in the way of Allah."

Although this is permissible in Arabic, I do not allow reciting with it, because of the consensus of the authoritative readers (al-qurra') against it. And if His saying "fi'ah" had come in the accusative, it would also be permissible on His saying "there has already been a sign for you in two armies which met," being different (armies).

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿They saw them as twice their number with the sight of the eye﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed in the recitation of this.

The reading of the people of Madinah is ﴿tarawnahum﴾ with the "ta," meaning: there has already been a sign for you, O Jews, in two armies which met, one fighting in the way of Allah, and the other disbelieving, you see the polytheists as twice the Muslims by sight. By this he intends to admonish them, saying: there is a lesson for you, O Jews, in what you saw of the small number of the Muslims and the large number of the polytheists, and the victory of these despite their small number over those despite their large number.

* *

The majority of the readers of Kufa and Basra and some Meccans recited ﴿yarawnahum mithlayhim﴾ with the "ya," meaning: the Muslims who fight in the way of Allah see the disbelieving group as twice the Muslims in number. So the interpretation of the verse according to their reading: there has already been, O company of Jews, a lesson and reflection in two armies which met, one fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving; these Muslims see, despite their small number, those polytheists in their large number.

* *

If someone says: What is the meaning of the interpretation of the one who recited with the "ya"? And which of the two armies saw its counterpart as twice its number? Was it the Muslim army that saw the polytheist army as twice its number, or the polytheist army that saw the Muslim army likewise, or someone else who saw one of them so?

It is said: the people of interpretation differed on this.

Some of them said: the army that saw the other as twice itself was the Muslim army; it saw the number of the polytheist army as twice the number of the Muslim army. Allah, may He be exalted, made it appear small in their eyes until they saw it as twice their own number. [His saying: "He made it small in their eyes" — because the polytheists were more than them in number, so Allah showed them their number as twice theirs and no more. The explanation will come shortly. See the following note.] Then He made it small in another state, so they saw it as equal to their own number.

Those who said this:

6681 - Musa narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi in a report he mentioned, from Murrah al-Hamdani, from Ibn Mas'ud: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving; they see them as twice their number with the sight of the eye": He said: this is the day of Badr. ʿAbd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: We looked at the polytheists and saw them doubling us, then we looked at them again and did not see them exceed us by a single man. That is the saying of Allah, may He be exalted: "And when He showed them to you when you met, few in your eyes, and He made you few in their eyes" [al-Anfal 8:44].

* *

The meaning of the verse according to this interpretation: there has already been, O company of Jews, a sign for you in two armies which met: one Muslim and the other disbelieving, the number of the disbelieving being large and the number of the Muslims small. The small-numbered party sees the large-numbered party as twice, meaning it sees it as increasing in number only by a single multiple, [In the printed edition: "...as twice, that they increase them..." — the correct reading is from the manuscript; the editor apparently missed the sense of restriction here and altered it. See the previous note.] so they see them as twice their number. So one of the two multiples at that point is the number equal to the number of the party that saw them, and the other multiple is the double added to their number. This is one meaning of the "making few" which Allah, may He be exalted, informed the believers that He made them few in their eyes.

The other meaning of it is the second making few, according to what Ibn Mas'ud said: that He showed them the number of the polytheists equal to their number, not exceeding them. This is the second making few which Allah, may His praise be exalted, mentioned: "And when He showed them to you when you met, few in your eyes."

* *

Others of the people of this view said: those who saw the polytheists as twice themselves were the Muslims. Only, the Muslims saw them with their actual number, and they were not made few in their eyes, but Allah strengthened them with His help. They said: That is why Allah, may He be exalted, said to the Jews: "There has already been a lesson for you in them," warning them thereby that there might befall them from among themselves a like of what befell the people of Badr at their hands.

Those who said this:

6682 - Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving": it was revealed concerning the lightening (of the burden) on the day of Badr, for the believers were on that day three hundred and thirteen men, and the polytheists were twice them. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving, they see them as twice their number with the sight of the eye," and the polytheists were nine hundred and sixty-six [sic: 26 and 600 as written], and Allah strengthened the believers. This was the lightening upon the believers.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This report contradicts what is corroborated by the reports about the number of the polytheists on the day of Badr. The people differed about their number in two ways.

Some said: their number was a thousand; and some said: between nine hundred and a thousand.

Those who said: "Their number was a thousand":

6683 - Harun ibn Ishaq al-Hamdani narrated to me, saying: Musʿab ibn al-Miqdam narrated to us, saying: Israʿil narrated to us, saying: Abu Ishaq narrated to us, from Harithah, from ʿAli, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) set out for Badr, and the polytheists outstripped us to it. We found in it two men, one of them a man of Quraysh and a client of ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muʿayt. As for the Qurashi, he escaped; as for the client of ʿUqbah, we captured him. We began to ask: How many are the people? He would say: They, by God, are many and their might is fierce! So the Muslims, whenever he said that, beat him, until they brought him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said to him: How many are the people? He said: They, by God, are many and their might is fierce! The Prophet (ﷺ) strove to make him tell how many they were, but he refused. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked him: How many do they slaughter of camels? He said: Ten each day. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The people are a thousand. [Report 6683: Tarikh al-Tabari 2: 269.]

6684 - Abu Saʿid ibn Yushaʿ al-Baghdadi narrated to me, saying: Ishaq ibn Mansur narrated to us, from Israʿil, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu ʿUbaydah, from ʿAbd Allah, who said: We captured a man of them, meaning of the polytheists, on the day of Badr, and we said: How many were you? He said: A thousand. [Report 6684: "Abu Saʿid ibn Yushaʿ al-Baghdadi" — I have found no biography of him in the books available to me; see also no. 6690.]

* *

Those who said: "Their number was between nine hundred and a thousand":

6685 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq said: Yazid ibn Ruman narrated to me, from ʿUrwah ibn al-Zubayr, who said: The Prophet (ﷺ) sent a group of his Companions to the water of Badr seeking news for him, [in the manuscript: "seeking for him concerning him," with a gap, and the printed edition completed it as in the text of Ibn Hisham.] and they came upon a water-carrier from Quraysh in whom were Aslam, a slave of the Banu al-Hajjaj, and ʿArid Abu Yasar, a slave of the Banu al-ʿAs. They brought the two to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them: How many are the people? They said: Many! He said: What is their number? They said: We do not know! He said: How many do they slaughter each day? They said: One day nine, and one day ten. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The people are between nine hundred and a thousand. [Report 6685: an abridgment of Sirah Ibn Hisham 2: 268–269, and Tarikh al-Tabari 2: 275.]

6686 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving, they see them as twice their number with the sight of the eye": that was the day of Badr; the polytheists were a thousand or near it, and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were three hundred and some men.

6687 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah regarding His saying: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one..." to His saying "with the sight of the eye," he said: They were doubled over them, and they killed seventy of them and captured seventy, on the day of Badr.

6688 - al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabiʿ regarding His saying: "There has already been a sign for you in two armies which met: one fighting in the way of Allah and another disbelieving, they see them as twice their number with the sight of the eye," he said: That was on the day of Badr, and the polytheists were nine hundred and fifty, and the Companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) were three hundred and thirteen.

6689 - al-Qasim narrated to me, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: The Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were three hundred and some, and the polytheists were between nine hundred and a thousand.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: All of these whom we have mentioned oppose the view we have related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning the number of the polytheists on the day of Badr. So, if what was said by those whose statement we have related — those who stated that their number exceeded nine hundred — is [correct], [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "If what was said by the one we related from, among those who stated that their number exceeded nine hundred, then the first interpretation ..." — an incoherent phrase and a common scribal error. I judged that the correct wording is "we related his statement" in the first place, with the addition of "correct" at the end of the sentence, as I have placed it between brackets.]] then the first interpretation we have given, based on the report we related from Ibn Mas'ud, is more fitting for the interpretation of the verse.
* *
Others said: The number of the polytheists exceeded nine hundred, and the Muslims saw their number differently from what it actually was. They said: God showed the Muslims the number of the polytheists as few, as a sign for the Muslims. They said: God, mighty and majestic, meant by His saying "they see them as twice their number" the addressees of His saying "There has already been a sign for you in the two hosts that met." They said: And they are the Jews, except that the address shifted to the report about an absent party, because it was a command from God, may He be praised, to His Prophet ﷺ to say that to them. So it was fine to address them once and to speak of them in the form of a report another time, as He said: ﴿Until, when you are in the ships and they sail with them with a good wind﴾ [Surah Yunus: 22].
They said: If someone says to us: how is it said "they see them as twice their number with their own eyes," when you know that the polytheists on that day were three times the Muslims?
We say to them: As a speaker says when he has a slave with him: "I need his like," and you need him and his like; then he says "I need twice his like," meaning that it is a report of his need of his like and of twice that like. And as a man says: "I have a thousand and I need twice that," so he needs three thousand. When he intends that the "thousand" is included in the meaning of "the like," the "like" becomes two, and two makes three. He said: A similar usage in speech is: "I see you as your like," as if he said: "I see you as your double," and "I see you as your two-fold." That means: I see you as double the two of you. They said: So this is in the sense of three times their number.
* *
Others said: Rather, the meaning is that God showed the disbelieving group the number of the Muslim group as twice their number.
This too contradicts what the apparent sense of the revelation indicates, because God, may He be praised, said in His Book: ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you few in their eyes﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 44], so He informed that each of the two groups made the other's number appear small in the other's sight.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: Others read it as ﴿turawnahum﴾ with a dammah on the ta', meaning: God shows them to them as twice their number.
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these readings is the reading of the one who reads "yarawnahum" with a ya', meaning: and another disbelieving group, which the Muslims see as twice their number — that is, twice the number of the Muslims — because God made them appear few in their eyes at one point, so their estimate of them was like that; then He made them appear fewer in their eyes than the first diminution, so they estimated them equal to the number of the Muslims, [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "twice the number of the Muslims" here as well, which is an obvious error; the preceding and following context indicates otherwise, so I have corrected it.]] then a third diminution, so they estimated them to be fewer than the number of the Muslims, as:
6690 - Abu Sa'id al-Baghdadi related to me, saying: Ishaq ibn Mansur related to us, from Isra'il, from Abu Ishaq, from Abu 'Ubaydah, from 'Abdullah, who said: They were made to appear few in our eyes on the day of Badr, until I said to a man beside me: "Do you see them as seventy?" He said: "I see them as a hundred." He said: Then we captured one of them and asked: "How many were you?" He said: "A thousand."
* *
It has been related from Qatadah that he used to say: If it were "turawnahum," it would be "mithlaykum" [i.e., "twice your number"].
6691 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad related to me, from Ibn al-Mubarak, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, with that.[[Report 6691: I have not definitively identified "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad." He appears previously as "'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad al-Kufi al-Qari" in nos. 3109 and 4077, but al-Muthanna is not recorded as transmitting from him except through an intermediary here, and the chain reads "al-Muthanna said, Ishaq related to us, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad," which I do not think is the same person. In Tarikh al-Tabari 1: 171 it reads "al-Muthanna said, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Hammad related to us ...", so the greater likelihood is that they are two different men. As for "Ibn al-Mubarak," I have preferred that it is "'Abdullah al-Mubarak." In the printed edition it was "from Ibn al-Mu'rak," and I did not find anyone known by this name; in the manuscript it reads "from Ibn al-Masral," which looks like a mim, a sin, a ra', and a kaf or lam. Perhaps it was originally written "Ibn al-Mubrak" without an alif between the ba' and the ra', and the copyist read it thus. And God knows best.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: In the two reports we have related from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud there is clarification of the variation in the Muslims' estimates of the number of the polytheists that day at different times. God, mighty and majestic, informed the Jews — regarding what occurred of variation in the states of their number in the eyes of the Muslims — according to what it was in their (the Jews') view, [[This is how it appears in the printed edition; it is a sentence that barely holds together. The phrase "the Jews" is the object of "God informed ...". The phrase "according to what it was in their view" is one whose meaning I have not found satisfactory. The manuscript reads: "God, mighty and majestic, informed of what occurred of variation in the states of their number in the sight of the Muslims, the Jews, according to what it was in their view," which is a disordered sentence and I fear something may have dropped out of it.]] while the Jews knew the magnitude of the number of the two groups, [[The sense of the passage as you see it is: "God, mighty and majestic, informed ... the Jews ... as a notice from Him to them."]] as a notice from Him to them that He supports the believers with His victory, so that they would not be deceived by their number and might, and so that they would beware lest He inflict upon them punishment at the hands of the believers, like what He inflicted upon the people of polytheism from Quraysh at their hands at Badr. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "at Badrihim" (at their Badr), which is not Arabic, so I preferred to omit the pronoun and render it "at Badr," unless there is a distortion in the text that I have not discerned. Moreover, as you see, the copyist in many of these pages has hastened, added, distorted, and omitted. May God forgive him.]]
* *
As for His saying "ra'y al-'ayn" (with their own eyes), it is a verbal noun from "ra'aytuhu," said: "ra'aytuhu ra'yan wa ru'yatan" and "ra'ayt fi al-manam ru'ya hasanah," (not inflected). It is said: "He is from me ra'y al-'ayn, and ri'a' al-'ayn" [[In the printed edition: "wa ra'y al-'ayn"; in the manuscript: "wa ra'a al-'ayn." The correct reading is what I have given. The first editor was prompted to read it that way because he did not find its text in the lexicons. But his later statement "and it is from al-ra'y like it" refers to this very word, as does what follows in the next sentence, "and the people are ri'a'," which he cites as evidence for it. However, the first editor did not read the manuscript well and altered it, which also helped him to alter the spelling of the preceding word, as we shall see in the following note. See also Majaz al-Qur'an by Abu 'Ubaydah 1: 88.]] in the accusative and nominative, meaning: wherever my sight reaches; and it is from "al-ra'y" like it. And "al-qawm ri'a'" [[In the printed edition: "wa al-qawm ra'u" — I do not know how the first editor wanted to read it, or what he thought it was! The correct reading is what I have given; in the manuscript it is written "wa al-qawm ra'a'" with a kasrah under the ra', and the correct reading is what I have given. See the preceding note.]] means when they sit where some of them see others.
* *
So the meaning is: they see them — where their sight reaches and their eyes behold them — as twice their number.
* *
On the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And God supports with His victory whom He wills. Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have sight﴾ (13)
Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may He be praised: "And God supports," He means: strengthens [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "He means by that, may He be praised," but the context as you see it requires what I have given.]] "with His victory whom He wills,"
* *
= from the speaker's saying: "I have supported so-and-so with such-and-such," when he strengthens him and helps him, "so I support him, support." Its "fa'ala" form from it: "adahu, so I uuid him, a'dan," and from it the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And remember Our servant Dawud, the possessor of strength﴾ [Surah Sad: 17], meaning: the possessor of might. [[The Tafsir of "al-ayd" and "ayyad" was given earlier: see 2: 319, 320; then 5: 379.]] [[Lexicons do not mention this triliteral verb as transitive; rather they say "ad ya'idu adan, if he became firm and strong." This is an addition I have not found in any work other than this noble tafsir.]]
* *
Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the speech is: There has been for you — O assembly of Jews — a sign in two groups that met, one fighting in the way of God and another disbelieving, which the Muslims see as twice their number with their own eyes. So We strengthened the Muslim group, though their number was small, against the disbelieving group, though their number was large, until they overcame them, [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "There had been for you a sign," and the mention of "sign" here is a slip of the copyist, since the sign was on his tongue earlier; the subject of "kana" comes shortly after, namely "one who takes heed and reflects," which is the meaning of "sign" here, as was mentioned at the beginning of the interpretation of this verse.]] a lesson for the one who takes heed and reflects. And God supports with His victory whom He wills.
* *
And He, may He be praised, said: "Indeed in that" — meaning: indeed in what We did with those whose matter We have described: Our strengthening of the Muslim group despite their small number, against the disbelieving group despite their large number — "is a lesson," meaning: a reflection and admonition for whoever understands and remembers and perceives the truth, as:
6692 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "Indeed in that is a lesson for those who have sight," he says: Certainly there was for them in these people a lesson and reflection; God strengthened them and gave them victory over their enemy.
6693 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the same.

**The Interpretation of His Words:** ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires: women, sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, means: love of what they desire, of women, of sons, and of all the rest that is enumerated, has been made attractive to people. He intended by this a rebuke of the Jews, who preferred this world and the love of leadership in it over following Muhammad ﷺ, even after they knew of his truthfulness.

* *

Al-Hasan used to say: "Who beautified it? No one is more critical of it than its Creator." [[In al-Qurtubi 4:28: "Who beautified it?" is an interrogative; "beautified" (zayyana) is a verb. I have not found the report from al-Hasan, but I recall having read it long ago. He was mocking the affairs of this world and saying: "Among its beauty is that the one who disparages and denounces it is the one who created it!" "Zayn" is the opposite of "shayn" (ugliness), a verbal noun from "zana al-shay' yuzayyinuhu zaynan" (he made the thing beautiful).]]

6694 – Ahmad ibn Hazim related to me this, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Abu al-Ash'ath related to us from him.

6695 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Jarir related to us, from 'Ata', from Abu Bakr ibn Hafs ibn 'Umar ibn Sa'd, who said: 'Umar said: "When this was revealed, 'Beautified for people is the love of desires,' I said: 'Now, O Lord, when You have beautified them for us!'" Then this was revealed: ﴿Say: Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear God, with their Lord are gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 15], and the verse.

* *

As for "al-qanatir" (heaped-up piles), it is the plural of "al-qintar" (a large weight).

The people of interpretation differed concerning the amount of the qintar.

Some of them said: It is one thousand and two hundred uqiyya (ounces).

Those who said this:

6696 – Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Abu Husayn, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, who said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred uqiyya."

6697 – Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Abu Bakr ibn 'Ayyash related to us, saying: Abu Husayn related to us, from Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd, from Mu'adh, the like of it.

6698 – Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Hafs ibn Maysara informed us, from Abu Marwan, from Abu Taybah, from Ibn 'Umar, who said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred uqiyya."

6699 – Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Malik al-Muzani related to us, saying: al-'Ala' ibn al-Musayyab informed me, from 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, who said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred uqiyya."

6700 – Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi related to us, saying: Hammad ibn Zayd related to us, from 'Asim ibn Bahdalah, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, the like of it. [[The report 6700: Ibn Kathir mentioned it in his tafsir 2:109-110, and referred to the narration of Ahmad: "'Abd al-Samad related to us, Hammad related to us, from 'Asim, from Abu Salih, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'The qintar is twelve thousand uqiyya, each uqiyya better than what is between heaven and earth.'" He mentioned the narration of Ibn Majah and Waki', and he affirmed that this report is mawquf (ending with a Companion), as narrated by Ibn Jarir and Waki'.]]

6701 – Zakariyya ibn Yahya al-Darir related to me, saying: Shababah related to us, saying: Mukhallad ibn 'Abd al-Wahid related to us, from 'Ali ibn Zayd, from 'Ata' ibn Abi Maymunah, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The qintar is one thousand uqiyya and two hundred uqiyya." [[The report 6701: "Zakariyya ibn Yahya al-Darir" is "Zakariyya ibn Yahya ibn Ayyub, Abu 'Ali al-Darir al-Mada'ini," who transmitted from Ziyad al-Bakka'i, Shababah ibn Sawwar, and Sulayman ibn Sufyan al-Juhani. Related from him were Muhammad ibn 'Ali known as Ma'dan, Muhammad ibn Ghalib al-Tammam, Yahya ibn Sa'id, and the judge al-Mahamili. He is biographed in Tarikh Baghdad 8:457. In the printed and manuscript editions it read "Zakariyya ibn Yahya al-Siddiq," which is an error; the correct reading is from Ibn Kathir's tafsir 2:110.
"Shababah" is "Shababah ibn Sawwar al-Fazari." Ahmad said: "I left him; I did not write from him because of his irja' (postponement doctrine); he was a propagandist." Zakariyya al-Saji said: "Truthful, calling to irja'. Ahmad used to attack him." Ibn Ma'in and Ibn Sa'd nonetheless deemed him trustworthy despite his irja'. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib. "Mukhallad ibn 'Abd al-Wahid" is Abu al-Hudhayl al-Basri, who transmitted from 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an, and from whom Shababah related. Ibn Hibban said: "Extremely unreliable in hadith." Abu Hatim said: "Weak in hadith." He is biographed in Lisan al-Mizan and Ibn Abi Hatim 4/1/348. "'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an" has passed under no. 40. "'Ata' ibn Abi Maymunah" transmitted from Anas, 'Imran, Jabir ibn Samurah, and others. Abu Zur'ah and al-Nasa'i deemed him trustworthy. Abu Hatim said: "His hadith is not used as proof, and he was a Qadari (follower of free will doctrine)." Ibn 'Adi said: "In his hadith there is some of what is objected to."
Ibn Kathir related this report in his tafsir 2:110 and said: "This is also a munkar (rejected) hadith." The more likely view is that it is mawquf upon Ubayy ibn Ka'b, like others from the Companions," meaning like the earlier report ending with Abu Hurayrah, and what preceded it from Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Ibn 'Umar.]]

* *

Others said: The qintar is one thousand dinars and two hundred dinars.

Those who said this:

6702 – 'Imran ibn Musa related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Warith ibn Sa'id related to us, saying: Yunus related to us, from al-Hasan, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred dinars."

6703 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Yunus related to us, from al-Hasan, who said: "The qintar: one thousand and two hundred dinars."

6704 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred dinars, and of silver, one thousand and two hundred mithqal."

6705 – It was related from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim say: "'The heaped-up piles' means the abundant wealth of gold and silver. The qintar is one thousand and two hundred dinars, and of silver, one thousand and two hundred mithqal."

* *

Others said: The qintar is twelve thousand dirhams, or one thousand dinars.

Those who said this:

6706 – 'Ali ibn Dawud related to me, saying: Abu Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiyah related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "The qintar is twelve thousand dirhams, or one thousand dinars."

6707 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn related to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, who said: "The qintar is one thousand dinars, and of wariq (silver) twelve thousand dirhams." [[Wariq (with fath on the waw and kasra on the ra'): silver, or dirhams made of silver.]]

6708 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, that the qintar is twelve thousand.

6709 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: 'Awf informed us, from al-Hasan: "The qintar is twelve thousand."

6710 – Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: .................... said: 'Awf informed us, from al-Hasan: "Twelve thousand." [[Report 6710: This is undoubtedly a defective chain, and I have placed these dots in place of the gap. The cause of this is that the copyist ended the page with his words "Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: related to us," and moved to the next page, beginning it with "said: 'Awf informed us," which was his error. The chain of "Muhammad ibn Bashshar" to "'Awf from al-Hasan" differs; for example, in chain no. 2570: "Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Yahya related to us, from Sa'id, from 'Awf, from al-Hasan," and others that I have not been able to trace now.]]

6711 – Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan, with the like of it.

6712 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn related to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from 'Awf, from al-Hasan, who said: "The qintar is one thousand dinars, the blood-money of one of you."

* *

Others said: It is eighty thousand of dirhams, or a hundred ratl of gold.

Those who said this:

6713 – Muhammad ibn Bashshar and Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna related to us, both saying: Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, from Sulayman al-Taymi, from Qatadah, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "The qintar is eighty thousand."

6714 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: 'Amr ibn 'Awn related to us, saying: Hushaym informed us, from 'Ali ibn Zayd, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "The qintar is eighty thousand."

6715 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, who said: "We used to be told that the qintar is a hundred ratl of gold, or eighty thousand of wariq."

6716 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, who said: "The qintar is a hundred ratl of gold, or eighty thousand dirhams of wariq."

6717 – Ahmad ibn Hazim related to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, who said: "The qintar is a hundred ratl."

6718 – Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "The qintar is a hundred ratl, and it is eight thousand mithqal."

* *

Others said: The qintar is seventy thousand.

Those who said this:

6719 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, "the heaped-up piles," who said: "The qintar: seventy thousand dinars."

6720 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

6721 – al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: 'Umar ibn Hawshab informed us, saying: I heard 'Ata' al-Khurasani say: "Ibn 'Umar was asked about the qintar and he said: 'Seventy thousand.'" [[Report 6721: "'Umar ibn Hawshab al-San'ani," who transmitted from Isma'il ibn Umayyah, and from whom 'Abd al-Razzaq related. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. Ibn al-Qattan said: "His state is not known." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, and in Ibn Abi Hatim 3/1/105.]]

* *

And others said: It is the filling of the hide of a bull with gold. [[Al-Maskh (with fath on the mim and sukun on the sin): it is the skin-sheath in which a bull or other animal is contained.]]

Those who said this:

6722 – Ibn Bashshar related to us, saying: Salim ibn Nuh related to us, saying: Sa'id al-Jurayri related to us, from Abu Nadrah, who said: "The filling of a bull's hide with gold."

6723 – Ahmad ibn Hazim related to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym related to us, saying: Abu al-Ash'ath related to us, from Abu Nadrah: "The filling of a bull's hide with gold."

* *

Others said: It is abundant wealth.

Those who said this:

6724 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, who said: "'The heaped-up piles': abundant wealth, some of it piled upon some."

* *

Some of the people of knowledge of Arabic speech have mentioned [[That is Abu 'Ubaydah Ma'mar ibn al-Muthanna, as he indicated by this many times before; see Majaz al-Qur'an of Abu 'Ubaydah 1:88.]] that the Arabs do not limit the qintar to a known measure of weight, but they say: "It is a measure of weight." [[The text of Abu 'Ubaydah: "It is the measure of a weight, they do not limit it," with "qadr" (measure) attached to "wazn" (weight). This is how it appears in the manuscript, but the printed edition added a waw, making it "qadr wa-wazn."]]

Abu Ja'far said: It should indeed be so, for if its quantity were fixed among them, there would not be all this disagreement among the earliest people of interpretation about it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this is to say: It is abundant wealth, as al-Rabi' ibn Anas said, and its weight is not restricted by a fixed limit, by forcing it. [[In the printed edition: "'ala ta'annuf (by harshness)," and in the manuscript: "'ala ta'annuf," undotted; I think the correct reading is what I have set.]] And what has been said has been said, from what we have narrated.

* *

As for "al-muqantara" (heaped up), it means "multiplied." It is as if "qanatir" is three and "muqantara" is nine. [[This is from al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:195, with some adaptation; its text is: "And the qanatir are three, and the muqantara are nine, thus I heard."]] And it is as al-Rabi' ibn Anas said: abundant wealth, some of it piled upon some, as:

6725 – Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "'The heaped-up piles of gold and silver': the muqantara is abundant wealth, some of it piled upon some."

6726 – It was related from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman informed us, who said: I heard al-Dahhak concerning His words, "the heaped-up piles," meaning abundant wealth of gold and silver.

* *

Others said: The meaning of "muqantara" is: struck into dirhams or dinars.

Those who said this:

6727 – Musa related to us, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: As for His words, "al-muqantara," he says: "Struck until they became dinars or dirhams."

* *

It has been related from the Prophet ﷺ concerning His words, "and you have given one of them a qintar" [Surah al-Nisa': 20], a report which, if its chain were sound, we would not refer to anything else. It is this:

6728 – Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Barqi related to us, with it, saying: 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah related to me, saying: Zuhayr ibn Muhammad related to us, saying: Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash and Humayd al-Tawil related to me, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Messenger of God ﷺ: "And you have given one of them a qintar" [Surah al-Nisa': 20], he said: "Two thousand mi'in" — that is, two thousand. [[The hadith 6728: Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Barqi: this is how it is in both the manuscript and the printed edition, and I did not know who he is. Ibn Kathir 2:110 transmitted this hadith from Ibn Abi Hatim's tafsir: "Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Raqqi informed us, 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah informed us..." I did not find "Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Raqqi" either, and Ibn Abi Hatim did not biograph him in al-Jarh wa-al-Ta'dil. It is very unlikely that he would not biograph his own teacher.
But among the teachers of al-Tabari is Ahmad ibn 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Barqi al-Hafiz. He related from him in no. 22 under the name "Ibn al-Barqi." And in no. 160, under the name "Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahim al-Barqi," attributed to his grandfather. And in no. 5444, under the name "Ibn al-Barqi." In the last narration he transmits from 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah, like the narration here.
So it is possible that he is the one meant here, and that the writing "Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman" in place of "Ibn 'Abd al-Rahim" is an error of the copyists.
But the agreement of "Ibn 'Abd al-Rahman" in Ibn Abi Hatim's narration and what is established here objects to this. For it is very unlikely that the copyists agreed on one specific error in two different books by two different authors, neither of whom copied from the other.
So perhaps "Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Raqqi" or "al-Barqi" is another teacher from whom al-Tabari and Ibn Abi Hatim related, whose biography has not reached us.
'Amr ibn Abi Salamah: his biography has passed under no. 5444.
Zuhayr ibn Muhammad al-Tamimi al-Khurasani al-Marwazi: trustworthy; Ahmad and others deemed him trustworthy.
Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash, whose name of Abu 'Ayyash is "Firuz": a Successor who transmitted from Anas, but he is weak. Ahmad said: "Munkar al-hadith (rejected in hadith)." Ibn Ma'in said: "His hadith is nothing." Abu Hatim said: "Matruk al-hadith (abandoned in hadith); he was a righteous man, but he was afflicted with poor memory." al-Bukhari said: "Shu'bah had a bad opinion of him."
But the weakness of Aban does not affect the soundness of this hadith, because Zuhayr ibn Muhammad heard it from him, and also heard it from "Humayd al-Tawil," and Humayd is trustworthy, as his biography has passed under no. 3877.
The hadith was also narrated by al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak 2:178, from Abu al-'Abbas al-Asamm, from Ahmad ibn 'Isa ibn Zayd al-Lakhmi, from 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah, from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad: "Humayd al-Tawil and another man related to us, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was asked about the words of God, 'the heaped-up piles' (Al 'Imran: 14)? He said: 'The qintar is two thousand uqiyya.'" Al-Hakim said: "This hadith is sound according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not narrate it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him. In the printed abridgment of al-Dhahabi that accompanies al-Mustadrak, "uqiyya" appears in the singular, which is a typographical error; it is correctly preserved in the manuscript of the abridgment in my possession, in agreement with the original of al-Mustadrak.
Ibn Kathir 2:110 transmitted it, as we said before, from the narration of Ibn Abi Hatim, from Ahmad ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Raqqi, from 'Amr ibn Abi Salamah, from Zuhayr ibn Muhammad: "Humayd al-Tawil and another man, whom he named, Yazid al-Raqashi, related to us, from Anas." And in it: "That is, one thousand dinars."
So the unnamed other man in al-Hakim's narration may be Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash, as in this narration of al-Tabari, and may be Yazid al-Raqashi, as in Ibn Abi Hatim's narration; Yazid ibn Aban al-Raqashi is also weak, as passed in the explanation of no. 6654.
As-Suyuti mentioned al-Hakim's narration at this place of the tafsir of the verse of Al 'Imran, 2:10, and mentioned al-Tabari's narration that is here, at its place in the tafsir of the verse 20 of Surah al-Nisa', al-Durr al-Manthur 2:133.
The wording of the hadith here has been confused in the copies: in the printed edition it reads "alfa mi'in, yaʻni alfayn" (two thousand mi'in, that is two thousand), and its corrector noted in the margin that this is in some copies, and that in some of them it reads "alfan wa-mi'in." The narration of al-Suyuti, quoting al-Tabari, reads: "alfan wa-mi'atayn, yaʻni alfayn" (one thousand and two hundred, that is two thousand).]]

This is the final part of al-Tabari's commentary on Surah 3, verse 14 (Jami al-Bayan).

"And my view is that all of this is a distortion, and that the correct wording is the one found in the narration of al-Hakim."]]
* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And the branded horses﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed over the meaning of "al-musawwamah" (the branded/marked ones).

Some of them said: it means the grazing ones.

Those who said this include:

6729 - Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "al-Khayl al-musawwamah" – he said: the grazing ones, which graze.

6730 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the like of it.

6731 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, the like of it.

6732 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Sufyan informed us, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: it is the grazing ones, meaning: the pasturing ones.

6733 - Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Talhah al-Qanad, who said: I heard Abdullah ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Abza say: the grazing ones.

6734 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, saying: my paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: "al-khayl al-musawwamah" – he said: the grazing ones.

6735 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, from al-Hasan: "al-khayl al-musawwamah" – those let loose to graze.

6736 - I was told by Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', his saying: "al-khayl al-musawwamah" – he said: the grazing horses.

6737 - I was told by Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Layth, from Mujahid: that he used to say: the grazing horses.

* *
Others said: "al-musawwamah" means the beautiful ones.

Those who said this include:

6738 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib, who said: Mujahid said: "al-musawwamah" – the well-proportioned (al-mutahhamah).

6739 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Habib ibn Abi Thabit, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "And the branded horses," he said: the well-proportioned, the beautiful.

6740 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: "And the branded horses," he said: well-proportioned in beauty.

6741 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

6742 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Nu'aym narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Habib, from Mujahid: well-proportioned.

6743 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub narrated to us, from Bashir ibn Abi 'Amr al-Khawlani, who said: I asked 'Ikrimah about "al-khayl al-musawwamah," and he said: its tasweem is its beauty. [[The report 6743: "Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Muqri'" is 'Abdullah ibn Yazid al-'Adawi, mawla of the family of 'Umar, listed in al-Tahdhib. "Bashir ibn Abi 'Amr al-Khawlani" is Egyptian; he narrated from 'Ikrimah and al-Walid ibn Qays al-Tujibi, and from him narrated Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub, al-Layth and Ibn Lahi'ah. He is trustworthy, listed in al-Tahdhib and in Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/377. In the printed and manuscript editions it reads "Bishr ibn Abi 'Amr al-Khawlani," which is an error.]]

6744 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Sa'id ibn Abi Ayyub informed me, from Bashir ibn Abi 'Amr al-Khawlani, who said: I heard 'Ikrimah say: "al-khayl al-musawwamah" – its tasweem: beauty. [[Report 6744: the manuscript and printed edition read "Bishr ibn Abi 'Amr al-Khawlani," which is an error. See the previous note.]]

6745 - Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "al-khayl al-musawwamah wa al-an'am" – the pleasing ones.

* *
This report was also narrated to me by 'Amr ibn Hammad other than Musa, who said: the grazing ones.

* *
Others said: "al-khayl al-musawwamah" means the marked ones.

Those who said this include:

6746 - Ali ibn Dawud narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas: "wa al-khayl al-musawwamah" – meaning: the marked ones.

6747 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "wa al-khayl al-musawwamah" – its sima is its shiyah. [["Al-shiyah": everything that differs in colour from the whole body of a horse or other animal; its plural is "shiyat," and its root is "al-washy" (embroidery). Washa al-thawb washyan and shiyah: he beautified it, decorated it, and embroidered it.]]

6748 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying: "wa al-khayl al-musawwamah," he said: the shiyah of horses on their faces.

* *
Others said: "al-musawwamah" means those prepared for jihad.

Those who said this include:

6749 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: "wa al-khayl al-musawwamah," he said: those prepared for jihad.

* *
Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views regarding His saying "wa al-khayl al-musawwamah" is: the marked ones by their markings (al-shiyat), the beautiful, those whose beauty pleases whoever sees them. This is because "al-tasweem" in the speech of the Arabs means "al-i'lam" (marking). Beautiful horses are marked by Allah's marking them with the beauty of their colours, markings and forms, and they are also "al-mutahhamah" (well-proportioned). On this is the saying of the poet Nabighah of the Banu Dhubyan describing horses:

*with lean ones like arrows, marked (musawwamat), upon them a band like jinn...*
[[From his Diwan, p. 86, from his poem composed when Banu 'Abs killed Nadlah al-Asadi, and Banu Asad killed two men from them. 'Uyaynah ibn Hisn wanted to aid Banu 'Abs and to remove Banu Asad from the alliance of Banu Dhubyan, so he said: "If you attempt wickedness against Asad, then I am not of you and you are not of me." Then he praised them and mentioned their days, including: "They advanced against Ghassan with a vast host, wide in its ranks, broad and tumultuous..." "With every cunning one like a lion that rises above the joints of a sturdy, strong man..." and "and lean ones like arrows..." The printed and manuscript editions read "bi-simar" (with spears), but it is not a description of horses to say "simar"; "simar" means spears. "Al-dumr" (with damma and sukun) is the plural of "damir," whose regular plural is "dawamir," but the plural of such adjectives of the form "fa'il" is sometimes formed on "fu'l," like "bazil/buzl" and "sharif/sharf," which they assimilated to "fu'ul" because of the similarity in the number of letters. Then Banu Tamim lighten "fu'l" by making its middle letter quiescent. "Al-qidah" is the plural of "qidh" (with kasra and sukun): the arrow when it has been straightened and feathered. Horses are likened to it when they are lean.]] He means by "musawwamat": the marked ones. And Labid's saying:

*And at dawn at the valley of al-Qurnatayn we came upon them, a crowd, among which the tasweem gleams...*
[[From the diwan of the poem, p. 16, verse 41. The verse is among verses in which he mentions his own honour and that of his people. Its opening: "I am a man whose lineage of 'Amir protected my oppression, though my adversaries have deviated against me..." Among its lines: "Hawi, al-Dhahab, and before it a day at Barqat Rahrahan, a noble one..." "Hawi," "al-Dhahab," "Barqat Rahrahan," and "Qa' al-Qurnatayn" are all places where his people had battles in which they were victorious. "Atinahum" – the pronoun refers to the horses, on which their riders were mounted; the other pronoun refers to his enemies. "Zujal" is the plural of "zujlah" (damma and sukun): a group of people and horses. The version in his diwan reads "rahwan," meaning successive. "Khilaluha": its middle.]]

So the meaning of those who interpreted it as "al-mutahhamah," "al-mu'lamah," and "al-ra'i'ah" is one.

* *
As for the view of those who interpreted it as "the grazing ones," they went by the saying of one who says: "asamtu al-mashiyah fa-ana usimuha isamah" – when one causes livestock to graze on herbage and vegetation, as Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And from it is a tree wherein you pasture (tusimun)﴾ [Surah al-Nahl: 10], meaning: you graze. Among its usage is al-Akhtal's saying:

*Like the son of Bazi'ah, or another like him – woe to you, O son of the one who pastures camels!*
[[From his diwan, p. 159; al-Aghani 8:319; Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara' p. 418; it appears again in the tafsir 14:60 (Bulaq). It is from his poem in which he raised the mention of 'Ikrimah ibn Rib'i al-Fayyad, secretary of Bishr ibn Marwan. Al-Akhtal came to Hawshab ibn Ruwaym al-Shaybani and said: "I have taken on two burdens so that I may preserve the blood of my people!" He rebuked him. Then he went to Shaddad ibn al-Bizi'ah (i.e. Shaddad ibn al-Mundhir al-Dhuhli, brother of al-Hudayn ibn al-Mundhir, bearer of 'Ali's banner at Siffin), who questioned him, and Shaddad apologised to him. Then he went to 'Ikrimah al-Fayyad and informed him of what the two men had said to him. 'Ikrimah said: "As for me, I shall neither rebuke you nor apologise to you, but I will give you one of them as gold and the other as goods." Al-Akhtal praised him and satirised the two men, saying: "You have truly bestowed favour upon all of Rabi'ah, and sufficed every weak, forsaken one..." "Tight-fisted in both hands, withholding from giving, whose qualities are not moistened by moisture..." "Like Ibn al-Bazi'ah, or another like him – woe to you, O son of the pasturer of camels!" "When you ask the miser, you dumbfound him, while the generous one you see rejoicing like the proud..." In the manuscript it reads "awla ibn musiyamah," which is an error. "Ibn al-Bazi'ah" is "Ibn Bazi'ah" in al-Tabari's narration here. "Al-Bazi'ah" (on the pattern of "karimah") is the mother of Shaddad ibn al-Mundhir. I had vocalised her name in the diminutive in Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara', following what is vocalised with the pen in Tarikh al-Tabari, but here I correct that, and I hold that I was right here: "al-Bazi'ah" is a pleasant, beautiful, clever-hearted slave-girl. Shaddad ibn Bazi'ah was mentioned before Ziyad ibn Abi Sufyan regarding witnesses; he was Ziyad ibn Sumayyah, son of his father. When it was said "Ibn Bazi'ah," he said: "Does this one have a father to be attributed to? Throw this one out of the witnesses." It was said to him: "He is the brother of Hudayn ibn al-Mundhir!" He said: "Then attribute him to his father." This reached Shaddad, who said: "Woe to me, son of the adulteress! Is his mother not more knowledgeable than he about his father? By God, he is only attributed to his mother Sumayyah!" (Tarikh al-Tabari 6:151).]]

meaning: the herder of camels. And if it is intended that the livestock were the ones that grazed, it is said: "sامت al-mashiyah tasumu sawman" (the livestock grazed), and so it is said "ibl sa'imah" (grazing camels), meaning: pasturing. However, it is not common in their speech to say "sawwamtu al-mashiyah" meaning "I caused the livestock to graze"; rather, when that is intended, one says "asamtuha."

* *
Given that this is so, directing the interpretation of "al-musawwamah" to mean "the marked ones," in accordance with the meanings mentioned above, is more correct.

* *
As for what Ibn Zayd said, that they are those prepared in the way of Allah, that interpretation of the meaning of "al-musawwamah" is far from correct.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And the cattle and the tilth﴾

Abu Ja'far said: "Al-an'am" is the plural of "na'am," and they are the eight pairs He mentioned in His Book: from sheep, goats, cattle and camels. [[In Surah al-An'am: 142-144.]]

* *
As for "al-harth," it is the crops. [[See the interpretation of "al-harth" above, 4:240-243, 397.]]

* *
The meaning of the speech is: the love of desires has been made attractive to people: of women, of sons, of such and such, of such and such, and of cattle and tilth.

* *
On the interpretation of His words: ﴿That is the enjoyment of the worldly life; and Allah has with Him the finest return (husn al-ma'ab) (14)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be majestic, "that," He means all that was mentioned in this verse: women, sons, the heaped-up hoards of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle and tilth. He used "that" to refer to all of them together. This shows that "that" encompasses many things of differing meanings, and is used to refer to all of them.

* *
As for His words, "the enjoyment of the worldly life," this is a report from Allah that all of that is something whose people enjoy in this world while they live; they provide for themselves by it and make it a means of their livelihood and a cause for fulfilling their desires, the love of which has been made attractive to them in the immediate world, without its being a provision for their return and a means of drawing near to their Lord, except what is spent in His way and what is given in accordance with His command. [[In the manuscript: "zayyana lahum hamlaha," which is one of the errors of our copyist. See the interpretation of "al-mata'" above, 1:539-540; then 3:55; then 5:260.]]

* *
As for His words, "and Allah has with Him the finest return," He means by it, may His majesty be exalted: and with Allah is the finest return, that is, the finest place of return, as narrated:

6750 - Musa narrated to me, saying: 'Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "and Allah has with Him the finest return," he says: the finest place of return, and it is Paradise.

* *
"Al-ma'ab" is a verbal noun on the pattern of "mafal," from the saying: "ab al-rajul ilayna" when the man returned; "yu'ib it'aban, awbatan, aybatan, and ma'aban." ["Aybah," with fatha or kasra on the hamza and sukun on the ya', is an alternation from the waw.] Except that the position of the fa' in it is hamzated, and the 'ayn has been changed from waw to alif because its vowel was shifted to fatha. Since its proper vowel was to be fatha, and its vowel was transferred to the letter before it, the first radical, it became an alif, just as in "qala," where the 'ayn of the verb became an alif because its proper vowel is fatha. "Al-ma'ab" is like "al-maqal," "al-ma'ad," and "al-majal," all of them of the pattern "mafal," whose 'ayn vowel is transferred to the fa', and whose waw or ya' becomes an alif because of the fatha before it. [In the manuscript and printed edition: "al-mahal" with ha', but the correct reading is what is written here.]

* *
Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: How is it said "and Allah has with Him the finest return," when you know what He has there on that day of painful punishment and severe retribution?

It is said: That is specifically meant for a certain category of people, and the meaning is: and Allah has with Him the finest return for those who fear their Lord. He has informed us of this in the verse that follows.

* *
If it is asked: What is "the finest return"? It is said: It is what He, may His praise be majestic, described it as: the return to gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and to pure spouses and the good pleasure of Allah.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who fear God is gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever, and pure spouses, and approval from God." And God is Seeing of His servants﴾ (3:15).

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: Say, O Muhammad, to the people whom the love of desires—of women, sons, and all the other things our Lord, may His praise be exalted, has mentioned—has been made attractive to: "Shall I inform you" (ﺃﺅﻧﺒﺌﻜﻢ), that is, shall I tell you and make you know (see the explanation of "anba" in what has preceded, 1:488-489), "of something better than that," meaning: of something better and more excellent for you "than that," meaning than what has been made attractive to you in this world, the love of its desires: women, sons, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, and the various kinds of wealth that are the enjoyment of this worldly life.

* *

Then the scholars of Arabic grammar (ahl al-'arabiyya) differed over the point at which the interrogation in this statement ends.

Some of them said: It ends at His saying "than that," and then the report begins concerning what is for those who fear God in their Lord's presence, so it is said: "For those who fear God in their Lord's presence are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever." Therefore "the gardens" is in the nominative.

* *

Whoever holds this view does not permit anything other than the nominative in His saying "gardens beneath which rivers flow," because it is the predicate of an inceptive subject, not subordinated to "something better." The genitive would be permissible if it were so subordinated. Although it is an inceptive predicate according to them, it serves to clarify the meaning of the "better" which God, mighty and majestic, commanded His Prophet ﷺ to say to the people: "Shall I inform you of it?" On this view, "the gardens" is in the nominative by virtue of the preposition "for" (lam) in His saying "for those who fear God in their Lord's presence."

* *

Others among them said something similar to this view, except that they said: If the "lam" in His saying "for those who fear" is taken as connected to "informing," then "the gardens" may be either genitive or nominative: the genitive by way of agreement with "something better," and the nominative on the basis that His saying "for those who fear God" is the predicate of an inceptive subject, as we have explained earlier.

* *

Others said: Rather, the end of the interrogation is His saying "in their Lord's presence," and then a new beginning: "gardens beneath which rivers flow." They said: The sense of the statement is: "Say, shall I inform you of something better than that for those who fear God in their Lord's presence?" Then it is as if it were said: "What is for them?" or "What is that?" [In the printed and manuscript editions, after this, and it was said, the text reads: "Or on the basis that it is said: What is for them? Or what is that?" It is clear that this is a repetition without meaning, and is a copyist's error, the copyist being very prone to error. For this reason I have removed it from the main text.] Then he said: it is "gardens beneath which rivers flow," etc.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views in my opinion is the view of those who hold that the interrogation ends at His saying "something better than that," and that what follows is a new subject concerning whom the gardens belong to, by His saying "for those who fear God in their Lord's presence are gardens." Thus its form is that of a statement, and it explains the "better" about which it was said: "Shall I inform you of it?" [In the manuscript and printed editions: "inform you of it," and the correct reading is what I have written; see the detailed treatment in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:195-198.] Then no pronoun is needed in the sentence. Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari said: As for His saying "abiding therein forever," it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (qat').

[At this point ends the last section of the old division from which our copy was taken, and in it the following text appears: "It is followed by: As for His saying: ﴿abiding therein forever﴾, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier. And God bless our master Muhammad, the Prophet, and his pure family, and greet them abundantly." It is followed by the text: "In the name of God, the Most Compassionate, the Most Merciful." "Qat'" means the circumstantial (hal), as explained in 2:392 and its references; see also the glossary of terms in the earlier volumes, and then see what follows: p. 270, note 3.]

* *

The meaning of His saying "for those who fear God" is: for those who fear God and obey Him by performing His obligations and avoiding His prohibitions. [See the explanation of "taqwa" in the lexical indexes under the root w-q-y.] "In their Lord's presence" means: for them are gardens beneath which rivers flow in their Lord's presence.

* *

"The gardens" are orchards, and we have demonstrated this with evidence earlier. That His saying "beneath which rivers flow" means: beneath the trees; that "abiding" therein means lasting permanence therein; and that "pure spouses" are the women of Paradise, who have been purified from every impurity found among the women of the worldly people, such as menstruation, seminal emission, urine, postnatal bleeding, and similar impurities—this has been sufficiently treated so that it need not be repeated here. [See the explanation of "paradise" in the earlier volumes: 1:384, then 5:535, 542; and of "abiding" in 1:397-398, 2:286, 4:317, 5:429; and of "pure spouses" in 1:395-397.]

* *

As for His saying "and approval from God," it means: and the good pleasure of God. It is a verbal noun from the speaker's saying: "God was pleased with so-and-so, and he is pleased with him, approval (rida)," with the defective forms "ridwanan, rudwanan, and mardatan." As for "ruduwan" with a dammah on the ra', it is the dialect of the Qays tribe, and 'Asim used to recite it thus.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His praise be exalted, mentioned among what He prepared for those who fear Him in His presence of good things His approval, because His approval is the highest of the honored stations of the people of Paradise, as:

6751 - Ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri narrated to me, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir, from Jabir ibn 'Abdullah, who said: When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, God, blessed and exalted, says: "I shall give you something better than this!" They say: "O our Lord, what is better than this?" He says: "My approval."

[The report: 6751 - This is a report that is not traced to the Prophet, but its corroboration from the traced report is what al-Bukhari narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ said: God says to the people of Paradise: 'O people of Paradise!' They say: 'Here we are, our Lord, at Your service and pleasure!' He says: 'Are you content?' They say: 'And why would we not be content, when You have given us what You have not given anyone of Your creation!' He says: 'I shall give you something better than that!' They say: 'O Lord, what is better than that?' He says: 'I shall let My approval descend upon you, so I shall never be angry with you again.'"

The hafiz Ibn Hajar alluded to the hadith of Jabir in Fath al-Bari 11:364, saying: "In al-Bazzar, and Ibn Hibban authenticated it." I did not find its wording.]

* *

As for His saying "and God is Seeing of His servants," it means: God is possessed of sight regarding the one among His servants who fears Him and is mindful of Him [see the explanation of "Seeing" in the earlier volumes: 2:140, 376, 506; then 5:76, 167], so that He obeys Him and prefers what is with Him—what He has mentioned He has prepared for those who fear Him—over the love of what has been made attractive to him in the immediate life of this world, namely the desires of women, sons, and all else that He, exalted is His mention, has enumerated. And He is aware of the one who does not fear Him in awe, but disobeys Him, obeys Satan, and prefers what has been made attractive to him in this world, the love of the desires of women, sons, and wealth, over the lasting bliss that is with Him. God, exalted is His mention, is Knowing of every group among them, so that He will repay each of them on their return to Him: the doer of good according to his good, and the doer of evil according to his evil.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 16:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words: ﴿Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."﴾ (3:16)

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of that is: Say, "Shall I inform you of something better than that? For those who are mindful of God [are] gardens..." Those who say, "Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins and protect us from the punishment of the Fire."

* *

The phrase "those who say" may be read in two ways in terms of i'rab (grammatical analysis): in the genitive, as a restatement of the first "those" (alladhina), or in the nominative, as a new subject (mubtada'), since it begins another verse distinct from the one containing the first "those." Its nominative reading would then be like the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Indeed, God has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾ (9:111), and then He said, at the beginning of the following verse: ﴿The repentant, the worshippers﴾ (9:112). Had it come in the genitive, it would also have been permissible. [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1: 198.]]

* *

The meaning of His words "those who say, 'Our Lord, indeed we have believed, so forgive us our sins'": those who say, "Indeed we have affirmed You and Your Prophet and what he has brought from You." "So forgive us our sins": that is, conceal our sins for us by Your pardon of them and Your leaving off punishing us for them. "And protect us from the punishment of the Fire": repel from us Your punishment of us by the Fire, that You not punish us with it. The meaning of that is only: "Do not punish us, O our Lord, with the Fire."

They specifically asked that He protect them from the punishment of the Fire, because whoever is distanced from the Fire on that Day has indeed attained salvation from God's punishment and a good return.

* *

The origin of His words "qina" (protect us) is from the speaker's saying, "God protected so-and-so from such-and-such," meaning: He repelled it from him, so He "protects" him (yaqihi). When a petitioner asks with that, he says, "qinī such-and-such" (protect me from such-and-such). [[See the explanation of "qina" and "waqa" above, 4: 206.]]

The interpretation of His words: ﴿the patient, the truthful, the obedient, and those who spend﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "the patient" (al-sabirin) He means those who are patient in adversity (al-ba'saa') and hardship (al-darraa') and at the time of battle (hina al-ba's).

By "the truthful" (al-sadiqin) He means those who are truthful to God in their words, by confirming their affirmation of Him and of His Messenger and of what he brought from Him, by acting upon what He commanded them and refraining from what He forbade them.

By "the obedient" (al-qanitin) He means those who obey Him.

* *

We have already explained all these words and their meanings, with evidence supporting what we have said about them and with reports from those who spoke about them in the past, in a way that makes repeating it in this place unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "al-sabirin" earlier, 2:11, then 3:214, 349 = and the explanation of "al-sadiqin" earlier, 3:356 = and the explanation of "al-qanitin" earlier, 2:538, 539, then 5:228-237.]]

* *

Qatada used to say about this:

6752 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: "the patient, the truthful, the obedient, and those who spend." "The truthful": people whose mouths speak truth, and whose hearts and tongues are upright, and who are truthful in secret and in public. "The patient": people who are patient in obedience to God and patient in refraining from His prohibitions. "The obedient": those who obey God.

* *

As for "those who spend" (al-munfiqin), they are those who pay the zakat of their wealth and place it as God commanded them to place it, and who spend their wealth in the ways God, may His majesty be exalted, has permitted them to spend it. [[See the explanation of "spending" (al-infaq) earlier, 5:555, 580.]]

* *

As for "the patient" and "the truthful" and the rest of these words, they are in the genitive case (makhfud), as a response to His words: "those who say, 'Our Lord, indeed we have believed.'" The genitive in these words indicates that His words "those who say" are also in the genitive, as a response to His words: "for those who are mindful of God, with their Lord." [[See Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:199.]]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿and those who seek forgiveness at dawn﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed concerning the people to whom this description applies.

Some of them said: They are those who pray at the dawns.

Mention of those who said that:

6753 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "and those who seek forgiveness at dawn," they are the people of prayer.

6754 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Qatada: "and those who seek forgiveness at dawn," he said: They pray at the dawns.

* *

Others said: They are those who seek forgiveness.

Mention of those who said that:

6755 - Ibn WakI' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Hurayth ibn Abi Mutar, from Ibrahim ibn Hatib, from his father, who said: I heard a man at the time of dawn in a corner of the mosque, saying: "My Lord, You commanded me and I obeyed You, and this is the dawn, so forgive me." I looked and it was Ibn Mas'ud. [[The report 6755: "Hurayth ibn Abi Mutar 'Amr al-Fazari, Abu 'Amr al-Hannat," who narrated from al-Sha'bi and al-Hakam ibn 'Utayba, and from whom Sharik, Ibn Numayr and Waki' narrated. Ibn Ma'in said: "Nothing," and Abu Hatim said: "weak in narration." al-Bukhari said: "There is concern about him; he is not strong according to them." al-Bukhari cited him in "al-Adahi," and he is mentioned in al-Tahdhib. As for "Ibrahim ibn Hatib," I have not found a biography for him or for his father "Hatib," and I fear there is an error or omission in his name, and that this "Hatib" is "Hatib ibn Abi Balta'a," companion of the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The report with this exact wording is in Tafsir Ibn Kathir 2:113, and he said nothing about it.]]

6756 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: I asked 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yazid ibn Jabir about the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: "and those who seek forgiveness at dawn." He said: Sulayman ibn Musa narrated to me, saying: Nafi' narrated to us: that Ibn 'Umar used to spend the night in prayer, then he would say: "O Nafi', has dawn come?" He would say: "No." So he would return to prayer. When I said: "Yes!" he would sit and seek forgiveness and supplicate until morning.

6757 - Ibn Wakic' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from some Basrans, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: We were commanded to seek forgiveness at dawn seventy times.

6758 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Zayd ibn al-Hubab narrated to us, saying: Abu Ya'qub al-Dabbi narrated to us, saying: I heard Ja'far ibn Muhammad say: Whoever prays at night and then seeks forgiveness at the end of the night seventy times is recorded among those who seek forgiveness at dawn.

* *

Others said: They are those who attend the dawn prayer in congregation.

Mention of those who said that:

6759 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn Muslima, brother of al-Qa'nabi, narrated to us, saying: [[His brother is "Abd Allah ibn Maslama ibn Qa'nab al-Harithi al-Qa'nabi," a teacher of al-Bukhari, Muslim and Abu Dawud.]] Ya'qub ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated to us, saying: I said to Zayd ibn Aslam: Who are "those who seek forgiveness at dawn"? He said: They are those who attend the dawn prayer.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings concerning the interpretation of His words "and those who seek forgiveness at dawn" is the saying of the one who said: They are those who ask their Lord to conceal their shame for them.

* *

"Bil-asḥar" is the plural of "saḥar."

* *
