The most evident meaning of this is that their asking Him is by way of supplication. It may also be that it means: their seeking His forgiveness through deeds and prayer, except that the most evident meaning is what we have mentioned, which is supplication.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 18:

The explanation of His saying: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those possessed of knowledge — standing firm in justice. There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise.﴾ (18)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels bear witness, and those possessed of knowledge.

"The angels" is conjoined with them to the name "God," and "that He" is in the accusative governed by "bore witness."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Some of the Basran grammarians interpreted His saying "God bears witness" as "God decreed," and read "the angels" in the nominative, meaning: "and the angels are witnesses, and those possessed of knowledge." [[This is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah in Majaz al-Qur'an 1:89, though al-Tabari does not name him but says "some Basrans." See al-Tabari's refutation of it on p. 272.]]

* *

Likewise, the reciters of the Muslim community read "that He" with a fathah on the alif, according to what I have mentioned of "bore witness" governing the first "anna," and read the second "inna" with a kasrah on its alif, as the start of a new clause. [[That is, in His saying at the beginning of the next verse: "Indeed, the religion with God is Islam."]] Except that some later Arabic grammarians [[This is al-Kisa'i; see al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:200, and al-Qurtubi's tafsir 4:42-43.]] read all of it with fathah on both alifs, meaning: "God bears witness that there is no god but He, and that the religion with God is Islam." He thus conjoined "that the religion" to the first "that He," with the conjunction "wa" omitted, though it is intended in speech. He argued for this by saying that Ibn 'Abbas read it: ﴿God bears witness that there is no god but He﴾ and so on, then read "that the religion" with a kasrah on the first "inna" and a fathah on the second "anna," with "bore witness" governing it, making the first "inna" an interjected clause that governs nothing. He also claimed that Ibn Mas'ud read "God bears witness that there is no god but He" with fathah on "anna" and kasrah on "inna" in "Indeed the religion with God is Islam," meaning that "bearing witness" governs the first "anna," while the second "anna" begins a new clause. He claimed that by reading both with fathah he combined the readings of Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud. [[See al-Farra', Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:199-200.]] By his reading, which differs from what I have described, he opposed all the reciters of the Muslim community, earlier and later, on the basis of an interpretation he attributed to Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud, claiming they had said it and recited it so. What he attributed to them is not known from any sound or weak report. Sufficient as evidence of the error of his reading is that it departs from the reading of the Muslim community.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Since the matter is as we have described regarding the reading, the correct view is fathah on the alif of the first "anna" and kasrah on the alif of the second "inna," that is, in His saying "Indeed, the religion with God is Islam," as a fresh start.

* *

It has been transmitted from al-Suddi, in interpreting this, a statement that points to the soundness of the reading mentioned by the grammarians regarding the fathah of "anna" in "that the religion." It is:

6760 – Musa related to me, saying: 'Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, regarding "God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels…" down to "There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise," he said: God bears witness, He and the angels and the scholars among mankind, that the religion with God is Islam. [[In the printed edition: "Indeed God bears witness," but in the manuscript: "that God bears witness," and the correct reading seems to be what I have adopted.]]

* *

This interpretation shows that "the witnessing" governs only the second "anna" in His saying "that the religion with God is Islam." On this interpretation, two possible readings are permissible for the first "anna": [[In the printed edition: "in the first 'anna' there are two possibilities," but the manuscript has a small "in" written above "anna," as if he meant "permissible in the first," with "anna" omitted, since there is no mark indicating an addition. So I have dropped it.]]

— One: that the first be in the accusative as a conditional clause, meaning: God bore witness that He is one; so it is fathah, which in the view of some grammarians is in the genitive and in the view of others in the accusative, and "the witnessing" governs the second "anna," as if you said: God bears witness that the religion with God is Islam, because He is one; then "because He is one" is moved forward, and you read it with fathah on that interpretation.

— Two: that the first "inna" be kasrah as a beginning, since it is an interjected clause, and "the witnessing" falls on the second "anna." The meaning of the speech is: God bears witness — indeed He, there is no god but He — and the angels, that the religion with God is Islam, like the speaker who says: "I bear witness — indeed I am truthful — that you are free of what is reproached in you," so the first "inna" is kasrah because it is interjected, and "the witnessing" falls on the second "anna." [[See the explanation of this also in al-Farra', Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:200.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: As for His saying "standing firm in justice," it means: He is the one who maintains justice among His creatures.

* *

"Al-qist" is justice, from the expressions "he is muqsit" and "he has acted justly" when one is just.

* *

"Standing" (qa'iman) is in the accusative by way of qat' (separation). [["Qat'" here means the circumstantial accusative (hal), as mentioned shortly before, p. 261, note 3. al-Farra' explained it in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:200, saying: "It is in the accusative by way of qat', because it is indefinite and qualifies a definite noun." He showed that the circumstantial is a kind of qualifier: one says "Zayd the rider came to me" in the nominative, making it a qualifier because a definite is qualified by a definite; but if one qualifies with an indefinite, one may not say "Zayd rider came to me" in the nominative, unless one makes it an apposition to the definite. The correct approach is to detach it from the qualifier's case and put it in the accusative, making it a hal. That is the explanation of qat' as hal, and I did not find its explanation in any book at hand. It is, I think, Kufan terminology, given al-Farra's usage and al-Tabari's frequent mention of it in the Kufan views, as noted above, and as will become clear from al-Tabari's later statement "that it is a hal" in the following sentences.]]

* *

Some Basran grammarians claimed it was a circumstantial clause of the "He" in "there is no god but He."

* *

Some Kufan grammarians claimed it was a circumstantial clause of the name "God" in His saying "God bears witness," so the meaning is: God, standing firm in justice, bears witness that there is no god but He. It has been mentioned that in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud it is likewise: ﴿and those possessed of knowledge, standing firm in justice﴾, with the article removed from "standing," making it indefinite while qualifying a definite, so it is in the accusative.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The more correct of the two views in my opinion is the view of those who made it a qat' [a circumstantial accusative], [[See note above.]] as a qualifier of God, may His praise be exalted, since "the angels and those possessed of knowledge" are conjoined to it. Likewise, the sound view is that His saying "standing" is a hal of Him.

* *

As for the interpretation of His saying "There is no god but He, the Mighty, the Wise," it denies that anything deserves worship other than the One who has no partner in His dominion. [[His word "al-'ubudah" is a verbal noun from "'abada," on the pattern of "sharafa"; one says "he is an 'abd between 'ubudah, 'ubudiyyah and 'abadiyyah." Al-Tabari used it in this sense earlier, 3:347, see the note there. It means submission and humbling, so here too he seems to mean: nothing deserves submission and humbling except the One who has no partner in His dominion. Ibn al-Qatta' in Kitab al-Af'al 2:337 explicitly states the verbal noun of "'abada ya'buduhu" is "'ibadah, 'ubudah, 'ubudiyyah," meaning to serve and to be humbled utterly.]]

* *

"The Mighty" means He whom nothing He wills can resist, and whom no one who punishes or takes vengeance on Him can overcome. [[See the explanation of "al-'Aziz" earlier, 3:88, and then p. 168-169, and the language indices (ʿ-z-z).]] "The Wise" means in His management, so that no defect enters it. [[See the explanation of "al-Hakim" earlier, 3:88, and the language indices (ḥ-k-m).]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: God, may His praise be exalted, meant by this verse only the denial of what the Christians who argued with the Messenger of God ﷺ about Jesus ascribed to him of sonship, and what all the people of polytheism ascribed to Him of having a partner, and their taking gods besides Him. So God informed them about Himself that He is the Creator of all that is other than Him, and that He is the Lord of everything that every unbeliever and polytheist took as a lord besides Him, and that this is what He, His angels, and the people of knowledge among His creatures bear witness to. He, may His praise be exalted, began with Himself, exalting Himself and declaring Himself free of what the polytheists who were mentioned ascribed to Him, just as He prescribed for His servants to begin their affairs by mentioning Him before mentioning others, disciplining His creation thereby.

The purpose of the speech is information about the witness of those whom He approved among His creatures and who sanctified Him: [[In the manuscript and printed edition: "they glorified Him," which seems to mean "beginning with mention of Him, exalted be He," but if so it would be better to say "they mentioned Him"; from the context of his speech I infer the meaning of declaring Him free, so I consider it a corruption of "sanctified Him."]] His angels and the scholars among His servants. He informed them that His angels, whom those who worship other than Him among the polytheists venerate and many of them worship, and the people of knowledge among them, [[The sentence reads: "He informed them that His angels... and the people of knowledge among them, deny..."]] deny what they persist in of their unbelief and their saying about Jesus, and the saying of whoever takes a lord other than Him among all creatures. [[His saying "and the saying of whoever takes a lord other than Him" is in the accusative, conjoined to "their saying," and it is the object of "deny."]] So He said: The angels and those possessed of knowledge bear witness that there is no god but He, and that everyone who takes a lord besides God is a liar, as an argument from Him to His Prophet, peace be upon him, against those of the delegation of Najran who argued with him about Jesus.

* *

He interjected, by mentioning God and His attribute, as I have explained, [[In the printed edition: "as we explain," which is an error; the correct reading is from the manuscript, though he did not read it well.]] just as He, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿And know that whatever you gain of spoil, a fifth of it is for God﴾ [Surat al-Anfal: 41], beginning the speech with His name. [[The meaning is that the mention of "God" in this verse of al-Anfal is merely the opening of speech. Abu Ja'far said in its explanation (10:3 Bulaq): "Some said: His saying 'a fifth of it is for God' is the key of the speech, and to God belong this world and the next and what is in them. The meaning of the speech is: a fifth of it is for the Messenger." This is the view al-Tabari preferred in the explanation of that verse.]] Likewise He began with His name and praise of Himself, bearing witness to what we have described: denying divinity of anything other than Him, and rejecting the polytheists who associated others with Him.

* *

As for what the one whose words we mentioned said, that by "He bears witness" He meant "He decreed," this is not known in the language of the Arabs or non-Arabs, because "witnessing" is one meaning and "decreeing" is another. [[This is a rebuttal of Abu 'Ubaydah's view in Majaz al-Qur'an, as mentioned on p. 267, note 2.]]

* *

Something like what we have said about this has been related from some earlier scholars.

6761 – Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding "God bears witness that there is no god but He, and the angels and those possessed of knowledge": contrary to what they said — meaning: contrary to what the Christian delegation of Najran said — "standing firm in justice," that is, with justice. [[Report 6761 is what Ibn Hisham related from Ibn Ishaq's Sirah 2:227; it is among the remaining reports whose last, previously, was no. 6649.]]

6762 – al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "with justice": with justice.

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of "ad-din" (religion, here: submission and humbling) in this passage is obedience and abasement, from the words of the poet: [[I have not yet identified who the poet is.]]

"And the day of al-Hazn, when Ma'add was gathered, and all the people, except us, were subservient (dinan)."

[[This verse will come in the commentary at 26:115 (Bulaq edition), together with a verse we will mention there. The second half of the first verse is in Lisan (d-y-n) and in other lexicons. I doubt the soundness of this verse, and I did not know what "yawm al-hazn" refers to. I think "hushidat" is "hushirat," from "al-hashr." The verse that follows it is: "We disobeyed the decree of the tyrant, until we attacked al-Jurf with a thousand marked horsemen."

I have corrected it here as such, from the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra', the manuscript commentary on Surah Qaf. In the printed text of the commentary (26:115) it reads "sahibna al-khawf akuffan" (we accompanied fear with palms), which is meaningless. Al-Tabari, after this verse there, said: "It is also narrated as al-Hawf. He said: by the tyrant he meant al-Mundhir, because of his rule." The correct reading is "al-Jurf." If that is so, my strong opinion is that it is "al-Jurf" as I have written it (with a damma on the jim and sukun on the ra'), a place in al-Hira where the dwellings of al-Mundhir were.

In al-Tabari there, "sahibna" is an error. "Sabbahna" comes from the expression "sabbaha al-qawm sharran," meaning he brought them evil, and "sabbahtuhum al-khayl," meaning horses came to them at dawn. "Alfan" means a thousand horses with their riders. "Al-mu'allim" is a horseman who makes a mark for himself as a sign of the brave, or a horse marked with a sign. The meaning: we raided the stronghold of al-Mundhir the tyrant and his dwellings, and attacked them at dawn, destroying his dwellings upon him. In al-Tabari it reads "hurmat al-jabbar" (the sanctity of the tyrant), and the correction is from the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra', as I have already noted.]]

He means by this: obedient in a manner of humiliation. From it is the saying of al-Qatami:

"Nawwar used to make you (tadinuka) subservient to all manner of states." [[His Diwan: 15, from good verses in which he described his beloved, named "Umayma," and named her "Janub" in the verse Tabari transmitted, and named her "Nawwar," and it is narrated as "Zalum." Among what he said:

"She shot the vitals of your heart, after Janub had been subjecting you to her (tadinuka) states."

"Ay" means: she does to you all sorts of deeds. It is said: she enslaves you, or: she tortured you. Or tadinuka: she requites you.

"And I see the young women are only a madness, resembling the winds, changing their hues.

So when they call you to their uncle, do not respond, for there purity finds no place.

A lineage that increases your lowliness in their sight, and humiliation upon the prime of their youth.

When they promise, they are the most false of promisers, and the most fair of those who swear and break their oaths.

And when they see in youth some softness, they seem to make your ropes into threads!"

This is brilliant, forward-moving poetry.]]

He means: makes you abased. And the saying of al-A'sha Maymun ibn Qays:

"He subdued (dana) the Rabab when they disliked the religion (ad-din), by raiding and assault." [[The explanation of this verse has passed earlier, 3:571.]]

By his words "dana" he means: made submissive, and by "they disliked the religion" he means obedience.

* *

Likewise "Islam," which is submission with humility and lowliness; its verb is "aslama," meaning he entered into peace (silm), as one says "aqhata al-qawm" when they entered into drought, and "arba'u" when they entered into spring. Likewise "aslamu" means they entered into peace, which is submission with humility and abandoning resistance. [[See the explanation of "Islam" and "silm" earlier, 2:510, 511; then 3:73, 74, 92, 94, 110; then 4:251–255.]]

* *

Since that is so, the interpretation of His words, "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam," is: indeed, the obedience which is obedience with Him is obedience to Him, and the affirmation by tongues and hearts of His servitude and humility, and their submission to Him in obedience to what He commands and forbids, and their humbling themselves to Him in that, without arrogance toward Him, and without deviating from Him, without associating anyone of His creation with Him in worship and divinity. [[In the printed edition: "in worship and divinity"; I have kept what is in the manuscript, and the use of "ubudah" was already noted earlier, p. 271, note 1. "Uluhah, ilahah, uluhiyyah": worship; see what passed at 1:124 and before.]]

* *

Many people of interpretation have said something like what we have said.

Those who said that:

6763 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam." Islam is the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the affirmation of what came from Allah [[The phrase "what came" refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), as if he said: "the testimony that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," and the testimony is not complete without it, may my father and mother be ransom for him. Thus al-Suyuti mentioned it verbatim in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:12, and attributed it also to Abd ibn Humayd in this wording.]] and it is the religion of Allah which He prescribed for Himself, sent His messengers with, and guided His friends to. He accepts nothing other than it and rewards with nothing but it.

6764 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: Abu al-'Aliyah narrated to us regarding His words: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam." He said: "Islam is sincerity to Allah alone, worshipping Him without partner, establishing prayer, giving zakat, and the rest of the obligations follow from this."

6765 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "We have submitted (aslamna)" [Surah al-Hujurat: 14], he said: we entered into peace (as-silm), and abandoned war. [[The report 6765 will come in the commentary on Surah al-Hujurat (26:90 Bulaq), in a different wording at length: "Aslamna: we surrendered, we entered into peace, and abandoned fighting and combat." Its chain is the same.]]

6766 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam," that is: what you are upon, O Muhammad, of monotheism toward the Lord and affirmation of the messengers. [[The report 6766: Ibn Hisham narrated it in his Sirah from Ibn Ishaq 2:227, dropping the "min" in "min al-tawhid." It is among the remaining reports whose last is number 6761.]]

* *

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: those who were given the Gospel, which is "the Scripture" mentioned by God in this verse, did not differ regarding the matter of Jesus, and their fabrication against God in what they said about him of the statements by which their disagreement multiplied, and their word was scattered, and some of them separated from others, until some of them made the blood of others lawful, ="except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves," meaning: except after they knew the truth in what they differed about concerning his matter, and became certain that in what they say about him of grave slander they are liars. [[See the explanation of "al-baghy" earlier, 2:342; then the explanation of similar verses earlier, 4:281, 282.]] Thus God informed His servants that they committed what they committed of falsehood, and said of the speech which is disbelief in God, knowing the error of what they said, and that they did not say that out of ignorance of its error, but they said it and differed in it the difference they are upon, transgressing of some against others, and seeking leadership, kingship and authority, as:

6767 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words: "And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves," he said: Abu al-'Aliyah said: except after the Scripture and knowledge had come to them, "out of rivalry among themselves," he says: rivalry over worldly things, and seeking its kingship and authority, so they killed one another over the world, after they had been the scholars of people.

6768 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Ibn Umar: that he used to recite this verse often: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam. And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of rivalry among themselves," he says: rivalry over worldly things, and seeking its kingship and authority. "From their side, by Allah, we were brought! It did not matter to us who would rule over us, after he establishes among us the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Prophet, but we were brought from their side."

6769 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: When Moses was near death, he summoned seventy rabbis of the Children of Israel, and entrusted them with the Torah, making them trustees over it, each rabbi a portion of it, [[This wording appears the same in the manuscript, and in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:13, as if he said: he entrusted each rabbi a portion of it. It is a phrase with its own difficulties.]] and Moses appointed Joshua son of Nun as successor. When the first generation passed, and the second passed, and the third passed, division occurred among them — those who had been given knowledge from the sons of those seventy — until they shed blood among themselves, and evil and disagreement occurred. All of that came from those who had been given knowledge, out of rivalry among themselves over the world, seeking its authority, kingship, treasures and adornment. So God empowered their tyrants over them. Then God said: "Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam," to His words: "and Allah is Seer of the servants."

* *

The saying of al-Rabi' ibn Anas here indicates that he understood that the one meant by "those who were given the Scripture did not differ" is the Jews of the Children of Israel, to the exclusion of the Christians among them and others. [[His words "to the exclusion of the Christians among them" mean: to the exclusion of the Christians among those given knowledge. As for "and others," meaning: to the exclusion of non-Christians among those given knowledge, pointing to what came in the report of Ibn Umar above, no. 6768.]]

* *

Others directed this toward the meaning that it refers to the Christians who were given the Gospel.

Those who said that:

6770 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "And those who were given the Scripture did not differ except after knowledge had come to them," which came to you, meaning that God is the One with no partner, "out of rivalry among themselves," meaning by this the Christians. [[The report 6770: Ibn Hisham narrated it in his Sirah from Ibn Ishaq 2:227; it is the remainder of the reports whose last is number 6766. His words "meaning by this the Christians" are not in Ibn Hisham, and seem to be Tabari's own explanation of the report.]]

* *

The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning (19).﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this He means: whoever denies the proofs of God and His signs which He set up as a reminder for those who understand, and as evidence for those who take heed and remember, then indeed God records against him his deeds which he did in this world, and will recompense him for them in the Hereafter. He, may His praise be exalted, is "swift in reckoning," meaning: swift in enumeration. The meaning is only that He is a Guardian over every doer of his deed, with no need for a count as His creatures count with their palms, or retain with their hearts, but He preserves that for them, without effort or burden, and without the struggle that others undergo in reckoning. [[See the meaning of "kufr" and "ayat" earlier in the language indexes (k-f-r) and (a-b-y). The explanation of "swift in reckoning" earlier: 4:207, and also 4:274, 275; then: this: 101, 102.]]

* *

Just as we have said regarding the meaning of "swift in reckoning," Mujahid used to say:

6771 – Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: "And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning," he said: His enumeration of them.

6772 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "And whoever disbelieves in the signs of Allah, then indeed Allah is swift in reckoning," His enumeration.

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿And if they dispute with you, say: "I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me."﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: "If they dispute with you, O Muhammad, the group of Christians of Najran concerning the matter of ʿIsa (Jesus), may God's blessings be upon him, and argue with you about it falsely" [[See the explanation of "ḥājja" in earlier passages: 3:120, 201; then 5:429, 430.]], then say: "I have surrendered to God alone, with my tongue, my heart, and all my limbs." God, may His remembrance be exalted, specifically commanded him to say "I have submitted my face to God" because the face is the most honourable of the son of Adam's limbs. In it lie his radiance and dignity. So when his face submits to something, the limbs of his body that are lower than it in honour have submitted to it too. [[See the explanation of "aslama wajhahu" in earlier passages: 2:510–512, and the explanation of "al-Islam" in the references I mentioned just before, p. 275, note 1.]]

* *

As for His words "and so have those who follow me," He means: "and let those who follow me also submit their faces to God along with me." The "man" (wa-man) is conjoined to the "tā'" in "aslamtu" (I have submitted), as in the following report:

6773 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "If they dispute with you," that is, with what they bring to you of falsehood, from their saying "We created, we did, we made, we commanded," for these are but false analogies, whose truth they know. [Then] "say: I have submitted my face to God, and so have those who follow me." [[The report 6773: Ibn Hisham relates it in his Sirah 2:227, and it is among the remaining reports, the last of which is number 6770.]]

* *

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿And say to those who were given the Book and to the unlettered: "Have you submitted?" If they submit, then they are guided.﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: "Say" (O Muhammad) "to those who were given the Book," from the Jews and Christians, "and to the unlettered," who have no Book, from the idolaters of the Arabs: "Have you submitted?" That is, say to them: Have you singled out monotheism and purified worship and divinity for the Lord of the worlds, apart from all the rivals and partners that you associate with Him in your worship of them and your acknowledgement of their lordship? [["Ashrāk" is the plural of "sharīk" (partner), as one says yatīm and aytām, sharīf and ashrāf. Its regular plural would be shurakāʾ, like sharafāʾ.]] And you know that there is no lord other than Him and no god besides Him. "If they submit," that is, if they yield to the singling out of God's oneness and the purification of worship and divinity for Him, "then they are guided," meaning: they have found the path of truth and taken the road of right guidance. [[See the explanation of the words of this verse in the earlier linguistic indexes. For the explanation of "al-ummiyyīn," see the earlier passage 257–259, the report number 5827, and in al-Tabari's own words 5:441, note 2.]]

* *

If someone says: How is it said, "If they submit, then they are guided," following an interrogative? Is it permissible in speech to say to a man, "Will you stand? If you stand, I will honour you"?

It is said: That is permissible when the speech is intended as a command, even if it takes the form of a question, as He, may His praise be exalted, said: ﴿And it hinders you from the remembrance of God and from prayer. So will you not desist?﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 91], meaning: desist. And as He, may His praise be exalted, related about the disciples, that they said to ʿIsa: ﴿O ʿIsa son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ [Surah al-Ma'idah: 112]. It is only a request, as a man says, "Will you refrain from us?" meaning: refrain from us. And as a man says to another, "Where, where?" meaning: stay, do not move. For this reason the interrogative was given the conditional form, just as the command was, in the reading of ʿAbd Allah: ﴿Shall I direct you to a commerce that will save you from a painful punishment? Believe (āminū)﴾ [Surah al-Saff: 10, 11]. He explained it with the command, [[Al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:202 says: "He explained (hal adullukum) with the imperative," and what is here is also close to the correct. Moreover, our reading in our codex is "you believe in God" (tu'minūna billāh) in place of "āminū" in the reading of ʿAbd Allah.]] while in our reading it is in the form of a statement. So the conditional in our reading is on His words "Shall I direct you," and in the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is on His words "Believe," which is in the imperative, because that is the explanation. [[This is the exact text of what is in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:202.]]

* *

Some of the people of interpretation said things in agreement with the meaning of what we have said:

6774 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salama related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "And say to those who were given the Book and the unlettered," who have no Book, "Have you submitted? If they submit, then they are guided," the verse. [[Report 6774: Ibn Hisham in his Sirah, from Ibn Ishaq, 2:227; it is the remainder of the reports, the last of which is number 6773.]]

6775 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "And say to those who were given the Book and the unlettered," he said: The unlettered are those who do not write.

* *

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿But if they turn away, then your duty is only to deliver the message, and God is seeing of the servants.﴾ (3:20)**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "But if they turn away," He means: if they turn their backs, averting from what you call them to of Islam and the purification of monotheism for God, Lord of the worlds [[See the explanation of "tawallā" in earlier passages: 2:162–164, 298, 299; then 3:115, 131; then 4:237.]], then you are only a messenger who delivers, and it is not incumbent upon you except to deliver the message to those to whom I have sent you from among My creation, and to fulfil what I have charged you with of My obedience. "And God is seeing of the servants" [[See the explanation of "seeing of the servants" in the earlier passage just before: 262. And the references in the footnote: 3.]], meaning: God has knowledge of those of His servants who accept what I have sent you with to them and obey you by submitting to Islam, and of those who turn away from it, averting, so that they reject what I sent you with to them, and disobey you by refusing Islam.

* *

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be exalted, "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God," that is: they deny the proofs and signs of God and call them lies, from the people of the two Books, the Torah and the Gospel, as in:

6776 - Ibn Humayd related to me, saying: Salama related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: Then He gathered the people of the two Books together and mentioned what they had introduced and innovated, of the Jews and the Christians, and said: "Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right," up to His words "Say: O God, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will." [[Report 6776: Ibn Hisham 2:227, from the remaining earlier reports, the last of which is number 6774.]]

* *

As for His words "and kill the prophets without right," He means by it: that they used to kill the messengers of God who were sent to them to forbid what they did of disobedience to God, and to undertake what they used to undertake of matters that God had already warned them against in their books, such as Zechariah and his son Yahya, and others like them among the prophets of God. [[See the explanation of "killing the prophets without right" in earlier passages: 2:140–142.]]

**The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And they kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: The readers (*qurra'*, transmitters of the Qur'anic readings) differed concerning the recitation of this.

The majority of readers of Madina, the Hijaz, Basra, Kufa and the rest of the reading centres recited it: ﴿وَيَقْتُلُونَ الَّذِينَ يَأْمُرُونَ بِالْقِسْطِ﴾ (*wa-yaqtuluna*, "and they kill"), meaning killing.

Some later readers of Kufa recited it: ﴿وَيُقَاتِلُونَ﴾ (*wa-yuqatiluna*, "and they fight"), meaning fighting. He did so by interpreting it in light of the reading of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, and claimed that in the codex of ʿAbdullah it is: ﴿وَقَاتَلُوا﴾ (*wa-qatalu*, "and they fought"). So he recited, on the basis of that interpretation, ﴿وَيُقَاتِلُونَ﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is the recitation of those who read "*wa-yaqtuluna*" (and they kill), because the authoritative readers unanimously agree upon it, [[Thus it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition. It is a phrase I do not approve of; I think its correct form is "*li-ijmaʿi al-ḥujjati min al-qurrāʾi ʿalā al-qirāʾati bihi*" (because of the consensus of the authoritative readers upon reciting it thus). See al-Farrāʾ, *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān* 1: 202, on the explanation of this reading of al-Kisaʾi.]] along with the interpretation transmitted from the people of interpretation (*ahl al-taʾwil*) that this is its meaning.

Mention of those who said so:

6777 – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿĪsā, from Ibn Abi Najīh, from Maʿqil ibn Abi Miskīn, concerning the words of God: ﴿and they kill the prophets without right, and they kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾. He said: Revelation used to come to the Children of Israel, and they would admonish [their people] – and no book used to come to them – and they would be killed. [[Thus al-Ṭabarī's text states it. Al-Durr al-Manthūr 2: 13 transmits it likewise, and I have added from it what is between the brackets. The meaning of his wording is that revelation used to come to the prophets of the Children of Israel, as is clear in the other reports narrated by al-Baghawī in his *Tafsīr* (margin of Ibn Kathīr) 2: 117, 118, and al-Qurṭubī 4: 46.]] Then men who followed them and believed them would stand up, admonish their people, and be killed. These are the ones who enjoin justice among mankind.

6778 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from Qatāda, concerning His words: ﴿and they kill the prophets without right, and they kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾. He said: These are the People of the Book. The followers of the prophets used to forbid them and admonish them, and they would kill them.

6779 – Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: Al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said, concerning His words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾: There were people from the Children of Israel who did not read the Book; revelation used to come to them, and they would admonish their people, and be killed for that. [[His words "*kāna nāsun min banī isrāʾīla … kāna al-waḥyu yaʾtīhim*" (there were people of the Children of Israel … revelation used to come to them), with the first "kāna" (was) omitted in its predicate, is an eloquent and well-formed expression in Arabic, to which I have drawn attention several times before.]] They are the ones who enjoin justice among mankind.

6780 – Abu ʿUbayd al-Raṣṣābī Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ narrated to me, saying: Ibn Ḥimyar narrated to us, saying: Abu al-Ḥasan, mawlā of the Banū Asad, narrated to us, from Makḥūl, from Qabīṣa ibn Dhuʾayb al-Khuzāʿī, from Abu ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ, who said: I said: O Messenger of God, which people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection? He said: "A man who killed a prophet, or a man who commanded what is evil and forbade what is good." Then the Messenger of God ﷺ recited: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God and kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾ [[In the manuscript and printed edition, and in al-Durr al-Manthūr 2: 13: "*alladhīna yaqtulūna al-nabiyyīna*", while in other sources it is "*wa-yaqtulūna*". I have adopted what appears in the narration of Ibn Abi Ḥātim, as cited by Ibn Kathīr in his *Tafsīr* 2: 118, and it is the text of the recitation.]] until he reached: ﴿and they have no helpers﴾. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O Abu ʿUbayda, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day, in a single hour!" Then a hundred and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, and they commanded those who killed them with what is right and forbade them what is wrong, so they were all killed by the end of that day; and they are the ones whom God, mighty and majestic, mentioned.

[[The report: 6780 – "Abū ʿUbayd al-Wiṣābī: Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ al-Ḥimṣī", whose biography has passed under no. 129 (and see what will come under no. 7009). In the isnad there was "*ḥaddathanī Abū ʿUbayd al-Wiṣābī, qāla ḥaddathanā Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ*" (narrated to me Abu ʿUbayd al-Wiṣābī, he said: narrated to us Muḥammad ibn Ḥafṣ). My brother Sayyid Aḥmad preferred that it is an error, and he was right; and the better course would have been to omit "qāla ḥaddathanā" (he said: narrated to us) from that isnad.

In the printed edition and manuscript here it reads "Abū ʿUbayd al-Raṣāfī Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar", and the correct form is from Ibn Kathīr's *Tafsīr* 2: 118. "Ibn Ḥimyar" is: "Muḥammad ibn Ḥimyar ibn Unays al-Quḍāʿī", who narrated from Ibrāhīm from Abu ʿAbla, and Muḥammad ibn Ziyād al-Alhānī, Muʿāwiya ibn Sallām and others. Aḥmad was asked about him and said: "I know nothing but good." Ibn Maʿīn said: "Trustworthy (*thiqa*)." Ibn Abi Ḥātim said: "His hadith is written down but not used as proof." In the printed edition it reads "Ibn Ḥumayd" with a dal, which is an error; the correct form is from Ibn Kathīr and al-Baghawī in the margin, 2: 118. He is biographed in *al-Tahdhīb*. Ibn Abi Ḥātim, in *al-Jarḥ wa-l-taʿdīl*, mentioned this Abu ʿUbayd al-Wiṣābī and said: "I met him and sought to hear from him, but some people of Ḥimṣ told me: he is not truthful; and he did not meet Muḥammad ibn Ḥimyar, so I left him." As for "Abu al-Ḥasan, mawlā of the Banū Asad", the Ḥāfiẓ (Ibn Ḥajar) mentioned him in *Lisān al-Mīzān* 6: 364, saying: "Abu al-Ḥasan al-Asadī: narrated to us from him Abu Kurayb. Unknown (*majhūl*)." Abu Kurayb did not narrate from him alone, for Muḥammad ibn Ḥimyar also narrated from him. In his narration it reads "mawlā of the Banū Asad, from Makḥūl", and al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Abi Ḥātim recorded his hadith; Abu Ḥātim mentioned him among those whose name is not known. Al-Baghawī also transmitted it by way of Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Ḥannān al-Kalbī, from Muḥammad ibn Ḥimyar (in the margin of Ibn Kathīr's *Tafsīr* 2: 118).]]

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of the verse, then, is: Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of God, and kill the prophets without right, and kill those who command them with justice in the matter of God's command and prohibition, those who forbid them from killing the prophets of God and from committing His disobedience.

* * *

**The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment (21). Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no helpers (22)﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: He means by His words, exalted is His praise: "So give them tidings of a painful punishment": inform them, O Muhammad, and make them aware, that for them, with God, is a punishment that is painful to them, that is, agonizing. [[See the meaning of "*bashshir*" (give tidings) above, 1: 383; 2: 393; 3: 221. Then the explanation of "*alīm*" (painful) above, 1: 283; 2: 140, 377, 469, 540; 3: 330.]]

* * *

As for His words: "Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter," by "those" He means those who disbelieve in the signs of God. The meaning of that is: those we have mentioned are "those whose deeds have become worthless", that is: their deeds have become void [[See the explanation of "*ḥabiṭa*" (became void) above, 4: 317.]] "in this world and the Hereafter." As for in this world, they gained no praise or commendation from people, because they were upon error and falsehood, and God did not raise for them any mention by it; rather He cursed them and exposed their concealments, and displayed on the tongues of His prophets and messengers, in His books that He sent down to them, what they used to hide of their vile deeds, so He left them with blame for as long as the world lasts. That is its voiding in this world. As for the Hereafter, He has prepared for them therein the punishment described in His Book, and He informed His servants that their deeds will become dust (*būran*), with no reward for them, because they were disbelief in God, so the recompense of its people is eternal abiding in the Hellfire.

* * *

As for His words: "and they will have no helpers," He means: these people have no helper from God who will help them if He takes vengeance upon them for their past crimes and their audacity against Him, so as to rescue them from Him. [[See the explanation of "*naṣr*" (help) above, 2: 35, 36, 489, 564; then 5: 581.]]

**The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And they kill those who enjoin justice among mankind﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: The readers (*qurra'*, transmitters of the Qur'anic readings) differed concerning the recitation of this.

The majority of readers of Madina, the Hijaz, Basra, Kufa and the rest of the reading centres recited it: ﴿وَيَقْتُلُونَ الَّذِينَ يَأْمُرُونَ بِالْقِسْطِ﴾ (*wa-yaqtuluna*, "and they kill"), meaning killing.

Some later readers of Kufa recited it: ﴿وَيُقَاتِلُونَ﴾ (*wa-yuqatiluna*, "and they fight"), meaning fighting. He did so by interpreting it in light of the reading of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud, and claimed that in the codex of ʿAbdullah it is: ﴿وَقَاتَلُوا﴾ (*wa-qatalu*, "and they fought"). So he recited, on the basis of that interpretation, ﴿وَيُقَاتِلُونَ﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation in this matter, in our view, is the recitation of those who read "*wa-yaqtuluna*" (and they kill), because the authoritative readers unanimously agree upon it, [[Thus it stands in the manuscript and the printed edition. It is a phrase I do not approve of; I think its correct form is "*li-ijmaʿi al-ḥujjati min al-qurrāʾi ʿalā al-qirāʾati bihi*" (because of the consensus of the authoritative readers upon reciting it thus). See al-Farrāʾ, *Maʿānī al-Qurʾān* 1: 202, on the explanation of this reading of al-Kisaʾi.]] along with the interpretation transmitted from the people of interpretation (*ahl al-taʾwil*) that this is its meaning.

He said: Revelation used to come to the Children of Israel, and they would admonish [their people] – and no book used to come to them – and they would be killed. [[Thus al-Ṭabarī's text states it. The meaning of his wording is that revelation used to come to the prophets of the Children of Israel, as is clear in the other reports narrated by al-Baghawī in his *Tafsīr* (margin of Ibn Kathīr) 2: 117, 118, and al-Qurṭubī 4: 46.]] Then men who followed them and believed them would stand up, admonish their people, and be killed. Then the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "O Abu ʿUbayda, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day, in a single hour!" Then a hundred and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up, and they commanded those who killed them with what is right and forbade them what is wrong, so they were all killed by the end of that day; and they are the ones whom God, mighty and majestic, mentioned.

**The Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 3, Verse 23**

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, being invited to the Book of God so that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turn away while they are opposed?﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: ﴿Have you not seen﴾, O Muhammad,¹ ﴿those who were given a portion of the Scripture﴾, meaning those who were given a share of the Book, ﴿being invited to the Book of God﴾.²

* *

The people of ta'wil (interpretation) differed regarding "the Book" that God meant by His words, ﴿being invited to the Book of God﴾.

Some said: It is the Torah. He invited them to accept what is in it, since the sects that claimed to follow the scriptures acknowledged it and what is in it, that it was the rulings of God before some of it was abrogated.

Those who said this:

6781. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of Zayd ibn Thabit, narrated to me, saying: Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Ikrimah narrated to me, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered the house of study (bayt al-midras)³ upon a group of Jews, and he invited them to God. Nu'aym ibn Amr⁴ and al-Harith ibn Zayd said to him: "Upon what religion are you, O Muhammad?" He said: "Upon the creed and religion of Abraham." They said: "Abraham was a Jew!" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Come to the Torah; it is between us and you!" But they refused him. So God, mighty and majestic, revealed: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, being invited to the Book of God so that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turn away while they are opposed?﴾ up to His words: ﴿what they used to fabricate﴾.

6782. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, client of the family of Zayd, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr or Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) entered the house of study, and he mentioned something similar, except that he said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: "Come, both of you, to the Torah,"⁵ and he also said: God revealed concerning them both: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture﴾, and the rest of the narration is like the narration of Abu Kurayb.

*Note on the two reports, 6781 and 6782:* Ibn Hisham, Sirah 2:201; Tafsir al-Qurtubi 4:50; Tafsir al-Baghawi (in the margin of Ibn Kathir) 2:119; al-Durr al-Manthur 2:14.

* *

Others said: Rather, it is the Book of God that He sent down to Muhammad, and only a group of them was invited to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) so that he might judge between them with truth, but they refused.

Those who said this:

6783. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, being invited to the Book of God so that it may judge between them, and then a faction of them turn away while they are opposed?﴾ They are the enemies of God, the Jews. They were invited to the Book of God so that it might judge between them, and to His Prophet so that he might judge between them, while they found it written among them in the Torah and the Gospel, yet they turned away from it while they were opposed.

6784. al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Qatada: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture﴾, the verse. He said: They are the Jews; they were invited to the Book of God and to His Prophet, and they found it written among them, then they turned away while they were opposed!

6785. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words: ﴿Have you not seen those who were given a portion of the Scripture, being invited to the Book of God so that it may judge between them﴾. He said: The People of the Book were invited to a book so that it might judge between them with truth, in what occurs, and in the hudud (prescribed punishments).⁶ The Prophet (ﷺ) used to invite them to Islam, and they turned away from it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the interpretations, in my view, is to say: God, mighty and majestic, informs of a group of Jews, those who lived among the emigrants of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in his time, who had been given knowledge of the Torah, that they were invited to the Book of God, which they acknowledged to be from God, which is the Torah, regarding some matter over which they and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) disputed. It may be that their dispute was over the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ) and his prophethood, and then they were invited to the Torah's ruling on it, but they refused to comply. It may be that it was over the matter of Abraham, the Friend of the Merciful, and his religion. It may be that it was over what they were invited to regarding Islam and affirming it. It may be that it was over a hadd. For all of these are matters over which they disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and he invited them to the ruling of the Torah concerning them, but they refused to comply and some of them concealed it.

There is no indication in the verse as to which of these it was,⁷ so it is permissible to say: it is this and not that. We have no need to know that, because the matter to which they were invited to judge is something that was obligatory upon them to comply with in their religion, and they refused it. So God, mighty and majestic, informed of their apostasy, their denial of what is in their Book, and their repudiation of what had been taken as a covenant and binding pledge from them to uphold and act upon. Their denial of Muhammad and what he brought of truth is therefore no different from their denial of Moses and what he brought, while they claim to adhere to him and affirm him.

* *

As for His words: ﴿then a faction of them turn away while they are opposed﴾,⁸ it means: they turn their backs on the Book of God to which they were invited to judge, turning away from it and departing, while they know its reality and its proof.⁹

* *

We have only said that this "Book" is the Torah because they were deniers of the Qur'an, and they were affirmers of the Torah according to their claim. So the proof against them, by their denial of what they themselves claim to affirm, is more forceful and more decisive in removing excuse.

**Translator's notes (for the study app):**

1. Ibn Jarir's own wording addresses the Prophet directly; the verse is an address to him.
2. The editors' footnotes were not included in the body of the commentary above.

**The interpretation of His words:** ﴿That is because they said, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."  And their fabrications have deluded them in their religion.﴾ (3:24)

His, exalted is His praise, saying "because they said," means: because these people who were called to the Book of God so that it might judge between them in truth, regarding what they disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ), refused to accept the ruling of the Torah and what it contains of truth, because of their saying [[The phrase "because of their saying" explains the meaning of the particle *bi-* in His words "That is because they said." For its explanation and clarification, see what preceded at 2:139, in the commentary on His words, "That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of God."]] "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days," which are forty days, the days in which they worshipped the calf [[See the commentary on their saying "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days" above, 2:274–278.]], after which our Lord will bring us out of it. They were deceived by this, "by what they used to fabricate," meaning: by the lies and falsehoods they invented, in their claim that they are the sons of God and His beloved, and that God had promised their father Jacob that He would not admit any of his descendants into the Fire except as a *tahillat al-qasam* (the fulfilment of an oath). [[*Tahillat* (with a *fatḥa* on the *tā'*, a *kasra* on the *ḥā'*, and a doubled *lām* with a *fatḥa*) is what expiates one's oath. It is said: "He did not do this matter except *tahillat al-qasam*," meaning he did not do it except to the extent that it dissolves his oath and releases him from it, without exceeding in that act. The meaning is that the Fire will touch them only with a brief touch, like the fulfilment of the oath of one who swears.]] So God refuted them concerning all of these statements of theirs, and informed His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) that they are the people of the Fire, where they will abide forever, unlike the believers in God, His messengers, and what they brought from Him.

* *

Those who engage in *ta'wil* (interpretation of the Qur'an's meaning) have said things similar to what we have said.

**Mention of those who said so:**

6786 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding "That is because they said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days'": They said, "The Fire will not touch us except for the *tahillat al-qasam* during which we worshipped the calf, and then the oath and the punishment will end for us." God, mighty and majestic, said: "And their fabrications have deluded them in their religion," meaning they said, "We are the sons of God and His beloved."

6787 – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words, "That is because they said, 'The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days'," the verse. He said: They said, "We will not be punished in the Fire except for forty days." He said: meaning the Jews. He said: And Qatadah said the like of it. He said: These are the days in which they set up the calf. God, mighty and majestic, says: "And their fabrications have deluded them in their religion," when they said, "We are the sons of God and His beloved."

6788 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: Mujahid said regarding His words, "And their fabrications have deluded them in their religion": What deluded them was their saying, "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days."

The interpretation of His words: ﴿So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt, and every soul is paid in full what it has earned, while they will not be wronged?﴾ (3:25)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is His praise, "So how will it be when We gather them," [He means]: what will be the state of those people who said this statement, and did what they did of turning away from the Book of God, deceiving themselves regarding their Lord, and fabricating lies? This is a severe warning from God, Mighty and Majestic, to them, and a harsh threat.

He only means by His words, "So how will it be when We gather them" (and the verse): how great will be what they encounter of the punishment of God and His retribution upon them, when He gathers them for a Day on which every doer is paid the reward of his deed in accordance with what he deserves, without being wronged therein, for no one is punished therein except for what he committed, and no one is held to account except for what he did. The good-doer is recompensed for his good, and the evildoer for his evil; none of His creatures fears on that day any injustice or diminution from Him.

[[See the words of this verse explained earlier, and seek them in the lexical indices of the previous volumes.]]

* *

If someone says: Why is it said, "So how will it be when We gather them for a Day about which there is no doubt," and not "on a Day about which there is no doubt"?

It is said: Because the meaning of the "lam" (li-) in this place differs from the meaning of "fi" (in). For if "fi" were in place of "lam," the sense of the statement would be: "So how will it be when We gather them on the Day of Resurrection, and what punishment and retribution will there be for them?" That meaning is not conveyed by the particle "lam," but its meaning with "lam" is: "So how will it be when We gather them for what will take place on a Day about which there is no doubt, and for what will occur on that Day of God's decisive judgment between His creatures; what punishment and painful torment will they have then?" So with the "lam" in "li-yawmin la rayba fihi" there is an implied verb and an understood object, whose mention has been omitted; the indication given by the entry of "lam" upon "yawm" suffices for it. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "the mention of which has been omitted finally by the indication of the entry of lam upon yawm" — a phrase devoid of meaning. The evident sense, as we have established it, is: "the indication of the entry of lam upon yawm sufficed for it." The "min" was placed after it as is his habit in such constructions throughout his work.]] This is not the case with "fi," and therefore "lam" was chosen and attached to "yawm" rather than "fi." [[See the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 202, 203, whose wording there is: "You say in speech: They gathered for Thursday (li-yawm al-khamis), as if the lam implies a hidden verb with 'Thursday,' as if they gathered for what will be on Thursday. But if you say: They gathered on Thursday (fi yawm al-khamis), you have not implied a verb. And His words: We gathered them for a Day about which there is no doubt, i.e., for reckoning and recompense."]]

* *

As for the interpretation of His words, "about which there is no doubt," it means: there is no doubt about its coming. We have shown that this is so by sufficient proofs, together with mention of those who have said this in its interpretation earlier, in a manner that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[See what has preceded: 1: 228, 378; then 6: 221.]]

* *

By His words, "and every soul is paid in full" (wuffiyat), meaning that God pays in full, "what it has earned," that is, what it has done of good and evil [[See the explanation of "kasb" earlier: 2: 273, 274; 3: 101, 128; 4: 449; 6: 131.]], "while they will not be wronged," meaning that He does not diminish the reward of the good-doer for his good, nor does He punish the evildoer for other than his crime.

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Say: O Allah﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: As for the interpretation of "Say: O Allah," it means: Say, O Muhammad: "O Allah."

* *

The grammarians (ahl al-'arabiyya, the scholars of Arabic) differed over the vowelling of the "m" in "Allahumma" (O Allah). It is a vocative, and the rule for a singular vocative that is not annexed is that it takes the nominative case. They also differed over the addition of the "m" to it, since the original form is "Allah" without the "m."

Some of them said: The two "m"s were added to it because it is not called with "ya" (O) in the way that names without an "alif" or "lam" are called. Names without an "alif" or "lam" are called with "ya," as when one says, "Ya Zayd, ya 'Amr." He said: So the "m" was placed in it as a substitute for "ya," just as they say "fam" (mouth), "abnam" (son), "hum," "zurqum," [[In the printed edition and the manuscript it reads "wa-dum" (and dum), and the first is certainly an error, and its correction will come a few lines later, when he mentions all three together: "fam, wa-abnam, wa-hum," in line with the printed edition's treatment there of the manuscript's text, so as to agree with what he wrote here.

As for his words "wa-hum" (and hum), I do not know of an acceptable explanation for it. This word appears in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:203, and it will also appear in the same form a few lines later. I checked it in my manuscript copy of Ma'ani al-Qur'an, and it is indeed "wa-hum," with a mark over the "m" resembling a shadda in both manuscripts, which the printed edition omitted. The editor of Ma'ani al-Qur'an commented on it with the following text: (Apparently he means the pronoun "hum," whose original form is "hum," as it is the plural of "hu," so the "w" was dropped and the plural "m" added, although this view is attributed to the Basrans. See Radi's commentary on al-Kafiya in the section on pronouns.) Some editors of Tafsir al-Tabari commented: (His words "wa-dum": so it is in the copies, and the two words are "dum" and "hum," perhaps distorted from "abnam" and "dalhum" or "dalqum," from the words to which the "m" was added at the end. al-Suyuti mentioned them in al-Muzhir 2:135.)

What the editors of Ma'ani al-Qur'an said does not hold, because the "m" in "hum," although in one respect an added letter, was brought for a meaning different from what the addition in "fam" and "abnam" conveys, and for a reason over which the grammarians disagreed greatly. As for what the editor of al-Tabari said, that it is distorted from "dalhum or dalqum," it is nothing, because the printed and manuscript copies of al-Tabari agree on it, and it is strange that the distortion should coincide with the distortion of two copies of Ma'ani al-Qur'an from which al-Tabari quotes the text of its words. After all this, I find myself utterly unable to know the origin of this word, or any acceptable way of correcting, distorting or reading it. I have investigated its case as far as I could, but I have gained nothing from the research. Perhaps I will find with others the knowledge that God has withheld from me, and over every possessor of knowledge is one more knowing.]] and "wustahum" [["Zurqum" and "wusthum" (both with a damma on the first, a sukun on the second, and a damma on the third): a man is zurqum and a woman is zurqum, meaning extremely blue-eyed. When the "alif" is removed from its beginning, the "m" is added at its end. Likewise "rajul sathum" and "imra'a sathum" (a man and a woman): the buttocks, meaning one with a very large buttock and a large rear, who has had done to him what he did to his companion. A rajiz (rhymed-verse) poet said of a woman:

She is not kahla' (with kohl-black eyes), but zurqum,
Nor rashha' (with a large-hipped gait), but sut-hum.]] and the like, from names and epithets from which a letter is removed and an "m" substituted in its place. He said: In the same way, the "ya" with which names of the type we have described are called was removed from "Allahumma," and the "m" was placed as its substitute at the end of the name.

* *

Others denied this view and said: We have heard the Arabs call "Allahumma" with "ya," as they call it without the "m." They said: If the one who said this were correct in his claim, the Arabs would not have used "ya," since they brought the substitute for it. [[In the printed edition: "lam tadkhulhu al-'arab ya" (the Arabs did not enter it with ya); in the manuscript: "lam tadkhulhu al-'arsa ya," which is a hasty error by the copyist. I have restored both to their proper form.]] They recited as evidence from Arab usage:

What harm is it to you, to say whenever
You pray or glorify, "O Allahuma"?
Return to us our sheikh, safe.

[[Its composer is unknown. The verses appear in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:203, al-Zajaji's al-Jumal p. 177, al-Insaf p. 151, al-Khizana 1:359, Lisan al-'Arab (under *alh*), and other books of Arabic and grammar, with variations in their transmission. They were brought as evidence for the addition of "ma" after "ya-Allahumma," so in the version of some of them it is "ya Allahumma ma." After the verses comes an addition the Kufans added:

From wherever, however, and wherever,
We shall never lack its goodness.]]

It is also transmitted as: "Sabbahta aw kabbarta" (you glorified or magnified). They said: We have not seen the Arabs add this "m" except lightened, in defective names like "fam," "abnam," and "hum." [[In the printed edition: "like fam, dam, and hum." I have kept the manuscript text, which agrees with al-Farra's wording in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:203; it is his exact words.]] They said: We hold that it is a word to which "umm" was joined, meaning "O Allah, may You protect us with good." It became common in speech and mixed into it. They said: The damma in the "h" of the "hamza" of "umm," when it was dropped, moved to what preceded it. They said: We hold that the Arabs' saying "halumma ilayna" (come to us) is similar: it was originally "hal," to which "umm" was joined, and it was left in its fatha. They said: Some Arabs say, when the "m" is dropped: "Ya Allahu, ighfir li" and "Ya 'Allahu, ighfir li," with the "hamza" of "Allah" pronounced once and its connection pronounced another time. Whoever drops it treats it according to its original form, since it is an "alif-lam," like the "alif-lam" that enter definite nouns as extra letters. Whoever pronounces the hamza imagines that it belongs to the root, since it is not dropped from it. They recited in support of the hamza on its "alif":

Blessed is he, and whoever named him
After Your name, O Allahumma, O Allah.

[[Its composer is unknown. The two verses appear in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:203; al-Insaf p. 150; and Lisan al-'Arab (under *alh*).]]

They said: "Allahumma" has become common in speech, so that its "m" was lightened in some dialects, and they recited:

Like the oath of Abu Riyah,
Which the greatest of them hears, the Allahum.

[[It is the verse of al-A'sha. Diwan p. 193; Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:203; al-Khizana 1:345; Lisan al-'Arab (under *alh*), and others. It is from a qasida in which he reproaches the Banu Jahdar, with whom he had a feud, which he mentions in several of his poems. Before the verse, and the opening of the qasida, is:

Did you not see Iram and 'Ad?
Night and day destroyed them.

They perished, and when they were consumed,
Qudar followed in their footsteps.

Like the oath . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .

"Awdaha bi-ha" means destroyed them and took them away. His words, "fa-lamma an ta'adaw," come from the saying "ta'adda al-qawm ta'adiyan wa-ta'addaw ta'adiyan," meaning they died in succession. Its root is from "adda al-rajul," meaning that a man was armed, having put on his weapon of war, that is, they took up their arms and fought until they were wiped out. Whoever explained "ta'adaw" in the verse as meaning "they helped each other and multiplied" has erred and taken a false path. He says: When Iram and 'Ad perished, Thamud came after them. "Qudar" is the one who hamstrung the she-camel of Thamud, and the tribe was named after him, since he was the cause of their destruction, when their Lord crushed them and leveled them. Abu Riyah (with an underdot 'ya') was a man from the Banu Dubay'a who had killed a man of the Banu Sa'd ibn Tha'laba who was their neighbour. They asked him to swear an oath, or to pay the blood-money, so he swore to them, but he was killed after his oath. The Arabs made him a proverb for an oath that avails nothing. In the printed edition it reads "Riyah" with a single-dotted "b," which is an error. This last verse appears in this place of the poem in his diwan, but the more probable reading is what Abu 'Ubayda transmitted in al-A'sha's words to the Banu Jahdar:

You swore we would not give you
Except 'irar, so this is 'irar.

"Al-'irar" means fighting. He says: You swore that you would not give us anything except after fighting, so this is the fighting; it has been decreed upon you as I decreed upon Abu Riyah his false oath, when his Greatest Lord heard it. "Al-Kibar" (with a damma on the kaf) is the intensive form of "kabir" (great).]]

And the transmitters recite it:

"Yasma'uha lahuhu al-kibar" (Like the oath, the great ones hear it).
Some of them recited it as:
"Yasma'uha Allahu wa-Allahu kubar" [[Al-Farra said: "Al-Kisa'i recited to me."]]

[[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "yasma'uha Allahu wa-l-kibar," which is an error by the copyist. The correct form is what appears in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:203, and what has preceded is entirely from his words with slight alteration. Likewise its commentator on his diwan transmitted it, and so do all the other books. Abu 'Ubayda transmitted: "yasma'uha al-wahid al-kibar."]]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Owner of Sovereignty. You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means by this: O Owner of Sovereignty, O He to whom belongs the sovereignty of this world and the next, exclusively, with none other, as:

6789 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding His words, "Say: O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty," that is, Lord of the servants and of sovereignty; none judges among them but You. [[The report 6789: Sira of Ibn Hisham 2:227, whose text is: "that is, Lord of the servants, and the sovereign over whom none other judges," and it is the remainder of the earlier reports, the last of which is numbered 6776.]]

* *

As for His words, "You give sovereignty to whom You will," it means: You give sovereignty to whom You will, so that he possesses it and You empower him over whom You will.

As for His words, "and You take sovereignty away from whom You will," it means: and You take sovereignty away from whom You will to take it from, [[The printed edition omitted: "meaning: and You take sovereignty from whom You will"; I have restored it from the manuscript.]] so the mention of "to take it from him" is omitted, being sufficiently indicated by His words, "and You take sovereignty from whom You will," as one says: "Take what you wish, and be in what you wish," meaning: take what you wish to take, and be in what you wish to be in. Likewise His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In whatever form He willed, He composed you﴾ [Surat al-Infitar: 8], meaning: in whatever form He willed to compose you in, He composed you. [[What preceded is an abridgement of what is in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:204-205, and it has fulfilled its right.]]

* *

It has been said: This verse was revealed to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in answer to his request to his Lord that He give the kingdom of Persia and Rome to his community. [[See the interpretation of "al-mulk" (sovereignty) in what preceded: 1:148, 149; 2:488; 5:312, 315, 371.]]

Those who said this:

6790 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) asked his Lord, may His praise be exalted, to give the kingdom of Persia and Rome to his community. So God, may He be mighty and majestic, revealed: "Say: O Allah, Owner of Sovereignty, You give sovereignty to whom You will" down to "Truly You are powerful over everything."

6791 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us, and God knows best, that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) asked his Lord, may He be mighty and majestic, to give the kingdom of Persia and Rome to his community, and then he mentioned the same.

* *

It is reported from Mujahid that he used to say: The meaning of "sovereignty" (al-mulk) in this place is prophethood.

The report from him to this effect:

6792 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words, "You give sovereignty to whom You will and You take sovereignty away from whom You will," he said: Prophethood.

6793 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿You exalt whom You will and You abase whom You will. In Your hand is the good. Truly You are powerful over everything﴾ (26)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: "You exalt whom You will" by giving him sovereignty and authority, and extending power to him. "And You abase whom You will" by stripping him of his kingdom and empowering his enemy over him. "In Your hand is the good": that is, all of that is in Your hand and toward You; none is able to do that except You, because You are powerful over everything, apart from all Your creatures, and apart from whomever the idolaters among the People of the Book and the unlettered Arabs took as a god and lord to worship besides You, such as the Messiah and the rivals that the unlettered ones took as lords, as:

6794 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding His words, "You give sovereignty to whom You will," etc., that is: this is all in Your hand, not toward anyone else. "Truly You are powerful over everything," that is: none other than You can do this by Your authority and Your power. [[The report 6794: Sira of Ibn Hisham 2:227, and it is the remainder of the reports, the first of which is numbered 6789.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 27 (part 1 of 2):

The explanation of His saying: ﴿He causes the night to pass into the day and causes the day to pass into the night﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His majesty be exalted, "tuwlij" means "tudkhil" (He makes enter). It is said of it: "Fulan has walked into (waleja) his house" when he entered it, "so he enters it (yalijuhu) waljan and wuluджан and wulijatan" [[His saying "waljan" is a verbal noun not mentioned in the books of lexicography. And "lijah" is of the pattern "iddah" and "wazinah".]] — and "I caused him to enter (awlajtuhu)" when I made him enter.
* *
And by His saying, "He causes the night to pass into the day": He makes enter into the hours of the day what you have subtracted from the hours of the night, so that the increase in this is the decrease of that. "And causes the day to pass into the night": He makes enter into the hours of the night what you have subtracted from the hours of the day, so He increases the hours of the night by what has been subtracted from the hours of the day, as:

6795 - Musa narrated to me, saying: Amr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "He causes the night to pass into the day and causes the day to pass into the night", until the night becomes fifteen hours and the day nine hours; and He makes the day enter the night until the day becomes fifteen hours and the night nine hours.

6796 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Hafs ibn Umar narrated to us, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "What is decreased from the day He places in the night, and what is decreased from the night He places in the day." [[The report 6798 (sic): "Hafs ibn Umar al-Adani", whose biography is in al-Kabir 1/2/362 and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/182. This chain has passed as no. 533, 1406, and will come again as no. 6814. In the manuscript and printed edition here it reads "Hafs 'an Umar", which is an error.]]

6797 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu Asim narrated to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of God: "He causes the night to pass into the day and causes the day to pass into the night", he said: what is decreased from one of them enters into the other, they alternate — or: they succeed one another, Abu Asim doubted — that is of the hours. [[In the printed edition: "what is decreased from one of them enters into the other, they alternate...", with the addition of "yadkhulu" which is not in the manuscript; see the following report. His saying "ya'taqibani" in the manuscript is "mu'taqibani" without dots, which is a distortion; what is in the printed edition is an alteration with no meaning.]]

6798 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "He causes the night to pass into the day and causes the day to pass into the night", what is decreased from one of them is in the other; they alternate that amount of hours.
