* *

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "The word" is 'Isa.

7062 – Ibn Wakic narrated to us, he said: My father narrated to us, from Isra'il, from Simak, from 'Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying "When the angels said: O Maryam, indeed Allah gives you good tidings with a word from Him," he said: 'Isa is the word from Allah.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The view nearest to the truth in my judgment is the first view: that the angels gave Maryam the good tidings of 'Isa from Allah, may He be exalted, with His message and His word, which He commanded her to cast to her: that Allah creates from her a child without a husband and without a male. For this reason He, may He be exalted, said: "his name is the Messiah," using the masculine, and did not say "her name" with the feminine. The word "kalima" is feminine, but the "word" is not intended as the name meaning "so-and-so"; rather it carries the sense of good tidings, so its pronoun is made masculine, just as the pronouns of "dhurriyya" (offspring), "dabba" (creature), and titles are made masculine, as we have explained earlier in what preceded.
[["Kinaya" means the pronoun, as has been mentioned many times before, and it is a term from the Kufan usage.]]
[[See what preceded, 2:210, then this part, pp. 362–363, and other places.]]

* *

The interpretation of that is as we have said just now: that the meaning of it is: indeed Allah gives you good tidings with glad tidings. Then he clarified the glad tidings, saying that it is a child whose name is the Messiah.

* *

Some grammarians of Basra claimed that He mentioned it by saying "his name is the Messiah," although He had said "with a word from Him," and that "the word" in their view is 'Isa, because in meaning it is so, just as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Lest a soul should say: "Alas for me!"﴾, then He said ﴿"Yes, indeed My signs came to you, but you denied them"﴾ [Surat al-Zumar: 56–59]. And just as one says "dhu al-thudayya" (the one with the little breast), because his hand was short and close to his breast,
[[The report of Dhu al-Thudayya is well known; see Sunan Abi Dawud, "Chapter on fighting the Kharijites," 4:334–338.]]
so he made it as if its name were "thudayya," and if not for that, the "ha'" would not enter the diminutive.

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa, in agreement with the view of those grammarians of Basra we mentioned, said that the "ha'" refers to "the word" (kalima), but he differed with him concerning the meaning for which he mentioned His saying "his name," when "the word" had been mentioned before it. He claimed that it was only said "his name," although "the word" had been put first, and he did not say "her name," because it is the custom of the Arabs to do that with nouns, titles, and names that were not designed to identify the one named by them, like "so-and-so" and "so-and-so," and like "dhurriyya," "khalifa," and "dabba." For that reason, in his view, it is permissible to say "dhurriyya tayyiba" and "dhurriyyatan tayyiban" (a good offspring), but it is not permissible to say "Talha came" (with the feminine ending on the verb) and "Mughira stood" (with the masculine).
[[See what preceded in this part, pp. 362–363.]]

* *

Some people denied the argument of those who reasoned in this matter from "dhu al-thudayya," and they said: the "ha'" was added in "dhu al-thudayya" because by it is meant a piece of the breast, just as it is said "we were in a piece (lahma) and a fragment (nabidha)," meaning a piece of it. This view is similar to our view which we have stated on this matter.

* *

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 44 (part 2 of 2):

As for His saying, ﴿His name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary﴾, He, mighty is His praise, informed His servants of Jesus' lineage, that he is the son of his mother Mary. By this He negated what the atheists among the Christians attributed to Him, mighty is His praise, in ascribing sonship to God, mighty and majestic is He, and what the slanderers among the Jews had falsely accused his mother of. [[In the printed edition: "qadhafat bihi" (she was accused of it), but the correct reading is from the manuscript. Qarafa al-rajul bi-su'in means he accused him of it and charged him with it, so he is maqrūf. And His saying "al-muftariyah" is in the nominative as the subject of "qarafat ummuhu bihi" (his mother was accused of it), meaning the slanderous group.]] As related:

7063 - Ibn Humayd narrated to me, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding ﴿When the angels said, "O Mary, indeed God gives you good tidings of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus, son of Mary, distinguished in this world and the Hereafter and among those brought near"﴾: that is, this was His command, not what they say about him. [[The report 7063: Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:229-230. It is among the remaining reports, the last of which is 7060, and its text reads: "not as you say about him."]]
* *
As for "al-Masih" (the Messiah), it is "fa'il" transferred from "maf'ul" to "fa'il," and its origin is "mamsuh," meaning God wiped him and purified him from sins. For this reason Ibrahim said: "al-Masih" is the truthful one ... [[There is undoubtedly a lacuna at these dots in my view, and I infer that it is a single chain of transmission to "Ibrahim," followed by report no. 7064, which states that the Messiah is the truthful one, as mentioned. In the manuscript and printed edition, at the place of these dots, there was: "Others said: he was anointed with blessing," which is a statement that does not hold, as you see, so I moved this sentence to its place before report no. 7066, and I deemed it permissible to do so, because it is so evident that no doubt or hesitation remains.
Moreover, there are many other opinions regarding the interpretation of "al-Masih," which I do not think al-Tabari overlooked, but I suspect that the copy has an ancient lacuna, which is why the copyist was confused here. This is if al-Tabari did not omit them intentionally in abridgment.]]
7064 - Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: my father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, the same.
7065 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Mansur, from Ibrahim, the same.
* *
Others said: he was anointed with blessing.
7066 - Ibn al-Barqi narrated to us, saying: Amr ibn Abi Salamah narrated to us, saying: Sa'id said: He was named "al-Masih" only because he was anointed with blessing.

The interpretation of His words: ﴿honored in this world and the Hereafter, and among those brought near﴾ (45).

Abu Ja'far said: By His words "honored" (wajihan) He means one who has a face (wajh), a lofty station with God, and nobility and dignity. From this is derived the term for a man who is esteemed and whom kings and people hold in high regard: "wajih." It is said of him: "So-and-so was wajihan (distinguished); he became wajih and gained standing (wajaha)," and "Indeed he has standing (wajh) with the ruler, and influence (jah) and prominence (wajahah)." The word "jah" is a metathesis: its initial waw was moved to the position of the 'ayn, so it was said "jah," when in fact it is "wajh." Its verbal form from jah is "jaha yajuhu," which is heard from the Arabs: "I fear that he will confront me (yajuhani) with more than this," meaning: that he will meet me face to face with something greater than it.

* *

As for the accusative case of "wajih," it is in the sense of a circumstantial qualifier (qat') of "Isa," because "Isa" is definite and "wajih" is indefinite, and it describes him. Had it been in the genitive, agreeing with "the word," it would have been permissible.

* *

As for our statement that the interpretation of this is: honored in this world and the Hereafter with God, Muhammad ibn Ja'far said, as has reached us:

7067 - Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "wajihan," he said: honored in this world and the Hereafter with God.

* *

As for His words "and among those brought near," He means that he is among those whom God will bring near on the Day of Resurrection, settling him in His neighborhood and drawing him close to Himself, as follows:

7068 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words "and among those brought near," he said: among those brought near to God on the Day of Resurrection.

7069 - I was told by Ammar ibn al-Hasan, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' regarding His words "and among those brought near," he said: among those brought near to God on the Day of Resurrection.

7070 - Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the same.

**The interpretation of His saying:** ﴿And he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity, and he is among the righteous﴾ [3:46]

Abu Ja'far said: As for His saying, ﴿and he will speak to the people in the cradle﴾, its meaning is: God gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, honored in the sight of God and speaking to the people in the cradle.

= As for ﴿yukallimu﴾ (he speaks), although it is in the nominative, because it is in the form of ﴿yafʿalu﴾ (he does) without any governing particle affecting it, it is in fact in the accusative position. This is like the saying of the poet, whose author is unknown:[[Ma ʿarraftu qāʾilahu.]]

*bittu uʿashshīhā bi-ʿaḍbin bātirin ... yaqṣidu fī aswuqihā wa-jāʾirin*

[I spent the night feeding her with a cutting sword ... it strikes at her shanks, neither moderately nor excessively.]

[[Maʿānī al-Qurʾān by al-Farrāʾ 1:213; Amālī Ibn al-Shajarī 2:167; al-Khizāna 2:345; Lisān (k-h-l). Al-Baghdādī noted variant readings of the poem. "Yuʿashshīhā" means feeding her at the evening meal (ʿashāʾ). It describes the generosity of a noble man who slaughters his camels when guests arrive at his settlement. ʿAḍb is a cutting sword, bātir is one that cleaves the struck body. Asʾuq is the plural of sāq (shank). Yaqṣidu means to be moderate, not exceeding the limit. The meaning: he strikes their shanks with his sword without caring whether he is moderate or excessive, out of his haste and his hospitality to his guest.

Also see al-Farrāʾ's detailed treatment of what Abu Ja'far said in Maʿānī al-Qurʾān 1:213–214.]]

* *

As for ﴿al-mahd﴾ (the cradle), it refers to the place where a child lies while nursing, as:

7071 – Al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Ibn ʿAbbās said, regarding ﴿and he will speak to the people in the cradle﴾: "It is the place where the child lies while nursing."

* *

As for His saying, ﴿wa-kahlan﴾ (and in maturity), it means: one who has reached the age beyond youth [[It is said: "ghulām bayna al-ghulūma wa-l-ghulūmiyya wa-l-ghulāmiyya," like "al-ṭufūla wa-l-ṭufūliyya."]] but before old age. From it one says: "rajul kahl" (a middle-aged man) and "imraʾa kahla" (a middle-aged woman), as the rajiz (rajaz-poet) said:[[He is ʿAdhāfir al-Fuqaymī.]]

*wa-lā aʿūdu baʿdahā kariyyā ... umārisu al-kahlata wa-l-ṣabiyyā*

[And I shall not return after her as a kariyy (a muleteer), ... I will have intercourse with the middle-aged woman and the young girl.]

[[Al-Jamhara 3:339; al-Mukhaṣṣaṣ 1:40; Amālī al-Qālī 2:215; al-Simṭ 836; Sharḥ Adab al-Kātib by Ibn al-Sayyid 217, 389; and by al-Jawaliqī 295; Lisān (k-h-l), (k-r-y), (sh-ʿ-f-r), (ʾ-m-m), and elsewhere. ʿAdhāfir used to hire out his camels to Mecca. A man from Banū Ḥanīfa, from the people of Basra, hired from him a camel for himself and his wife, whose name was Shaʿfar. So he composed a rajaz about them:

*law shāʾa rabbī lam akun kariyyā ... wa-lam asuq bi-Shaʿfara l-muṭayyā*

[If my Lord had willed, I would not have been a muleteer, nor would I have driven Shaʿfar's mounts.]

*baṣriyyatun tazawwajat baṣriyyā ... yuṭʿimuhā l-māliḥa wa-l-ṭarriyyā*

[A Basran woman who married a Basran man, who feeds her salted and fresh food.]

*wa-jayyida l-birri lahā maqliyyā ... ḥattā nattat surrutuhā natiyyā*

[And the finest wheat, fried for her, until her navel protruded.]

*wa-faʿalat thunnatuhā fariyyā ...* [...]

The rajaz transmitted after these verses appears to be different. Kariyy means the one who hires out, the one who rents out his mount. After the two verses transmitted by Abu Ja'far comes:

*wa-l-ʿazaba l-munaffahata l-ummiyyā*

Al-munaffah is one whose travel has exhausted him and whose strength has failed, so that he weakened and collapsed. Al-ummī is the one who is dull, rough, coarse, and speaks little.]]

* *

God, may His praise be exalted, only meant by His saying, ﴿and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, that he would speak to the people as a child in the cradle = as an indication of the innocence of his mother from what the slanderers had attributed to her [[In the printed edition: "qadhfahā" (slandered her); see above, p. 413, note 3.]] and as proof for him of his prophethood; and as an adult, having reached maturity after his youth, = by the revelation of God that He revealed to him, His command and prohibition, and what He sent down to him of His Book. [[In the printed edition: "wa-mā taqūlu ʿalayhi" (and what he said about it), but God forbid that this be so!! The word in the manuscript is poorly written, corrupted and corrected, but it is nonetheless clear to anyone who grasps some of the meanings of the discourse!!]]

* *

God, may He be exalted, only informed His servants of this concerning the matter of the Messiah, and that he was indeed so, although it is the general pattern of people that they speak in maturity and old age = as an argument against those among the people of disbelief in God, the Christians, who spoke falsehood about him [[In the printed edition: "bi-l-bāṭil" (with falsehood), which is an alteration of Ṭabarī's phrase that the reader of his book is familiar with. The word "al-bāṭil" is in the accusative as the object of "al-qāʾilīn" (those who say).]] and that he was = [from the time He created him] an infant child and then an adult, [[In the printed edition: "wa-annahu kāna fī maʿnāhu ashyāʾ mawlūdan..." and in the manuscript: "wa-annahu kāna fī maʿānīhi ashyā mawlūdan..." I have been unable to find any meaning for any of that that I accept, and I have struggled for a long time to determine its corruption or distortion, until I became exhausted by it, and until I suspected that something had dropped from the copyist which would make this statement sound correct, along with the likelihood of corruption and distortion. So I decided to put in the parentheses what makes the statement sound correct, and to leave the original of this sentence blank. This is while I believe that "maʿahu ashyā" is "mundhu anshaʾahu" as I have recorded it. The context: "that he was ... moving among the events."]] changing with the passing of times and days, from childhood to adulthood, and from state to state = and that if he had been, as the atheists say about him, that would not have been permissible for him. Thus He refuted what the delegation from the people of Najrān said, those who disputed with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning him, and He used it as an argument against them for His prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), informing them that he was like the rest of the children of Adam, except for the honor that God singled him out with, which distinguished him from them, as:

7072 – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Isḥāq, from Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn al-Zubayr: "and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity and he is among the righteous": He informs them of his states through which he passes in his life, like the passing of the children of Adam through their lives, as children and as adults, except that God singled him out with speaking in the cradle as a sign of his prophethood, and as an introduction for the servants to the places of His power. [[The report: 7072 – Sīrat Ibn Hishām 2:230; it is part of the continuation of the reports whose last is number 7067.]]

7073 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatāda: "and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity and he is among the righteous," he says: he will speak to them as a child and as an adult.

7074 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ: "and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity," he said: he will speak to them as a child and as an adult.

7075 – Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid: "and in maturity and he is among the righteous," he said: the kahl is the forbearing one.

7076 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: He spoke to them as a child, as an adult, and in maturity. = Ibn Jurayj said: Mujāhid said: the kahl is the forbearing one.

7077 – Muḥammad ibn Sinān narrated to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Ḥanafī narrated to us, from ʿAbbād, from al-Ḥasan, regarding His saying: "and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity," he said: He spoke to them in the cradle as an infant, and He spoke to them as an adult.

* *

Others said: The meaning of His saying, ﴿and in maturity﴾, is that he will speak to them when he appears.

Those who said that:

7078 – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: I heard him – meaning Ibn Zayd – say regarding His saying: "and he will speak to the people in the cradle and in maturity," he said: Jesus has already spoken to them in the cradle, and he will speak to them when the Dajjāl is killed, and he will be then a middle-aged man.

* *

The word ﴿kahlan﴾ is in the accusative as a conjunction with the position of ﴿wa-yukallimu al-nās﴾.

* *

As for His saying, ﴿and he is among the righteous﴾, it means: among their number and their allies, because the people of righteousness are of one another in religion and virtue.

The explanation (ta'wil, interpretation) of His words, ﴿She said, "My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?" He said, "Thus Allah creates what He wills. When He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,' and it is."﴾ (47)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Maryam said, when the angels had said to her, "Indeed, Allah gives you good news of a word from Him,"[[See the explanation of "anna" above: 4:398–416 / 5:312, 447 / 6:358.]] "My Lord, how can I have a child?" By what means can I have a child? Will it be from a husband I marry and a spouse I wed, or will You originate a creation in me without a spouse or a stallion [[In the manuscript: "ay tabtadi'" ("that You originate"), which is an error. In the printed edition: "aw tabtadi'" ("or You originate"). I have preferred what I have adopted.]] and without a man touching me?

Then Allah said to her, "Thus Allah creates what He wills," meaning: In this way Allah creates a child for you from you, without a man touching you, and makes him a sign and a lesson for the people. He creates what He wills and does what He desires. He grants a child to whom He wills, with or without a stallion, and withholds it from whom He wills among women, even if she has a husband, because nothing is beyond His power to create whatever He intends to create. He only has to command when He wants something, and He says to it, "Be," and it is, whatever He wills, however He wills, and in whatever way He wills, as:

7079: Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding "She said, 'My Lord, how can I have a child when no man has touched me?' He said, 'Thus Allah creates what He wills,'" [meaning] He does what He intends and creates what He wills, whether human or not, "when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, 'Be,'" whatever He wills and however He wills, "and it is," what He intends.[[Report 7079: Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:230, from the remaining reports, the last of which is no. 7072. In the printed edition and the manuscript it read: "ay: idha qada amran ..." ("that is, when He decrees a matter..."). It is evident that "ay" has no place here, and the text of Ibn Hisham from Ibn Ishaq confirms this, so I have removed it. The manuscript and printed edition also read: "fa-innama yaqulu lahu kun fayakun, mimma yashaa ..." It is also evident that "fayakun" here is an addition, since the context requires its omission here, and it will come later, as in the text of Ibn Hisham's report from Ibn Ishaq, so I have moved it from this place too. In Sirat Ibn Hisham it reads: "fayakun, kama arada" ("and it is, as He intends"), and both are correct.]]

**On the interpretation of His words: ﴿And He will teach him the Book, and the wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel﴾ (3:48)**

Abu Ja'far said: The reciters differed over the recitation of this.

The majority of the reciters of the Hijaz and Medina, and some of the reciters of Kufa, recited ﴿wa-yu'allimuhu﴾ with the *ya'* (third person, "He will teach him"), as a response to His words ﴿Thus God creates what He wills﴾ and ﴿and He will teach him the Book﴾. They thus attached the report in His words ﴿and He will teach him﴾ to the similar report in His words ﴿He creates what He wills﴾ and His words ﴿So He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾.

The majority of the reciters of Kufa and some of the reciters of Basra recited ﴿wa-nu'allimuhu﴾ with the *nun* (first person plural, "We will teach him"), conjoining it to His words ﴿We reveal it to you﴾, as if He had said: "That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you," and "We will teach him the Book." They said: what follows "We reveal it" in its relative clause extends to His words ﴿it is﴾, and then He conjoined ﴿and We will teach him﴾ to it.

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this, in our opinion, is that these are two different recitations which do not differ in meaning. Whichever of the two a reciter reads, he is correct, because the meanings of the two recitations agree: both are a report from God that He will teach Jesus the Book, and what He mentioned that He would teach him.

This is the beginning of a report from God, Mighty and Majestic, to Mary about what He will do with the child whose good news He gave her, of honour, elevation of rank and excellence. He said: Thus God creates a child from you without a father or a husband, and He will teach him the Book, which is the writing that he writes with his hand; and the wisdom, which is the Sunnah that He reveals to him outside of a book; and the Torah, which is the Torah that was sent down to Moses, which was among them from the time of Moses; and the Gospel, the Gospel of Jesus, which did not exist before him. But God informed Mary before Jesus was created that He would reveal it to him.

He informed her of that and named it for her because she had known, from what was sent down of the Scriptures, that God would raise up a prophet to whom He would reveal a book named the Gospel. So God, Mighty and Majestic, informed her that this prophet (ﷺ), whose description she had heard, and whom He had promised to His prophets earlier, upon whom would be sent down the Book called the Gospel, was the child whom He had granted her and given her the good news of.

Scholars of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said on this. Those who said this:

7080 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said concerning ﴿and We will teach him the Book﴾: "By his hand."

7081 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah concerning ﴿and We will teach him the Book and the wisdom﴾: "The wisdom is the Sunnah."

7082 – Al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Qatadah concerning His words ﴿and He will teach him the Book and the wisdom and the Torah and the Gospel﴾: "The wisdom" is the Sunnah; "and the Torah and the Gospel": Jesus used to read the Torah and the Gospel.

7083 – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij concerning ﴿and We will teach him the Book and the wisdom﴾: "The wisdom is the Sunnah."

7084 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, who said: He informed her – meaning God informed Mary – of what He intended, so He said: ﴿and He will teach him the Book and the wisdom and the Torah﴾, which was among them from the time of Moses, ﴿and the Gospel﴾, another book which He would reveal to him, of which they had no knowledge except its mention that it would occur from the prophets before him. [[The report: 7084 – Sirat Ibn Hisham 2: 230, a completion of the reports whose last is number 7079. In Ibn Hisham: "they had nothing but its mention that it would occur from the prophets after him," omitting "its knowledge" and "before him" instead of "after him." The correct wording is the text of al-Tabari in his transmission from Ibn Ishaq.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):

The discussion of His saying: ﴿and a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying], "I have come to you with a sign from your Lord"﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His majesty be exalted, "and a messenger," [the meaning is]: "and We make him a messenger to the Children of Israel." The mention of "and We make him" is omitted because the context indicates it, as the poet said:

*"And you saw your husband in the battle, / girded with a sword and a spear."* [[The verse has passed, with its takhrij, in 1:140.]]

* *

As for His saying, "that I have come to you with a sign from your Lord," it means [[In the printed edition: "bi-ma'na" (meaning); the correct reading is from the manuscript.]] "and We make him a messenger to the Children of Israel, as a prophet, a bearer of good news and a warner." [[In the printed edition: "nabi wa-bashir wa-nadhir"; the correct reading is from the manuscript. Moreover, His saying "and We make him a messenger..." up to "and a warner" explains the words of God the Exalted to Mary, "a messenger to the Children of Israel." Then he began explaining the words of Jesus, peace be upon him, "that I have come to you with a sign," so Jesus, peace be upon him, said: "And my proof of my truthfulness in that..." In the manuscript and the printed edition it read "ʿala ṣidqī ʿala dhālika," which is not correct; it is an error or a lapse of the copyist, and the correct form is what has been adopted.]] "And my proof of my truthfulness in that is: 'that I have come to you with a sign from your Lord'," meaning: a mark from your Lord that confirms my word and verifies my report that I am a messenger from your Lord to you. As related:

**7085** – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr: "And a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying], 'I have come to you with a sign from your Lord'," i.e., by it he confirms my prophethood, that I am a messenger from Him to you. [[The report: 7085 – Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:230, a continuation of the reports whose last number is 7084. In the printed edition it read "tuhaqqiqu bi-ha nubuwwati, wa-anni rasul..."; I have adopted what is in the manuscript, which agrees with the narration of Ibn Hisham.]]

* *

The discussion of His saying: ﴿that I create for you from clay [the form] of a bird, then I breathe into it, and it becomes a bird by the permission of Allah﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: "and a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying], 'I have come to you with a sign from your Lord'." Then He explained what the sign is, saying: "that I create for you."

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: "and a messenger to the Children of Israel, [saying] that I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, namely that I create for you from clay [the form] of a bird."

* *

"Al-tayr" (the birds) is the plural of "ta'ir" (a bird).

* *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of this.

Some of the people of the Hijaz recited: ﴿ka-hay'at al-ta'ir fa-anfukh fihi fa-yakunu ta'iran﴾ [in the singular], in unity.

* *

Others recited: ﴿ka-hay'at al-tayr fa-anfukh fihi fa-yakunu tayran﴾ [in the plural], in agreement in both places.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The recitation most pleasing to me in this is the recitation of the one who recites "ka-hay'at al-tayr fa-anfukh fihi fa-yakunu tayran" in agreement in both places together, because that was among the attributes of Jesus, that he does this by the permission of Allah, and because it accords with the orthography of the Mushaf. Following the orthography of the Mushaf, together with the soundness of the meaning and the wide transmission of the reading, is more pleasing to me than departing from the Mushaf. [[In the printed edition: "ʿala al-jimāʿ kilayhimā"; in the manuscript "kulihimā" also, without the diacritic of the kaf, as if he had intended to write "kilayhimā," then corrected himself, leaving the kaf as it was so that it could be turned into "fīhimā" (in both); and so he wrote it.]]

* *

The creation of Jesus was what he created from birds, as related:

**7086** – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq narrated to us that Jesus, peace be upon him, sat one day with boys from the scribes' school. He took some clay and said: "Shall I make for you a bird from this clay?" They said: "Can you do that?" He said: "Yes, by the permission of my Lord." Then he shaped it until, when he had made it in the form of a bird, he breathed into it and said: "Be a bird by the permission of Allah," and it flew off between his palms. The boys went out with this matter from him and told their teacher, and they spread it among the people. He grew up, and the Children of Israel intended harm to him. When his mother feared for him, she carried him on a donkey of hers and set out with him, fleeing. [["Ḥumayyir" (with a dammah on the ḥāʾ, a fatḥah on the mīm, and a shaddah on the yāʾ with kasrah), the diminutive of "ḥimār" (donkey), is vocalized so in the manuscript, and it is correct.]]

* *

It is mentioned that when he wanted to create the bird from clay, he asked them: "Which bird is the strongest in its creation?" It was said to him: "The bat." As related:

**7087** – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij, who said regarding His saying, "that I create for you from clay [the form] of a bird": He said: "Which of the birds is strongest in its creation?" They said: "The bat, for it is only flesh." He said: "So he did it."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: How is it said "then I breathe into it" when it was said "that I create for you from clay [the form] of a bird"?

It is said: Because the meaning of the statement is: "then I breathe into the bird." If it had been "then I breathe into it" (feminine), it would have been sound and permissible, as He said in al-Ma'ida, ﴿fa-tanfukhu fīhā﴾ [5:110] [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "fa-anfukh fīhā," which differs from the recitation in Surat al-Ma'ida; it is an error of the copyist due to the proximity of the verse of Al 'Imran, and the publishers followed him.]], meaning: "then you breathe into the form." [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "fa-anfukh" also, which follows the earlier error.]] It has been mentioned that in one of the two recitations it is "fa-anfukhhā," without "fī." [[This is the text of the statement of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:214, which reads: "And in one of the two recitations: 'fa-anfukhhā,' and in the recitation of ʿAbd Allāh, without 'fī,' and this is of what the Arabs say: 'Rubba laylatin qad bittu fīhā wa-battuhā' (many a night I spent in it and spent it)." It may be an alteration and abbreviation by al-Tabari himself, as is his habit with what he transmits from al-Farra'; and my view is that there is an error in al-Farra's text, and its correct form is: "wa-hiya qirā'at ʿAbd Allāh..."]] The Arabs do something like this, saying: "Rubba laylatin qad battuhā, wa-bittu fīhā" (many a night I have spent it, and I have spent in it). The poet said: [[He is Yazid ibn Rabi'a ibn Mufarrigh al-Himyari.]]

*"Not torn was a collar, nor did a wailing woman stand over you, / nor did mourning horses weep for you at the spoils."* [[Al-Aghani 17:68, and Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:215. It is from verses concerning which the story goes that Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad was an enemy of Ibn Mufarrigh. When the companions of al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd killed him on the day of al-Zab, Ibn Mufarrigh said about him, and about his tyranny against him, a lesson for every tyrant and oppressor:

*"He who lived as a deceiver by his covenant, / and lived a slave, the slain of God at al-Zab. / The slave to the slave, neither root nor branch, / Clawed and fanged things tore him to pieces. / Indeed, when the deaths visit a tyrant, / they tear away the curtains between the gates. / Had you, when you met the hosts of Nizar, / been a man of Nizar, not doubting. / You neither jostled for a kingdom so as to defend it, / nor did you reach out to a people with ropes."*

*"Not torn was a collar, nor did a wailing woman mourn you..."*

The narration in al-Aghani is "nahatak" (mourned you), which runs according to analogy: one says "nāḥat al-mar'a" (the woman wailed), intransitively, and "nāḥat al-mar'a zawjahā" (the woman wailed for her husband), transitively. As for the narration of al-Farra' and Abu Ja'far, it is the one in which the preposition is omitted from "qāmatk," which is from "qāmat ʿalayk" (stood over you). "Al-asālīb" is the plural of "salb" (with two fatḥahs), which is what is on the warrior and the man of his clothing and battle garments; when he is killed, his slayer takes his spoils, that is, what is upon him of clothing and weapons, and what is with him of a mount. He says: You were not a horseman of the people of war and battles, for your horse would love you and weep for you at your downfall.]]

In the sense of: "and no one stood over you" (wa-lā qāmat ʿalayk). Like what the other said: [[I do not know who said it.]]

*"One of the Banu ʿAyyidhallah, with whom he went on, / sweet of its juice, until the trumpet is blown."* [[Banu ʿAyyidhallah (with a shaddah on the yāʾ with kasrah) are the Banu ʿAyyidh Allah ibn Saʿd al-ʿUshayra of Madhhij. "Istamarra bihā": he went off with her. "Ḥulw al-ʿuṣāra": sweet of disposition. "Al-ʿuṣāra" and "al-ʿuṣīr" are what drips from a thing when it is pressed. He says: he went off with her, so she will not return until the Day of Judgment.]]

* *

The discussion of His saying: ﴿and I heal the blind and the leper﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying "wa-ubri'" (and I heal) he means "wa-ashfī" (and I cure). From it is said: "Abra'a Allāh al-marīḍ" (God healed the patient) when He cured him of it; "so He heals him with healing"; and "bara'a al-marīḍ fa-huwa yabra' bar'" (the patient recovered). It is also said: "bura'a al-marīḍ fa-huwa yubra'" (the patient was healed). These are two well-known dialects.

* *

The people of interpretation differed regarding the meaning of "al-akmah" (the blind from birth).

Some of them said: He is the one who cannot see at night but sees by day.

Those who said this:

**7088** – Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His saying, "wa-ubri' al-akmah": He said: "The akmah is the one who sees by day and does not see by night, so he is mukmah (groping)." [[It is said: "kharaja yatakammahu fī al-arḍ," when he went out bewildered and wandering, riding his head, not knowing where to head.]]

**7089** – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

* *

Others said: He is the blind one whom his mother bore thus.

Those who said this:

**7090** – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, who said: "We used to be told that the akmah is the one who was born blind, with his eyes ghammūm (covered)." [[In the printed edition it read "madmūm al-ʿaynayn" (with closed eyes); in the manuscript it is nearly "maghmūm al-ʿaynayn." I incline that this is the correct one, so I have adopted it according to my reading of the script. The akmah is blind, whether his eyes are closed or not, but it is from "ghamm al-shay'," when it covers, so he is maghmūm: covered. From it is "al-ghamāma," which is a covering tied over the eyes of a she-camel or a bull or others.]]

**7091** – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from Qatada, regarding His saying, "wa-ubri' al-akmah wa-l-abras": He said: "We used to be told that the akmah is the one who is born blind, with his eyes madmūm (closed)." [[In the printed edition it read "madmūm al-ʿaynayn," and in the manuscript it is nearly "maghmūm al-ʿaynayn"; I incline that the latter is correct, so I have adopted it according to my reading of the script. The akmah is blind, whether his eyes are closed or not, but it is from "ghamm al-shay'," when it covers, so he is maghmūm: covered. From it is "al-ghamāma," which is a covering tied over the eyes of a she-camel or a bull or others.]]

* *

**7092** – It was related to me from al-Minjab, who said: Bishr narrated to us, from ʿImara, from Abu Rawq, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn ʿAbbas who said: "The akmah is the one born blind."

* *

Others said: Rather, he is the blind man.

Those who said this:

**7093** – Musa ibn Harun narrated to me, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "wa-ubri' al-akmah": he is the blind man.

**7094** – Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: Al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Juraij who said: Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The blind."

**7095** – Al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatada regarding His saying, "wa-ubri' al-akmah": He said: "The akmah is the blind."

**7096** – Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi narrated to us, from ʿAbbad ibn Mansur, from al-Hasan regarding His saying, "wa-ubri' al-akmah": He said: "The blind."

* *

Others said: He is the one with weak eyesight [al-a'mash].

Those who said this:

**7097** – Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Hafs ibn ʿUmar narrated to us, from al-Hakam ibn Aban, from ʿIkrima regarding His saying, "wa-ubri' al-akmah": He said: "The a'mash."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: What is known among the Arabs for the meaning of "al-kamah" is blindness. From it is said: "Kamihat ʿaynuhu fa-hiya takmahu kamahan, wa-akmahtuhā anā" (his eye became blind, and it is blind, and I blinded it), when I blinded it, as Suwayd ibn Abi Kahil said:

*"His two eyes became blind until they turned white, / so he blames himself, when he stumbled."* [[Al-Mufaddaliyyat 405; al-Lisan (k-m-h). In the printed edition: "kimihat ʿaynāhu," and it is the narration of al-Mufaddaliyyat, in which it is "kamihat ʿaynāhu limmā abyaḍḍatā." The verse is from his unique ode. In these verses preceding this verse, he mentions some of his enemy, who wanted to bring him down after his strength and severity, and how enmity was inherited from his fathers; so he strove as his fathers had striven, and gained nothing from Suwayd. So he struck for himself an example of the rock that cannot be reached, and said that his enemy remained crouching, hurling a rock that is not thrown in the peaks of a high, rugged, steep height: *"A stronghold whose inhabitant is safe, / which those before him failed to uproot. / It overcame ʿAd and those after them, / then refused, and so it is not lowered. / The people do not see it except above them; / it comes as it wills and leaves. / He throws at it, but will never reach it, / like the folly of the ignorant who is content with what he has done."* "His eyes became blind..." He says: he became blind from the severity of what he suffered, or it blinded him by its severity. When he ceased and stumbled, he went on blaming himself for having exposed himself to it.]]

And from it is the saying of Ru'ba:

*"I roared, and he recoiled like the blind man's recoil / amid the perils of the bewildered, wandering one."* [[His Diwan 166; al-Lisan (k-m-h), (h-r-j), (t-h-t-h); Majaz al-Qur'an 1:93; and Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:230. From a poem in which he mentions himself and his days, of which many verses have passed. Before it he mentions an opponent who had exaggerated in his misguidance, so he repulsed him and rebuked him. "Harraja bi-l-sabʿ": he shouted at it and rebuked it. "Al-ghā'ilāt": those that destroy and ruin him. "Al-mutahtih": the one who wanders in falsehoods, that is, hesitates in them. The Diwan's version is "fī ghā'ilāt al-khā'ib...", which is close to it.]]

* *

God, may He be exalted, only informed about Jesus, peace be upon him, that he says that to the Children of Israel, as an argument from him by these lessons and signs against them concerning his prophethood. That is because blindness and leprosy have no treatment, so that one with medical knowledge could be capable of healing them by remedy. So that was among his proofs of the truth of his saying that he is a messenger of God, because it is among the miracles, along with the other signs God gave him as evidence of his prophethood.

* *

As for what ʿIkrima said, that "al-kamah" is weak eyesight, and what Mujahid said, that it is poor sight at night, neither has any meaning. Because God does not argue against His creatures with a proof that gives them a path to contest it. If what Jesus argued to the Children of Israel regarding his prophethood were that he heals the one with weak eyesight, or the one who sees by day and cannot see by night, they would have been able to contest him by saying: "What proof is this for you? Among us are people who treat that, and they are not prophets or messengers of God."

In that is clear evidence for the soundness of what we have said: that "al-akmah" is the blind one who sees nothing, neither at night nor by day. It is closer to what Qatada said, that he is the one born thus, because treatment of such a condition is not claimed by any human, except one whom God has given the like of what He gave Jesus. And likewise the treatment of the leper.

* *

The discussion of His saying: ﴿and I raise the dead by the permission of Allah, and I inform you of what you eat and what you store in your houses﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The reviving of the dead by Jesus was by the supplication of God: he would supplicate for them, and He would respond to him, as related:

**7098** – Muhammad ibn Sahl ibn ʿAskar narrated to me, saying: Isma'il ibn ʿAbd al-Karim narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil narrated to me: that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "When Jesus reached twelve years of age, God revealed to his mother, while she was in the land of Egypt, and she had fled from her people when she bore him to the land of Egypt: 'Ascend with him to al-Sham.' She did what she was commanded. She remained in al-Sham until he was thirty years old, and his prophethood lasted three years, then God raised him to Himself." He said: Wahb claimed that there would gather around Jesus, from the sick in one group, fifty thousand; whoever among them was able to reach him, reached him, and whoever among them was unable, Jesus would come to him walking; and he would only treat them by supplicating to God.

* *

As for His saying, "and I inform you of what you eat," it means: "and I will tell you what you eat, of what I did not see or witness with you at the time you ate it," "and what you store," meaning by that: what you set aside and hide, and do not eat.

= He informs them that among the proofs of his prophethood, along with the miracles he told them he would perform as evidence of his prophethood and of the truth of his report that God sent him to them, is creating a bird from clay, healing the blind and the leper, and raising the dead by God's permission. No human can do these things unless God grants him the ability, as a sign of his truthfulness and a proof of the reality of his message, to whichever of His prophets and messengers, and whichever of His creatures, He loves. [[His words "his informing" are the predicate of "that" in his earlier words: "that among his proofs also for his prophethood... his informing."]] His informing them of the unseen, which no human whose path is like his can reach, is also (a proof) for him. [[His words "for him" complete his earlier words: "which no human can reach..."]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: If someone says: "What proof of his truthfulness was there in his saying to them, 'I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses,' since we have seen astrologers (al-mutanajjimah) and soothsayers (al-mutakahhinah) often tell such things and be correct?"

It is said: The astrologer and the soothsayer are known, to those they inform, to derive their information through some means that leads to knowledge of it. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "to the one who informs him of it," but the context of the pronouns requires what I have adopted.]] This was not the case with Jesus, peace be upon him, or with any of God's other prophets and messengers. Jesus would report such things without seeking them out, without any trickery to learn them, but by beginning with what God had informed him of, without any prior basis that he imitated, relied upon, or resorted to, as the astrologer resorts to his calculation and the soothsayer to his *ra'iy*. [[The *ra'iy* is the companion from among the jinn, whom a person or soothsayer sees, who becomes familiar with him, visits him, and tells him things, falsehoods about the unseen.]] This is the distinction between the knowledge of the prophets of the unseen and their reports about it, and the knowledge of the rest of those who lie against God or claim such knowledge. As follows:

7099 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said: When Jesus reached nine or ten years of age or thereabouts, his mother enrolled him in the school, so they claim. He was with a man from among the teachers of writing who taught him as one teaches boys. [[*Al-mukattib* (with a *damma* on the *mim*, a *fatha* on the *kaf*, and a shadda on the *ta'* with a *kasra*), on the pattern of *mu'allim*, is the one who teaches young children writing. It is also said *al-mukatib* (with a *damma* on the *mim*, a *sukun* on the *kaf*, and a *kasra* on the *ta'*), on the pattern of *mubsir*, which also means teacher.]] He did not teach him anything of what boys learn except that Jesus outdid him in knowing it before he taught it to him, saying: "Do you not marvel at this widow's son? I never teach him anything but he already knows it better than I do!"

7100 - Musa related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: When Jesus grew up, his mother gave him to be taught the Torah. He would play with the boys of the village where he lived and tell the boys what their fathers were doing.

7101 - Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, regarding God's words: "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses." He said: Jesus son of Mary, when he was in the school, would inform them of what they ate in their houses and what they stored.

7102 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hushaym related to us, saying: Isma'il ibn Salim informed us, saying: I heard Sa'id ibn Jubayr say: "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses." He said: Jesus son of Mary would say to a boy in the school: "O so-and-so, your family has hidden for you such-and-such food, will you give me some of it?"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Thus did the prophets and their proofs act. They bring what they bring of proofs through something that may be reached by some stratagem, but not in the way that others bring it, rather in a way that makes creation know that it cannot be reached by that means through any stratagem except by God's power.

* *

What we have said concerning the interpretation of His words "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses" is what the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said.

Those who said that:

7103 - Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding God's words: "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses," he said: "What you ate yesterday and what you hid of it." Jesus son of Mary said this.

7104 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shabl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the same.

7105 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said - meaning regarding His words "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses" - : "The food and things they store in their houses, unseen things which God taught him."

7106 - al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding God's words: "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses," he said: "What you eat": what you ate of food yesterday, and what you hid of it.

7107 - Musa ibn Harun related to me, saying: Amr related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, who said: He - meaning Jesus son of Mary - would tell the boys, while he was with them in the school, what their fathers were doing, what they were lifting for them, and what they were eating. He would say to a boy: "Go, for your family has lifted for you such-and-such, and they are eating such-and-such." The boy would go and weep over his family until they gave him that thing. [["Weeps over them" means he insists on them with weeping; he used *bakā* with *'alā* because it is embedded with the meaning of "insisting."]] They would say to him: "Who told you this?" He would say: "Jesus!" = This is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses." = So they kept their children away from him, saying: "Do not play with this sorcerer!" They gathered them into a house, and Jesus came looking for them. They said: "They are not here." He said: "What is in this house?" They said: "Pigs." Jesus said: "So they shall be!" They opened it, and there they were: pigs. That is God's words: "Cursed were those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel by the tongue of David and Jesus son of Mary" [Qur'an 5:78].

7108 - Muhammad ibn Sinan related to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi related to us, from 'Abbad, from al-Hasan, regarding God's words: "and what you store in your houses," he said: "What you hide out of fear of the One who withholds that He may replace it." [[In the printed edition: "What you hide out of fear of the One who withholds that He not replace it with anything," adding "not" and "anything" to the manuscript text. The manuscript has "...the One who withholds that He replace it." Both are meaningless. The manuscript letters are disordered at this point, and I fear the correct sentence is: "What you hide out of fear for it, what you hold back out of fear for it." I have left the manuscript text as it stands.]]

* *

Others said: He only meant by His words "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses": what you eat of the table (al-ma'idah) that descends upon you, and what you store of it.

Those who said that:

7109 - Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses": when the people asked for the table, and it was a spread (khiwan) that descended upon them wherever they were, with fruit from Paradise, [[In the printed edition: "it was a bag (jirab) that descended upon it," which is an undoubted error. In the manuscript it is "hawaban" without dots, and the correct reading is what I have adopted. The *ma'idah* is the *khiwan*, and the lexicographers said: "It is not called *ma'idah* until there is food on it; otherwise it is a *khiwan*."]] God commanded the people not to betray it, not to hide, and not to store for tomorrow; it was a trial God tested them with. Whenever they did any of that, Jesus son of Mary would inform them of it, saying: "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses."

7110 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, regarding His words "And I will tell you what you eat and what you store": He said: "I will tell you what you eat from the table and what you store of it." He said: A covenant was taken from them regarding the table when it descended: that they should eat and not store. They stored and betrayed, so they were made pigs when they stored and betrayed. That is God's words: "But whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment with which I have not punished anyone from among the worlds" [Qur'an 5:115].
= Ibn Yahya said: 'Abd al-Razzaq said: Ma'mar related to us, from Qatadah, from Khallas ibn 'Amr, from 'Ammar ibn Yasir, the same.

* *

The verb *yaddakhirun* (they store) is originally from the form *yaftaʿilun* (*yadtakhirun*) from the saying of the speaker: "*dhakhartu al-shay'*" (I stored the thing) with a *dhal*, "so I *adhkhuruhu*." Then it was said *yaddakhiru*, as it was said *yaddakiru* from "*dhakartu al-shay'*," intended as *yadhtakiru*. When the *dhal* and the *ta'* came together, and they are close in articulation, their pronunciation was heavy on the tongue, so one was assimilated into the other, and both became a shadda-ed *dal*. They made it a middle ground between the *dhal* and the *ta'*. [[His words "a middle ground," meaning intermediate between them; this is the exact wording of al-Farra' in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1:215.]] Some Arabs favor the *dhal* over the *ta'*, assimilating the *ta'* into the *dhal*, and say: "*wa ma tadhdhakhirun*," and "*wa huwa mudhakhar lak*," and "*wa huwa mudhakkir*."

The dialect on which the recitation is based is the first, namely assimilating the *dhal* into the *ta'* and making them a shadda-ed *dal*. It is not permissible to recite otherwise, because the transmission from the reciters in it is consistent. It is the dialect of *al-judaa* [[*Al-judaa* is a form *fu'la* from *al-ajwad* like *afdal* and *fudla*. I have not seen it used except rarely among the scholars of Abu Ja'far's generation. See what al-Farra' said in *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1:215, 216.]], as Zuhayr said:

Indeed the generous one is he who gives you his bounty freely,
and is wronged at times, so he wrongs in return. [[His *Diwan*, p. 152; Sibawayh 2:421; *al-Mukhassas* 2:206, 207; *Lisan* (z-l-m); and others. Abu Ja'far quoted it this way, but the correct transmission is what is in his *Diwan*, since before it is: "Indeed the miser is blameworthy wherever he is, but the generous one, despite his faults, is old," and so on. Consult the various transmissions of the verse, and the explanation of those transmissions in these and other books.]]

It is narrated with the *zay* (*yazzallam*), meaning *yaftaʿil* from *al-zulm* (wrong), and it is also narrated with the *ta'*.

* *

On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Surely in that is a sign for you, if you are believers﴾ [Qur'an 3:49].

Abu Ja'far said: By this, His mention, exalted be His praise, means: Surely in My creating from clay a bird by God's permission, and in My healing the blind and the leper, and My raising the dead, and My informing you of what you eat and what you store in your houses - beginning without any calculation or astrology, nor soothsaying or divination - there is a lesson for you and a matter for reflection, that you may reflect on it and take warning from it that I am truthful in my saying to you, "I am a messenger from your Lord to you," and that you may know by it that in what I call you to of God's command and prohibition I am truthful ["if you are believers"], meaning: if you confirm God's proofs and signs, acknowledge His unity, and confirm His prophet Moses and the Torah that came to you with him.

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and I have come to you confirming what was before me of the Torah." Accordingly, "confirming" (*musaddiqan*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "I have come to you."

The evidence that it is in the accusative as referring to "I have come to you," and not as a conjunction with "[made] honored" (*wajihan*), is the phrase "what was before me of the Torah." Had it been conjoined with "wajihan," the sentence would have read: "and confirming what was before him of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you." [See al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1: 216.]

* *

As for the phrase "confirming what was before me of the Torah" [see the discussion of "what is before me" and "what is before him" earlier in this volume: 160, 161], it is said because Jesus, upon him be God's blessings, believed in the Torah and affirmed it, and that it was from God. Likewise all the prophets confirm everything that came before them of the books and messengers of God, even if some of their legal rulings differ, because God varied the laws among them in that respect. Moreover, Jesus, as we have been informed, acted in accordance with the Torah and did not oppose any of its rulings, except that God lightened for its people, through the Gospel, what had been made burdensome for them in it. As follows:

7111: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ishaq related to us, he said: Abd al-Karim related to us, he said: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil related to me, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "Jesus was upon the law of Moses (ﷺ), and he would observe the Sabbath and face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). He said to the Children of Israel: 'I have not summoned you to oppose a single letter of what is in the Torah, except to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you, and to lift from you the *asar*.'" [*Al-asar* is the plural of *isr* (with a kasra and then a sukun), meaning a covenant, i.e., a heavy binding obligation upon them, such as their killing themselves, cutting away the skin when it is touched by impurity, and other burdensome rulings.]

7112: Bishr related to me, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding "confirming what was before me of the Torah and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you": "What Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought. Among what Moses had brought, camel meat and *thurub* had been forbidden to them, as well as certain birds and fish." [*Thurub* is the plural of *thirb* (with a fatha and then a sukun), which is the thin fat that covers the stomach, the intestines and the entrails of slaughtered livestock.]

7113: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ishaq related to us, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words: "confirming what was before me of the Torah and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you." He said: "What Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought. He said: Camel meat and *thurub* had been forbidden to them in what Moses brought in the Torah, so he made them lawful for them through the tongue of Jesus; and fats were forbidden, and were made lawful for them in what Jesus brought; and [he made lawful] some fish and some birds that have no *sisiyah*, [*Sisiyat* al-dik (with a kasra on the first and second sad and a fatha on the final ya') and its plural *al-sayasi* is the spur on a rooster's leg. The horns of cattle are also called *al-sayasi*, and from this the fortresses were called *al-sayasi*, because fighters take refuge in them as cattle take refuge in their horns.] and in other things He had forbidden them and made burdensome for them. So Jesus came to them with the lightening of it in the Gospel. Thus what Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought, upon him be God's blessings."

7114: Al-Qasim related to us, he said: Al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words: "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you": "[It refers to] camel meat and fats. When Jesus was sent, he made them lawful for them, and he was sent to the Jews, but they disagreed and scattered."

7115: Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding "confirming what was before me of the Torah," meaning: "what preceded me of it," and "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you," meaning: "I inform you that it had been forbidden to you, and you abandoned it; then he made it lawful for you as a lightening upon you, so that you attain its ease and leave off its consequence." [The report 7115 is in Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 231, and it is the continuation of the reports whose last was number 7085. His words "and leave off its consequence" mean: from its sin, which would follow you if you committed it. *Al-tabi'ah* and *al-tiba'ah* (with a kasra on the ta') is what carries a sin for which its doer is held accountable. It is said: "He has no *tabi'ah* from God in this, nor *tiba'ah*."]

7116: Muhammad ibn Sinan related to me, he said: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi related to us, from Abbad, from al-Hasan regarding "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you," he said: "He had forbidden them certain things, and Jesus came to make lawful for them what had been forbidden to them, seeking thereby their gratitude."

* *

Regarding His words: ﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means by this: "And I have come to you with a proof and a lesson from your Lord, by which you will know the reality of what I say to you." As follows:

7117: Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, he said: Abu Asim related to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord": "[It is] what Jesus clarified for them of all things, and what his Lord gave him."

7118: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, he said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord": "What Jesus clarified for them of all things."

* *

By His words "from your Lord," He means: "from your Lord's presence."

* *

Regarding His words: ﴿So fear God and obey me. Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means by this: "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord by which you will know with certainty the truth of what I say," "so fear God," O assembly of the Children of Israel, in what He commanded you and forbade you in His Book that He sent down to Moses; "so fulfill His covenant that you made with Him in it," "and obey me" in what I call you to, [namely] confirming me in what my Lord and your Lord has sent me with to you. "So worship Him, for He sent me to you with this, and with the lawfulness of some of what had been forbidden to you in your Book." That is the upright road and the firm guidance that has no crookedness in it. [See the discussion of "the straight path" earlier: 1: 170–177 / 3: 140, 141.] As follows:

7119: Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding "So fear God and obey me. Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord": disavowing what they say about Him, meaning what the Christians say about Him, and arguing with His Lord against them. "So worship Him; this is a straight path," meaning: "This is what I have carried you to and brought you with." [The report 7119 is in Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 231, and it is part of the remaining reports whose last was number 7115.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed regarding the recitation of His words: "Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him."

The majority of the readers of the major cities recited it: ﴿Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾ with a kasra on the alif of "inna," as the beginning of a predicate.

* *

Some of them recited it: ﴿That God is my Lord and your Lord﴾ with a fatha on the alif of "anna," with the interpretation: "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, that God is my Lord and your Lord," making "that" (*an*) a restatement of "the sign" and an apposition to it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation according to us is what the readers of the major cities hold, namely the kasra on the alif of "inna" as a beginning, because of the consensus (*ijma'*) of the authoritative readers upon the soundness of this. What they have unanimously agreed upon is a proof (*hujjah*), and what one reader alone has held apart from them is an opinion. Opinion may not be set against proof.

* *

Although the apparent meaning of this verse is information, in it is the conclusive proof from God to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) against the delegation of the people of Najran who disputed with him, through God's informing, mighty and majestic is He, that Jesus was innocent of what those who attributed to him something other than what he described himself as having ascribed to himself, namely that he is a servant of God like His other servants among the people of the earth, except for what God, may His praise be exalted, specially granted him of prophethood and the proofs that He gave him as evidence of his truthfulness, just as He gave all the other messengers other signs and proofs of their truthfulness, and as a proof of his prophethood. [In the printed edition it reads "and a proof of their prophethood," but I have kept what is in the manuscript, which is correct. His words "and a proof of his prophethood" are conjoined to "as evidence of his truthfulness," and the pronoun refers to Jesus; what lies between the conjoined and what it is conjoined to is a parenthetical interruption.]

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, and I have come to you confirming what was before me of the Torah." Accordingly, "confirming" (*musaddiqan*) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*) of "I have come to you."

The evidence that it is in the accusative as referring to "I have come to you," and not as a conjunction with "[made] honored" (*wajihan*), is the phrase "what was before me of the Torah." Had it been conjoined with "wajihan," the sentence would have read: "and confirming what was before him of the Torah, and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you." [See al-Farra's *Ma'ani al-Qur'an* 1: 216.]

* *

As for the phrase "confirming what was before me of the Torah" [see the discussion of "what is before me" and "what is before him" earlier in this volume: 160, 161], it is said because Jesus, upon him be God's blessings, believed in the Torah and affirmed it, and that it was from God. Likewise all the prophets confirm everything that came before them of the books and messengers of God, even if some of their legal rulings differ, because God varied the laws among them in that respect. Moreover, Jesus, as we have been informed, acted in accordance with the Torah and did not oppose any of its rulings, except that God lightened for its people, through the Gospel, what had been made burdensome for them in it. As follows:

7111: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ishaq related to us, he said: Abd al-Karim related to us, he said: Abd al-Samad ibn Ma'qil related to me, that he heard Wahb ibn Munabbih say: "Jesus was upon the law of Moses (ﷺ), and he would observe the Sabbath and face Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). He said to the Children of Israel: 'I have not summoned you to oppose a single letter of what is in the Torah, except to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you, and to lift from you the *asar*.'" [*Al-asar* is the plural of *isr* (with a kasra and then a sukun), meaning a covenant, i.e., a heavy binding obligation upon them, such as their killing themselves, cutting away the skin when it is touched by impurity, and other burdensome rulings.]

7112: Bishr related to me, he said: Yazid related to us, he said: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding "confirming what was before me of the Torah and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you": "What Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought. Among what Moses had brought, camel meat and *thurub* had been forbidden to them, as well as certain birds and fish." [*Thurub* is the plural of *thirb* (with a fatha and then a sukun), which is the thin fat that covers the stomach, the intestines and the entrails of slaughtered livestock.]

7113: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Ishaq related to us, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words: "confirming what was before me of the Torah and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you." He said: "What Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought. He said: Camel meat and *thurub* had been forbidden to them in what Moses brought in the Torah, so he made them lawful for them through the tongue of Jesus; and fats were forbidden, and were made lawful for them in what Jesus brought; and [he made lawful] some fish and some birds that have no *sisiyah*, [*Sisiyat* al-dik (with a kasra on the first and second sad and a fatha on the final ya') and its plural *al-sayasi* is the spur on a rooster's leg. The horns of cattle are also called *al-sayasi*, and from this the fortresses were called *al-sayasi*, because fighters take refuge in them as cattle take refuge in their horns.] and in other things He had forbidden them and made burdensome for them. So Jesus came to them with the lightening of it in the Gospel. Thus what Jesus brought was gentler than what Moses brought, upon him be God's blessings."

7114: Al-Qasim related to us, he said: Al-Husayn related to us, he said: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words: "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you": "[It refers to] camel meat and fats. When Jesus was sent, he made them lawful for them, and he was sent to the Jews, but they disagreed and scattered."

7115: Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding "confirming what was before me of the Torah," meaning: "what preceded me of it," and "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you," meaning: "I inform you that it had been forbidden to you, and you abandoned it; then he made it lawful for you as a lightening upon you, so that you attain its ease and leave off its consequence." [The report 7115 is in Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 231, and it is the continuation of the reports whose last was number 7085. His words "and leave off its consequence" mean: from its sin, which would follow you if you committed it. *Al-tabi'ah* and *al-tiba'ah* (with a kasra on the ta') is what carries a sin for which its doer is held accountable. It is said: "He has no *tabi'ah* from God in this, nor *tiba'ah*."]

7116: Muhammad ibn Sinan related to me, he said: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi related to us, from Abbad, from al-Hasan regarding "and to make lawful for you some of what was forbidden to you," he said: "He had forbidden them certain things, and Jesus came to make lawful for them what had been forbidden to them, seeking thereby their gratitude."

* *

Regarding His words: ﴿And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means by this: "And I have come to you with a proof and a lesson from your Lord, by which you will know the reality of what I say to you." As follows:

7117: Muhammad ibn Amr related to me, he said: Abu Asim related to us, from Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord": "[It is] what Jesus clarified for them of all things, and what his Lord gave him."

7118: Al-Muthanna related to me, he said: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, he said: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord": "What Jesus clarified for them of all things."

* *

By His words "from your Lord," He means: "from your Lord's presence."

* *

Regarding His words: ﴿So fear God and obey me. Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him. This is a straight path﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He means by this: "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord by which you will know with certainty the truth of what I say," "so fear God," O assembly of the Children of Israel, in what He commanded you and forbade you in His Book that He sent down to Moses; "so fulfill His covenant that you made with Him in it," "and obey me" in what I call you to, [namely] confirming me in what my Lord and your Lord has sent me with to you. "So worship Him, for He sent me to you with this, and with the lawfulness of some of what had been forbidden to you in your Book." That is the upright road and the firm guidance that has no crookedness in it. [See the discussion of "the straight path" earlier: 1: 170–177 / 3: 140, 141.] As follows:

7119: Ibn Humayd related to us, he said: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr, regarding "So fear God and obey me. Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord": disavowing what they say about Him, meaning what the Christians say about Him, and arguing with His Lord against them. "So worship Him; this is a straight path," meaning: "This is what I have carried you to and brought you with." [The report 7119 is in Ibn Hisham's *Sirah* 2: 231, and it is part of the remaining reports whose last was number 7115.]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The readers differed regarding the recitation of His words: "Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him."

The majority of the readers of the major cities recited it: ﴿Indeed God is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him﴾ with a kasra on the alif of "inna," as the beginning of a predicate.

* *

Some of them recited it: ﴿That God is my Lord and your Lord﴾ with a fatha on the alif of "anna," with the interpretation: "And I have come to you with a sign from your Lord, that God is my Lord and your Lord," making "that" (*an*) a restatement of "the sign" and an apposition to it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct recitation according to us is what the readers of the major cities hold, namely the kasra on the alif of "inna" as a beginning, because of the consensus (*ijma'*) of the authoritative readers upon the soundness of this. What they have unanimously agreed upon is a proof (*hujjah*), and what one reader alone has held apart from them is an opinion. Opinion may not be set against proof.

* *

Although the apparent meaning of this verse is information, in it is the conclusive proof from God to His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ) against the delegation of the people of Najran who disputed with him, through God's informing, mighty and majestic is He, that Jesus was innocent of what those who attributed to him something other than what he described himself as having ascribed to himself, namely that he is a servant of God like His other servants among the people of the earth, except for what God, may His praise be exalted, specially granted him of prophethood and the proofs that He gave him as evidence of his truthfulness, just as He gave all the other messengers other signs and proofs of their truthfulness, and as a proof of his prophethood. [In the printed edition it reads "and a proof of their prophethood," but I have kept what is in the manuscript, which is correct. His words "and a proof of his prophethood" are conjoined to "as evidence of his truthfulness," and the pronoun refers to Jesus; what lies between the conjoined and what it is conjoined to is a parenthetical interruption.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 52 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them, he said, "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" The disciples said, "We are God's helpers. We believe in God, and bear witness that we are Muslims."﴾ (3:52)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, may His majesty be praised, "Then when Jesus sensed disbelief from them," he means: when Jesus found disbelief among them.

* *

"Al-ihsas" (sensing) means finding, and from it is the saying of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿Do you sense any of them?﴾ [Surah Maryam: 98].

As for "al-hass" without an alif, it means annihilation and killing, and from it is His saying: ﴿When you were killing them by His permission﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 152].

"Al-hass" also means tenderness and compassion, and from it is the verse of al-Kumayt:

Is there anyone who weeps over the abode, hoping that it might feel for him,
or that the abode might weep for him, the flowing tear-water that is abundant?[[Al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 217; Majalis Tha'lab: 486; Islah al-Mantiq: 240; Lisan al-Arab (h-s-s). "Al-khadil" is that which flows continuously, constantly and abundantly. He marvels at the one who weeps over the ruins of his beloved ones, and asks what he hopes from them: that they feel for him, or that they weep for his weeping? He belittles what he does. For the rest of what has been said about this root in language, see the references mentioned above.]]

By His words "an tuhissa lahu" (that it feel for him) he means: that it feel tenderness for him.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: when Jesus found among the Children of Israel, to whom God had sent him, denial of his prophethood, rejection of his word, and turning away from what he called them to of God's command, he said, "Who are my helpers (ansari) in the cause of God?" By this he means: Jesus said, "Who will assist me against those who deny God's proof, those who turn away from His religion, and those who reject the prophethood of His prophet, in the cause of God, mighty and majestic?"[[See the explanation of "al-ansar" above: 2: 489 / 5: 581.]]

* *

By His words "ila Allah" (in the cause of God) he means "ma'a Allah" (with God).

The reason it is proper to say "ila Allah" in the sense of "ma'a Allah" is that it is the custom of the Arabs, when they join one thing to another and then wish to report about the two by joining one with the other, that they sometimes put "ila" in place of "ma'a," and sometimes they report about them with "ma'a." So they say: "al-dhawd ila al-dhawd ibil" (the camel to the camel is a herd), meaning: when you join one camel to another they become a herd.
