This report was narrated by al-Bukhari (al-Fath 7:109–110) through the route of Fudayl ibn Sulayman, from Musa ibn Uqba, with the same wording as al-Tabari, with some differences.

At this point a section of the old division of the text ends. The manuscript contains the following:

"Followed by the explanation of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ' Indeed, the people most worthy of Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe, and Allah is the Guardian of the believers.'"

"And praise be to Allah for (..!!). And may Allah bless Muhammad, his family, and grant them peace."

Then there follows the text:

"In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. My Lord, make it easy."

"Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated to us."

This is something new that has appeared in this copy. All that preceded was the end of the old division, the narration of Abu Muhammad al-Farghani from Abu Ja'far Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari. Then the narration of the tafsir began with another chain, from a man other than Abu Muhammad al-Farghani, who is well known for narrating the tafsir. I therefore record the chain in the body of the tafsir. Thus it is necessary to introduce Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi here, so that we may later see how the narration of the tafsir proceeds: is it the narration of Abu Muhammad al-Farghani to the end of the book, except for a part narrated by Abu Bakr, or did the narration of Abu Muhammad al-Farghani end, and did the narration of Abu Bakr begin from this point?

The narrator of this tafsir from the beginning of this point is: "Muhammad ibn Dawud ibn Sulayman Sayyar ibn Bayan, al-Baghdadi, the jurist, Abu Bakr," who settled in Egypt and narrated there from Abu Ja'far al-Tabari and Uthman ibn Nasr al-Ta'i. Abu al-Fath Abd al-Wahid ibn Muhammad ibn Masrur al-Balkhi narrated from him, and he was trustworthy. Al-Khatib al-Baghdadi said in his history, 5:265, with his chain to Abu Sa'id ibn Yunus: "Muhammad ibn Dawud ibn Sulayman, known as Abu Bakr, Baghdadi, came to Egypt. He used to serve as judge at Tinnis, and he narrated the books of Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari from him. A group of Baghdadis narrated from him. He was clean and sensible. He held the office of endowments in Egypt. He died on Thursday, three days before the end of Jumada al-Akhira in the year 336 AH."

I have found no biography of him other than this in Tarikh Baghdad, nor in al-Kindi's Qudat Misr, nor in any other book available to me now. Perhaps I will find elsewhere in the tafsir something that reveals his narration of the tafsir, beyond this amount that I have reached. And Allah is the Granter of success.]]

Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Dawud ibn Sulayman informed us, saying: Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari narrated to us:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe﴾, and Allah is the Guardian of the believers.

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, "Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham," may He be glorified and exalted, He means: the most worthy of people of Abraham, of his support and his guardianship, are "those who followed him." That means those who took his path and his method, who affirmed the oneness of Allah, sincere to Him in religion, who practised his sunnah (way), who established his laws, and who were ḥanīfs (upright monotheists) submitting to Allah, not associating anything with Him. "And this Prophet" means Muhammad (ﷺ). "And those who believe" means those who affirmed Muhammad and what came to them from Allah. "And Allah is the Guardian of the believers" means: Allah is the helper of the believers in Muhammad, those who affirm him in his prophethood and in what came to them from Him, against those who oppose them among the people of the other religions and creeds.

* *

Those who interpret (the Qur'an, ahl al-ta'wil) have said the same as what we have said about this.

Those who said so:

7214 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham are those who followed him," meaning: those who followed him in his creed, his sunnah, his method and his natural disposition (fitrah). "And this Prophet," who is the Prophet of Allah, Muhammad. "And those who believe" with him, who are the believers who affirmed the Prophet of Allah and followed him. Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and those who were with him among the believers, were the closest of people to Abraham.

7215 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

7216 – Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna, Jabir ibn al-Kirdi, and al-Hasan ibn Abi Yahya al-Maqdisi narrated to us, saying: Abu Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every prophet has walis (protectors) from among the prophets, and my wali among them is my father and the Friend of my Lord," then he recited: "Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham are those who followed him, and this Prophet, and those who believe, and Allah is the Guardian of the believers."

[[Hadith 7216: Jabir ibn al-Kirdi ibn Jabir al-Wasiti al-Bazzar: trustworthy, one of the teachers of al-Nasa'i, whose biography is in al-Tahdhib.

Al-Hasan ibn Abi Yahya al-Maqdisi: I have not reached knowledge of who he is.

Abu Ahmad: he is al-Zubayri, Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr al-Asadi.

Sufyan: he is al-Thawri.

His father: Sa'id ibn Masruq al-Thawri al-Kufi, a known trustworthy narrator whom the authors of the six canonical books related from.

Abu al-Duha: he is Muslim ibn Subayh (with diminutive form). His biography has passed at 5424.

Masruq: he is Ibn al-Ajda' ibn Malik al-Hamdani. His biography has passed at 4242.

This is a sound, connected isnad.

Following it, and with a broken isnad: through the route of Abu Nu'aym, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, from Abdullah – that is Ibn Mas'ud – broken, with the dropping of "Masruq" between Abu al-Duha and Ibn Mas'ud.

Abu al-Duha did not meet Ibn Mas'ud. Ibn Mas'ud died in the year 33 (AH). Abu al-Duha died in the year 100. This hadith has been transmitted in the collections in both ways: connected and broken. The connected version is an addition from a trustworthy narrator, and so it is accepted.

Al-Tirmidhi (4:80–81) related it from Mahmud ibn Ghaylan, from Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, with this isnad, connected, like the version of al-Tabari here through Abu Ahmad.

Likewise al-Bazzar related it through Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri, as reported by Ibn Kathir (2:163).

Abu Ahmad al-Zubayri was not alone in connecting it by mentioning "Masruq" in the isnad. Two trustworthy narrators followed him in this.

Al-Hakim related it in al-Mustadrak (2:292), through Muhammad ibn Ubayd al-Tanafisi, from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, from Abdullah, raised and connected. Al-Hakim said: "This is a sound hadith according to the conditions of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), but they did not include it." Al-Dhahabi agreed with him.

Ibn Kathir (2:161–162) reported that Sa'id ibn Mansur related it: "Abu al-Ahwas narrated to us, from Sa'id ibn Masruq [he is the father of Sufyan], from Abu al-Duha, from Masruq, from Ibn Mas'ud..." – and he mentioned it.

Abu al-Ahwas Sallam ibn Sulaym: a trustworthy, precise, memorising narrator, whose biography has passed at 2058. He related it raised and connected, from Sa'id al-Thawri – the father of Sufyan – just as Sufyan related it from his father.

This favours the version of those who related it from Sufyan connected over the version of those who related it from him broken. When the transmission from Sufyan differs between connection and break, it does not differ from Abu al-Ahwas.

Indeed, the apparent view to me is that this is not a difference regarding Sufyan; rather, Sufyan himself sometimes connected it and sometimes broke it. Such things are common in isnads.]]

7217 – Ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Abu Nu'aym al-Fadl ibn Dukayn narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, from Abdullah – I think he said: from the Prophet (ﷺ) – and he mentioned something similar.

[[Hadith 7217: This is the broken version of this hadith. Al-Tabari related it through Abu Nu'aym from Sufyan, broken.

Likewise al-Tirmidhi (4:81) related it from Mahmud, who is Ibn Ghaylan, from Abu Nu'aym, with this isnad.

Other trustworthy narrators followed Abu Nu'aym in relating it thus, broken:

Ahmad related it in al-Musnad (3800), from Waki', from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, from Abdullah – that is Ibn Mas'ud – raised.

Likewise al-Tirmidhi (4:81) related it from Abu Kurayb, from Waki'.

However, Ibn Kathir (2:163–164) transmitted it from the tafsir of Waki', with this isnad, in which it reads "from Abu Ishaq" instead of "from Abu al-Duha." I hold that this is an error by some copyists of the tafsir of Waki', preferring the narration of Ahmad from Waki' and that of al-Tirmidhi through Waki' – in which it reads "from Abu al-Duha."

Ahmad also related it (4088) from Yahya, who is al-Qattan, and from Abd al-Rahman, who is Ibn Mahdi – both from Sufyan, from his father, from Abu al-Duha, from Abdullah, raised.

Al-Tirmidhi preferred the broken version, which is a preference without a valid basis. The connection is an addition accepted without doubt from a trustworthy narrator.

In this narration of al-Tabari is the phrase "I think he said: from the Prophet (ﷺ)," which implies doubt about its being raised as well. This doubt is perhaps from Ibn al-Muthanna, the teacher of al-Tabari, or from al-Tabari himself, because al-Tirmidhi's narration through Abu Nu'aym contains no doubt about its being raised.

The hadith is mentioned by al-Suyuti (2:42) without distinguishing the connected from the broken narrations; he added its attribution to Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, but did not mention its attribution to the Musnad of Ahmad or to al-Bazzar.]]

7218 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali, from Ibn Abbas: Allah, glorified is He, says: "Indeed, the closest of people to Abraham are those who followed him," and they are the believers.

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿A group of the People of the Book wish that they could mislead you, but they mislead none except themselves, and they do not perceive﴾ (69).

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, glorified is His praise, "wadda" means they wish (tamanna) [[See the explanation of "wadda" above, 2:470 / 5:542.]] "ta'ifah" means a group, "min ahl al-kitab" means the People of the Book, namely the Jews, who possess the Torah, and the Christians, who possess the Gospel. "Law yudillunakum" means they say: if only they could turn you away, O believers, from Islam and bring you back to the unbelief they themselves follow, thereby destroying you.

* *

"Al-idlal" (misguiding) in this context means destruction (al-ihlak), [[See the explanation of "dalla" above, 1:195 / 2:495, 496.]] as in the saying of Allah, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿And they say, "When we have gone astray in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ (32:10), meaning: when we have perished. And from it is the saying of al-Akhtal in satirizing Jarir:

"You were the chaff in a turbid, foaming sea,
which the torrent cast forth, and it went astray in error."
[[Its takhrij and explanation were given earlier, 2:496.]]

meaning: it perished a perishing. And the saying of the Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan:

"So the ones who misled him returned with a clear sign,
and left behind at al-Jawlan were resolve and bounty."
[[From his Diwan, p. 83, and Lisan (dalla) (jala), from his famous elegy on the death of Abu Hujr al-Nu'man ibn al-Harith ibn Abi Shamir al-Ghassani. The verse preceding it: "If you have bid farewell, not blameworthy, to the comforts of a kingdom the ancients had established, then do not be far off; death is an appointed meeting, and every man's state will one day pass away. There was between the good, had he come back safe, Abu Hujr, only a few nights. If I live, I shall not tire of my life; and if you die, there is no benefit in life after your death." Then: "So the ones who misled him..."

The transmission of al-Asma'i and Abu 'Ubaydah has "fa'aba musloh" with the unpointed sad. Al-Asma'i explained it, saying: "He meant: the first arrival came with news of his death, and they did not verify it, did not confirm it, and did not believe it. Then came the ones who arrive later, who came after the first report, following its trail, and reported what it had reported, 'with a clear sign': that is, with a true, widely-transmitted report confirming his death and affirming the first report. He took it from the one who precedes and the one who follows (among horses)." Abu 'Ubaydah said: "Musloh means the people of prayer, i.e., the monks and the religious among them."

What al-Asma'i said is very strange, and I reject it for its remoteness, its extreme strangeness, and the contrivance that does not avail. Had he said "musloh" means those who escort him, who will soon follow his traces to the place where he ended, which is the grave, it would have been better and more deeply rooted in Arabic! But thus do opinions sometimes lead the imams of knowledge astray. What Abu 'Ubaydah said, despite its weakness, is better than what al-Asma'i said. I choose the reading that al-Tabari transmitted, and it has two explanations. One is what al-Tabari said, which implies that al-Nu'man died by being killed, and I have found no report supporting that, since it is not possible for "musloh" to mean "muhlikuh" except in this sense. The other: "mudillu" means those who buried him, i.e., they hid him and concealed him in the earth; this is the well-known usage in their speech, like the saying of al-Mukhabbal: "The Banu Qays ibn Sa'd lost their chief and their horseman in the age, Qays ibn 'Asim." So the meaning of the Nabigha's words is: the people denied the report of al-Nu'man's death when it first came; then, when those who buried him came with news of what they had witnessed, they confirmed the first report. This is the best that can be said about the meaning of the verse. "Al-Jawlan" is a mountain in the region of Damascus, in the district of Hauran. It is clear from the Nabigha's poetry that al-Nu'man's dwellings, palaces and houses were there.]]

meaning: those who destroyed him.

* *

"Wa ma yudillun illa anfusahum" — and they destroy none but themselves by their attempt to turn you from your religion; by "themselves" is meant their followers and partisans in their creed and religions. They destroyed themselves and their followers by what they attempted of that, because by their deed they earned from Allah His wrath and deserved His anger and curse, for their disbelief in Allah and their breaking of the covenant that Allah took from them in their Book, regarding following Muhammad (ﷺ), affirming him, and acknowledging his prophethood.

Then He, mighty is His praise, informed about them that they do what they do, attempting to turn the believers from guidance to error and ruin, out of ignorance of what Allah has prepared for them of His punishment and stored for them of His painful torment. So He, exalted is His remembrance, said: "wa ma yash'urun" — and they do not perceive that they mislead none but themselves by their attempt to mislead you, O believers.

* *

The meaning of His saying "wa ma yash'urun" is: they do not know and are not aware.

* *

We have explained the interpretation of this with its evidence in another place, so repeating it is unnecessary. [[See the explanation of "sha'ara" above, 1:277, 278.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 70:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you witness [their truth]?﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: "O People of the Scripture," from among the Jews and the Christians, "why do you disbelieve," meaning: why do you deny "the signs of God," meaning: what is in the Book of God, which He sent down to you through the tongues of your prophets, of its signs and proofs, "while you witness" that it is the truth from your Lord.

* *

This is only from God, mighty and majestic, a rebuke to the People of the Two Scriptures for their disbelief in Muhammad (ﷺ) and their denial of his prophethood, while they find it in their books, together with their testimony that what is in their books is true and that it is from God. As [the reports] say:

7219 - Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you witness [their truth]?﴾ He said: You testify that the description of Muhammad, the Prophet of God (ﷺ), is in your book, and then you disbelieve in him, deny him, and do not believe in him, while you find him written among you in the Torah and the Gospel: ﴿the unlettered Prophet who believes in God and His words﴾.

7220 - Al-Muthanna narrated to us, he said: Ishaq narrated to us, he said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you witness [their truth]?﴾ He said: You testify that the description of Muhammad is in your book, and then you disbelieve in him and do not believe in him, while you find him among you in the Torah and the Gospel: ﴿the unlettered Prophet﴾.

7221 - Muhammad narrated to me, he said: Ahmad narrated to us, he said: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi, concerning ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you witness [their truth]?﴾: "the signs of God" refers to Muhammad, and as for "while you witness," they testify that he is the truth, finding him written among them.

7222 - Al-Qasim narrated to us, he said: Al-Husayn narrated to us, he said: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you witness [their truth]?﴾ that the religion with God is Islam, and there is no religion with God other than it.

[[Report 7222: The printed edition and the manuscript omitted "al-Qasim narrated to us, he said," so I have restored it. This is a chain that recurs in the tafsir from its beginning, the closest instance being no. 7200, and it will come shortly in its correct form, no. 7226.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 71:

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you mix truth with falsehood﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: O people of the Torah and the Gospel, "why do you mix" — that is, why do you confuse — "truth with falsehood."

* *

Their mixing of truth with falsehood was their outward profession with their tongues of belief in Muhammad ﷺ and in what he brought from God, while what was in their hearts was other than that: Judaism and Christianity.

As related:

7223 - Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Ibn Ishaq, from Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, from Ikrimah or Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Abdullah ibn al-Sayyif, Adi ibn Zayd, and al-Harith ibn Awf said to one another: "Come, let us believe in what has been revealed to Muhammad and his companions at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve in it at its end, so that we may confuse their religion for them; perhaps they will do as we do and turn back from their religion!" So God, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them: "O People of the Scripture, why do you mix truth with falsehood" down to His saying: "And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing." [Report 7223: Sirat Ibn Hisham 2:202; this continues the earlier report no. 7202.]

7224 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "O People of the Scripture, why do you mix truth with falsehood," meaning: why do you mix Judaism and Christianity with Islam, when you know that the religion of God, which He accepts no other than, is Islam, and He recompenses only by it?

7225 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' with the like of it, except that he said: "The one He accepts from no one other than it is Islam," and did not say: "and He recompenses only by it." [In the printed edition: "and He does not accept nor recompense except by it," read so by the editor due to the corruption of the copyist's script; the correct reading is what is recorded here. In the manuscript: "la yujza al-aya," which is an ugly distortion.]

7226 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His saying: "O People of the Scripture, why do you mix truth with falsehood": Islam with Judaism and Christianity.

* *

Others said, regarding this:

7227 - Yunus related this to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, concerning the saying of God, mighty and majestic: "why do you mix truth with falsehood": "The truth" is the Torah which God revealed to Moses, and "the falsehood" is what they wrote with their own hands.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have already explained the meaning of "confusion" (labs) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [See what has preceded, 1:567–568.]

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿and you conceal the truth while you know﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Why do you conceal, O People of the Scripture, the truth?

* *

The "truth" which they concealed is what was in their books of the description of Muhammad ﷺ, his sending, and his prophethood, as related:

7228 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah concerning His saying: "and you conceal the truth while you know": They concealed the matter of Muhammad, while they found him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel, commanding them to what is right and forbidding them from what is wrong.

7229 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' concerning His saying: "and you conceal the truth while you know," meaning: they conceal the matter of Muhammad ﷺ, while they find him written with them in the Torah and the Gospel: commanding them to what is right and forbidding them from what is wrong.

7230 - Al-Qasim related to me, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "conceal the truth": Islam, and the command of Muhammad ﷺ; "while you know": that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and that the religion is Islam.

* *

As for His saying "while you know," He means: while you know that what you conceal of the truth is truth, and that it is from God. This statement from God, mighty and majestic, is a report about the People of the Scripture's deliberate disbelief in it and their concealment of what they knew of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ, which they found in their books and which their prophets had brought them.

The Interpretation of His words, may His praise be exalted: ﴿And a group of the People of the Book said: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may turn back."﴾ (3:72)

Abu Ja'far said: The commentators differed concerning the nature of the matter which this group was commanded to do: belief at the beginning of the day, and disbelief at its end.

Some of them said: That was a command from them to one another to affirm the Prophet ﷺ in his prophethood and in what he brought from God, and that it is true, outwardly, without affirming it with resolve and conviction of the hearts, and to disbelieve in him and deny all of that at its end.

Mention of those who said this:

7231 - Al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, concerning His words: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end." He said: Some of them said to others: "Give them satisfaction with their religion at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, for that is more likely to make them believe you, and to make them know that you have seen in them what you dislike, and it is more likely that they will turn back from their religion."

7232 - Al-Muthanna related to us, saying: Mu'alla ibn Asad related to us, saying: Khalid related to us, from Husayn, from Abu Malik, concerning His words: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end." He said: The Jews said: "Believe with them at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may turn back with you."

7233 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi, concerning: "And a group of the People of the Book said: Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may turn back." He said: The rabbis of the villages of 'Uraynah (or 'Urayna) were twelve rabbis, and they said to some of them: "Enter into the religion of Muhammad at the beginning of the day, and say: 'We testify that Muhammad is true and truthful,' and when it is the end of the day, disbelieve and say: 'We returned to our scholars and rabbis and asked them, and they told us that Muhammad is a liar, and that you are not upon anything, and we have returned to our religion, which is more pleasing to us than your religion,' that perhaps they may doubt. They will say: 'These were with us at the beginning of the day, so what has happened to them?'" Then God, Mighty and Majestic, informed His Messenger ﷺ of that.

7234 - It was related to me on the authority of 'Ammar, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from Husayn, from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, who said: The Jews said to one another: "Embrace Islam at the beginning of the day, and apostatize at its end, that perhaps they may turn back." So God made known their secret, and God, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: "And a group of the People of the Book said: Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end, that perhaps they may turn back."

* *

Others said: Rather, what they were commanded to believe in was the prayer, attending it with them at the beginning of the day, and abandoning it at its end.

Mention of those who said this:

7235 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the words of God, Mighty and Majestic: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day." The Jews said: They prayed the dawn prayer with Muhammad, and disbelieved at the end of the day, by way of deceit, to show the people that misguidance had appeared in him after they had followed him.

7236 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

7237 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning his words: "And a group of the People of the Book said: Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day," the verse, and that is because a group of the Jews said: "When you meet the companions of Muhammad ﷺ at the beginning of the day, believe, and when it is the end of it, pray your prayer, that perhaps they will say: 'These are the People of the Book, and they are more knowledgeable than us!' Perhaps they will turn back from their religion, and do not believe except in one who follows your religion."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the speech is then: "And a group of the People of the Book" — meaning: of the Jews who read the Torah — "believe" — affirm — "in what has been revealed to those who believe" — that is, what Muhammad ﷺ brought them of the true religion, its laws and its ways — "at the beginning of the day" — meaning: the first part of the day.

* *

He called its beginning "its face" (wajh) because it is its best part and the first thing that confronts the one who looks at it and sees it, just as the first part of a garment is called "its face," and as Rabi' ibn Ziyad said:

"Whoever is glad at the killing of Malik, let him come to our women with the face of the day."

*(Footnote in the original: the verse is from a poem in which he lamented his close kinsman Malik ibn Zuhayr; the commentators explained that the Arabs wailed for their slain only after avenging them, and the poet's meaning is that he had already exacted vengeance swiftly that very morning.)*

* *

Similar to what we have said concerning this has been stated by a group of the commentators.

Mention of those who said this:

7238 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, concerning his words: "the face of the day" — the beginning of the day.

7239 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi': "the face of the day" — the beginning of the day, "and disbelieve at its end" — he says: the end of the day.

7240 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believe at the beginning of the day, and disbelieve at its end." He said: Pray with them the dawn prayer, and do not pray with them at the end of the day, perhaps you will cause them to slip by that.

* *

As for His words "and disbelieve at its end," He means by it that they said: Deny what you affirmed of their religion at the beginning of the day, at the end of the day, "that perhaps they may turn back" — meaning: that perhaps they will turn back from their religion with you and abandon it, as:

7241 - Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah: "that perhaps they may turn back" — he says: that perhaps they will abandon their religion and return to that in which you are.

7242 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', similarly.

7243 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd related to me, saying: My father related to me, saying: My paternal uncle related to me, saying: My father related to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "that perhaps they may turn back" — that perhaps they will turn over from their religion.

7244 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "that perhaps they may turn back" — that perhaps they will doubt.

7245 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, his words: "that perhaps they may turn back" — he said: they will turn back from their religion.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 73:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And do not believe except to one who follows your religion﴾

Abu Ja'far said: Its meaning, by His, may His majesty be exalted: "Do not believe [i.e., do not trust or affirm] except one who follows your religion, being a Jew."

* *

This is a report from God about the words of the group who said to their Jewish brethren: "Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day."

* *

The "lam" in His words "li-man tabi'a dinakum" (to one who follows your religion) is similar to the "lam" in His words: ﴿Perhaps some of what you seek to hasten has drawn near to you﴾ [Surah al-Naml: 72], meaning: "radifakum" (has drawn near to you).

* *

The people of interpretation have said things similar to what we have said regarding this interpretation.

Mention of those who said this:

7246 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "And do not believe except to one who follows your religion" — this is the statement of some of them to others.

7247 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' the like of it.

7247 (m) - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And do not believe except to one who follows your religion," he said: "Do not believe except to one who follows Judaism."

7248 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words: "And do not believe except to one who follows your religion," he said: "Do not believe except to one who believes in your religion, and whoever opposes it, do not believe him." [[In the printed edition: "la man khalafahu fala tu'minu bihi" with an added "la", and in the manuscript: "man khalafahu fala tu'minu bihi"; the correct reading is the added waw as I have established, and also "tu'minu lahu", and that is a scribal error.]]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God — that someone be given the like of what you were given, or that they argue with you before your Lord﴾

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation differed regarding the interpretation of this.

Some of them said: His words "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God" are an interjection in the middle of the speech, a report from God that clarification is His clarification and guidance is His guidance. They said: The rest of the speech after that is connected to the first speech, as a report about the saying of the Jews to one another. So the meaning of the speech according to them is: "And do not believe except one who follows your religion, and do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you were given, or that they will argue with you before your Lord" — i.e., "Do not believe that anyone will argue with you before your Lord." Then God, the Mighty and Majestic, said to His Prophet ﷺ: "Say, O Muhammad: 'Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills,'" and "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God."

Mention of those who said this:

7249 - Muhammad ibn Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid regarding His words: "That someone be given the like of what you were given," out of envy of the Jews that prophethood would be in others, and wanting that they be followed in their religion.

7250 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

* *

Others said: The interpretation is: "Say, O Muhammad: 'Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that clarification is the clarification of God, that someone be given'" — they said: its meaning is: no one from among the nations will be given the like of what you were given, just as He said: ﴿God makes clear to you lest you go astray﴾ [Surah al-Nisa: 176], meaning: lest you go astray; and as in His words: ﴿Thus We have inserted it into the hearts of the criminals; they do not believe in it﴾ [Surah al-Shu'ara: 200–201], meaning: that they not believe. "The like of what you were given" — he says: the like of what you, O Muhammad, and your community were given of Islam and guidance. "Or that they argue with you before your Lord" — they said: the meaning of "aw" (or) is "illa" (except), i.e., "except that they argue with you," meaning: except that they dispute with you before your Lord regarding what your Lord did to them. [[See the detailed account of this view in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 222–223.]]

Mention of those who said this:

7251 - Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: God, the Mighty and Majestic, said to Muhammad ﷺ: "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that someone be given the like of what you were given," meaning: the like of what you were given, O community of Muhammad, "or that they argue with you before your Lord." The Jews say: God has done such-and-such honor to us, until He sent down upon us the manna and the quail. So: indeed what I have given you is greater; so say: "Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills," and so on, the verse.

* *

On this interpretation, this entire speech is a command from God to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to say it to the Jews, and it is connected in its parts without interjection. The second "guidance" is a response to the first "guidance," and "an" (that) is in the nominative position as the predicate regarding "guidance."

* *

Others said: Rather, this is a command from God to His Prophet to say it to the Jews. They said: Its interpretation: "Say," O Muhammad, "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that someone among mankind be given" "the like of what you were given" — meaning: the like of what you, O assembly of Jews, were given of the Book of God and of your Prophet. So do not envy the believers for what I have given them, like what I have given you of My bounty, for bounty is in My hand; I give it to whom I will.

Mention of those who said this:

7252 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah regarding His words: "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that someone be given the like of what you were given," he means: when God sent down a Book like your Book and sent a Prophet like your Prophet, you envied them for that. "Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God," and so on.

7253 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi' the like of it.

* *

Others said: Rather, the interpretation is: "Say," O Muhammad: "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that someone be given the like of what you were given," you, O assembly of Jews, from the Book of God. They said: This is the end of the statement that God commanded our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ to say to the Jews from this verse. They said: His words "or that they argue with you" are linked back to His words "And do not believe except to one who follows your religion."

The meaning of the speech according to the proponents of this view is: "And do not believe except to one who follows your religion, so that you abandon the truth — that they argue with you by it before your Lord, from whose religion you have followed and chosen: that it is true, and that you find its description in your Book." Then, according to these people, His words "or that they argue with you" are linked back to an omitted prohibition.

Mention of those who said this:

7254 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words: "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that someone be given the like of what you were given," he means: this matter in which you are: that someone be given the like of what you were given. "Or that they argue with you before your Lord," he said: some of them said to others: Do not inform them of what God has made clear to you in His Book, so that they argue with you — he said: that they dispute with you — "before your Lord." "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God."

* *

[Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these views is that His words "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God" are an interjection, and the rest of the speech follows one context.] Then its interpretation is: "And do not believe except one who follows your religion, and do not believe that anyone will be given the like of what you were given" — meaning: no one will be given the like of what you were given — "or that they argue with you before your Lord, by [your] faith, because you are more honored by God through what He has favored you with over them." So the whole speech is a report about the statement of the group of whom God, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "And a group of the People of the Book said: Believe in what has been revealed to those who believed at the beginning of the day," apart from His words "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God." Then the speech begins with a refutation of their saying, "Say," O Muhammad, to those who said what they said to their followers among the Jews: "Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God" — that success is the success of God and clarification is His clarification — "and indeed bounty is in His hand; He gives it to whom He wills," not what you Jews have wished for.

We have chosen this from the other views we have mentioned, because it is the soundest in meaning and the most correct in the usage of Arabic, and the most consistent with the arrangement and context of the speech. As for other opinions, they are strained and far from correctness, with extreme forcing of the speech.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing﴾ (73)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His majesty be exalted, He means: "Say," O Muhammad, to these Jews whose statement I have described to their followers: "Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God," indeed success for faith and guidance to Islam are in the hand of God and to Him, not yours nor that of the rest of His creation. "He gives it to whom He wills" of His creatures, meaning: He gives it to whomever of His servants He wishes, as a refutation by God, the Mighty and Majestic, of them in their saying to their followers: "No one will be given the like of what you were given." So God, the Mighty and Majestic, said to His Prophet ﷺ: Say to them: That is not up to you; it is up to God, in whose hand all things are, and to Him belongs bounty, and in His hand; He gives it to whom He wills. "And God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing" — meaning: God possesses vastness in His bounty toward whomever He wills to favor, and All-Knowing of those who are worthy of bounty among them.

7255 - al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Suwayd ibn Nasr narrated to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us by reading, from Ibn Jurayj regarding His words: "Say: Indeed, bounty is in the hand of God; He gives it to whom He wills," he said: Islam.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 74:

The discussion of the interpretation of His words: ﴿He singles out for His mercy whom He wills, and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By His words, "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills," "yakhtassu" (he singles out) is of the form "yaftaʿilu," from the saying of the speaker, "I singled out so-and-so with such-and-such, I single him out with it" (khassastu fulanan bi-kadha, akhussuhu bihi). [See the explanation of "yakhtassu" earlier as well, 2:471.]

* *

As for "His mercy" in this place, it is Islam and the Qur'an, together with prophethood, as follows:

7256 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills": he said: prophethood; He singles out for it whom He wills.

7257 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Abu Huthayfa related to us, saying: Shibl related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, the like of it.

7258 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Ishaq related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills": he said: He singles out for prophethood whom He wills.

7259 - Al-Muthanna related to me, saying: Suwayd related to us, saying: Ibn al-Mubarak informed us by recitation, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding "He singles out for His mercy whom He wills": he said: The Qur'an and Islam.

7260 - Al-Qasim related to us, saying: Al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, the like of it.

* *

As for "and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty," it means: He is the Possessor of a bounty which He bestows upon whomever He loves and wills from among His creation. Then He described His bounty as great, saying, "His bounty is great," because it is incomparable in the greatness of its station with respect to the one upon whom it is bestowed, [a bounty] from the bounties of His creation, [note: in the printed edition: "incomparable ... whom He favoured with a bounty from the bounties of His creation"; in the manuscript: "incomparable ... from whom He favoured with bounties from the bounties of His creation." I saw that some words were dropped by the manuscript copyist, which I have added between the brackets so the sentence is sound.] nor does anything approach it in the majesty of its worth, nor come near to it.

**The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him.﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: This is information from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that among the People of the Book, who are the Jews of the Children of Israel, there are people of trustworthiness who return what is entrusted to them and do not betray it, and among them is one who betrays his trust, the immoral one who swears falsely and considers it lawful [[The manuscript may have a lacuna. The correct reading is probably "the one who considers lawful the wealth of the unlettered Arabs" or "the one who considers lawful the wealth of the believers," as becomes clear from the rest of the commentary on the verse.]].

* *

If someone says: What is the purpose of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informing His Prophet ﷺ of this, when you know that people have always been this way, some returning their trusts and some betraying them?

It is said: By informing the believers of their condition, as He has explained in His Book through these verses, Allah intended to warn them against entrusting them with their wealth, and to frighten them against being deceived by them, since many of them consider the wealth of the believers lawful.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: "And among the People of the Book is one who, O Muhammad, if you entrust him with a great amount of wealth, will return it to you and will not betray you concerning it; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will betray you concerning it and will not return it to you, unless you press him with demands and insistence."

* *

The "bi" (with/for) in His words "bi-dinar" and the "ʿalā" (over) interchange in this context, just as one says "marartu bihi" and "marartu ʿalayhi" (I passed by him).

* *

The interpreters differed concerning the meaning of His words: ﴿unless you keep standing over him﴾.

Some of them said: "Unless you keep demanding it from him."

Those who said this:

7261: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him": unless you seek it and pursue it.

7262: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him," he said: "You demand it from him."

7263: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him," he said: "Persistently."

7264: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: "unless you keep standing at his head." [[In the printed edition it reads "unless you keep standing over him," with the added word "ʿalayhi," which is an error. The correct reading is from the manuscript.]]

Those who said this:

7265: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him," he said: He acknowledges his trust as long as you are standing at his head. When you stand and then come seeking it, he denies your right. [[ "Kafarahu haqqahu" means he denied his right.]] Such are the one who returns it and the one who denies it. [[His words "the one who returns it and the one who denies it" explain the two groups mentioned in the verse: this one returns it, and that one denies it.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the two interpretations of the verse is the statement of the one who said: "The meaning is: unless you keep standing over him in demand and pursuit." This is from their saying: "So-and-so stood on my behalf against so-and-so until he extracted it for me," meaning he worked to secure it and strove to extract it from him until he obtained it. This is because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only described them as considering the wealth of the unlettered lawful, and that among them is one who does not pay what he owes except with intense demand and insistence. Standing at the head of the one who owes the debt does not necessarily move him from his state of considering lawful what he holds unlawfully, but it may be that, even while he considers it lawful to take what he owes from the creditor, the way to extract it is through demand, litigation, and dispute. [[The sentence structure is "it may be ... the way to extracting it is through demand ...," and there is a separation between the two parts.]] That demand is the creditor's standing to extract his right from the one who owes it.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿That is because they said, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, the Mighty and Majestic means: whoever among the Jews considers betrayal lawful and denies the rights of the Arab that he owes him, not paying what the Arab entrusted him with except as long as the Arab keeps demanding it from him, does so because he says: "There is no sin or blame upon us for what we have taken from the wealth of the Arabs, because they are not upon the truth and they are polytheists." [[For the interpretation of "al-ummiyyun" (the unlettered), see earlier volumes 2: 257–259; then 5: 442 in al-Tabari's own words; then 6: 281; then the reports numbered 5827, 6774, 6775.]]

* *

The interpreters differed concerning the interpretation of this, and some of them said something similar to what we said.

Those who said this:

7266: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered,'" the verse: the Jews said: "There is no blame upon us for what we have taken from the wealth of the Arabs."

7267: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered," he said: "There is no blame upon us concerning the polytheists," meaning those who are not People of the Book.

7268: Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered,'" he said: It is said to him: "Why do you not return your trust?" He says: "There is no blame upon us regarding the wealth of the Arabs; Allah has made it lawful for us!"

7269: Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yaʿqub al-Qummi narrated to us, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr: When the verse was revealed, "And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him—that is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered,'" the Prophet ﷺ said: "The enemies of Allah have lied. Everything from the time of ignorance is under my feet, except trust; it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked alike." [[Report 7269: "Yaʿqub ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Ashʿari al-Qummi," and "Jaʿfar" is "Jaʿfar ibn Abi al-Mughirah al-Khuzaʿi al-Qummi," both of whom occurred in number 617. My brother Sayyid Ahmad said regarding a similar chain earlier: "This is a marfuʿ hadith (traced to the Prophet), but it is mursal (missing a companion), since Saʿid ibn Jubayr is a Successor, though its chain to him is a good chain." Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 2: 169–170 from the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim, and it is cited in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 44, attributed also to ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir.]]

7270: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Hisham ibn ʿUbayd Allah narrated to us, from Yaʿqub al-Qummi, from Jaʿfar, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr who said: When the Jews said, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered," meaning the seizing of their wealth, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, and then he mentioned something similar, except that he said: "Everything is under these two feet of mine, except trust, which is to be returned," and he did not add anything more.

7271: Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered.'" That is because the People of the Book used to say: "There is no sin upon us regarding what we have taken from these people, because they are unlettered." So this is His saying: "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered," to the end of the verse.

* *

Others said concerning this, that:

7272: al-Qasim narrated to us with this, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered,'" he said: Some Muslims had traded with the Jews in the time of ignorance. When they became Muslim, they demanded from them the price of their sales. The Jews said: "You have no trust with us, and you have no claim against us, because you have abandoned your religion which you were upon!" He said: They also claimed that they had found this in their book. So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, said: "And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know."

7273: Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: Sufyan narrated to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'sa'ah who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas: "We raid the People of the Book and obtain some of their fruit?" He said: "Do you say what the People of the Book said: 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered'!?" [[Report 7273: "Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani," as shown in the following report. "Sa'sa'ah ibn Yazid," also said to be "Sa'sa'ah ibn Zayd." al-Bukhari mentioned the disagreement about his name and pointed to the narration of this report in al-Kabir 2/2: 321–322, and Ibn Abi Hatim 2/1: 446. See the note on the following report.]]

7274: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Abu Ishaq al-Hamdani, from Sa'sa'ah: that a man asked Ibn ʿAbbas, saying: "We obtain from the raid, or [the palm cluster] (the doubt is from al-Hasan), from the wealth of the dhimmis, a hen and a sheep." Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Then what do you say?" He said: "We say: there is no harm in that for us!" He said: "This is like what the People of the Book said: 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered'! When they pay the poll tax (jizyah), their wealth is not lawful for you except with their good will." [[Report 7274: This is another route for the earlier report, with different wording. Abu ʿUbayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated it in Kitab al-Amwal (p. 149, no. 415) through ʿAbd al-Rahman, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'sa'ah, with different wording. al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan 9: 198 through "Shu'bah, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'sa'ah, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas," with wording different from all of the above. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 2: 169 from the tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq, where it reads "from Abu Sa'sa'ah ibn Yazid," which is an error; the correct form is "Sa'sa'ah." He said: "Similarly al-Thawri narrated it from Abu Ishaq with similar wording." al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 4, attributing it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim. al-Zamakhshari quoted it in his tafsir of the verse, in Abu Ja'far's wording, and al-Qurtubi 4: 118–119, and Abu Hayyan in his tafsir from the tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq also, 2: 501. In all of them it reads "We raid in the lands," except al-Qurtubi, whose version reads "We only obtain in the reserves," and al-Bayhaqi, whose version reads: "We come to the village in the countryside and open the door," and in al-Amwal: "We travel in the land of the dhimmis and obtain from them."

In the manuscript and printed edition of al-Tabari, there was: "We obtain in the al-ʿurf or al-ʿadhq (the doubt is from al-Hasan)," which I did not find anywhere, and which has no meaning either. All of those we mentioned who transmitted from the tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq with this same chain agreed on one wording: "We obtain in the raid," so I have recorded it so. As for what al-Hasan ibn Yahya doubted, I have placed it between brackets, as it has no meaning. My strongest opinion is that it is "or: the raid (ghazwah), the doubt is from al-Hasan," or it may be "or: the village (qaryah), the doubt is from al-Hasan."]]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, the Mighty and Majestic means: those among them who say, "There is no blame upon us regarding the wealth of the unlettered Arabs that we betray them concerning it," say this, claiming that Allah has made that lawful for them, so there is no blame upon them for betraying them and abandoning paying them. [[His words "al-kadhib" (the lie) are the object of "yaqulun" (they say), and there is separation between them.]] They speak falsehood about Allah deliberately, incurring sin by claiming that Allah has made that lawful for them. This is His statement, the Mighty and Majestic: "while they know," as:

7275: Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know" means the one among them who says, when he is asked, "Why do you not return your trust?": "There is no blame upon us regarding the wealth of the Arabs; Allah has made it lawful for us!"

7276: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know," meaning their claim that they found in their book the saying: "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered."

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Yes! Whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah—indeed Allah loves the righteous.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is information from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about what is for the one who returns his trust to the one who entrusted him with it, out of fear and awareness of Allah, with Him. [[In the printed edition: "This is information from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about the one who returns his trust to the one who entrusted him with it, out of fear of Allah, his awareness of Him, and his threat." The text here is that of the manuscript, which is the pure correct version. The context is: "This is information from Allah ... about what is for the one who returned his trust ... with Him." His words "ittiqa' Allah wa muraqabatahu" (fear of Allah and awareness of Him) are in the accusative, as objects of purpose.]] So He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: The matter is not as those liars against Allah among the Jews say, that there is no blame or sin upon them regarding the wealth of the unlettered. Then He said: "Yes," but "whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah," meaning: but rather the one who fulfills his covenant, which is the charge He gave them in the Torah, to believe in Muhammad ﷺ and in what came to them. [[For the meaning of "awfa" (fulfills), see earlier volumes 1: 557–559 and 3: 348. For the interpretation of "al-ʿahd" (covenant), see earlier volumes 1: 410–414, then 557–559, 3: 20–24, 348–349.]]

* *

The pronoun "hu" (his) in His words "whoever fulfills his covenant" refers to the name "Allah" in His words "and they speak falsehood about Allah."

* *

He says: Yes, whoever fulfills the covenant of Allah which He made with them in His Book, and believes in Muhammad ﷺ, confirms him, and confirms what came to him from Allah—including returning trusts to those who entrusted them, and other matters of Allah's commands and prohibitions—"and fears Allah," meaning he fears what Allah forbade him, which is disbelief in Him and all His acts of disobedience that He forbade him, avoiding them out of awareness of Allah's threat and fear of His punishment. "Indeed Allah loves the righteous," meaning: indeed Allah loves those who fear Him, fear His punishment, and beware of His torment, so they avoid what He forbade them and prohibited for them, and obey Him in what He commanded them.

* *

It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to say: It is fear of polytheism (shirk).

7277: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah narrated to us, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words "Yes! Whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah," he says: "He fears polytheism," "indeed Allah loves the righteous," meaning: those who fear polytheism.

* *

We have already explained the disagreement of the interpreters concerning this and the correct statement about it, with the evidences that indicate it, in what has passed of our book, sufficiently so that we need not repeat it. [[See the interpretation of "ittaqa" (fear) and "taqwa" (fear of God/piety) in earlier volumes 1: 232, 233, 364; 2: 181, 457; 4: 162, 244, 425, 426; then 6: 261.]]

**The Interpretation of His Words: ﴿And among the People of the Book is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar, will return it to you; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will not return it to you unless you keep standing over him.﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: This is information from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, that among the People of the Book, who are the Jews of the Children of Israel, there are people of trustworthiness who return what is entrusted to them and do not betray it, and among them is one who betrays his trust, the immoral one who swears falsely and considers it lawful [[The manuscript may have a lacuna. The correct reading is probably "the one who considers lawful the wealth of the unlettered Arabs" or "the one who considers lawful the wealth of the believers," as becomes clear from the rest of the commentary on the verse.]].

* *

If someone says: What is the purpose of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informing His Prophet ﷺ of this, when you know that people have always been this way, some returning their trusts and some betraying them?

It is said: By informing the believers of their condition, as He has explained in His Book through these verses, Allah intended to warn them against entrusting them with their wealth, and to frighten them against being deceived by them, since many of them consider the wealth of the believers lawful.

* *

So the meaning of the statement is: "And among the People of the Book is one who, O Muhammad, if you entrust him with a great amount of wealth, will return it to you and will not betray you concerning it; and among them is one who, if you entrust him with a dinar, will betray you concerning it and will not return it to you, unless you press him with demands and insistence."

* *

The "bi" (with/for) in His words "bi-dinar" and the "ʿalā" (over) interchange in this context, just as one says "marartu bihi" and "marartu ʿalayhi" (I passed by him).

* *

The interpreters differed concerning the meaning of His words: ﴿unless you keep standing over him﴾.

Some of them said: "Unless you keep demanding it from him."

Those who said this:

7261: Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him": unless you seek it and pursue it.

7262: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him," he said: "You demand it from him."

7263: Muhammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abu ʿAsim narrated to us, from ʿIsa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him," he said: "Persistently."

7264: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Hudhayfah narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: "unless you keep standing at his head." [[In the printed edition it reads "unless you keep standing over him," with the added word "ʿalayhi," which is an error. The correct reading is from the manuscript.]]

Those who said this:

7265: Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi concerning His words "unless you keep standing over him," he said: He acknowledges his trust as long as you are standing at his head. When you stand and then come seeking it, he denies your right. [[ "Kafarahu haqqahu" means he denied his right.]] Such are the one who returns it and the one who denies it. [[His words "the one who returns it and the one who denies it" explain the two groups mentioned in the verse: this one returns it, and that one denies it.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the two interpretations of the verse is the statement of the one who said: "The meaning is: unless you keep standing over him in demand and pursuit." This is from their saying: "So-and-so stood on my behalf against so-and-so until he extracted it for me," meaning he worked to secure it and strove to extract it from him until he obtained it. This is because Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, only described them as considering the wealth of the unlettered lawful, and that among them is one who does not pay what he owes except with intense demand and insistence. Standing at the head of the one who owes the debt does not necessarily move him from his state of considering lawful what he holds unlawfully, but it may be that, even while he considers it lawful to take what he owes from the creditor, the way to extract it is through demand, litigation, and dispute. [[The sentence structure is "it may be ... the way to extracting it is through demand ...," and there is a separation between the two parts.]] That demand is the creditor's standing to extract his right from the one who owes it.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿That is because they said, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, the Mighty and Majestic means: whoever among the Jews considers betrayal lawful and denies the rights of the Arab that he owes him, not paying what the Arab entrusted him with except as long as the Arab keeps demanding it from him, does so because he says: "There is no sin or blame upon us for what we have taken from the wealth of the Arabs, because they are not upon the truth and they are polytheists." [[For the interpretation of "al-ummiyyun" (the unlettered), see earlier volumes 2: 257–259; then 5: 442 in al-Tabari's own words; then 6: 281; then the reports numbered 5827, 6774, 6775.]]

* *

The interpreters differed concerning the interpretation of this, and some of them said something similar to what we said.

Those who said this:

7267: al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Maʿmar informed us, from Qatadah concerning His words "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered," he said: "There is no blame upon us concerning the polytheists," meaning those who are not People of the Book.

7268: Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered,'" he said: It is said to him: "Why do you not return your trust?" He says: "There is no blame upon us regarding the wealth of the Arabs; Allah has made it lawful for us!"

7271: Muhammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbas: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered.'" That is because the People of the Book used to say: "There is no sin upon us regarding what we have taken from these people, because they are unlettered." So this is His saying: "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered," to the end of the verse.

* *

Others said concerning this, that:

7272: al-Qasim narrated to us with this, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "That is because they said, 'There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered,'" he said: Some Muslims had traded with the Jews in the time of ignorance. Abu ʿUbayd al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated it in Kitab al-Amwal (p. 149, no. 415) through ʿAbd al-Rahman, from Sufyan, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'sa'ah, with different wording. al-Bayhaqi narrated it in al-Sunan 9: 198 through "Shu'bah, from Abu Ishaq, from Sa'sa'ah, who said: I said to Ibn ʿAbbas," with wording different from all of the above. Ibn Kathir cited it in his tafsir 2: 169 from the tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq, where it reads "from Abu Sa'sa'ah ibn Yazid," which is an error; the correct form is "Sa'sa'ah." He said: "Similarly al-Thawri narrated it from Abu Ishaq with similar wording." al-Suyuti cited it in al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 4, attributing it to Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim. al-Zamakhshari quoted it in his tafsir of the verse, in Abu Ja'far's wording, and al-Qurtubi 4: 118–119, and Abu Hayyan in his tafsir from the tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq also, 2: 501. In all of them it reads "We raid in the lands," except al-Qurtubi, whose version reads "We only obtain in the reserves," and al-Bayhaqi, whose version reads: "We come to the village in the countryside and open the door," and in al-Amwal: "We travel in the land of the dhimmis and obtain from them."

In the manuscript and printed edition of al-Tabari, there was: "We obtain in the al-ʿurf or al-ʿadhq (the doubt is from al-Hasan)," which I did not find anywhere, and which has no meaning either. All of those we mentioned who transmitted from the tafsir of ʿAbd al-Razzaq with this same chain agreed on one wording: "We obtain in the raid," so I have recorded it so. As for what al-Hasan ibn Yahya doubted, I have placed it between brackets, as it has no meaning. My strongest opinion is that it is "or: the raid (ghazwah), the doubt is from al-Hasan," or it may be "or: the village (qaryah), the doubt is from al-Hasan."]]

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, the Mighty and Majestic means: those among them who say, "There is no blame upon us regarding the wealth of the unlettered Arabs that we betray them concerning it," say this, claiming that Allah has made that lawful for them, so there is no blame upon them for betraying them and abandoning paying them. [[His words "al-kadhib" (the lie) are the object of "yaqulun" (they say), and there is separation between them.]] They speak falsehood about Allah deliberately, incurring sin by claiming that Allah has made that lawful for them. This is His statement, the Mighty and Majestic: "while they know," as:

7275: Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know" means the one among them who says, when he is asked, "Why do you not return your trust?": "There is no blame upon us regarding the wealth of the Arabs; Allah has made it lawful for us!"

7276: al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: "And they speak falsehood about Allah while they know," meaning their claim that they found in their book the saying: "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered."

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿Yes! Whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah—indeed Allah loves the righteous.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is information from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about what is for the one who returns his trust to the one who entrusted him with it, out of fear and awareness of Allah, with Him. [[In the printed edition: "This is information from Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, about the one who returns his trust to the one who entrusted him with it, out of fear of Allah, his awareness of Him, and his threat." The text here is that of the manuscript, which is the pure correct version. The context is: "This is information from Allah ... about what is for the one who returned his trust ... with Him." His words "ittiqa' Allah wa muraqabatahu" (fear of Allah and awareness of Him) are in the accusative, as objects of purpose.]] So He, the Mighty and Majestic, said: The matter is not as those liars against Allah among the Jews say, that there is no blame or sin upon them regarding the wealth of the unlettered. Then He said: "Yes," but "whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah," meaning: but rather the one who fulfills his covenant, which is the charge He gave them in the Torah, to believe in Muhammad ﷺ and in what came to them. [[For the meaning of "awfa" (fulfills), see earlier volumes 1: 557–559 and 3: 348. For the interpretation of "al-ʿahd" (covenant), see earlier volumes 1: 410–414, then 557–559, 3: 20–24, 348–349.]]

* *

The pronoun "hu" (his) in His words "whoever fulfills his covenant" refers to the name "Allah" in His words "and they speak falsehood about Allah."

* *

He says: Yes, whoever fulfills the covenant of Allah which He made with them in His Book, and believes in Muhammad ﷺ, confirms him, and confirms what came to him from Allah—including returning trusts to those who entrusted them, and other matters of Allah's commands and prohibitions—"and fears Allah," meaning he fears what Allah forbade him, which is disbelief in Him and all His acts of disobedience that He forbade him, avoiding them out of awareness of Allah's threat and fear of His punishment. "Indeed Allah loves the righteous," meaning: indeed Allah loves those who fear Him, fear His punishment, and beware of His torment, so they avoid what He forbade them and prohibited for them, and obey Him in what He commanded them.

* *

It has been narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to say: It is fear of polytheism (shirk).

7277: al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Muʿawiyah narrated to us, from ʿAli, from Ibn ʿAbbas concerning His words "Yes! Whoever fulfills his covenant and fears Allah," he says: "He fears polytheism," "indeed Allah loves the righteous," meaning: those who fear polytheism.

* *

We have already explained the disagreement of the interpreters concerning this and the correct statement about it, with the evidences that indicate it, in what has passed of our book, sufficiently so that we need not repeat it. [[See the interpretation of "ittaqa" (fear) and "taqwa" (fear of God/piety) in earlier volumes 1: 232, 233, 364; 2: 181, 457; 4: 162, 244, 425, 426; then 6: 261.]]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 77 (part 1 of 2)

The explanation of His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price - those will have no share in the Hereafter, and Allah will not speak to them or look at them on the Day of Resurrection, nor will He purify them, and they will have a painful punishment.﴾ (3:77)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, His majesty, the Exalted, means: Indeed, those who exchange, by their abandonment of the covenant of Allah which He made with them, and His charge which He enjoined on them in the Scriptures that Allah sent down to His prophets, by following Muhammad, affirming him, acknowledging him, and acknowledging what he brought from Allah, and by their false oaths with which they make lawful what Allah has forbidden them, [namely] the wealth of people entrusted to them [[The context of the sentence: "Indeed, those who exchange, by their abandonment of the covenant of Allah ... and by their false oaths ... a price..."]] - "a price", meaning a base return and an inferior substitute from the goods of this world and its trash. [[See the explanation of "purchase" (ishtara) earlier: 1:311-315, 565 / 2:316, 317, then 341, 342, then 452 / 3:328. And see the explanation of "a small price" earlier: 2:565 / 3:328.]] - "Those will have no share in the Hereafter": He says, indeed those who do this have no portion in the good things of the Hereafter, and no share in the bliss of Paradise and what Allah has prepared there for its people, apart from others. [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "apart from others" (feminha dun ghayrih), but the context requires what is recorded here.]]

* *

We have already explained, earlier, the differences among the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) regarding the meaning of "khalaq" (share), and we have indicated the most correct of their opinions on this, with sufficient detail. [[See what has passed: 2:452-454 / 4:201-203.]]

* *

As for His saying "nor will Allah speak to them": it means, Allah will not speak to them in a way that pleases them. "Nor will He look at them": He says, He will not show them kindness, as a sign of His wrath against them, like the saying of one man to another, "Look at me with the look of Allah upon you," meaning: show compassion to me with the compassion of Allah toward you, with goodness and mercy. And as one says to a man, "May Allah not hear your supplication," meaning: may Allah not answer you, though nothing is hidden from Allah. And as the poet said: [[He is Shumayr ibn al-Harith al-Dabbi, and it is said "Sumayr" with an unpointed initial, diminutive. He is from the pre-Islamic period.]]

"I called upon Allah until I feared that Allah would not hear what I say"

[[Nawadir Abi Zayd: 124; al-Khizanah 2:363; al-Lisan (s-m-'); and after it: "So that He might carry me upon a horse, for I am weak in walking, and bearing for the lowly."]] And "hear what I say" means: answer, as in our saying, "Allah hears those who praise Him."

* *
