Others said: "Rather, that is the sincerity of monotheism (tawhid) to Allah."

Mention of those who said that:

7573 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya regarding His saying: "And hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together," he says: hold fast to sincerity to Allah alone.

7574 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His saying: "And hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together," he said: "The rope is Islam." And he recited: "And do not separate."

* * *

The interpretation of His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And do not separate﴾

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means by His saying "And do not separate": and do not separate from the religion of Allah and His covenant which He has entrusted to you in His Book, of harmony and togetherness in obeying Him, obeying His Messenger (ﷺ), and abiding by His command. As follows:

7575 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "And do not separate, and remember the blessing of Allah upon you," – Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has disliked for you division, and has warned you against it in advance, and cautioned you about it, and forbidden you from it, and has approved for you hearing and obedience, harmony and community. So be pleased for yourselves with what Allah has been pleased with for you, if you are able; there is no power except through Allah.

7576 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-'Aliya: "And do not separate," – do not be hostile over it; he means: over sincerity to Allah; and be brothers upon it. [[In the manuscript it reads "and be brothers upon it," and the correct form is what is in the printed edition, and al-Durr al-Manthur 2: 61.]]

7577 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiya ibn Salih narrated to me, that al-Awza'i related to him that Yazid al-Raqashi related to him that he heard Anas ibn Malik say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The Children of Israel split into seventy-one sects, and my community will split into seventy-two sects, all of them in the Fire except one." He said: It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is this one?" He said: He grasped his hand and said: "The community," and "Hold fast to the rope of Allah, all together, and do not separate." [[The hadith 7577: Yazid al-Raqashi is Yazid ibn Aban, Abu Amr, the Basran storyteller (qass). We indicated in the explanation of 6654 and 6728 that he is weak. Shu'ba used to speak about him, said al-Bukhari in al-Kabir 4/2/320; al-Nasa'i said in al-Du'afa': "abandoned"; and Ibn Sa'd 7/2/13 said: "He was weak, a Qadari." The hadith was narrated by Ibn Majah, 3993, by way of al-Walid ibn Muslim: "Abu Amr [that is al-Awza'i] narrated to us, Qatada narrated to us, from Anas," and he mentioned it similarly, raised; but its ending in his version is: "all of them in the Fire except one, which is the community." Al-Busiri said in his additions: "Its chain is sound; its narrators are trustworthy." And so he said. So al-Awza'i narrated it from two shaykhs, one of whom is weak, and the other trustworthy; and the weak one – Yazid al-Raqashi – added the citation of the verse. There is no harm in that, as the meaning is close. Al-Suyuti mentioned it 2: 60, and added its attribution to Ibn Abi Hatim.]]

7578 – Abdullah ibn Abi Umayr al-Karim narrated to me, saying: al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Awza'i narrate, from Yazid al-Raqashi, from Anas ibn Malik, from the Prophet (ﷺ), similar to it. [[The hadith 7578: This hadith repeats the one before it. Abd al-Karim ibn Abi Umayr, the shaykh of al-Tabari: al-Dhahabi mentioned him in al-Mizan 2: 144 with the nickname "al-Dahhan," and said: "There is obscurity in him, and the report is odd" – he means another hadith, which the Hafiz explained in Lisan al-Mizan 4: 50–51, from Tarikh Baghdad, in the biography of another man. It is in Tarikh Baghdad 3: 242, and in that chain the name of this shaykh is: "Abd al-Karim ibn Abi Umayr al-Dihqan." I have not found a biography of him or any mention of him elsewhere.]]

7579 – Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: al-Maharibi narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Thabit ibn Qutba al-Madani, from Abdullah: that he said: "O people, upon you is obedience and community, for it is the rope of Allah which He commanded, and what you dislike in community and obedience is better than what you desire in division." [[The report 7579: "Thabit ibn Qutba al-Madani al-Thaqafi," is recorded in al-Kabir 1/2/168 and al-Jarh 1/1/457. Al-Bukhari said: "He heard Ibn Mas'ud; al-Sha'bi and Abu Ishaq related from him." Ibn Abi Hatim added: "Ziyad ibn Ilaqa and Salim ibn Abi al-Ja'd." In the printed edition in this place and in the next two reports it reads "Thabit ibn Qutna" with an n, which is an error. In the manuscript in this report it reads "Fatnah" without dots, and the ba' is pointed in the next two reports. In the manuscript and printed edition: "al-Marri" in this report and in no. 7581; the correct form is "al-Madani" as I have written it, and Thabit is Thaqafi, not Marri.]]

7580 – Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan al-Sukkari narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Yazid informed us, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, from al-Sha'bi, from Thabit ibn Qutba, who said: I heard Ibn Mas'ud while he was giving a sermon, and he was saying: "O people," then he mentioned something similar. [[The report 7580: In the printed edition: "Abd al-Hamid ibn Bayan al-Yashkuri," which is an error; the correct is the manuscript. A similar error has passed in no. 7378; see the note on it there.]]

7581 – Isma'il ibn Hafs al-Ablli narrated to us, saying: Abdullah ibn Numayr Abu Hisham narrated to us, saying: Mujalid ibn Sa'id narrated to us, from Amir, from Thabit ibn Qutba al-Madani, who said: Abdullah said: "Upon you is obedience and community, for it is the rope of Allah which He commanded," then he mentioned something similar. [[The report 7581: "Isma'il ibn Hafs ibn Amr al-Ablli, Abu Bakr al-Awdi al-Basri, and 'al-Ablli' (with a damma on the hamza, a single ba' and a shadda on the lam with a kasra) is a nisba to 'al-Ablah.' In some books it is 'al-Ayli' with a ya'. He narrated from his father, Hafs ibn Ghiyath, Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman and others. Al-Nasa'i and Ibn Majah narrated from him, and Ibn Khuzayma and a group. Abu Hatim heard from him. Ibn Abi Hatim said: "I asked my father about him, and he said: 'I wrote from him and from his father, and his father was a liar, and he is different from his father.' I said: 'Is there no harm in him?' He said: 'I cannot say there is no harm in him.'" Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat. He is biographed in al-Tahdhib and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/1/165.]]

* * *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And remember the blessing of Allah upon you when you were enemies, so He brought together your hearts, and you became by His blessing brothers﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "And remember the blessing of Allah upon you," – remember what Allah has bestowed upon you of harmony and togetherness in Islam.

The scholars of the Arabic language (ahl al-'arabiyya) differed regarding His saying: "When you were enemies, so He brought together your hearts."

Some grammarians of Basra said regarding this: the speech ends at His saying "And remember the blessing of Allah upon you," then it is explained by His saying "so He brought together your hearts," and it informs about what they were in before the joining, just as you say: "The wall held back from falling."

Some grammarians of Kufa said: His saying "when you were enemies, so He brought together your hearts" follows His saying "And remember the blessing of Allah upon you," not separated from it.

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this, in my opinion, is that His saying "when you were enemies, so He brought together your hearts" is connected to His saying "And remember the blessing of Allah upon you," not cut off from it.

Its interpretation: And remember, O believers, the blessing of Allah upon you, which He has bestowed upon you, when you were enemies in your polytheism [[In the printed edition: "that is, with your polytheism," which is not correct. In the manuscript: "that is your polytheism," which has no meaning; it has an extra alif "that is," and the "in" is "fi." So what I have written is the correct form and context.]], killing one another out of tribal partisanship, not in obedience to Allah or obedience to His Messenger. So Allah brought together your hearts through Islam, and made some of you brothers to others after you were enemies, connected by the affection of Islam and the unity of your word upon it. As follows:

7582 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: "And remember the blessing of Allah upon you, when you were enemies, so He brought together your hearts": you were slaughtering one another in it, the strong among you devouring the weak, until Allah brought Islam, and bound you together in brotherhood with it, and joined you together with it. By Allah, besides whom there is no god, indeed harmony is a mercy, and division is a punishment.

7583 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His saying: "And remember the blessing of Allah upon you, when you were enemies": killing one another, and the strong among you devouring the weak, until Allah brought Islam, and joined you together with it, and gathered your assembly upon it, and made you brothers upon it.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The blessing which Allah bestowed upon the Ansar, which He, may His remembrance be exalted, commanded them in this verse to remember, is the harmony of Islam and the unity of their word upon it; and the enmity that was between them, of which Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "when you were enemies," is the enmity of wars which was between the two clans of al-Aws and al-Khazraj in the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam). The scholars of the Arabs' history (bi-ayyam al-'arab) claim that it stretched between them for a hundred and twenty years. As follows:

7584 – Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salama narrated to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq said: The war between al-Aws and al-Khazraj lasted a hundred and twenty years, until Islam came while they were still in that state, and their war was between them even though they were brothers of the same father and mother. No people had ever been known to have such enmity and war between them as existed between them. Then Allah, Mighty and Majestic, extinguished that with Islam, and joined them together through His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ). [[The report 7584: I have not been able to locate its place in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham at this time.]]

* * *

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 103 (part 2 of 3):

So the Mighty and Majestic One reminded them, when He admonished them, of the great affliction and misery they had been in during their jahiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam), through enmity among them, killing one another, and fear of one another, and of what they came to through Islam, following the Messenger (ﷺ), and believing in him and in what he brought, namely harmony and unity, the security of some from others, and the becoming of some of them brothers to others. And the cause of that was what:

7585- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, saying: Ibn Ishaq related to me, saying: Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah al-Madani related to us, from elders of his people, who said: Suwayd ibn Samit, brother of Banu Amr ibn Awf, came to Makkah for the hajj or the umrah. He said: Suwayd was called by his people among them "the Perfect" for his strength, poetry, lineage and nobility. He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) approached him as soon as he heard of him, and invited him to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and to Islam. He said: Suwayd said to him: "Perhaps what you have is like what I have!" He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "And what do you have?" He said: "The Majalla of Luqman," meaning: the wisdom of Luqman. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Show it to me." So he showed it to him, and he said: "Indeed this is a good saying, but what I have is better than this: the Qur'an, which Allah has sent down to me as guidance and light." He said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited the Qur'an to him and invited him to Islam, and he did not turn away from it, and said: "Indeed this is a good saying!" Then he departed from him and went to Madinah, and he did not remain long before the Khazraj killed him. His people would say: "He was killed while a Muslim." His killing was before the Day of Buath.

7586- Ibn Humayd related to us, saying: Salamah related to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Amr ibn Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, one of Banu Abd al-Ashhal, related to me: that Mahmud ibn Labid, one of Banu Abd al-Ashhal, said: When Abu al-Haysar Anas ibn Rafi came to Makkah, with a group of youths from Banu Abd al-Ashhal, among them Iyas ibn Mu'adh, seeking an alliance with Quraysh against their people, the Khazraj, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard of them, came to them, sat with them and said: "Is there for you something better than what you came for?" They said: "And what is that?" He said: "I am the Messenger of Allah; he sent me to the servants, calling them to Allah that they worship Allah and not associate anything with Him, and the Book was sent down to me." Then he mentioned Islam to them and recited the Qur'an to them. Iyas ibn Mu'adh, who was a young man, said: "O people, by Allah, this is better than what you came for!" He said: Then Abu al-Haysar Anas ibn Rafi took a handful of gravel from the valley and struck it against the face of Iyas ibn Mu'adh, and said: "Leave us of you, for by my life, we came for other than this!" He said: Iyas ibn Mu'adh fell silent, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rose from them, and they returned to Madinah. The battle of Buath took place between the Aws and the Khazraj. He said: Then Iyas ibn Mu'adh did not remain long before he died. He said: When Allah willed to make His religion manifest, to strengthen His Prophet (ﷺ), and to fulfil His promise to him, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) went out in the season in which he met the group of the Ansar, presenting himself to the tribes of the Arabs, as he used to do in every season. While he was at the Aqabah, he met a band of the Khazraj whom Allah wished good for.

=Ibn Humayd said, Salamah said, Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah related to me, from elders of his people, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) met them, he said to them: "Who are you?" They said: "A band of the Khazraj." He said: "Are you from the clients of the Jews?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you not sit so that I may speak with you?" They said: "Yes indeed!" He said: So they sat with him, and he invited them to Allah, presented Islam to them, and recited the Qur'an to them. He said: Among the things Allah arranged for them regarding Islam was that the Jews were with them in their land; they were People of the Book and knowledge, while they were people of polytheism, worshippers of idols, and the Jews had subjugated them in their land. Whenever there was something between them, the Jews would say: "A prophet is now about to be sent, whose time has drawn near; we will follow him and kill you with him, the killing of 'Ad and Iram!" When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) spoke with those men and invited them to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, some of them said to others: "O people, you know by Allah that he is the Prophet whom the Jews have threatened you with, so let them not outpace you to him!" They responded to what he invited them to, by believing him and accepting from him what he presented of Islam, and they said to him: "We have left our people, and there is no enmity and evil among any people as there is among them. Perhaps Allah will unite them through you. We will go to them, call them to your affair, and present to them what we have accepted from you of this religion; if Allah unites them upon it, there will be no man mightier than you." Then they departed from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), returning to their land, having believed and affirmed, and they were, as was related to me, six men. He said: When they arrived in Madinah among their people, they mentioned the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to them and invited them to Islam, until it spread among them, and there was no house of the Ansar except that the mention of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was in it. When the following year came, twelve men of the Ansar attended the season, and they met him at the Aqabah, which is the First Aqabah, and they pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with the pledge of women, and that was before fighting was enjoined upon them. [The pledge of women is the pledge mentioned in [Surah al-Mumtahanah: 12]; its text, as related by Ibn Ishaq through his two chains from Ubadah ibn al-Samit, who said: "We pledged to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the night of the First Aqabah that we would not associate anything with Allah, nor steal, nor commit adultery, nor kill our children, nor bring a slander we had fabricated between our hands and feet, nor disobey him in what is right. If you fulfil it, you will have Paradise; if you commit any of that and are punished for it in this world, it is an expiation for you; and if you conceal it until the Day of Resurrection, your affair is with Allah: if He wills, He punishes, and if He wills, He forgives." This is a pledge in which fighting and jihad, which Allah prescribed for men and not for women, were not mentioned; therefore it was called the pledge of women, because it corresponds to their pledge mentioned in Surah al-Mumtahanah.] [Report: 7586, Ibn Hisham's Sirah 2: 69-73; it follows the preceding report no. 7585.]

7587- al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Ayyub, from Ikrimah: that six men of the Ansar met the Prophet (ﷺ), believed in him and affirmed him, and he wished to go with them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, between our people there is war, and we fear that if you come in this state of yours, what you desire will not be achieved." They promised him the following year, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we will go, and perhaps Allah will reconcile that war!" He said: So they went and did so, and Allah the Mighty and Majestic reconciled that war, though they had thought it would not be reconciled; this was the day of Buath. They met him the following year with seventy men who had believed, and he took from them twelve chiefs as leaders, and that is when He says: "Remember Allah's favour upon you when you were enemies, and He joined your hearts."

7588- Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: As for "when you were enemies," it refers to the war of Ibn Sumayr; "and He joined your hearts" refers to Islam.

7589- al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Abu Sufyan related to us, from Ma'mar, from Ayyub, from Ikrimah, similarly, and he added in it: "When the matter of Aishah occurred what occurred," [The meaning is the account of the slander concerning Aishah the Mother of the Believers, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed the people, mentioning men who harmed him regarding his family and said untrue things about them, and the chief of hypocrisy, Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, took the lead in that along with men of the Khazraj. Usayd ibn Hudayr of the Aws stood and said: "O Messenger of Allah, if they are from the Aws, we will deal with them for you; and if they are from our brothers the Khazraj, command us with your order, for by Allah they deserve to have their necks struck." Then Sa'd ibn Ubadah of the Khazraj stood and said: "You lie, by the life of Allah! Their necks will not be struck! By Allah, you only said this because you knew they were from the Khazraj; had they been from your people, you would not have said this!" Usayd ibn al-Hudayr said: "You lie, by the life of Allah! But you are a hypocrite who argues on behalf of the hypocrites!" The people became agitated, until it nearly came to evil between these two tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj (Tarikh al-Tabari 3: 69).

I have not found mention of this report in any book, nor have I found in the books of occasions of revelation that this verse was revealed concerning Aishah, may Allah be pleased with her, nor concerning what was between the Aws and the Khazraj on that day. Abu Ja'far did not explicitly mention this in this place, nor did he mention it in the commentary of Surah al-Nur, where the verses of the account of the slander and the innocence of Aishah the Mother of the Believers appear.] and the two groups became agitated. Some said to others: "Our appointment is al-Harrah!" They went out to it, and this verse was revealed: "And remember Allah's favour upon you, when you were enemies and He joined your hearts, so you became by His favour brothers," to the end of the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came to them and kept reciting it to them until some of them embraced others, and until they were weeping, that is, weeping [with a sob-like sound] (khanin).

* *

As for "Sumayr," whose war al-Suddi claimed was meant by His saying "when you were enemies," it is Sumayr ibn Zayd ibn Malik, [In al-Aghani 3: 40 it is "Sumayr ibn Yazid ibn Malik," and it is mentioned at 3: 21 that he was the brother of "Darham ibn Yazid ibn Dabi'ah"; I preferred in the note on Tabaqat Fuhul al-Shu'ara of Ibn Sallam: 247, note 6, that it is "Darham ibn Yazid ibn Malik" of Banu Dabi'ah ibn Zayd ibn Malik ibn Awf ibn Amr ibn Awf. In both printed editions it appears as "Darham ibn Zayd," as here in mentioning his brother "Sumayr ibn Zayd."] one of Banu Amr ibn Awf, whom Malik ibn al-Ajlan mentioned in his saying:

Indeed Sumayr, I see his clan,
have leaned toward him and have grown indignant. [Jamharat Ash'ar al-Arab: 122; al-Aghani 20; al-Lisan (s-m-r). This verse and the next were written in the printed edition with a qaf: "abqu" then "alaqu," and in the manuscript they are unpointed; the pointing in al-Lisan (s-m-r) led them astray: "abqu" with ba and qaf, which is a pure error that must be corrected. Malik's poem is rhymed in fa', without doubt. The author of Jamharat Ash'ar al-Arab related it in full, and Abu al-Faraj related it and related with it its counter-poems by Darham ibn Yazid, then by Qays ibn al-Khatim long after this war, and Hassan ibn Thabit's response to it and his contention against it. The account of this poetry is long, in al-Aghani 3: 18-26, then 39-42. Then see what al-Tabari said after the verses.]

If the suspicion is true about the Banu al-Najjar,
they did not taste what they were fed. [In the version of Jamharah and al-Aghani: "sadiqan," and they are the same. In explaining this verse, Abu al-Faraj said in his Aghani: "'Alafu al-daym' means: when they acknowledge it; that is, my suspicion is that they will not accept oppression." This is a metaphor whose explanation you will rarely find in lexicons. A similar usage appears in the words of Subay' ibn Zurarah or Khalid ibn Nughaylah (al-Hamasah 1: 186): "When you are among a people who are enemies, not of them, then eat whatever you are fed, both the foul and the good." And the saying of al-Abbas ibn Mirdas (al-Hamasah 1: 225): "And do not eat what they feed you, for they came to you, despite their closeness, with a fabrication." It seems they mean by this: what is presented to you, which appears fair as if it were care and generosity, while its inner intent is harm and oppression; they used "feeding" because it is like deceiving the one to whom it is presented, as if he were a beast that does not perceive the hidden inner meaning. The editors of this tafsir have left these two verses in their corrupted state. Then some commentators came and wrote what no person of sense can accept, except on the saying of the speaker: "fa-kullu ma 'ulifta"!]

The scholars of the Ansar have mentioned that the origin of the enmity which stirred up the wars between their two tribes, the Aws and the Khazraj, and began them, was the killing of a client of Malik ibn al-Ajlan al-Khazraji, called "al-Harr ibn Sumayr" of Muzaynah, [I am not certain of this name "al-Harr ibn Sumayr," but I have not found it elsewhere; what they say in other accounts is that his name was "Ka'b ibn al-Ajlan," and other things are said.] who was an ally of Malik ibn al-Ajlan; then that enmity between them continued until Allah extinguished it through His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ). That is the meaning of al-Suddi's saying: "the war of Ibn Sumayr."

* *

As for His saying, "So you became by His favour brothers," it means: so you became, through Allah the Mighty and Majestic joining you together by Islam and the word of truth, and cooperating in supporting the people of faith, and standing together against those who opposed you among the people of disbelief, brothers who are sincere friends, with no rancour or envy between you, as:

7590- Bishr related to me, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His saying, "So you became by His favour brothers": and it was mentioned to us that a man said to Ibn Mas'ud: "How did you become?" He said: "We became brothers by the favour of Allah."

* *

The discussion concerning the interpretation of His saying: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, so He saved you from it﴾

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 103 (part 3 of 3):

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, may His praise be majestic, ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire﴾, he means: you, O believing community, of the Aws and the Khazraj, were on the edge of a pit of the Fire. This is only a parable for the disbelief in which you were before God guided you to Islam. He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: You were on the rim of Hell because of the disbelief you held before God bestowed upon you Islam, so that by your unity upon it you would become brothers. Between you and falling into it there was nothing but that you would die in that state of your disbelief and thus be among those who abide in it forever. But God rescued you from it through the faith to which He guided you.

* *

The "shafa" (edge) of a pit is its rim and its brink, like the "shafa" of a well or a cistern. From this is the saying of the rajiz (rajaz poet):

"We dug for the pilgrims the well of Sajla,
A sprouting herb grows above its lips."

[[I have not found this rajaz in this version in any book other than this tafsir. As for "Sajla," it is the well of al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi ibn Nawfal ibn 'Abd Manaf. It is said that 'Adi ibn Nawfal dug it; it is said that Hashim ibn 'Abd Manaf dug it; and it is said that Qusayy dug it. Ibn Hisham mentioned it in his Sirah (2:157), al-Azraqi in Tarikh Makkah (1:64, 65 / 2:175, 176), al-Baladhuri in Futuh al-Buldan (pp. 55, 56), al-Bakri in Mu'jam maAsta'jam (p. 724), and Mu'jam al-Buldan (under "Sajla"), and al-Rawd al-Unuf (1:101). Al-Mus'ab mentioned it in Nasab Quraysh (pp. 31, 197), but did not name it; he said: "the water-station of 'Adi, which is between the two sacred places (al-Mash'aran), between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and in it Mutrud al-Khuza'i says, praising 'Adi ibn Nawfal:

"The Nile, which comes with its ships held back,
is not more generous in its gift than 'Adi ibn Nawfal.
You dug between the two sacred places a water-station
for the pilgrims to the House of God, the finest watering place."

Abu al-Faraj, in his Aghani (13:5), attributed this poetry to Qays ibn al-Hadadiyya, among verses. As for the rajaz similar to this, which they mention in the earlier sources, its attribution has been disputed: to Qusayy, and to Khaldah bint Hashim. She says:

"We gave 'Adi a well
in soft, sweet, level ground,
it gives the pilgrims to drink, a gulp and then a gulp."

I have not been able to verify this further at present beyond this.]] That is, above its rim. It is said: "This is the edge of this well," with the word being maqsur (having a short final vowel), and "they are its two edges (shafawha)."

* *

He said: "then He rescued you from it," meaning: He rescued you from the pit. He returned the pronoun to "the pit," though he began speaking about "the edge," because "the edge" is part of "the pit." This is permissible, since the statement about "the edge" in the manner mentioned in this verse is a statement about "the pit," just as Jarir ibn 'Atiyya said:

"She saw the passing of years took from me
as the crescent's last sliver is taken from the moon."

[[From his Diwan (p. 426), Majaz al-Qur'an (p. 98), al-Kamil (1:324), and elsewhere. It will come later in the tafsir (12:94 / 13:109 / 19:39, Bulaq edition), from a qasidah in which he satirizes al-Farazdaq, which was not mentioned in their nақa'id (flytings). Before the verse he says:

"Leave me, for my grey hair has forbidden me,
and my experience, my grey hair, and my maturity.
She saw the passing of years..........
And who remains on the target of death,
and of days that pass with the nights?"

"Al-sirar" (with the sin vowelled either with a kasra or fatha) is the last night of the month, the night when the moon is hidden, i.e., disappears. Jarir meant by "al-sirar" in this verse the waning of the moon until it becomes its last crescent, until it is hidden on the last night. So this waning is what takes from it night after night. As for "al-sirar" which the lexicographers explained, it is the night the moon disappears, and that does not fit the meaning of this verse.]] He mentioned "the passing of years," then returned to speak about "the years," as al-'Ajjaj said:

"The length of nights has hastened in wearing me down,
they have folded my length and folded my breadth."

[[It is attributed to al-Aghlab al-'Ijli, as you will see in the sources, and Abu Muhammad al-A'rabi said in Farhat al-Adib: "This rajaz is not by al-Aghlab; it belongs to someone else, from the scattered rajaz."]] Diwan al-'Ajjaj (p. 80), Sibawayh (1:26), Kitab al-Mu'ammarin (p. 87), al-Aghani (18:164), al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin (4:60), al-Khizanah (2:168), al-'Ayni (margin of al-Khizanah, 3:395), Sharh Shawahid al-Mughni (p. 298), and elsewhere. The wording of this rajaz varies greatly. The version of Abu Muhammad al-A'rabi is:

"I have become one whose parts do not carry one another,
exhausted, I go like a worn-out camel.
The passing of nights.........
Then they have stripped the bark from my bones,
they have made me sit after long standing."

"Munaffah" is one who is weary and exhausted. "Naqd" is a worn-out camel. "Iltahat al-'ud min al-shajar" means it was stripped of its bark, and that is its peel. "Nahd" is flesh. He means: the nights have left him as bones, having eaten his flesh.]]

I have already explained the reason why it was said this way, in an earlier passage. [[5:77, 78.]]

* *

The commentators have said what we have said in this interpretation.

Those who said that:

7591. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: ﴿And you were on the brink of a pit of the Fire, and He rescued you from it. Thus God makes clear to you His signs﴾. This tribe of the Arabs was the most humiliated of people in humiliation and the most wretched in livelihood, [[His words: "and the most wretched in livelihood, and the most manifest in error..." with the pronoun returning to "the people," because the pronoun of the dual and plural after the comparative form "af'al" may be made singular or masculine; see the earlier commentary on the reports, nos. 5968, 6129, 7028, 7029.]] the most manifest in error, the most naked in skins, and the most hungry in bellies, pressed down (ma'kumin), [[In the printed edition: "ma'kumin," but the correct reading from the manuscript is: ka'ama fam al-ba'ir wa ghayrihi, meaning he tied the mouth of a camel or other beast shut during its agitation, lest it bite. The discussion of the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying: ﴿And let there be among you a community who invite to good, enjoin what is right, and forbid what is wrong. And it is they who are the successful.﴾ (3:104)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: "And let there be among you," O believers, "a community" (ummah), meaning a group [[See the explanation of "ummah" above: 1:221; 3:74, 100, 128, 141, 275-277.]], "who invite" the people "to good" (al-khayr), meaning to Islam and its laws which Allah has prescribed for His servants [[See the explanation of "al-khayr" above: 2:505.]], "and enjoin what is right" (al-ma'ruf). He says: they command the people to follow Muhammad (ﷺ) and the religion which he brought from Allah [[See the explanation of "al-ma'ruf" above: 3:293; 4:547, 548; 5:44, 76, 93, 137, 520.]], "and forbid what is wrong" (al-munkar). He means: they forbid disbelief in Allah and the denial of Muhammad and of what he brought from Allah, by struggling against them with their hands and limbs, until they submit to you in obedience.

* *

As for His saying: "And it is they who are the successful," He means: those who prosper with Allah, who remain in His gardens and His bounty.

* *

We have already shown the meaning of "iflah" (success) in another place, which is sufficient to dispense with repeating it here [[See above: 1:249, 250; 3:561.]].

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 3, Verse 105:**

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. For them there is a great punishment.﴾

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: ﴿And do not be﴾, O company of those who believe, ﴿like those who became divided﴾ from the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab), ﴿and differed﴾ concerning the religion of God, His command and His prohibition, ﴿after the clear proofs had come to them﴾, that is, the proofs of God. Concerning what they differed over, they knew the truth in it, yet they deliberately opposed it, defied the command of God, and broke His covenant and pledge out of audacity toward God. ﴿For them﴾, meaning for those who became divided and differed from the People of the Book after the proofs had come to them, ﴿there is a punishment﴾ from God, ﴿great﴾. He, may His praise be exalted, says: So do not divide, O company of believers, in your religion as these people divided in their religion, and do not do as they did, and do not follow their practice in your religion. Otherwise, you will have from the great punishment of God the like of what they have, as:

7598. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Ishaq narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His words: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them﴾. He said: They are the People of the Book. God forbade the people of Islam to divide and differ as the People of the Book divided and differed. God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And for them there is a great punishment.﴾

7599. Al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah ibn Salih narrated to me, from Ali ibn Abi Talhah, from Ibn Abbas, concerning His words: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed﴾. And similar to this in the Qur'an: God, may His praise be exalted, commanded the believers to unity (al-jama'ah), and forbade them from disagreement and division, and informed them that those before them were destroyed only through disputation and quarrels over the religion of God.

7600. Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi narrated to us, from Abbad, from al-Hasan, concerning His words: ﴿And do not be like those who became divided and differed after the clear proofs had come to them. And for them there is a great punishment.﴾ He said: They are the Jews and the Christians.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 106–107:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, words: ﴿On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."  And as for those whose faces turn white, they will be in the mercy of Allah, wherein they will abide eternally.﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: Those have a great punishment on a day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black.

* *

As for His words: "As for those whose faces turn black, 'Did you disbelieve after your belief?'" its meaning is: As for those whose faces turn black, it will be said to them: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." There is no substitute for "as for" (amma) with a response introduced by the fa' (then); when the response is omitted, the fa' is omitted along with it. The omission of the mention of "it will be said" is permissible because of what has been mentioned in the speech that indicates it.

* *

As for the meaning of His, may His praise be exalted, words: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?", the people of interpretation differed concerning who is meant by it.

Some of them said: It refers to the people of our qibla among the Muslims.

Those who said this:

7601 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black," the verse: Indeed, peoples disbelieved after their belief, as you hear. It has been related to us that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "By Him in whose hand is Muhammad's soul, some people among those who accompanied me will be brought to the Basin, until when they are lifted up to me and I see them, they will be pulled away from me, and I will say: 'My Lord! My companions! My companions!' And it will be said: 'You do not know what they innovated after you!'" = And His words: "And as for those whose faces turn white, they are in the mercy of Allah," these are the people of obedience to Allah and fulfillment of the covenant of Allah. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "They are in the mercy of Allah, wherein they abide eternally." [[The report 7601 is a mursal report; it was narrated by al-Bukhari in his Sahih with a different wording (al-Fath 11: 408, 412 and following), and by Muslim in his Sahih 17: 194. His words "were lifted up to me" mean that Allah made them manifest to him so that he saw them from afar. "Ikhtalaja al-shay'" means he pulled it out and drew it away.]]

7602 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black. As for those whose faces turn black, 'Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve,'" this refers to those among the people of the qibla who disbelieved when they fought one another.

7603 – Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Hammad ibn Salamah and al-Rabi' ibn Subayh, from Abu Mujalid, from Abu Umamah: "As for those whose faces turn black, 'Did you disbelieve after your belief?'" He said: They are the Kharijites.

* *

Others said: By this is meant: everyone who disbelieved in Allah after the belief in which he believed, when Allah took from the loins of Adam his offspring and made them testify concerning themselves, as He explained in His Book. [[This refers to the verse of Surah al-A'raf 7:172: "And when your Lord took from the children of Adam, from their loins, their offspring..." up to the end of the verse.]]

Those who said this:

7604 – al-Mathna narrated to me, saying: Ali ibn al-Haytham narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far informed us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, regarding His words: "On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black," he said: On the Day of Resurrection they become two groups. He says to those whose faces have turned black, and reproaches them: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." He said: It is the belief that existed before the difference, at the time of Adam, when their covenant and pledge were taken from them, and they all acknowledged servitude, and He created them upon Islam, so they were one community, Muslims. He says: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?", meaning: after that which existed at the time of Adam. And he said concerning the others: those who remained steadfast in that belief, sincerely devoting to Him religion and deed, so Allah whitened their faces and admitted them into His good pleasure and His Garden.

* *

Others said: Rather, those meant by His words "Did you disbelieve after your belief?" are the hypocrites.

Those who said this:

7605 – Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi narrated to us, from Abbad, from al-Hasan: "On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black," the verse, he said: They are the hypocrites, who were given the word of belief with their tongues, and denied it with their hearts and deeds.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the opinions we have mentioned concerning this is the view we have reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that by it is meant all the disbelievers, and that the belief for which they are rebuked for apostasy is the belief to which they acknowledged on the day it was said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we testify﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 172].

That is because Allah, may His praise be exalted, made all the people of the Hereafter into two groups: one whose faces are black, and the other whose faces are white. [[In the printed edition: "black ... white" (feminine forms); the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]] It is known—since there were no other than these two groups there—that all the disbelievers are included in the group whose faces are blackened, and that all the believers are included in the group whose faces are whitened. Therefore there is no basis for the statement of one who says: "By His words 'Did you disbelieve after your belief?' some of the disbelievers are meant, not others," since Allah, may His praise be exalted, has made the report about them all general. And when all of them are included in that, and there was no state for all of them in which they believed and then after that apostatized as disbelievers except one state, it is known that it is the one intended by that. [[In the printed edition: "the intended" without the feminine ending; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

So the interpretation of the verse is: They have a great punishment on a day when some peoples' faces turn white and other peoples' faces turn black. As for those whose faces turn black, it will be said: Did you deny the Oneness of Allah and His covenant and His pledge which you pledged to Him, that you would not associate anything with Him and would devote worship to Him, after your belief? = meaning: after your affirmation of Him? "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve," meaning: for what you used to deny in the world of what Allah had taken as your pledge to acknowledge and affirm. "And as for those whose faces turn white" from among those who remained steadfast upon the covenant and pledge of Allah, and did not change His religion, nor turned back on their heels after acknowledging the Oneness and bearing witness to their Lord's divinity, and that there is no god but Him: "they are in the mercy of Allah," meaning: they are in the mercy of Allah, that is, in His Garden and its bliss and what Allah has prepared for its people therein. "They abide therein eternally," meaning: they remain therein forever, without end or limit.

7604 – al-Mathna narrated to me, saying: Ali ibn al-Haytham narrated to us, saying: Ibn Abi Ja'far informed us, from his father, from al-Rabi', from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, regarding His words: "On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black," he said: On the Day of Resurrection they become two groups. He says to those whose faces have turned black, and reproaches them: "Did you disbelieve after your belief? Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve." He said: It is the belief that existed before the difference, at the time of Adam, when their covenant and pledge were taken from them, and they all acknowledged servitude, and He created them upon Islam, so they were one community, Muslims. He says: "Did you disbelieve after your belief?", meaning: after that which existed at the time of Adam. And he said concerning the others: those who remained steadfast in that belief, sincerely devoting to Him religion and deed, so Allah whitened their faces and admitted them into His good pleasure and His Garden.

* *

Others said: Rather, those meant by His words "Did you disbelieve after your belief?" are the hypocrites.

Those who said this:

7605 – Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi narrated to us, from Abbad, from al-Hasan: "On the day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black," the verse, he said: They are the hypocrites, who were given the word of belief with their tongues, and denied it with their hearts and deeds.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of the opinions we have mentioned concerning this is the view we have reported from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that by it is meant all the disbelievers, and that the belief for which they are rebuked for apostasy is the belief to which they acknowledged on the day it was said to them: ﴿Am I not your Lord? They said: Yes, we testify﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 172].

That is because Allah, may His praise be exalted, made all the people of the Hereafter into two groups: one whose faces are black, and the other whose faces are white. [[In the printed edition: "black ... white" (feminine forms); the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]] It is known—since there were no other than these two groups there—that all the disbelievers are included in the group whose faces are blackened, and that all the believers are included in the group whose faces are whitened. Therefore there is no basis for the statement of one who says: "By His words 'Did you disbelieve after your belief?' some of the disbelievers are meant, not others," since Allah, may His praise be exalted, has made the report about them all general. And when all of them are included in that, and there was no state for all of them in which they believed and then after that apostatized as disbelievers except one state, it is known that it is the one intended by that. [[In the printed edition: "the intended" without the feminine ending; the correct reading is what is in the manuscript.]]

* *

So the interpretation of the verse is: They have a great punishment on a day when some peoples' faces turn white and other peoples' faces turn black. As for those whose faces turn black, it will be said: Did you deny the Oneness of Allah and His covenant and His pledge which you pledged to Him, that you would not associate anything with Him and would devote worship to Him, after your belief? = meaning: after your affirmation of Him? "Then taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve," meaning: for what you used to deny in the world of what Allah had taken as your pledge to acknowledge and affirm. "And as for those whose faces turn white" from among those who remained steadfast upon the covenant and pledge of Allah, and did not change His religion, nor turned back on their heels after acknowledging the Oneness and bearing witness to their Lord's divinity, and that there is no god but Him: "they are in the mercy of Allah," meaning: they are in the mercy of Allah, that is, in His Garden and its bliss and what Allah has prepared for its people therein. "They abide therein eternally," meaning: they remain therein forever, without end or limit.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 108:

The explanation of His, the Exalted's, words: ﴿These are the verses of God, which We recite to you in truth. And God desires no injustice to the worlds﴾ (3:108)

Abu Ja'far said: By His, the Exalted's, words "These are the verses of God," He means: these are the verses of God.

* *

We have already explained how the Arabs used "tilka" (those) and "dhalika" (that) in place of "hadha" (this) and "hadhihi" (this, feminine), in other places earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[See what preceded, 1:225–228 / 3:335.]]

* * *

As for His words "verses of God" [[See the explanation of "ayah" (verse) earlier, in the indexes of language under the root "a-y-a".]] — He means: the admonitions of God, His lessons, and His proofs. "We recite them to you" [[See the explanation of "talā" (to recite) earlier, 2:409–411, 566–570 / 6:466.]] — We read them to you and relate them to you. "In truth" — meaning in sincerity and certainty.

By His words "These are the verses of God," He means: these are the verses in which He mentioned the affairs of the believers, from among the helpers of the Messenger of God ﷺ, and the affairs of the Jews, the Children of Israel, and the People of the Book, and what He will do to those who keep faith with His covenant, and to those who alter His religion and break His covenant after acknowledging it. Then the Mighty and Majestic informed His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ that He recites that to him in truth, and informed him that whoever of His creatures He punishes with what He has informed that He will punish them — [namely] blackening his face and making him abide forever in His painful torment and great punishment — and whoever He rewards from among them with what He rewards them — [namely] whitening his face, honouring him and elevating his station with Him, by making him abide forever in His everlasting bliss — it is not an injustice on His part toward any group of them, but rather in truth that they deserved, and for deeds they had earlier committed, for which He recompenses them. So the Exalted said: "And God desires no injustice to the worlds," meaning by that: God, O Muhammad, does not [desire], in blackening the faces of these people and making them taste the great punishment, and in whitening the faces of those and granting them bliss in His Garden, to place anything of what He has done in other than its proper place, which is its proper place. This is to inform His servants that in His wisdom He will not make right, in His creation, anything other than what He promised to the people of obedience and faith in Him, and what He threatened to the people of disobedience and disbelief in Him; and it is a warning from Him to these and a glad tidings from Him to those.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 109:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ (109).

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: He will punish those who disbelieve after their belief with the great punishment He has mentioned He will punish them with, and the blackening of faces, and He will reward the people of faith in Him, those who remained steadfast in affirmation and in fulfilling their covenants that they had pledged, with the reward He has described, which is abiding forever in His gardens, without any injustice from Him toward either of the two groups in what He does, because He has no need to commit injustice. That is because the unjust person only wrongs another in order to increase his honour through his wrongdoing, or to increase his authority to his authority, or his kingdom to his kingdom, or to make up for a deficiency in some of his means, completing through his wrong toward another what was lacking in his means to completion. As for one who possesses all that lies between the easts and the wests, and what is in this world and the Hereafter, there is no sense in his wronging anyone, and it is not permissible for him to wrong anything, since there is nothing deficient in his means that needs completion, so that it might be completed by wronging others. Exalted is Allah far above that. For this reason He, may His praise be exalted, said after His saying: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the worlds﴾, and ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and to Allah all matters are returned﴾.

* *

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed regarding the reason for the repetition of Allah's name, the Exalted, with His saying ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾ explicitly, when His name had already been mentioned explicitly with His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾.

Some grammarians from Basra said: This is like the saying of the Arabs: "As for Zayd, Zayd has gone" (ammā Zaydun fa-dhahaba Zaydun), and as the poet said:

"I do not see that death precedes death, something (shay') that has troubled death, the wealthy and the poor man."

The poet is ʿAdiyy ibn Zayd, though it is sometimes attributed to his son Sawada ibn ʿAdiyy, and sometimes to Umayya ibn Abi al-Salt.

[The verse appears in the sources as part of a larger poem on the vicissitudes of life and death; the transmitted text in the manuscript was corrupt and deficient, and is sound in the printed edition.]

So the noun was made explicit in a place where a pronoun would be expected.

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa said: That is not like this verse, because the second "death" in the verse is a place of a pronoun (kināya), since it is one word — "kināya" being what the rest of the grammarians call the pronoun. This is not so in the verse, because His saying ﴿To Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ is a statement, having nothing to do with ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾; each of the two statements is distinct in meaning from the other, each sufficient in itself, not needing the other. Whereas the poet's saying "I do not see death" requires completion of the predicate concerning it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: This second view is, in our opinion, closer to the truth, because the Book of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, is not to be directed in its meanings, and what it contains of clarity, toward the anomalous forms of speech and meanings; rather, in its eloquent discourse and in its manifest meanings that are understood, there is a sound and existing aspect.

As for His saying ﴿and to Allah all matters are returned﴾, He, may His praise be exalted, means: to Allah is the return of the affair of all His creation, the righteous among them and the wicked, the doer of good and the doer of evil, so that He will recompense each according to the measure of what they deserve from Him of recompense, without any injustice from Him toward any of them.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 110:**

**On the interpretation (ta'wil) of His words, glorified is His praise: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong, and believing in God﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) differed concerning the interpretation of His words: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind."

Some of them said: They are those who emigrated with the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from Mecca to Medina, specifically, from among the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

Mention of those who said this:

7606. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: 'Amr ibn Hammad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from Simak, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said concerning: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," he said: They are those who went out with him from Mecca.

7607. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Ibn 'Atiyya related to us, from Qays, from Simak, from Ikrima, from Ibn 'Abbas: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He said: They are those who emigrated from Mecca to Medina.

7608. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn related to us, saying: Ahmad related to us, saying: Asbat related to us, from al-Suddi: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said: "If God had willed, He would have said 'you (plural)', so that we would all be included. But He said 'you were' specifically of the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and whoever did the same as their deeds. They were the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong."

7609. Al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ikrima said: It was revealed concerning Ibn Mas'ud, Salim the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, and Mu'adh ibn Jabal.

7610. Abu Kurayb related to us, saying: Mus'ab ibn al-Miqdam related to us, from Isra'il, from al-Suddi, from one who related to him: 'Umar said concerning: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," it is for our first ones and not for our last ones.

7611. al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Isra'il informed us, from Simak ibn Harb, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He said: They are those who emigrated with the Prophet (ﷺ) to Medina. [[The report: 7611. Ahmad related it in the Musnad, nos. 2463, 2928, 2989, 3321, and its isnad is sound. al-Hakim related it in al-Mustadrak 2: 294 and said: "This is a sound hadith according to the conditions of Muslim, though they did not record it," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him.]]

7612. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said during a pilgrimage he performed, when he saw from the people a bad *ri'a* [[The *ri'a* (with a kasra on the ra and a fatha on the 'ayn) is originally from *wara'*, like *'idda* from *wa'd*. Al-ri'a means guidance and bad or good bearing, i.e., it means: manner, matter, and courtesy. In a hadith of al-Hasan: "They crowded around him, and he saw from them a bad *ri'a* and said: O God, to You," meaning bad manners, not showing restraint in what disgraces.]], then he recited this: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," the verse. Then he said: O people, whoever desires to be of that nation, let him fulfil God's condition from it. [[His words "God's condition from it" mean the condition of God which He demanded from it.]]

7613. Yahya ibn Abi Talib related to me, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, concerning His words: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He said: They are specifically the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), meaning: they were the transmitters (*ruwat*) and the callers (*du'at*) whom God commanded the Muslims to obey. [[The explanation of the meaning of "transmitters" has already passed in report no. 7597, along with the commentary on it.]]

* * *

Others said: The meaning of that is: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," if you are with these conditions by which He, glorified is His praise, described them. So the interpretation of that according to them is: You are the best nation, enjoining what is right, forbidding what is wrong, and believing in God, brought forth for mankind in your time.

Mention of those who said this:

7614. Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Najih, from Mujahid, concerning the saying of God, mighty and majestic: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," he says: On this condition: that you enjoin what is right, forbid what is wrong, and believe in God. He says: for those among whom you are, like His words: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 32].

7615. al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, His words: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He said: He says: You are the best of people for mankind, on this condition: that you enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and believe in God. He says: for those among whom you are, like His words: ﴿And We chose them knowingly over the worlds﴾ [Surah al-Dukhan: 32].

7616. Ibn Wakī' related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Sufyan, from Maysara, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayra: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He said: You are the best of people for mankind; you bring them in chains, you cause them to enter Islam. [[The report: 7616. al-Bukhari related it through Muhammad ibn Sufyan from Maysara. (Fath 8: 169) al-Hafiz said: "Maysara is Ibn 'Ammar al-Ash'ari, a trustworthy Kufan; he has in al-Bukhari nothing other than this hadith and another that has passed in the Beginning of Creation." And "Abu Hazim" is "Salman al-Ash'ari al-Kufi," and in Fath it is "Sulayman," which is an error and a misreading. The wording of al-Bukhari: "You bring them with chains around their necks, until they enter Islam."

Al-Hafiz has thoroughly treated in this place the discussion of the meaning of the verse, and mentioned most of the reports that have preceded and that will come after.]]

7617. 'Ubayd ibn Asbat related to us, saying: My father related to us, from Fudayl ibn Marzuq, from 'Atiyya, concerning His words: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He said: the best of people for mankind.

* * *

Others said: It was only said, "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," because they were the nation most responsive to Islam.

Mention of those who said this:

7618. I was told by 'Ammar ibn al-Hasan, who said: [[In the printed edition: "'Ammar ibn al-Husayn," which is an error; the correct reading is in the manuscript.]] Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His words: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." He said: No nation was more responsive to Islam than this nation; therefore He said: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind."

* * *

Some of them said: He meant by that that they were the best nation brought forth for mankind.

Mention of those who said this:

7619. Muhammad ibn Sinan related to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi related to us, from 'Abbad, from al-Hasan, concerning His words: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind, enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong." He said: What you hear of good has been in this nation.

7620. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, who said: al-Hasan used to say: We are its last and the most honoured of it before God.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of these sayings for the interpretation of the verse is what al-Hasan said, because:

7621. Ya'qub ibn Ibrahim related to me, saying: Ibn 'Ulayya related to us, from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "Verily you complete seventy nations; you are the last of them and the most honoured of them before God.

7622. al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Bahz ibn Hakim, from his father, from his grandfather: that he heard the Prophet (ﷺ) say, concerning His saying: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind," "You complete seventy nations; you are the best of them and the most honoured of them before God." [[The two hadiths: 7621 and 7622 are one hadith with two isnads. It has already passed with both isnads together, as a group, under no. 873. We have there traced it in detail, and we indicated its places here in the Bulaq edition. We add here that al-Hakim also related it in al-Mustadrak 4: 84, through 'Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, with the second isnad here. He said: "This is a hadith with a sound isnad, though they did not record it." al-Dhahabi agreed with him. Then al-Hakim pointed to the corroboration of Sa'id al-Juraysi, through his narration of it from Hakim ibn Mu'awiya. Then he related it through Yazid ibn Harun, from al-Juraysi. The narration of al-Juraysi has already been traced there from the narration of Ahmad in the Musnad.

Al-Hafiz mentioned it in Fath 8: 169, pointing to al-Tabari's narration of it, then said: "It is a sound hadith, good. It was recorded by al-Tirmidhi, who graded it good; Ibn Majah; and al-Hakim, who graded it sound."

Its meaning has also come, within a lengthy hadith from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, traced to the Prophet, which Ahmad related in the Musnad: 11609 (vol. 3, p. 61, Halabi). Its isnad is sound.]]

7623. Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada, who said: It was mentioned to us that the Prophet of God (ﷺ) said one day while he was leaning his back against the Ka'ba: "We will complete seventy nations on the Day of Resurrection; we are its last and its best."

* * *

As for His saying: "enjoining what is right," it means: you enjoin belief in God and His Messenger, and acting upon His laws; "and forbidding what is wrong," it means: you forbid associating partners with God, denying His Messenger, and acting upon what He has forbidden, as:

7624. 'Ali ibn Dawud related to us, saying: 'Abd Allah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Mu'awiya related to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: "You are the best nation brought forth for mankind." He says: You command them what is right: that they bear witness that there is no god but God, and the acknowledgement of what God has sent down, and you fight them over it; and "there is no god but God" is the greatest of what is right. And you forbid them what is wrong, and the wrong is denial, and it is the most wrong of wrongs.

* * *

The origin of "al-ma'ruf" (what is right) is everything whose doing is known, beautiful and deemed good, [[In the printed edition: "everything that is known, and its doing is beautiful and deemed good," they changed the wording of the manuscript, thinking that it was not correct, while it is more correct than what they confirmed!! Indeed it is the pure correct reading.]] not deemed reprehensible among the people of faith in God. The obedience to God is called "ma'ruf" only because it is what the people of faith recognize, and do not reject its doing. [[See the explanation of "ma'ruf" previously, shortly before, p. 91, note 2, and the references there.]]

* * *

The origin of "al-munkar" (what is wrong) is what God has rejected, and deemed its doing ugly; and for this reason the disobedience of God is called "munkar," because the people of faith in God reject its doing and regard its commission as grave. [[See the explanation of "munkar" previously, p. 91.]]

* * *

As for His saying: "and believing in God," it means: you affirm God, thereby sincerely devoting to Him the Oneness and the worship.

* * *

Abu Ja'far said: If a questioner asks and says: How is it said, "You are the best nation," when you have claimed that the interpretation of the verse is that this nation is the best of the past nations, and it is only said, "You were the best nation," to a people who were the best and then changed from what they had been upon?

It is said: The meaning of that is contrary to what you have gone to. Its meaning is: You are the best nation, as it is said: ﴿And remember when you were few﴾ [Surah al-Anfal: 26], and He said in another place: ﴿And remember when you were few, and He multiplied you﴾ [Surah al-A'raf: 86]. So inserting "kana" (was) in such a context and omitting it is with one meaning, because the speech is known in its meaning. [[See the Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1: 229.]] And if another speaker said also in this regard, "You were," meaning complete, its interpretation would be: You were created the best nation; or: You were found to be the best nation, it would be a correct meaning.

* * *

Some of the people of Arabic grammar claimed that the meaning of that is: You were the best nation with God in the Preserved Tablet, brought forth for mankind.

* * *

The first two sayings that we mentioned are more similar to the meaning of the report which we related earlier.

* * *

Others said: The meaning of that is: You were the best people of a path. And he said: "The nation" means the path. [[See the explanation of "umma" previously, 1: 221, then this, p. 90, and the references there in the note.]]

* * *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And if the People of the Book had believed, it would have been better for them. Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾ (110)

Abu Ja'far said: He, mighty is His remembrance, means by that: If the People of the Torah and the Gospel, from the Jews and the Christians, had affirmed Muhammad (ﷺ) and what came to them from God, it would have been better for them with God, in their immediate worldly life and their deferred hereafter. "Among them are believers," meaning: among the People of the Book, from the Jews and the Christians, the believers who affirm the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in what came to them from God, and they are: 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and his brother, and Tha'laba ibn Sa'ya and his brother, [[In the printed edition: "Tha'laba ibn Sa'id," which is an error; the correct reading is what I have confirmed from the manuscript, and "Sa'ya" with an unpointed sin, a fatha, and a yā' with two dots beneath. It will come in the correct form in the account of his conversion and his brother's conversion, shortly after, no. 7644.]] and those like them who believed in God and affirmed His Messenger Muhammad (ﷺ), and followed what came to them from God. "But most of them are defiant transgressors," meaning: those who leave their religion; and that is because from the religion of the Jews is following what is in the Torah and affirming Muhammad (ﷺ), and from the religion of the Christians is following what is in the Gospel and affirming it and what is in the Torah. In both books is the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), his attributes, and his mission, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "and in each of the two books..." which is a distortion; the correct reading is what I have given.]] and that he is the Prophet of God. Both groups, namely the Jews and the Christians, deny him, and that is their defiance and their departure from their religion which they claim they adhere to; concerning which His praise said: "But most of them are defiant transgressors."

* * *

Qatada said regarding this:

7625. Bishr ibn Mu'adh related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatada: "Among them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors." God condemned most people.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 111:

The interpretation of His words: ﴿They will not harm you, except for a little hurt﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: They will not harm you, O people of faith in God and His Messenger, these wicked people among the People of the Book, through their disbelief and their denial of your Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), any harm ["except a hurt"], meaning: but they will hurt you through their polytheism, by making you hear their disbelief, their statements about Jesus, his mother and Ezra, and their calling you to misguidance; and they will not harm you by that. [[In the printed edition: "wa-la yadurrunakum" ("and they do not harm you"), and in the manuscript: "wa-la yadurrukum"; the correct reading is what I have recorded.]]

* *

This is an exception of the disconnected kind (istithna' munqati'), which differs in meaning from what precedes it, as it is said: "He complained of nothing except good," and this is an expression transmitted from the Arabs by hearing.

* *

Those who engaged in interpretation have said things similar to what we have said on this matter.

Mention of those who said this:

7626: Bishr related to us, saying: Yazid related to us, saying: Sa'id related to us, from Qatadah, regarding His words: "They will not harm you, except for a little hurt," he said: They will not harm you except a hurt that you hear from them.

7627: It was related to me from Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far related to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', regarding His words: "They will not harm you, except for a little hurt," he said: a hurt that you hear from them.

7628: al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, from Ibn Jurayj, regarding His words: "They will not harm you, except for a little hurt," he said: their associating partners with God, regarding Ezra, Jesus and the cross.

7629: Muhammad ibn Sinan related to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi related to us, from Abbad, from al-Hasan, regarding His words: "They will not harm you, except for a little hurt," etc., he said: you hear from them lies about God, and they call you to misguidance.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And if they fight you, they will turn their backs to you; then they will not be helped﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His praise be exalted, He means: And if the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians, fight you, they will be routed from you, and they will turn their backs to you in flight.

* *

His words "they will turn their backs to you" are a metonymy for their defeat, because the one who is routed turns his back toward the pursuer, fleeing to a refuge and a shelter to which he takes refuge, out of fear for his own self, while the pursuer is on his trail. So the back of the one pursued is then opposite the face of the pursuer who routs him.

* *

"Then they will not be helped," meaning: then God will not help them, O believers, against you, because of their disbelief in God and His Messenger, and your faith in what your Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) has brought you. For God, mighty and majestic, has cast terror into their hearts, and He strengthened you, O believers, by granting you victory. [[In the printed edition: "qad alqa al-ru'b fi qulub ka'idikum" ("has cast terror into the hearts of your plotters"), which is a correction of what is in the manuscript: "qad alqa al-ru'b fi qulub fa-ayyadakum" ("has cast terror into the hearts, so He strengthened you"); it is evident that "qulub" should be "qulubihim" ("their hearts"), and the sentence is sound according to the manuscript.]]

* *

This is a promise from God, may He be exalted, to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ) and the people of faith, that He would give them victory over the disbelievers among the People of the Book.

* *

As for His words "then they will not be helped" being in the nominative, although His words "they will turn their backs to you" are in the jussive, this is because it follows as the answer to the conditional, a resumption of the speech, since the ends of the verses before it end in the nun; so He attached this one to them, as He said: ﴿And it will not be permitted for them, so they will not make excuses﴾ [Surah al-Mursalat: 36], in the nominative, and He said elsewhere: ﴿Nor will it be decreed for them, so that they die﴾ [Surah Fatir: 36], when it was not the end of a verse. [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Quran 1: 229.]]

The commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 112:

The explanation of His saying: ﴿They are struck with humiliation wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, may His praise be exalted, "they are struck with humiliation" (duribat 'alayhimu al-dhillah), He means: they are bound to humiliation. "Al-dhillah" is the form "fi'lah" from "al-dhull" (humiliation), and we have already explained this with its evidences in another place. [See the explanation of "they are struck with humiliation" in what preceded, 2:136.]

* *

"Wherever they are found" (aynama thuqifu) means: wherever they are met. [See the explanation of "thaqifa" in what preceded, 3:564.]

* *

He, may His praise be exalted, says: Humiliation is imposed upon the Jews who denied Muhammad (ﷺ), wherever they are on the earth, and in whatever place of its lands they are, whether in the lands of the Muslims or of the polytheists, "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," as:

7630 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar narrated to us, saying: Hawdhah narrated to us, saying: 'Awf narrated to us, from al-Hasan, concerning His saying: "They are struck with humiliation wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people, and they have returned with anger from Allah, and they are struck with destitution." [A phrase was omitted by the copyist: "and they returned with anger from Allah"; the printed edition followed that, so I have restored the reading of the recitation.] He said: This community overtook them, and the Magians (majus) collect the poll-tax from them.

7631 - Muhammad ibn Sinan narrated to me, saying: Abu Bakr al-Hanafi narrated to us, saying: 'Abbad narrated to us, from al-Hasan, concerning His saying: "They are struck with humiliation wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," he said: Allah humiliated them, so they have no protection, and Allah placed them under the feet of the Muslims.

* *

As for the "covenant" (habl) which Allah mentioned in this place, [See the explanation of "habl" in what preceded just above, pp. 70, 71.] it is the means by which they feel safe for their own selves from the believers, and for their property and their offspring: a pact and a guarantee of security whose contract was made for them before they were found in the lands of Islam. As:

7632 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, concerning His saying: "except under a covenant from Allah," he said: by a pact. "And a covenant from the people," he said: by their pact.

7633 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "They are struck with humiliation wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," meaning: except by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people.

7634 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya narrated to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: Ma'mar informed us, from Qatadah, the like of it.

7635 - Humayd ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, from 'Uthman ibn Ghiyath, who said: [In the manuscript: "'Uthman ibn 'Attab," and the correct reading is what is in the printed edition.] 'Ikrimah said: He says: "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," he said: by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people.
