7636 - Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," meaning: except by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people.

7637 - It was narrated to me from 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', concerning His saying: "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," meaning: except by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people.

7638 - Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, concerning His saying: "wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," it is a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people, as a man says: "the protection of Allah and the protection of His Messenger (ﷺ)," and it is the pledge.

7639 - al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, who said: Mujahid said: "wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," he said: by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people for them. Ibn Jurayj said: 'Ata' said: the covenant is the rope of Allah.

7640 - Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His saying: "wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," he said: except by a covenant, and they are Jews. He said: And the rope is the covenant. He said: This is the statement of Abu al-Haytham ibn al-Tayyihan to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when the Ansar came to him at 'Aqabah: "O man, we are severing for you ropes between us and the people," meaning: covenants. He said: The Jews are not safe in any land of the lands of Allah except by this rope which Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned. And he recited: "And We made those who followed you superior to those who disbelieved until the Day of Resurrection" [Surah Al 'Imran: 55]. He said: So there is no town in which there is any Christian except that they are above the Jews, east or west; they are humiliated in all the lands. Allah said: "And We divided them in the earth into communities" [Surah al-A'raf: 168], meaning the Jews. [The report 7640 was passed in abbreviated form under no. 7155.]

7641 - It was narrated to me from al-Husayn, who said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak concerning His saying: "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," he said: by a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people.

7642 - Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Yazid informed us, saying: Juwaybir informed us, from al-Dahhak, the like of it.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The scholars of Arabic differed concerning the meaning which brought the "ba'" (bi-) in His saying: "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people." Some of the grammarians of Kufa [this is al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:230] said: what brought the "ba'" in His saying "bi-habl" is a verb understood but whose mention has been dropped. He said: the meaning of the speech is: "they are struck with humiliation wherever they are found, unless they hold fast to a rope from Allah." So he supposed this to be understood, and he cited for his statement the verse of a poet: [This is Humayd ibn Thawr al-Hilali.]

She saw me with her two ropes and shrank in fear, while in the rope was a restive, fearful heart [Diwan: 35; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:230; al-Lisan (n-s-' and f-r-q); the version of the verse under (f-r-q) contains an ugly error and a corruption; its correct form is what appears in this tafsir. As for the version in the Diwan it is: "I came with her two ropes, and she turned back in fear, toward the self, a restive heart, fearful." "Ruw'a al-janan" means: very quick-witted, lively of spirit, high-spirited, as if there were fright in her from her sharpness and lightness of spirit. "Furuq" means: very frightened. He did not intend blame, but praised his she-camel for keenness of heart, startling at every sound in her alertness, as they said in praising her: "crazed." He says of his she-camel: she saw me come with the two ropes, to tighten my saddle upon her, so she shied away in fear. He describes her as noble, whom travels have not debased. Then he said: when I tightened the saddle upon her, she was in the rope clever and high-spirited, startling at every sound with her alertness and vigilance.]

And he said: He meant: "I came with her two ropes," and with the saying of the other: [This is Abu al-Tamhan al-Qayni, Hanzalah ibn al-Sharqi, of the Banu Kinanah ibn al-Qayn. He is one of the long-lived, and this poem is also attributed to 'Adi ibn Zayd, and to al-Mishhaj ibn Sabba' al-Dabbi.]

The ages' bendings bent me, until I seemed a stalker drawing near to game [Kitab al-Mu'ammarin: 57; Ma'ani al-Qur'an of al-Farra' 1:230; al-Aghani 2:353, 356, and also 12:347; Hamasah al-Buhturi: 202; Amali al-Qali 1:110; Amali al-Sharif 1:46, 257; Majmu'at al-Ma'ani: 123; al-Ma'ani al-Kabir: 1214, with great variation in the transmission; al-Lisan (kh-t-l), and others. Now, the printed edition and the manuscript confined themselves to the first verse, which is a very corrupt procedure and certainly not the work of Abu Ja'far, but a slip of the copyist. For Abu Ja'far transmitted al-Farra's statement from his Ma'ani al-Qur'an, and dropping the second verse, which is the verse of evidence, is a great corruption, so I have restored the verse, and also restored al-Farra's comment upon it, which is his saying: "He means: restrained by a fetter," and I have not placed this between brackets, because the copyist's slip is a matter established by clear evidence. In the manuscript and printed edition it read "ahnu li-sayd," which is an unquestionable corruption: Abu Ja'far is transmitting al-Farra's statement, and it is in al-Farra's book, and in what the transmitters quoted from it in the earlier sources, that it is recorded thus; this is together with the evident corruption and its proximity, the corruption's meaning being corrupt, and the absence of this strange version. "Khatil," meaning a hunter: it is said "khatala al-sayd," that is the hunter concealed himself behind something in order to shoot the game, and in pursuit of that he walks slowly, little by little, in secrecy, lest the game hear his movement. This is the khatl and the mukhatalah.]

Close of step, he thinks whoever sees me, and I am not shackled by a fetter.

So he made it necessary to supply a verb that is omitted, and to make manifest its complement which has been left out. [The "complement" here: the preposition and its object.] This, in the doctrines of Arabic, is weak, and far from the speech of the Arabs. As for what he cited of verses for his saying, it does not prove the soundness of his claim, because in the poet's saying "she saw me with her two ropes" there is clear evidence that she saw him holding the two ropes; in his report about her that "she saw him with her two ropes," there is a report from him that she saw him holding the two ropes. So what was apparent in the speech made the mention of "holding" unnecessary, and the "ba'" was a complement of his saying "she saw me," as in the saying of the speaker: [In the printed edition: "as in the saying of the speaker," with an added "fi," which corrupts the sentence more than this copyist's error in some of what is written. His saying "self-sufficient" is the predicate of "as the saying of the speaker," and "the hearer's knowledge" is conjoined to "in itself," meaning: self-sufficient in itself and in the hearer's knowledge of its meaning.] "I am with God," self-sufficient in itself, and the hearer's knowledge of its meaning, so that the "ba'" would require a speech which brings it other than what is manifest, and the meaning would be: "I am with God, seeking help."

* *

Some grammarians of Basra said: His saying "except under a covenant from Allah" is an exceptive clause excluded from the beginning of the speech. He said: this is no more strange than His saying: "they hear therein no vain talk, only 'Peace'" [Surah Maryam: 62].

* *

Other grammarians of Kufa said: It is a connected exception, and the meaning is: "they are struck with humiliation wherever they are found," that is, in every place, except in the place of a covenant from Allah, just as you say: "humiliation was struck upon them in the places, except in this place."

* *

This too is a seeking of truth that erred in its distinction. For he claimed it is a connected exception, and if it were connected as he claimed, it would be necessary that when the people are found under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people, the poverty would not be struck upon them. But that is not the attribute of the Jews, for wherever they are found, under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people, or without a covenant from Allah the Mighty and Majestic and without a covenant from the people, humiliation is struck upon them, as we have mentioned earlier from the people of interpretation. So if His saying "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people" were a connected exception, it would be necessary that when the people are found under a pact and a protection, humiliation would not be struck upon them. That contradicts what Allah described them by, and contradicts the state they are in. Thus it is also made clear by this that the saying of this speaker is corrupt as well.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: But the view we hold is that the "ba'" in His saying "except under a covenant from Allah" was introduced because the speech before the exception requires "ba'" in meaning. For the meaning of His saying "they are struck with humiliation wherever they are found" is: humiliation is struck upon them in every place where they are found. Then He said "except under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people," not in the manner of connection with the first, but in disconnection from it. Its meaning is: but they are found under a covenant from Allah and a covenant from the people, just as it is said: "It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by error" [Surah al-Nisa': 92]. The "error," although it is accusative by what operates before the exception, His saying is not an exception connected to the first in the sense of "except error," for he may kill him in that way; rather its meaning is: but he may kill him by error. Likewise His saying "wherever they are found, except under a covenant from Allah," although the verb that requires the "ba'" after "except" is the verb before "except," the exception is not connected to what precedes it in the sense that when the people are met, humiliation departs from them; rather humiliation is established in every state. But its meaning is what we have explained just above.

* *

The explanation of His saying, exalted be He: "And they have returned with anger from Allah, and destitution has been struck upon them. That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right."

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, means: "and they have returned with anger from Allah," that is, they bore the anger of Allah and departed bearing it, deserving it. We have explained the origin of this with its evidences, and the meaning of "destitution" (maskanah) as the humiliation of need and poverty and their submissiveness, and the meaning of "anger from Allah" in what has passed, sufficing without repeating it in this place. [See the explanation of "baa'a" in what preceded, 2:138, 345. And the explanation of "anger of Allah," 1:188, 189 / 2:138, 345. And the explanation of "were struck upon them," 2:136 / 7:110, and the explanation of "maskanah," 2:137, 292, 293 / 3:345 / 4:295.]

* *

As for His saying "That is because they used to disbelieve in the signs of Allah," He, may His praise be exalted, by His saying "that" means: their return, which they returned with, of the anger of Allah, and the striking of humiliation upon them, in exchange for what they used to deny: the signs of Allah and His proofs of the truth of His prophets, and what He imposed upon them of His obligations. "And they kill the prophets without right" means: and because they killed their prophets and the messengers of Allah sent to them, in transgression against Allah and audacity toward Him by falsehood, and without right that would have made killing them lawful.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: So the meaning of the speech is: they are bound to humiliation wherever they are found, except by a pact from Allah and a pact from the people; and they departed bearing the anger of Allah, and they bound themselves to the humiliation of need and the submissiveness of poverty, in exchange for what they used to deny the signs of Allah, His proofs and arguments, and kill His prophets without right, in wrongdoing and transgression.

* *

The explanation of His saying: "That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress" (112)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His praise be exalted, says: We did that to them because of their disbelief, and their killing of the prophets, and their disobedience to their Lord, and their transgression against the command of their Lord.

* *

We have explained the meaning of "transgression" (i'tida') in other places earlier in our book with what suffices without repeating it [See what preceded, 2:142, 167, 307 / 3:375, 376, 564, 580 / 4:583, 584, and others.].

* *

So our Lord, may His praise be exalted, informed His servants of what He did to these people of the Book, of the imposition of humiliation and disgrace upon them in the hastening of the world, together with what He stored for them in the hereafter of punishment, retribution, and painful torment, when they transgressed the limits of Allah and made lawful His prohibitions. This was a reminder from Him, may He be exalted, to them, and an alert to the place of trial from which they came, that they might turn back and remember, and an admonition from Him to our community that it not follow their way nor ride their course, lest it be made to walk their paths and there befall it of the vengeance and punishments of Allah what befell them. As:

7643 - Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress," [he said:] avoid disobedience and transgression, for by them were destroyed those among the people who were destroyed before you.

**The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, and they prostrate themselves (113)﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, exalted is His praise, "They are not all alike," He means that the People of the Book are not equal: the believers among them and the disbelievers are not alike. He means that they are not equivalent. They are unequal in righteousness and corruption, and in good and evil. [[See the explanation of "sawa'" (alike, equal) in what has passed before: 1:256.]]

* *

The reason it was said, "They are not all alike," is that the passage mentions the two groups of the People of the Book, whom God mentioned in His saying: ﴿Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are believers, but most of them are defiant transgressors﴾. [[This is the verse mentioned just before: 3:110.]] Then He, exalted is His praise, informed about the condition of the two groups before Him, the believing and the disbelieving, and said, "They are not all alike," meaning these are not alike, the believers among them and the disbelievers. Then He, exalted is His praise, began to describe the believing group of the People of the Book and to praise them and commend them, after He had described the transgressing group with what He described them with: cowardice, feebleness of heart, [[al-nakhb (with a fatha on the nun and a sukun after it) means cowardice and weakness of heart. A man who is mankhub al-janan or nakhib al-janan is a coward with no courage in him, as if his heart had been torn out so that he has no heart.]] alliance with humiliation and lowliness, constant poverty and neediness, and bearing the disgrace of this world and the exposure of the Hereafter. So He said: ﴿Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, and they prostrate themselves﴾, the three verses, up to His saying: ﴿And God knows well those who are mindful of Him﴾.

* *

So His saying [[In the printed edition it reads "qawluhu" without the fa' at its beginning; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]] "upright community" (ummah qa'imah) is in the nominative, governed by "from the People of the Book."

* *

A group of grammarians of Kufa and Basra, and the earliest of them in their craft, [[He means al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:230-231, and this is close to the wording of his speech and some of his evidences.]] have imagined that what follows "sawa'" in this place, namely "upright community," is a restatement (tarjamah) of "sawa'" and an explanation of it, [[Tarjamah here means badal (apposition). See its explanation in what has passed: 2:340, 374, 420, 424, 426, and other places in the index of terms.]] meaning: "Among the People of the Book, an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night is not equal to another that is disbelieving." They claimed that the mention of the other group was omitted, being sufficient with mention of one of the two groups, which is "the upright community." They illustrated this with the verse of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"I disobeyed my heart concerning her, though I am attentive to her command,
and I do not know whether her pursuit is rectitude (rushd)?"

[[This verse and its takhrij and explanation have passed: 1:327.]]

He did not say, "or not rectitude," being sufficient with his saying "rushd" for the mention of "or not rushd." And with the saying of another: [[I do not know who said it.]]

"I see you, and I do not know: is it a worry that I am worried about?
Indeed, the one who worries is of old humbled and diminished."

[[Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra' 1:231. In the printed edition it was "azala fala adri ..." which has no meaning; the correct reading is from the manuscript and Ma'ani al-Qur'an. I do not know whether he addresses a woman and says to her: the worry overpowers me when I see you, so I am humbled and diminished before you; or whether he means the worry and the plotting, saying that whoever conceals in himself something he intends, of plotting, hides his person until he reaches the utmost of his vengeance on his enemy. I do not prefer one meaning until I find the siblings of this verse.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: Along with this, their statement is an error, as is the speech of one who intends to say, "Equal whether you stood or sat," and says "Equal, you stood," without saying "or sat." They permit the omission of the second part only in speech that is complete with one part, and not in speech that is short of that. This is like "ma ubali" (I do not care) or "ma adri" (I do not know). They permitted "ma ubali aqamta" (I do not care whether you stood), and they mean "ma ubali aqamta am qa'adta" (I do not care whether you stood or sat), because "ma ubali" is complete with one part. The same is true of "ma adri." But they refused to permit it with "sawa'," because of its incompleteness, and because it is not complete with one part. So in their interpretation they neglected His saying, "They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, an upright community," according to what we have related from them, in favor of their interpretation and their grammatical schools [[His saying "madhahibahum" (their schools) is the object of "fa-aghfalu" (so they neglected). The context: fa-aghfalu fi tawjihihim qawlahu ila ma wajjahuhu ilayhi, madhahibahum fi al-'arabiyyah.]] since they permitted in it omission that is not permissible for them in speech with "sawa'." They erred in the interpretation of the verse. So "sawa'" in this place means completeness and sufficiency, not the meaning of the one whose interpretation we have related.

* *

It has been mentioned that His saying, "Among the People of the Book is an upright community," the three verses, was revealed concerning a group of Jews who converted to Islam and whose Islam was good.

Whoever said so:

7644. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad narrated to me, from Ikrimah or from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: When 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and Tha'labah ibn Sa'yah, and Usayd ibn Sa'yah, and Asad ibn 'Ubayd, and whoever of the Jews converted with them, converted, they believed, affirmed, desired Islam, and became firm in it, [[In the printed edition: "wa-manahu fihi" (and they were granted in it); in the manuscript: "wa-mahu" without dots, which is a misreading of what I have set down from the Sirah of Ibn Hisham.]] the rabbis of the Jews and the disbelievers among them said: None believed in Muhammad or followed him except our wicked ones! [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "ashrarana" as I have set it down, while in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham it is "sharrarana." The latter is better.]] Had they been of our best, they would not have abandoned the religion of their fathers and gone to another. So God, mighty and majestic, revealed in response to their saying: "They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, an upright community who recite the verses of God," up to His saying: "And those are among the righteous." [[The two reports: 7644, 7645. Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:206.]]

7645. Abu Kurayb narrated to us, saying: Yunus ibn Bukayr narrated to us, [[In the manuscript and the printed edition: "Yunus 'an Bukayr," which is an error. This isnad recurs often in tafsir; the nearest example is no. 7334.]] from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: Ibn Abi Muhammad, mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, narrated to me, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr or Ikrimah narrated to me, from Ibn 'Abbas, similarly. [[In the printed edition and the manuscript: "ashrarana" as I have set it down, while in the Sirah of Ibn Hisham it is "sharrarana." The latter is better.]]

7646. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, an upright community," the verse. He says: Not all the people perished; God still had a remnant among them. [[In the manuscript: "lillah fihim 'alayhi" (with an undotted word). I left what is in the printed edition, because it agrees with what is in al-Durr al-Manthur 2:64-65.]]

7647. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: "An upright community": 'Abdullah ibn Salam, and Tha'labah ibn Salam his brother, and Sa'yah, [[In the printed edition: "Sha'yah"; I have set down what is in the manuscript.]] and Mubashshir, and Usayd and Asad, the two sons of Ka'b.

* *

Others said: The meaning of that is: The People of the Book and the upright community of Muhammad's nation, who stand by the right of God, are not equal in the sight of God.

Whoever said so:

7648. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from al-Hasan ibn Yazid al-'Ijli, from 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, that he used to say concerning His saying, "They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, an upright community," he said: The People of the Book and the nation of Muhammad, ﷺ, are not equal. [[The hadith: 7648 - Abu 'Asim is al-Nabil, al-Dahhak ibn Makhlad; he has passed at 2155. 'Isa is Ibn Maymun al-Jurashi al-Makki; he has passed at 278. al-Hasan ibn Yazid al-'Ijli: a trustworthy Successor. Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat, and al-Bukhari in al-Kabir 1/2/306, and Ibn Abi Hatim 1/2/42, and they mention no criticism of him. This hadith was mentioned by Ibn Kathir 2:224 from Ibn Abi Najih without ascription of takhrij. Its continuation with this isnad will come at 7660. al-Suyuti collected them as a single hadith 2:65, as will come there.]]

7649. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "They are not all alike, among the People of the Book, an upright community," the verse. He says: These Jews are not like this nation which is upright.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: We have already shown that the more correct of the two opinions regarding this is the saying of the one who said: The narrative is complete at His saying "They are not all alike," as information from God about the matter of the believing People of the Book and the disbelieving among them; and that His saying "Among the People of the Book is an upright community" is a new statement praising their believers and describing them by their attributes, as said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatadah, and Ibn Jurayj.

* *

By His saying, exalted is His praise, "upright community" (ummah qa'imah), He means a steadfast group established upon the truth.

* *

We have already shown the meaning of "ummah" (community) earlier, in a way that makes repeating it unnecessary. [[See what has passed just before, p. 106 and footnote 2, where the references are.]]

As for "qa'imah" (upright), the people of interpretation (ta'wil) differed about its meaning.

Some of them said: Its meaning is: just.

Whoever said so:

7650. Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, saying: 'Isa narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid: "An upright community," he said: Just.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning is: that they stand upright upon the Book of God and what He commanded in it.

Whoever said so:

7651. Bishr ibn Mu'adh narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, concerning His saying "an upright community": he says: standing upon the Book of God, its obligations and its limits.

7652. I was told by 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', His saying: "an upright community," he says: standing upon the Book of God, its limits and its obligations.

7653. Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "Among the People of the Book an upright community," he says: a community guided, standing upon the command of God, not turning away from it and abandoning it as the others abandoned it and wasted it.

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of "qa'imah" is obedient.

Whoever said so:

7654. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "An upright community," the verse. He says: These Jews are not like this community which is qanitah (obedient) to God. "Qanitah" means obedient.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these opinions regarding its interpretation is what Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said, and whoever said as they said, as we have related from them, although the other opinions are close in meaning to what Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah said about it. That is because the meaning of His saying "qa'imah" is: upright upon guidance, the Book of God, His obligations, the laws of His religion, justice, obedience, and other causes of good, which are part of the description of the people of uprightness, according to the Book of God and the sunnah of the Messenger of God, ﷺ. The comparable report is that transmitted by al-Nu'man ibn Bashir from the Prophet, ﷺ, that he said:

7655. "The likeness of one who stands upon the limits of God and one who falls into them is like a people who boarded a ship," then he struck for them a parable. [[The hadith: 7655 - This is a sound hadith, which al-Tabari alluded to without mentioning it in full or giving its isnad.
Ahmad reported it in al-Musnad 4:268 (Halabi), from Abu Mu'awiyah, from al-A'mash, from al-Sha'bi, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, who said: The Messenger of God, ﷺ, said: The likeness of one who stands upon the limits of God, the Exalted, and one who compromises in them, is like a people who drew lots upon a ship at sea; some of them got its lower part and some got its upper part. Those in its lower part would climb up and draw water, and pour it upon those in its upper part. Those in its upper part said: We will not leave you to climb up and harm us. Those in its lower part said: Then we will pierce it from below and draw water! He said: If they seize their hands and prevent them, they will all be saved; and if they leave them, they will all drown.
Then Ahmad also reported it 4:269 from Yahya ibn Sa'id, from Zakariyya; and 4:270 from Ishaq ibn Yusuf, from Zakariyya ibn Abi Za'idah; and 4:273-274 from Sufyan, from Mujalid. Both Zakariyya and Mujalid, I mean, from al-Sha'bi, from al-Nu'man ibn Bashir, similarly.
al-Bukhari reported it 5:94 (Fath) from Abu Nu'aym, from Zakariyya, from al-Sha'bi.
Then he also reported it 5:216-217 from 'Umar ibn Hafs ibn Ghiyath, from his father, from al-A'mash, from al-Sha'bi, similarly.]]

* *

So the one who stands upon the limits of God is the one who is steadfast in holding to what God commanded him, and avoiding what God forbade him.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: So the meaning of the speech is: Among the People of the Book is a group that holds fast to the Book of God, adheres to it, and is steadfast in acting upon what is in it and what His Messenger, ﷺ, prescribed for them.

* *

The interpretation of His saying: ﴿They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, and they prostrate themselves (113)﴾

Abu Ja'far said: By His saying, "They recite the verses of God," He means they read the Book of God in the watches of the night. By His saying, "the verses of God," He means what He revealed in His Book of lessons and admonitions. He says: They recite that in the watches of the night, meaning in the hours of the night, and so they reflect upon it and ponder it.

* *

As for "watches of the night" (ana' al-layl), they are the hours of the night. Its singular is "inay" (or "ini"), as the poet said: [[He is al-Mutanakhkhil al-Hudhali, but he will come in al-Tabari attributed to "al-Mankhal al-Sa'di," which is an error I verified in its place afterwards.]]

"Sweet and bitter, like the bending of an arrow, its tautness,
in every watch the night has traversed, it puts on its sandals."

[[Diwan al-Hudhaliyyin 2:35, Majaz al-Qur'an 1:102, Sirah of Ibn Hisham 2:206, and Lisan al-'Arab, "anaa." It will come from the tafsir 16:168 (Bulaq), from his elegy for his son Uthaylah, and the verse is in describing his son. Ibn al-Anbari narrated it, as it comes in Lisan:
"The one who walks the frontier, its approaches feared,
in every watch the night has decreed, it puts on its sandals."
Al-Azhari mentioned the transmission of Ibn al-Anbari, and said: al-Jawhari recited it too, then cited the verse as it is in the tafsir, then said: "He attributed it also to al-Mankhal, so either it is this very verse, or another from a different poem." This is a speech which is without doubt weak, and what Ibn al-Anbari narrated is a mix of another verse from the poem, which he erred in transmitting. It is his saying before those verses: "The one who walks the breach, watchful over it, ..." Regarding the meaning of the verse he narrated in the tafsir: he means by "sweet and bitter" that he is easy for whoever is gentle with him and hard upon whoever is rough with him. "Like the bending of the arrow" means he is folded as the arrow is folded, then returns to its hardness and straightness. "Al-murrah" means strength and force. The reading of the Diwan and al-Tabari, "hadhahu al-layl," means the night cut him off in stride, and it is similar in meaning to "qadahu" (decreed), for "qadahu" means: made, decreed, and distinguished. "Put on sandals" means: took it as sandals, meaning traveled in it, heedless of what he encountered. Moreover, in the printed tafsir it was "qadahu al-layl" (the night decreed it), which an editor transferred from another place other than the tafsir, because in the manuscript it is "hadhahu," undotted, so its meaning was not known, and its correct form was not known; so they replaced it with what I have set down from Lisan or elsewhere.]] It has been said that the singular of "anaa'" is "ina" (inan) with a shortened vowel, as the singular of "am'a'" (intestines) is "ma'an."

* *

The people of interpretation differed concerning its meaning.

Some of them said: Its meaning is the hours of the night, as we said.

Whoever said so:

7656. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah: "They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night," meaning: the hours of the night.

* *

7657. I was told by 'Ammar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', who said: "The watches of the night": the hours of the night.

7658. al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Jurayj said: 'Abdullah ibn Kathir said: We heard the Arabs say: "The watches of the night," the hours of the night.

Others said: "The watches of the night" means the middle of the night.

Whoever said so:

7659. Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: "They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night." As for "the watches of the night," it is the middle of the night.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 3, verse 113 (part 2 of 2):

And others said: Rather, by this was meant a people who used to pray the late night prayer (al-'isha' al-akhira).[[In the printed edition: "al-'isha'" al-akhira"; the correct reading is from the manuscript.]]
Mention of those who said this:
7660 - Muhammad ibn 'Amr related to me, saying: Abu 'Asim related to us, saying: 'Isa related to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from al-Hasan ibn Yazid al-'Ijli, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, regarding His words: "They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night." [He said:] "The 'atama prayer. They pray it, and whoever else among the People of the Book does not pray it."[[The hadith: 7660 - This is the continuation of the previous hadith with this same chain: 7648, as we pointed out there. Al-Suyuti (2:65) combined them into a single hadith, attributing it to al-Firyabi, al-Bukhari in his History, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim. We did not find any of these sources except Ibn Jarir, and he related it in two separate hadiths, as you see. As for al-Bukhari's al-Tarikh al-Kabir, it does not relate it in full; rather, it related only this last part, briefly as is his custom, in the biography of al-Hasan ibn Yazid (1/2/306). He said: "Muhammad ibn Yusuf related from Warqa', from Ibn Abi Najih, from al-Hasan ibn Yazid al-'Ijli, from Ibn Mas'ud (They recite the verses of God in the watches of the night), he said: the 'atama prayer." And "Umar ibn Dharr related from al-Hasan ibn Yazid al-'Ijli, as a mursal (hadith)." See the two hadiths after this.]]
7661 - Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Yahya ibn Ayyub related to me, from 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr, from Sulayman, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ was detained from us one night; he was with some of his family and wives. He did not come to us for the 'isha' prayer until a portion of the night had passed. He came, and among us were those who were praying and among us were those who were lying down. He gave us good news and said: "No one among the People of the Book prays this prayer!" Then God revealed: "They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, while they prostrate" [[The hadith: 7661 - 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr al-Dammari al-Ifriqi: trustworthy (thiqa). Al-Bukhari declared him trustworthy as transmitted by al-Tirmidhi, as in al-Tahdhib; Ahmad ibn Salih also declared him trustworthy, as Abu Dawud related from him. Ahmad, Ibn Ma'in, and Ibn al-Madini weakened him. Ibn Abi Hatim (2/2/315) related from his father that he said: "Lenient in hadith." And from Abu Zur'a that he said: "There is no harm in him, truthful." Neither al-Bukhari nor al-Nasa'i mentioned him among the weak narrators. We hold that whoever spoke about him did so only because of a copy he narrates from 'Ali ibn Yazid al-Alhani, in which the blame lies with 'Ali ibn Yazid. See al-Tahdhib.
"Zahr" is with a fatha on the za' and a sukun on the unpointed ha'.
Sulayman is al-A'mash.
I fear that "from 'Asim" has dropped out of this chain, between Sulayman al-A'mash and Zirr ibn Hubaysh, for al-A'mash is not recorded as transmitting from Zirr; rather his narration from him is through 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud and his contemporaries of that tabaqa.
The hadith will come, similar to it, right after this, and its takhrij is there.]]
* *

7662 - Yunus related to me, saying: 'Ali ibn Ma'bad related to us, from Abu Yahya al-Khurasani, from Nasr ibn Tarif, from 'Asim, from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ came out to us while we were waiting for the 'isha' prayer - he meant the 'atama - and said to us: "On the earth there is no one of the people of religions who waits for this prayer at this time except you!" He said: Then it was revealed: "They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, while they prostrate" [[The hadith: 7662 - 'Ali ibn Mu'bad ibn Shaddad al-'Abdi al-Raqqi, resident of Egypt: trustworthy. Abu Hatim narrated from him and declared him trustworthy. Al-Hakim said: "A shaykh among the great hadith scholars."
Abu Yahya al-Khurasani: I did not identify who he is, after long search and investigation. There is much variation in the kunya "Abu Yahya" and in the nisba "al-Khurasani."
Nasr ibn Tarif, Abu Juza al-Qassab al-Bahili: very weak; they agreed on his weakness. Al-Bukhari included him in al-Kabir (4/2/105) and said: "They kept silent about him, he is gone (dhahib)." Ibn Sa'd (7/2/41) said: "He is nothing, and his hadith has been abandoned." Yahya said: "Among those known for fabricating hadith." Al-Fallas listed him among those upon whom the liars were agreed that they are not to be narrated from.
His kunya "Abu Juza": with a fatha on the jim and a kasra on the za', as al-Dhahabi vocalized it in al-Mushtabih, p. 104. The hadith is established, in similar wording, through another sound chain that makes these two chains of al-Tabari unnecessary: Ahmad related it in al-Musnad (3760), from Abu al-Nadr and Hasan ibn Musa, both from Shaybān, from 'Asim, from Zirr, from Ibn Mas'ud.
Al-Haythami mentioned it in Majma' al-Zawa'id (1:312) and said: "Ahmad, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar, and al-Tabarani in al-Kabir related it," then he mentioned it in similar wording, nearly the wording of the previous narration (7661). Then he said: "The narrators of Ahmad are trustworthy; among them there is none but 'Asim ibn Abi al-Najud, who is disputed as to being used as proof. In the chain of al-Tabarani is 'Ubayd Allah ibn Zahr, who is weak." Al-Suyuti mentioned it (2:65) and added its attribution to al-Nasa'i, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim.]] And others said: Rather, by this was meant a people who prayed between maghrib and 'isha'.
* *
Mention of those who said this:
7663 - al-Hasan ibn Yahya related to us, saying: 'Abd al-Razzaq informed us, saying: al-Thawri informed us, from Mansur, who said: It has reached me that it was revealed: "They are not all alike. Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night, while they prostrate," between maghrib and 'isha'.

Abu Ja'far said: These sayings I have mentioned, despite their differences, are close in meaning. This is because God, may He be remembered, described these people as reciting the verses of God during the hours of the night, and these are its watches (ana'uhu). Whoever recites them during the 'isha' prayer is reciting during the watches of the night, and likewise whoever recites them between maghrib and 'isha', and whoever recites them in the middle of the night; each reciter recites during the hours of the night. However, the most preferable of the sayings for the interpretation of the verse is the saying of the one who said: "It means the recitation of the Qur'an in the 'isha' prayer, because it is a prayer that none of the People of the Book pray." God thus described the nation of Muhammad ﷺ as praying it, unlike the People of the Book who disbelieved in God and His Messenger.

* *

As for His words "while they prostrate," some grammarians of Arabic claimed that the meaning of "sujud" (prostration) in this place is the name of the prayer, not the prostration itself, because recitation does not occur in prostration or in bowing. So the meaning of the statement, in their view, is: "they recite the verses of God in the watches of the night while they pray." [This is the view of al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an (1:231).]

* *

The meaning is not as he went, rather the meaning of the statement is: "Among the People of the Book is an upright community who recite the verses of God in the watches of the night during their prayer, and in addition to that they prostrate in it." So "sujud" is the well-known prostration of the prayer.

Commentary on the Words of Allah: ﴿They believe in Allah and the Last Day, and enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and hasten to good deeds. And those are among the righteous﴾ (3:114)

Abu Ja'far said: By His words, exalted is He and mighty, "They believe in Allah and the Last Day," He means: they affirm Allah and the resurrection after death, and they know that Allah will recompense them for their deeds. They are not like the polytheists, who deny the oneness of Allah, worship others besides Him, deny the resurrection after death, and reject the recompense for deeds, as well as reward and punishment.

* *

As for His words, "and enjoin what is right," He says: they command the people to believe in Allah and His Messenger, and to affirm Muhammad (ﷺ) and what has come to them from him. [[See the explanation of "al-ma'ruf" (what is right) above, p. 105, footnote 2, and the references there.]] "and forbid what is wrong," He says: and they forbid the people from disbelief in Allah and from denying Muhammad and what has come to them from Allah. [[See the explanation of "al-munkar" (what is wrong) above, p. 105, footnote 3, and the references there.]] He means by this: they are not like the Jews and Christians, who command the people to disbelieve and deny Muhammad regarding what has come to them, and forbid them from the right deeds, which is affirming Muhammad in what has been brought to them from Allah. "and hasten to good deeds," He says: they hasten to do good deeds, fearing that such deeds might escape them before death overtakes them.

* *

Then, may His praise be exalted, He informed that those who possess these attributes are among the people of the Book, and are counted among the righteous [[See the explanation of "al-salih" (the righteous) above, vol. 3, p. 91 / vol. 6, p. 380.]], because whoever among them was a wicked transgressor has incurred the anger of Allah for his disbelief in Allah and His signs, his killing of the prophets without right, and his disobedience to his Lord and his transgression against His limits.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: "And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them. And Allah is Knowing of the God-fearing" (3:115).

Abu Ja'far said: The reciters differed regarding the reading of this.

The majority of the reciters of Kufa read it, all of it, as: "And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them" (with the verb in the third person, yaf'alū and yukfarūhu), in response to the description of the people whom He, exalted is His praise, described as enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong.

The majority of the reciters of Madina and the Hijaz, and some of the reciters of Kufa, read it with the taʾ in both places: "And whatever good you do, it will not be denied you" (tafʿalū and tukfarūhu), meaning: whatever good you, O believers, do, your Lord will not deny you it.

* *

Some of the reciters of Basra held that both readings were permissible, with the yāʾ and the tāʾ, in both places.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct reading in our view is: "And whatever good they do, it will not be denied them" (yafʿalū and yukfarūhu), with the yāʾ in both places, meaning by it the report about the upright community, the ones who recite the verses of Allah.

We chose this because the verses preceding this verse are a report about them. Joining this verse to the meanings of the verses before it, since there is no indication in it that turns away from their description, is better than diverting it from the meanings of what precedes it. And it is with the reading we have chosen that Ibn ʿAbbas used to recite.

7664 – Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Taghlabi narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to us, from Harun, from Abu ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAla, who said: It reached me from Ibn ʿAbbas that he used to recite both of them with the yāʾ. [[Report 7664: Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Taghlabi has had his biography given under no. 5954. As for the printed edition, it dropped "al-Taghlabi," because the editor did not read the word well; in the manuscript it was written "al-Ta'labi," undotted and unclear, so the editor omitted it.]]

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The interpretation of the verse, then, according to the reading we have chosen, is: Whatever good this community does, and whatever deed it performs for Allah in which there is His pleasure, Allah will not deny them that; meaning: Allah will not nullify the reward of that their deed, nor leave them without recompense from Him for it, but He will bestow abundant reward upon them for it and multiply honour and recompense for them.

* *

We have already demonstrated the meaning of "kufr" (denial, concealment) earlier, with its evidences, and that its root is covering something (taghtiyat al-shay').

* *

Likewise, in His words "fa-lan yukfarūhu" ("it will not be denied them"): the good they have done will not be covered over so that they are left without reward, but they will be thanked for what they have done, and abundant reward will be given them for it.

* *

Those who interpreted it did so in a manner similar to what we have said. Those who said so:

7665 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada: "And whatever good you do, it will not be denied you," he says: it will not be lost to you.

7666 – It was reported to me from ʿAmmar, who said: Ibn Abi Ja'far narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

* *

As for His words "And Allah is Knowing of the God-fearing," He, may His remembrance be exalted, is saying: Allah has knowledge of those who fear Him, for their obedience and their avoidance of His disobedience, and He preserves their righteous deeds until He rewards them for them and recompenses them with them, as glad tidings from Him, exalted is His remembrance, in the world's immediate life, and as encouragement for them to hold fast to the righteous character they are upon, which He has approved for them.

Commentary on the interpretation of His words: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah. And those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.﴾ (3:116)

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: This is a warning from Allah, mighty and majestic, to the other sinful community of the People of the Book, concerning whom He informed that they are defiantly disobedient (fasiqun), and that they have incurred anger from Him, and to those among their counterparts from the people of disbelief in Allah and His Messenger and in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought from Allah.

He, exalted is His remembrance, says: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve﴾, meaning: those who denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and rejected him and what came to them from Allah. ﴿Neither their wealth nor their children will avail them anything against Allah﴾, meaning: their wealth that they gathered in this world and their children whom they raised in it will not repel from them any of Allah's punishment on the Day of Resurrection, if He delays it for them until the Day of Resurrection, nor in this world, if He hastens it for them therein.

* *

He specified their wealth and children because a man's children are the closest of his relatives to him, and he has more power over his wealth than over the wealth of others, and his authority over it is more permissible than his authority over the wealth of others. So if his offspring of his own loins and his wealth over which his command is effective do not avail him, then other of his relatives and all his kin and their wealth are further from availing him anything against Allah.

* *

Then He informed, mighty is His praise, that they are the people of the Fire, who are its inhabitants, by His saying: ﴿And those are the companions of the Fire﴾. He made them its companions because they are its people who will neither leave it nor part from it, like a man's companion whom he does not leave, and his associate whom he does not part from. [See the explanation of "companions of the Fire" previously: 1:286, 287 / 4:317 / 5:429 / 6:14.] Then He reinforced this by informing about them that they are ﴿abiding therein eternally﴾, that their companionship with it is a companionship without cessation, since among things there are those that part from their companion in some states and depart from him at some times; but the companionship of those who disbelieve with the Fire that they have roasted is not so, rather it is a lasting companionship with no end and no cessation. We seek refuge in Allah from it, and from whatever draws near to it of speech and deed.

**The interpretation of His words: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind in which is a freezing cold, which strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves, and destroys it﴾**

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His mention be exalted, He means: the likeness of what those who disbelieve spend, that is, the likeness of what the disbeliever gives in charity from his wealth, [[See the explanation of "nafaqah" (expenditure) in earlier passages: 5:555, 580 / 6:265.]] giving it to whoever receives it, seeking nearness to his Lord, while he denies the oneness of God and denies Muhammad ﷺ, regarding the fact that it does not benefit him because of his disbelief, and that it vanishes when he needs it, and perishes after he had hoped for its benefit and return to him. It is like a wind in which is severe cold, which strikes the tilth of a people, [[See the explanation of "harth" (tilth, cultivated field) in earlier passages: 4:240, 397 / 6:257.]] meaning: the crop of a people who had hoped for its ripening and expected its yield and benefit to return to them, ﴿who have wronged themselves﴾, meaning: the owners of the crop, who disobeyed God and transgressed His limits, ﴿and it destroys it﴾, meaning: the wind in which is the freezing cold destroys their crop, after what they had been in of hope and expectation of its benefit returning to them.

He, may His mention be exalted, says: Likewise God acts toward the expenditure and charity of the disbeliever in his life, when he meets Him: He nullifies its reward and disappoints his hope in it. The likeness was brought forth for the expenditure, and what is meant by "the likeness" is God's dealing with the expenditure. This is made clear by His words ﴿like a wind in which is a freezing cold﴾. It is, as we have already explained in His similitude, ﴿Their likeness is like the likeness of one who kindled a fire﴾ [[See what preceded: 1:318–328.]] [Surat al-Baqarah: 17], and similar to that.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The meaning of the statement is: The likeness of God's nullifying the reward of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind in which is freezing cold. The omission of mention of "God's nullifying the reward of that" is permissible because the end of the statement indicates it, namely His words ﴿like a wind in which is a freezing cold﴾, and because the hearer knows its meaning.

* *

The people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil, those versed in tawil, i.e. exegesis) differed regarding the meaning of "nafaqah" (expenditure) mentioned in this verse.

Some of them said: It is the expenditure well known among people.

Those who said this:

7667 – Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, saying: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, from 'Isa, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding the words of God, may He be mighty and majestic: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life﴾, he said: the expenditure of the disbeliever in this world.

* *

Others said: Rather, it is his statement that he says with his tongue, which he does not believe in his heart.

Those who said this:

7668 – Muhammad ibn al-Husayn narrated to me, saying: Ahmad ibn al-Mufaddal narrated to me, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi: ﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like a wind in which is a freezing cold that strikes the tilth of a people who have wronged themselves, and destroys it﴾, he says: the likeness of what he says and it is not accepted from him, is like this crop when the wrongdoing people sow it, and a wind in which is freezing cold strikes it and destroys it. Likewise, they spent and their polytheism destroyed them.

* *

We have already explained which of these is more correct.

* *

The interpretation of "the worldly life" has already been sufficiently explained earlier, so there is no need to repeat it here. [[See what preceded: 1:314, 316.]]

* *

As for "ṣirr" (freezing cold), it is severe cold, and it occurs with a blowing from the north in the form of heavy dew and mist, on a dark morning following a clear night. [[This explanation of the meaning of "ṣirr" is rarely found in lexicographical books.]] As follows:

7669 – Humayd ibn Mas'adah narrated to us, saying: Yazid ibn Zurai' narrated to us, from 'Uthman ibn Ghiyath, who said: I heard 'Ikrimah say: ﴿a wind in which is ṣirr﴾, he said: severe cold.

7670 – al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, saying: Ibn Juraij said: Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿a wind in which is ṣirr﴾, he said: severe cold and frost.

7671 – 'Ali ibn Dawud narrated to us, saying: 'Abdullah ibn Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding his words: ﴿a wind in which is ṣirr﴾, he says: cold.

7672 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyan, from Harun ibn 'Antarah, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: "al-ṣirr" is cold.

7673 – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatadah, regarding his words: ﴿like a wind in which is a freezing cold﴾, that is: severe cold.

7674 – I was told by 'Ammar, from Ibn Abi Ja'far, from his father, from al-Rabi', the like of it.

7675 – Muhammad narrated to us, saying: Ahmad narrated to us, saying: Asbat narrated to us, from al-Suddi regarding "al-ṣirr": severe cold.

7676 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My uncle narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas: ﴿like a wind in which is a freezing cold﴾, he says: a wind in which is cold.

7677 – Yunus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said: ﴿a wind in which is ṣirr﴾, he said: "ṣirr" is a cold wind that destroyed their tilth. He said: The Arabs call it "al-ḍarīb" (hoarfrost); the wind comes cold and in the morning there is ḍarīb, having burned the crop. [[al-ḍarīb: frost and ice.]] They say: "It was struck last night," meaning it was struck by the frost of that ṣirr that struck it.

7678 – Yahya ibn Abi Talib narrated to me, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Juwaybir narrated to us, from al-Dahhak: ﴿a wind in which is ṣirr﴾, he said: a wind in which is cold.

* *

The interpretation of His words: ﴿And God did not wrong them, but they wronged themselves﴾ (117)

Abu Ja'far said: By this, may His mention be exalted, He means: God did not do to these disbelievers what He did to them, by nullifying the reward of their deeds and voiding their wages, as an injustice from Him toward them. That is, He would have placed what He did to them in other than its proper place and with other than its people. Rather, He placed His action in its proper place and did to them what they deserved. For the deed they performed was not for God, while they were submitting to Him in oneness, obeying His command, and affirming His messengers. Rather, it was from them while they were associating others with Him, opposing His command, and denying His messengers, after He had previously made clear to them that He does not accept any deed from a doer unless it is accompanied by sincerity in monotheism toward Him, acknowledgment of the prophethood of His prophets, affirmation of what they brought them, and His confirmation of the proofs of that against them. So He did not, by His action toward one who disbelieved in Him and opposed His command in that, after the giving of excuse to him, [[In the printed and manuscript editions: "al-i'tidhar ilayhi" (the making of an excuse to him), which is a clear error. "A'dhara i'dharan" means he reached the utmost point in conveying (the warning), and from it the saying: "A'dhara man andhar" (he who warned has been excused), meaning he went to the limit in warning until his excuse became evident, when he brought upon the one he warned what would distress him. And his words "wafr 'amalihi" mean the abundance and fullness of his deed. The word "wafr" (with fatha then sukun). In the printed edition it was "wafir 'amalahu," and what is in the manuscript has been adopted.]] regarding the nullifying of the abundance of his deed, wrong him. Rather, the disbeliever is himself the one who wronged himself, by acquiring for it the disobedience of God and opposition to His command, which brought it to the Fire of Hell, and by which it will burn in the blaze of Saqar. [[The context of the sentence: "fa-lam yakun ... lahu zalimanan," and what lies between them is an explanatory clause related to "zalimanan," but placed before it.]]

**Commentary of al-Ṭabarī (Jāmiʿ al-Bayān) on Sūrah 3, verse 118 (part 1 of 2)**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates (biṭānah) those other than your own, who spare no effort to corrupt you and love what distresses you﴾**

Abū Jaʿfar (al-Ṭabarī) said: By this, exalted is His remembrance, He means: O you who have affirmed God and His Messenger, and acknowledged what their Prophet brought to them from their Lord, ﴿do not take as intimates﴾, that is, do not take as allies and friends for yourselves, ﴿those other than your own﴾, that is, other than the people of your religion and community, meaning those who are not believers.

* *

The word *biṭānah* (lit. "lining," the garment worn next to the body, used figuratively for an intimate confidant) is used as a metaphor for a man's close friend. He likened him to what is worn next to the belly of garments, because such a friend is placed in the position of what clothes the body, by virtue of his knowledge of one's secrets and what one conceals from distant persons and many relatives.

* *

God therefore forbade the believers to take as intimates and confidants those among the disbelievers. Then He informed them of what those disbelievers concealed within themselves of deceit and treachery, and of their desire to inflict harm upon them. Thereby He warned them against them and against befriending them. So He, exalted is His remembrance, said: ﴿They spare no effort to corrupt you﴾, meaning they do not spare their strength in doing evil to you. It is from *alawtu āluwwan* (I withheld, I spared). It is said: "So-and-so did not spare such-and-such," meaning he did not manage it (*mā istaṭāʿa*), as the poet said:[[This is Abū al-ʿIyāl al-Hudhalī.]]

*Jahrāʾu lā taʾlū, idhā hiya aẓharat, ... baṣaran, wa lā min ʿaylatin tughnīnī*

*(A blind one who does not spare, when she displays, sight, nor from poverty does she enrich me.)*

[[Dīwān al-Hudhaliyyīn 2: 263; al-Ḥayawān 3: 535; al-Maʿānī al-Kabīr: 690; Lisān al-ʿArab (ʾ-l-y), (j-h-r). This is a fine poem in exchange of verses between him and Badr ibn ʿĀmir al-Hudhalī. Badr ibn ʿĀmir recited verses when he heard that a nephew of Abū al-ʿIyāl had sided with his opponents, and he disowned that and claimed he was not one who would bring evil upon his brother Abū al-ʿIyāl. Abū al-ʿIyāl denied him, so Badr hastened to refute him. All of it is good poetry in its meaning. Abū al-ʿIyāl likened Badr's poetry about himself and his praise of him to a gift, and said to him:

*Aqsamta lā tansā shabāba qaṣīdatin ... abadan! Fa-mā hādhā alladhī yunsīnī?*
*(You swore you would never forget the youth of a poem, ever! What is this that makes me forget?)*

*Falasawfa tansāhā wa taʿlamu annahā ... tabaʿun li-ābiyati al-ʿiṣābi zabūni*
*(You will surely forget it and know that it is a follower of the stubborn, reluctant camel-herd.)*

*Wa-manaḥtanī fa-raḍītu zayya manīḥatī ... fa-idhā bihā, wa-abīka, ṭayfu junūni*
*(You gave me a gift and I was content with the appearance of my gift; then, by your father, it was a phantom of madness.)*

*Jahrāʾa lā taʾlū ...*

*Al-jahrāʾ* is the one who cannot see in the sun, a weakness of sight. It is said: *ʿāla yaʿīlu ʿaylan wa ʿaylatan* (he became poor). He means: you gave me poetry, praise and speech, and I was content with it; then, when the matter is examined and made clear, there is nothing but words and talk. When the matter is revealed and manifest, this poem becomes blind and extinguished. When the crisis comes, your speech avails nothing. Rather, you were as I said to you a moment ago:

*Fa-laqad ramaqtuka fī al-majālisi kullihā ... fa-idhā, wa-anta tuʿīnu man yabghīnī*
*(I have watched you in all the gatherings; then, when you help the one who seeks to harm me...)*]]

It means: you cannot see clearly at midday.

* *

By His words, exalted is His remembrance, ﴿They spare no effort to corrupt you﴾, He means the intimates whom He forbade the believers to take in preference to them. So He said: these intimates do not leave off their utmost capacity to bring corruption upon you, that is, they do not abandon their effort in that which brings you corruption. [[Abū Jaʿfar went far in his stretching of the meaning of "lā yaʾlūnakum" (they spare no effort to you). The explanation of the lexicographers about the meaning of this word in Arabic is more truthful and complete than his. They mentioned the meaning he mentioned, then said: "I did not spare that: meaning I did not manage it; and I did not spare doing it: meaning I did not leave it." And they said: "It is among the antonyms: *alā*: to slacken and weaken; and *alā*: to strive." So refer to that in the books of Arabic.]]

* *

The root of *al-khabl* and *al-khabāl* is corruption (*al-fasād*), and then it is used in many meanings. This is shown by the report from the Prophet ﷺ:

**7679** – "Whoever is struck by *khabl* or by wounds..."[[The report: 7679 – Abū Jaʿfar narrated it without a chain (*ghayr musnad*). Aḥmad narrated it in his Musnad 4: 31, and al-Bayhaqī in al-Sunan 8: 53. The version of Aḥmad is through his teacher Muḥammad ibn Salamah al-Ḥarrānī, from Ibn Isḥāq, and Yazīd ibn Hārūn said: Anbaʾanā Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, from al-Ḥārith ibn Faḍīl, from Faḍīl, from Sufyān ibn Abī al-ʿAwjāʾ, – Yazīd said: al-Sulamī – from Abū Shurayḥ al-Khuzāʿī who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said – and Yazīd said: I heard the Messenger of God ﷺ say: "Whoever is struck by blood or *khabl* (= wounds) has the choice between one of three: either he takes retaliation, or he takes the blood-money, or he pardons. If he wants a fourth, take hold of his hand. If he does any of that and then transgresses after, and kills, then for him is the Fire, abiding in it forever."

He means by blood: the killing of a soul; and by *khabl* or wounds: the severing of a limb. I have left what is in al-Ṭabarī as it is: "or wounds," and indicated with punctuation that it seems to be another narration for his words "*khabl*," the doubt of the narrator. But the context of the report leads me to think it is: "i.e., wounds," because the explanation of *khabl* as wounds has come in the same hadith itself.]]

* *

As for His words, ﴿and love what distresses you﴾, He means: they love your distress. He says: they wish for you hardship and harm in your religion and what grieves you and does not please you. [[See the explanation of *al-ʿanat* above, 4: 358–361.]]

* *

It is mentioned that this verse was revealed concerning people among the Muslims who used to associate with some Jews, their allies, and with the hypocrites among them, and maintained affection with them through the ties that existed between them in their pre-Islamic ignorance. So God forbade them from that, and from seeking their counsel in any of their affairs.

Those who said this:

**7680** – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Salamah narrated to us, from Muḥammad ibn Isḥāq, who said: Muḥammad ibn Abī Muḥammad narrated, from ʿIkrimah, or from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, from Ibn ʿAbbās who said: Some men among the Muslims used to maintain relations with some men of the Jews, because of the neighbourliness and alliance that existed between them in the Jāhiliyyah. So God, mighty and majestic, revealed concerning them, forbidding them from intimacy with them, fearing the trial upon them from them: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾ up to His words: ﴿and you believe in the Book, all of it﴾.[[The report: 7680 – Sīrat Ibn Hishām 2: 207; it follows the two previous reports, nos. 7644 and 7645.]]

**7681** – Muḥammad ibn ʿAmr narrated to me, saying: Abū ʿĀṣim narrated to us, saying: ʿĪsā narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid concerning the words of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own, who spare no effort to corrupt you﴾, [he said:] concerning the hypocrites of the people of Madinah. God, mighty and majestic, forbade the believers to take them as allies.

**7682** – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, concerning His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own, who spare no effort to corrupt you, and love what distresses you﴾. God, mighty and majestic, forbade the believers to admit the hypocrites into their inner circle [[His words "yastadkhilū" mean: to take them as friends. *Istadkhalahu*: he took him as an intimate (*dakhīl*), like their saying *istaṣḥabahu*: he took him as a companion. The *dakhīl* and *mudākhil* is one who enters into a man's affairs entirely. This form "*istadkhalahu*" is among what the books of the language have overlooked, and it is an Arabic word of ancient origin, as you see.]] or to befriend them, or to take them as allies in preference to the believers. [[In the printed edition: "i.e., they take them as allies," and in the manuscript: "that they take them as allies," and the correct reading is what I have written.]]

**7683** – Muḥammad ibn Saʿd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn ʿAbbās, concerning His words: ﴿do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾: they are the hypocrites.

**7684** – It was narrated to me from ʿAmmār, who said: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ, concerning His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own, who spare no effort to corrupt you﴾, he says: Do not admit the hypocrites into your inner circle [[See p. 141, note 3.]], take them as allies in preference to the believers.

**7685** – Abū Kurayb and Yaʿqūb ibn Ibrāhīm narrated to us, both saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab informed us, from al-Azhar ibn Rāshid, from Anas ibn Mālik who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "Do not seek light from the fire of the people of polytheism, and do not engrave on your rings *ʿarabiyyan*." He said: We did not know what that meant, until they came to al-Ḥasan and asked him. He said: Yes. As for his words "do not engrave on your rings *ʿarabiyyan*," he means: do not engrave on your rings "Muḥammad." As for his words "do not seek light from the fire of the people of polytheism," he means by it the polytheists; he means: do not consult them about anything of your affairs. He said: al-Ḥasan said: The confirmation of that is in the Book of God, then he recited this verse: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾. [[The report: 7685 – al-Azhar ibn Rāshid al-Baṣrī: trustworthy (*thiqah*). Al-Bukhārī included him in al-Kabīr 1/1/455, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim 1/1/313, and he mentioned no criticism of him.

There is another narrator named "al-Azhar ibn Rāshid al-Kāhilī," who was of Kufa, and he is other than the Baṣrī, and later than him. Al-Bukhārī and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also included him. The Baṣrī has narrated from him "al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab," who died in 148 AH, while the Kufan al-Kāhilī has narrated from him "Marwān ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Fazārī," who died in 193 AH. Marwān ibn Muʿāwiyah is among the teachers of Aḥmad, and al-ʿAwwām ibn Ḥawshab is among the teachers of his teachers. So this and that are worlds apart.

Despite this clear difference, the great ḥāfiẓ al-Mizzī erred: he mentioned in *al-Tahdhīb al-Kabīr* that Abū Ḥātim said about the Baṣrī: "unknown" (*majhūl*). He was followed by the ḥāfiẓ (Ibn Ḥajar) in *Tahdhīb al-Tahdhīb*, and by al-Dhahabī in *al-Mīzān*. It increased the confusion further, for he mentioned that Ibn Maʿīn declared him weak.

But Ibn Maʿīn and Abū Ḥātim only said that about the Kufan Kāhilī. Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated in the biography of "al-Kāhilī" 1/1/313, no. 1180, from Ibn Maʿīn who said: "Azhar ibn Rāshid, the one from whom Marwān ibn Muʿāwiyah narrated: weak." Then he said: "I asked my father about Azhar ibn Rāshid, and he said: he is unknown."

The ḥāfiẓ Ibn Ḥajar did not verify, and the statements in the two biographies were confused for him. He said in the biography of "al-Kāhilī," after the biography of "al-Baṣrī": "I fear that they are one person! But Ibn Maʿīn distinguished between them." The difference between them is as clear as the sun.

The hadith was narrated in Aḥmad's Musnad: 11978 (vol. 3, p. 99, Ḥalabī edition), from Hushaym, with this chain, without al-Ḥasan's statement, who is al-Baṣrī.

Al-Bukhārī also narrated it in al-Kabīr 1/1/455, without al-Ḥasan's statement, from Musaddad, from Hushaym, with it. Then al-Bukhārī explained part of it, saying: "Abū ʿAbd Allāh [he is al-Bukhārī himself] said: *ʿarabiyyan*, meaning 'Muḥammad, Messenger of God.' He says: do not write like the Prophet's seal: 'Muḥammad, Messenger of God.'"

Abū Yaʿlā narrated it at length, like al-Ṭabarī's version or slightly longer, and in it is al-Ḥasan's statement. He narrated it from Isḥāq ibn Isrāʾīl, from Hushaym, with this chain. Ibn Kathīr transmitted it from him, 2: 227, then said: "Thus did the ḥāfiẓ Abū Yaʿlā, may God have mercy on him, narrate it. Al-Nasāʾī also narrated it, from Mujāhid ibn Mūsā, from Hushaym, with it. Imam Aḥmad narrated it from Hushaym with the same chain, without mention of the explanation of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī. And this explanation is open to scrutiny" – to the end of what he said. I did not find it in the Sunan of al-Nasāʾī, so perhaps it is in al-Sunan al-Kubrā.

Al-Suyūṭī mentioned it, 2: 66, and added its attribution to ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, and al-Bayhaqī in *Shuʿab al-Īmān*. He did not attribute it to al-Nasāʾī, nor to the *Tārīkh* of al-Bukhārī.]]

**7686** – Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad ibn al-Mufaḍḍal narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾. As for "*biṭānah*" (intimates), they are the hypocrites.

**7687** – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, concerning His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾ – the verse – he said: A believer should not admit a hypocrite into his inner circle in preference to his brother. [[See p. 141, note 3, and p. 142, note 1.]]

**7688** – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said concerning His words: ﴿O you who believe, do not take as intimates those other than your own﴾ – the verse – he said: These are the hypocrites. And he recited His words: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾ – the verse.

* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: They differed concerning the interpretation of His words: ﴿and love what distresses you﴾.

Some of them said its meaning is: they love that you go astray from your religion. [[See the explanation of *al-ʿanat* above, 4: 358–361.]]

Those who said this:

**7689** – Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Aḥmad narrated to us, saying: Asbāṭ narrated to us, from al-Suddī: ﴿and love what distresses you﴾, he says: that you go astray.

* *

Others said:

**7690** – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj: ﴿and love what distresses you﴾, he says: in your religion; meaning: they love that you be distressed in your religion.

* *

Abū Jaʿfar said: If someone says to us: How is it said "*wadda mā ʿanittum*" (they love what distresses you), bringing the report about "*biṭānah*" (intimates) in the past tense in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), and as a detached clause (*qaṭʿ*) after the completion of the report, whereas circumstantial clauses can only be in the forms of nouns and imperfect verbs, not the perfect?[[See "*al-qaṭʿ*" above, 6: 270, note 3, and the other indexes of technical terms.]]

It is said: The matter is not as you suppose, that His words "and love what distresses you" are a circumstantial clause of "*biṭānah*." Rather, it is a second report about them, separate from the first and not connected to it. The meaning of the speech is: O you who believe, do not take as intimates those whose attribute is such-and-such, whose attribute is such-and-such. So the report about the second attribute is not connected to the first attribute, even though both are attributes of one person.

* *

Some of the grammarians of Arabic have claimed that His words "and love what distresses you" are a relative clause (*ṣilah*) of "*biṭānah*," and since it has been connected by His words "they spare no effort to corrupt you," there is no room for another relative clause after the completion of "*biṭānah*" with its relative clause. [[See "*al-ṣilah*" above, 5: 299, note 5, and it is the description of an indefinite noun (*naʿt al-nakirah*).]] But the statement about this is as we explained before: that His words "and love what distresses you" are a predicate of a subject concerning "*biṭānah*," different from the first predicate, and neither a circumstantial clause of "*biṭānah*" nor a detached clause from it. [[See "*al-qaṭʿ*" above, 6: 270, note 3, and the other indexes of technical terms.]]

* *

**On the interpretation of His words: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾**

Abū Jaʿfar said: By this, exalted is His praise, He means: Hatred has already appeared, of these whom I forbade you, O believers, to take as intimates in preference to you, ﴿from their mouths﴾, meaning by their tongues. What has appeared to them from them by their tongues is their persistence in their disbelief and their enmity toward those who oppose the misguidance in which they persist. That is among the strongest causes of their hostility toward the people of faith, because that is enmity over religion, and enmity over religion is enmity that does not cease except by one of the two opponents transferring to the other's creed. That transfer is from guidance to error, which was error for the one who transfers to it before that. So their displaying that to the believers, and their persisting in it, was the clearest proof for the people of faith of the hatred and enmity they harbour.

* *

Some of them said: The meaning of His words "Hatred has already appeared from their mouths" is: their hatred toward the people of faith has already appeared to their allies among the hypocrites and the people of disbelief, by some of them informing others of it. The proponents of this view claimed that those meant by this verse are the people of hypocrisy, and not those who openly held disbelief among the Jews and the people of polytheism.

Those who said this:

**7691** – Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazīd narrated to us, saying: Saʿīd narrated to us, from Qatādah, concerning His words: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾, he says: Hatred has already appeared from the mouths of the hypocrites to their brethren among the disbelievers, from their deceit toward Islam and its people, and their hatred of them.

**7692** – It was narrated to me from ʿAmmār, who said: Ibn Abī Jaʿfar narrated to us, from his father, from al-Rabīʿ: ﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾, he says: from the mouths of the hypocrites.

* *

This statement which we have mentioned from Qatadah is a statement that has no meaning. For Allah, may He be exalted and remembered, only forbade the believers to take as confidants (biṭānah) those whom they have come to know as deceiving Islam and its people and as harboring hatred, either by clear evidence indicating that this is their attribute, or by the open display of enmity, hostility and opposition toward them by those described with it. As for those whom they have not come to recognize with certainty as the ones whom Allah, mighty and majestic, forbade them from befriending and taking into their inner circle, [[In the printed edition: "فأما من لم يتئسوه معرفة"; this has no meaning. In the manuscript: "لم سوه معرفة" without dots, and the correct reading is what I have established. It is said: "أثبته معرفة," meaning he knew him with full knowledge.]] it is not permissible that they were forbidden from befriending and making him a companion except after making them known to them, either by their persons and names, or by attributes by which they have been recognized.
